Before I begin, this is my first strategy game of this kind of "ultra" strategy genre.
How the game works:
In HOI4 you can take on the role of every nation present during the second world war although only the most important ones in the conflict get their own individual progression and customization. It is your goal to either avoid the conflict or win it by force, it is important to note that you can switch sides in a kind of alternate history way as youre able to, for example,  research a focus which lets you conquer Great Britain while playing as the United States. Next to focuses there are other technologies which you have to research to upgrade your army, infrastructure or anything else really. Then of course you have to see to it that you get all the ressources you need to continue your war efforts. You get ressources by basically conquering strategic factories in which there are ressources being produced. Although you can conquer the world I have not yet encountered a way to "win" the game. You can stop at any time and you will be brought to a scoreboard which will show you how well you performed in contrast to the other nations but there is no end as far as i experienced.
Criticism:
The DLC Policy is garbage. With every DLC you get more individual focusses for countries who hadnt had any before. Which is great until you realize that most of these DLCs have existed in the modding community long before the DLC came out. Just dont buy the DLCs, youre better off downloading mods from the steam workshop.
Naval Battles:
Theyre broken, there is no way around it. I've experienced this to the extent that i dont even want to play nations anymore where i have to focus on navy. When you build a huge fleet which is able to control an ocean the AI starts "breaking". The AI engages your fleet just to instantly flee again... This process sometimes happens several times a second. This wouldnt even be that bad if all of your Invasions werent dependent on you controlling the oceans along its path, because as long as there is an enemy fleet in the ocean your invasion has to pass through you risk your convoys being attacked and your army being decimated before even landing on shore. But whats even worse than losing your army, is your army being stuck for minutes on its way to the invasion point because enemy fleets keep engaging and fleeing again, because the longer your army is not supplied the more attrition they suffer which puts you at a disadvantage.
All in all though, if you know about these things you can work around them, of course its not ideal and paradox also doesnt seem to keen on fixing anything but between naval battles and stupid DLCs I really enjoy this game for its historical accuracy mode and the alternate routes to go in the war like, as mentioned before, joining the AXIS as the US. If however youre not interested in history and you only want a good "ultra" strategy game this is not for you...
It's a really great strategy game! I really recomend it! (it also has a ton of amazing mods)

Axiom Verge starts off great. A science experiment goes wrong and you wash ashore in a strange new world. Jump around, shoot baddies, discover secret areas. It's fun.

Item hunting becomes a tedious chore and the game begins to punish you for not discovering every little secret, and most of this occurs in the level with most annoying BS indian chanting music. You really want to print that garbage on a vinyl? No thanks.

However! Axiom Verge does not hold your little Trump hands across the finish line. You'll feel like♥♥♥♥♥♥when you play, but also incredibly accomplished when you wiggle your way through that tough spot or spit on a boss's boots.
The story is weird and cryptic with some unexpected twists. The levels are varied and grotesque, and always feel fresh when you discover a new one. They snap together like a pile of lincoln logs and the game encourages backtracking as you nab new items and abilities, giving you access to previously unreachable areas.
In conclusion, Axiom Verge fits together in an oddly frustrating way.

I have been addicted to video games since 1982.  I have owned nearly every console and PC configuration released in North America since the Atari and MS DOS.  Taking this into account, I can comfortably claim that Axiom Verge is perhaps the best platformer I have ever played.  That truely says a lot.
What is Axiom Verge?  At first glance, it looks like a clone of the original Metroid for the NES.  But no.  It's much more of a cleverly crafted love letter to the era.
Back in the day, NES titles often suffered from bugs known as address corruption.  These would usually take the form of glitched or discolored blocks or enemies.  The original Metroid was notorious for this.
What was a bug in Metroid, Axiom Verge utilises as a fully intentional (and functional) feature.  For the sake of spoiler protection, I won't go much further than this.
Every area is beautifully crafted, perfectly matching the style of the time - but with oh so much love and polish.  Indeed, polish is perhaps this game's strongest asset.
The music?  Pulse-pounding.  I know of no other way to describe it.  The developer has turned chiptune into a veritable art form.
The story is "meta" - confusing, alluring, and possibly brilliant.  I would truly love to see it expanded upon in a sequel.
Game-length is perfect.  Slightly longer than any 2D Metroid title, including Fusion and Zero Mission.
In the "metroidvania" genre, it checks off ALL the right boxes.  If you're a fan of said genre, take the advice of this old gamer:  Buy it.  You won't regret it, and it's worth the full asking price.

Yes, you can carry lots of guns, like 40 sniper-rifles and a silenced pistol that fires peas, and even if the bugs that haunt this game calm down, your super-soldier-friend-that-is-Rambo-and-Charlie-Sheen-combined-and-never-dies has killed all of the enemy AI, who, in most times, stands in the open because hiding in cover is too mainstream. And yes, there are scenes where you are in the back of a Jeep with a badass MG at hand... Yet you'll fire it, like, 0 to none times.
Just no/10

The positive is that you can technically shoot people with a gun and they do actually die, so the basic premise of the game works on a technical level. The problems start with the game being literally just a reskin of their manhunter game, which is why these came out like 4 months apart (although this one actually works and opens up correctly). You are given three snipers (for some unknown reason, because the bolt action is just strictly worse) and a silenced pistol that you can't use because stealth isn't an option ever. The bad guys can shoot you with machine guns from 200 yards away while you miss them with a rifle, and they always know where you are, and can shoot you from behind trees and bushes where you can't see them. Every level you shoot the same looking guy, or do a turret section, nothing ever changes. You run through these open boring grey levels with 2006 graphics on a 2013 game.
This game loves turret section more than those old beachhead games, which were turret only. In one part I was on a stationary turret section, then you beat it and the immediately go to a truck turret section (I'm not kidding). Now I wanted to beat the game, because I secretly hate myself, but I was unable to. Because there is no saving besides the checkpoints, you are at the developer's mercy, and they don't apparently get how checkpoints work. In the back to back turret sections I mentioned before, the second one is super long, and as usual you get shot by guys behind trees and bushes from super far away, and you can't see them. Unlike running around however, you can't hide and keep taking damage. Well the genius developers chose that if you die during the second section you have to start the FIRST ONE OVER....... *collective facepalm*. Since I did not know quite how bad and poorly designed the game was, I played on the hardest difficulty. After having to redo both turret sections multiple times because I was getting killed by guys I couldn't see in the second turret section and couldn't do anything about it, I decided to give up. Oh yeah and there is no real story, although that's probably a blessing in disguise. Oh yeah and my favorite part, the explosive red barrels in the game don't actually blow up when you shoot them. Genius.  2/10.

A game this bad, I'd normally just give an up vote and some joking review but not this one. I'm far too INSULTED with how bad it is. I didn't expect much, especially given that I bought this game solely on the principle is was really cheap at the time and called "CHERNOBYL COMMANDO". I didn't say I was expecting much but holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ This has to be the worst FPS I've ever played. For starters, the first thing I notice is the game is really bloody dark and you can't at all change that. The graphics settings aren't even an option, you have to back out of the game entirely and start the launcher if you want to adjust. What is this, 2001? The game's super laggy and runs like my computer is a toaster. Turning down the graphics didn't really fix this. 10/10 optimization; already off to a good start I see.
The next is; there is no run in this game. "Forward" is equate to a casual stroll through the park and the "SPRINT" (I dare call it) ups your speed by about 75% for LITERALLY 10 feet. I say again; LITERALLY 10 feet (about 2-3 meters)
Yeah, see this crap? I started on the closest edge of the shadow. THIS is where your guy tires out. And he takes about 30 seconds after that to catch his breath. Didn't know you could join the CHERNOBYL COMMANDOS now regardless of being an overweight asthmatic. I should also note; this is a game where you do A LOT of walking with A LOT OF NOTHING to do.
The third thing I notice after about 10 minutes of god awful game-play is when I go to look up at the sky.. For some reason I can't explain, THE SUN IS BLUE. What? Why? I'm not going to nitpick this WEIRD "aesthetic" choice but why?... So I go on for a ways, I'm in some weird middle-ground between "Oh god what am I doing with my life" and laughing my♥♥♥♥♥off with the friends I'm streaming this for, at just HOW BAD THIS GAME IS.
So I'm about 30 minutes into the game on like.. level 3 or 4 or something, and I climb a ladder. Now, this is a ladder I *have* to climb to progress the story. I get stuck inside the ladder about 3 different times. I'm forced to restart, play the first 3-5 minutes of the level again up to that point and try over and over until the game finally lets me climb it. Alright, I do some sniping bit then have to climb back down. Joy. So now we're near the end of the section and there sits a truck we escape in. Thank god, no more walking! The truck travels at about 5 miles per hour and is stuck to invisible rails. The turret in back I'm forced to man is hilarious, as it has no ammo, cool down, or reload. That's right, you can just hold the trigger down as long as you'd like until you get bored. Doing this causes the muzzle flash to break away from the gun and drift off the screen somewhere. I'm in tears by this point.
The next loading screen takes about 10 minutes like they all seem to, I get bored and turn the game off. Me and another friend joke about how this must be some piece of crap FPS from the early PS1 era, to which he jokingly tells me he'll look it up. A couple moments later he returns with dread in his voice. "It came out last year..." We stop laughing.
TL;DR - A complete piece of crap, 2/10

-This cannot be classified as an MMO, as I have not seen other players in the game at all.

Overall, the idea is cool, the implementation a failure. Not worth trying at the moment.

Well, what can I say....the game used to be lots of fun 'back in the old days', only for everything that I enjoyed about it to get wrecked after the big update when they went 'stage 2' and F2P.
Originally, the 'hunters' had to actually hunt for the 'monster', which allowed for cat-and-mouse game. Most of people who chose the 'monster' didn't realize that 'hey, I have to be stealthy before I grow', which lead to them making a lot of noise, practically spamming the 'hunters' map with location markers to chase after not to mention all the footprints. But if you had a player who knew what he was doing, he'd be able to literally sneak right past them, having them running around entire map clueless as to where he was. And -that- is what I loved in the game. The thrill of actual hunt, leaving behind fake footprints, leading them into completely wrong directions only to duck and sneak right between them. Eventually evolving, and growing from prey to predator, or even picking them off one at a time if they separated.
After Stage 2 all that was stripped. Sure, the 'moster' got boosted and made able to kill entire hunter team in weakest stage of evolution, but all that was there to make it a hunt got stripped. Respawn timers on hunters decreased to practically none, a 'Monster is this way' skill they could just pop at any time with not long enough reuse delay. From a stealthy/hunting game they turned it into a 'RUNRUNRUNRUN WAAAAGH BASHY BASH'.
Could I recommend it? That's hard to tell. I wouldn't recommend the Stage 2 version. If you can get people to play with on the 'Legacy' version, then certainly, yes go for it! Alas, it just doesn't seem like anyone plays it anymore.

Gameplay: 5/10 - Very simple gameplay involving jumping around and shooting things with various guns that may or may not have upgrades buyable for them. .

Amazing game if you enjoy Metroid games.  Perfect art style, music, and gameplay to bring up nostalgic feelings toward classics like Super Metroid.  Could not put it down.

What if Super Metroid had been drawn by H.R. Giger? You'd probably end up with something like Axiom Verge.
Axiom Verge initially seems like a straight clone of Super Metroid. That's hardly a bad thing. Super Metroid is fantastic and lots of games could learn from it. That said, Axiom Verge quickly establishes an identity of its own. It could have taken the easy way out and copied the abilities found in other Metroidvania games, but Axiom Verge has plenty of unique ideas to throw at you.

Axiom Verge is one of those games you play and get an immediate sense that you'll be going back and replaying it a lot. Thomas Happ is a fantastic developer and this game is a shining example of how to make a game. The controls are tight and there is no uncertainty about where you're going to be moving while you're in control. The story is deep, but you don't need to know the story to beat the game, with the journals/logs providing a deep sense of worldbuilding. The soundtrack is top-notch electronica, and you need to listen to it with headphones to fully enjoy it. And of course, the spritework is just. So perfectly done.
The added speedrun mode is the icing on the cake. After my first playthrough, 100% completion over 30 hours, i played on hard mode, beat it in 10 hours, and now i speedrun the game whenever I'm feeling down or want a quick game fix (1:38:45, baybee).
This game is fantastic, and I heartily encourage you to get it if you want a great, well-crafted indie game.

Hearts of Iron IV is the best Grand Strategy game I've ever played. You can command the entire war machine of the Axis powers or stand and fight for liberty and democracy as the Allies. With the addition of mods you can relive the most important moments of recent history and change the fate of the modern world. This game could only be better with more in depth political challenges and decisions. Even still I would recommend Hearts of Iron IV to anyone who loves being in control of an entire nation and rewriting the course of history.

First off, a disclaimer. I only got the game to play the Kaiserreich mod (highly recommended), and have not yet played the vanilla version. Nevertheless the core gameplay is unchanged with the mod.
If you've played other paradox games, you may have some idea what to expect from this; it runs on the same engine as EUIV and CKII. It is mostly maps and charts, but that's typical for the genre. Where this game is different from its siblings is that it is much more focused on war rather than general nation-building and map-blobbing. This means that you will need to pay much more attention to the details of your army and strategy, which makes for a somewhat higher learning curve; after having played trial-and-error for 125 hours over one-and-a-half games I still don't really understand some things like the division designer, naval gameplay, or the fine points of using multiple armies and plans for maximum effect (in lieu of having one giant front of 200 divisions). This stuff has to be learned from outside sources like guides and videos.
It also means that it can be less rewarding to play as a weak minor country, as you will not have centuries to become stronger and there isn't a whole lot to do in peacetime. Especially since in the vanilla version most of these countries currently lack focus trees.
Nevertheless, particularly if you are playing with mods that add detail, there is a lot of potential for alternate-history-building, and like other grand strategy games this one can be very engrossing and has a lot of replay value.
There is one thing in the game which is just plain bad, and that's the AI. Seriously, it sucks. It doesn't seem to know any strategy other than "put a bunch of troops on a line and push on it." It has no understanding of the victory point/national unity system (where taking a few key cities from a disordered country can cause a capitulation) and therefore can take over a year to win a fight that a player could have finished in two or three months. Sometimes it does things that simply make no sense, like sitting outside an undefended capital city without taking it, or conversely leaving a major coastal city defenseless and letting it be taken by one enemy division (looking at you Leningrad). It's creation and placement of armies/generals is seemingly random. God forbid the AI needs to do a naval invasion (spoiler alert, half the time they simply won't). This can be incredibly frustrating if you are in a war where the performance of your allies is crucial, and you seem them totally throwing themselves away through amazingly dumb decisions (several times in singleplayer I had to load a save as an ally for a couple turns just to take a simple action that would prevent them from losing needlessly. This also makes it even harder to play as a faction-aligned minor in singleplayer.
These AI problems are especially bad in light of the battle plan system. This system places your divisions on the line in an optimal way to prepare for an offensive and to evenly distribute weakened divisions. This exists to reduce micromanagement. But with larger armies/fronts, the AI will be moving these constantly in search of an ever-changing perfect set-up, which causes a penalty to the computer-assesed readiness of the plan, which means that the AI may just sit there endlessly shuffling its divisions back and forth instead of seizing on an opportunity.
There are also some other things that don't make any sense, like the capitulation system (which tends to give capitulated territory to a nation other than the one that actually did the fighting, and therefore isn't present to defend it), the awful border-gore created by the AI during peace conferences, and the lack of a spearhead plan without buying overpriced DLC.
On the whole this game has some significant flaws (which I hope will be improved in various patches), but can still be pretty fun. I would recommend picking it up when it is on a big sale.

IL-2 Sturmovik: 1946 is a compilation release (2006) of IL-2 Sturmovik,Forgotten Battles, FB:Ace Expansion Pack, Pacific Fighters, and finally PE-2. The series begins in 2001 and has stretched into 2016 with the Battle of Stalingrad game with it's expansion the Battle of Moscow and a new IL-2 game "Battle  of Kuban is TBD.

If you want to fully experience this game to it's peak, you will need to dedicate bandwith and time to installing the BAT mod. Having played the Gold Edition of Guacamelee almost to the end I was hesitant about buying this edition that would require me to restart the whole game as each area was modified and so saves would not be compatible. I'm glad I took the plunge (with a major discount helping) as this is the definitive version of the game.
Guacamelee is one of the finest action-platformers ever made with outstanding level design and gameplay fusing superb and intelligently designed platforming with great beat-em-up mechanics all in a beautiful, colourful and musically pleasing setting. It has a metroidvania-style exploration system where new abilities enable exploring previously locked areas of the game and the map is filled with chests to find and interesting challenges to reach them. Each new move doubles as both a combat-ready combo-expanding ability while also enabling greater environment traversal. The level design smartly teaches you how to apply them while offering extremely creative ways of using them both individually and combined with previous abilities. The story and characters are fun and the music is fantastic and the traiditional Mexican art style is great too.
The gameplay in this version has been enhanced compared to the Gold Edition and the few areas that used to feel frustrating no longer do so, they feel challenging but fair and skill-based. The visual upgrades are a nice touch with enhanced lighting and generally more colour tastefully applied. The new areas are nice additions expanding the backstory and there are a few new secret chests to find with the new Pollo bomb ability. Technically the game engine seems to have been enhanced too as it feels smoother (although that is subjective and may just be an impression).
Just buy this game, it's one of the best games ever made, rarely has a game been so fun.

10/10.
+ Small number of heroes (yes this is a good thing!) very easy to keep track.
+ All units level up (+medals is cool also)
+ Campaign allows for continuing the same hero. Need to get some good income of magic first though.
+ Equipment for heroes can be easily bought. (In most similar games i've tried, buying new equipment is "late game"
+ Auto-combat can speed things up.
- Hero balance is pretty awful. Scout is OP, Wizard is good, Warrior has uses, Commander is pretty much worthless.
- Lots of useless units. Mostly tier 1.
- Crashes, nothing too bad from what i've had and it autosaves frequently so rarely will you lose more than 3 minutes.
- Difficulty of units you're fighting to reach the opponent can be "too hard". i.e i had to literally go through some semi difficult dungeons too "get lucky" and find a bow which let me kill some harder stuff which i couldnt find how to dodge to even reach the opponents side of the map to kill him.
- 1 "playable" race, but hireables from others is interesting (but a little too unreliable)
- Starting can sometimes be slow (depends on randomness of finding easy dungeons)
Basics for new players:
Get scout with either barbarians or swordsman (get 2-3), i recommend swordsman as they're easier to keep alive. Do not even bother with the other units. Bowman's can be added later on if you really want or elf if you get lucky as a mercenary.
Protect scout with units whilst it slaughters stuff. When he levels increase his damage & precise strike/ammo when possible
Exploring closer to your capital is more likely to find weaker enemies. Once the scout reaches level 10 select archer and win from there.
Buy him better equipment when possible pretty much as soon as your income allows.
You can figure out the rest.
Also, speed up the combat speed to max in the settings, yes it looks a little silly but so much better.
Might seem i have more negatives than positives, but i've managed 60 hours in barely over a week and seeing i work and  do other stuff, this is pretty much all i've been playing.
Highly enjoyable and worth a shot.

This game is badly designed, plain and simple.
The controls are okay-good on a gamepad, but borderline dumb on a keyboard, you get the mouse advantage and that's it.
The missions are easily the worst part of the game for me, they seem so rushed and done to "add more content to the game" that it's obvious how flawed they are.
For starters, you don't have much mission variety, pick some coins, get from point A to B, kill X enemies... all with a time limit.
The problem is the map is not prepared for those missions, they are so luck-reliant that it hurts. Want to win that race in Factory? Not as long the green goo fountain activates as soon you reach it, or the platforms are in the opposite side at the start, you just need to have the luck to get everything so you can cross at the start, otherwise your opponent (who is a ghost) will win 95% of the times.
The game shows care and laziness in some parts of the game, you can see they clearly did a great effort about the monsters, giving them stories and things, the visuals are really well done as I said, that was a great part of the game.
In other hand, the luck factor and the occasional BS death or falling in spikes is about as much challenge this game is going to give you. Every monster/boss is easy, their AI is really basic, altough there are a lot of weapons there is not any difference between them but fire rate, damage, ammo and design. The grenades are seriously OP
I hate how this game relies so much in Quicktime Events to the point that is literally a core mechanic of the game. They are unneeded, feel forced, and are no fun at all after doing the same QTE 10 times. Death animations get old pretty fast too.
You can tell this was not a game going for an amazing plot, but if you take away the subpar plot, the QTE and the badly implemented missions, all the fun you are going to get from the game is figuring how you are going to defeat some monsters (only some, because most are just shooting them).
After that, the postgame content are just even more missions and to be honest I left the game after getting all the achievements, there is no fun at all in 100% it when the missions are so bad (and I haven't talked about the Handle your Fuel mission in Cute Land where you are given no indications whatsoever as where the goal is and only a few seconds) and zones appear to not be complete for some weird reason (they all linger at about 90%)
This game doesn't even give a fraction of what it should give to 15 dollars. Get it free or don't get it at all.

I got it for sale, and to be honest, for the first several hours I deeply regretted buying the game. It wasn't horrible, per say, but the story writing was subpar and the characters were super shallow. Despite how cheap it was, if I were to ask myself, "Well, did I really need this in my life?" The answer was no, I really didn't. Each playthrough was incredibly short and the only thing that kept me playing was that I was bored and spent good money on it. Think low quality light novel writing. It's lighthearted and kind of interesting and fun, but I honestly gained very little from it. Except Nageki, still not writted super well but I just honestly loved Nageki. Anghel was pretty interesting too.
But then... Then came the BBL ending. And well heck did that mess me up. First off, heads up guys, that thing is a massive MONSTER. I kept expecting it to end soon because the others were so short, and it just. Kept. Going. Which, don't misunderstand, was fantastic and I loved every moment of it. But it was really bad for my self control and I literally went to bed at 6 AM on a Monday morning. orz
The writing was still what it was, and wasn't amazing prose or anything. Probably an issue of translating Japanese to English. But the plot really made up for it, and the music really set the mood. Things got INTENSE. Like, so much intrigue and all those little hints you get about two certain characters relations, and the Hawk Party, and all that, well... It just all comes together and you're honestly just mind boggled.
Okay, so maybe not actually mind-blowing. Again, written kind of like a (translated) light novel. But maybe it's just me (and a large portion of other players...?), but something about it really drags you in and refuses to let go. Maybe it's the tone shift, maybe it's the mystery. Maybe it's how these two dimensional characters interact in a very three dimensional manner. In the end though, this was actually one of my favorite games.
Overall probably:
Characters are a 4/10 (but 7.5/10 for Nageki so sweet)
Plot 9/10
Ambiance 8.5/10

The game starts out like a really fun fast paced overly violent brawler type game. It is actually pretty fun for about the first 20 bosses. However after that the game gets really repetative and old fast. The game had some fun designs like a jetpack and some really fun weapons, but also made some very strange decisions as well. First and the thing that I disliked the most is how long some of the animations took to play. The game feels like it is designed to play fast and fun, but the flow is slowed way down for the kill animaitons. Second, there are many instant death traps. This means there are many times you could spend quite some time collecting coins you need to upgrade and buy more weapons, only to hit a spike while still at full health and instantly lose all the progress. This mechanic should not be in a game like this and made the game way less fun. Given everything about the game I feel the first part of the game is decently fun and could be a 7 or 8 out of ten, but after playing through the rest of the game I would have to say it is a 3/10.
TL;DR - The game starts out fun but gets old fast. Some strange game decisions make the game not as fun as it could be and it suffers because of these choices.

A very fun vehicle building game with multiplayer mechanics and a powerful method of building which can be used to create anything you can think of. There are weapons and enemies to use them against but I don't want to spoil too much. You can obviously fight other players in your vehicles which is good fun, and since the devs have an armour plating system planned, thats gonna get really interesting.
There is a varied map with roads, a swamp, large bodies of water, mountains and sand - so you can test your vehicle offline or with friends on a variety of surfaces/environments. The map hides lots of secrets, I haven't found them all and the community is still trying to figure out a few of the more enigmatic ones.
People seem to be complaining that it is difficult to use, I have to say I wouldn't agree. I have nearly 42 hours on record at the time of writing this plus more before it was on steam. At hour 42+ I'm obviously a much better builder than I was at hour 0, but even at the start the system seemed intuitive and anything I didn't understand was cleared up by tutorials or help from the amazing community and dev support on the website.
It's in alpha yes, and I am apprehensive about buying games in alpha sometimes but not with this one. There are bugs present as with all alphas, but there are no major gamebreakers. There has been regular updates and the devs are literally in constant communication with the players, and I know if I had a pressing issue with the game or needed help with mechanics of the game I'd be able to get it faster than pretty much any of the other games in my library, plus the community are always happy to help on the chat on the homebrew website or the group chat on steam.
Overall a really good sandbox vehicle builder with massive potential that is going in the right direction. I'd reccomend it, just take half an hour to learn the building system at the start using tutorials (like you have to do with all other sandbox building games like KSP etc) and you'll have a blast.

This game IS a fantastical example of what an impressive feat
man can achieve when building a good game from start to finish. And immdeately we come to a reason
one person shouldn't do it to a scale that Axiom Verge tried to pull everything off: it is lacking in all the component fields as a result...
Artwork is nice, but not varied enough;
music is ok but doesn't have thought continuation throughout;
story is interesting to start with and then goes into an incoherent vector and I'm still not sure if I understood what Tom was trying to convey. After playing it through it seems much more could've been done in the universe and storyline.
gameplay mechanics are good but some parts are really fiddly to work with and the variety of weapons was there just for the sake of it. It didn't add anything different and I played 96% of it using combination of two weapons again with a ratio of 80% to 20% where long range was a necessity. The amount of unnecessary gadgetry was baffling almost to a level of a point-and-click adventure game where you would get a shiny new item with a dedicated button only to use it in 3 locations throughout the map.
The area that I could not get any complains at is the technical side. No crashes, runs impossibly smoothly, loads fast, and didn't end up in any unforseen scenario throughout the whole run (never stuck in a wall or anything of the sorts).
Most of luck in the future Tom, I really really hope your next game will be with a full(er) team, at least one guy in each sector to get all the distractions out of the way!
Bottom line:
It was a nice journey, but I wouldn't play it again.
Could be regarded as a decent pickup on a sale.

Should have been called "Bullsh*t Quotes on Meh Island"
Being more serious, though, this game is unfortunate because it feels like it has a lot of potential to be interesting.  The island contains a variety of setpieces ranging from a large Buddha statue to a tree house to a playground in an orchard to beach bungalos... lots of things that should be tons of fun.  However, outside of collecting sea shells and apples, the game lacks any kind of interactivity (the treehouse is inaccessible because you clip through the ladder, what a rip).  Also, the visuals are really somewhat subpar, with 3d models that come across as lazily crafted and certainly lazily textured.  The movement of the player is also really floaty and annoying in that subtle way that never allows you to get used to it.  The MMO aspect adds literally nothing to the gameplay, interactivity, or experience at all.
Not to mention that the game world is scattered with these books which apparently only contain one "philosophical" quote each.  In a somewhat hamfisted attempt to give the game some sort of intellectual or faux zen aspects, the most shallow guru quotes (which can only be mistaken as deep by college freshmen stoners) are tossed into random places, putting the finishing touch on this game's status as an absolute mess of random assets thrown together with no thought.
All in all, the game feels like a collection of half baked ideas, lazy execution, and lack of direction that isn't really meant for anyone.  I usually enjoy laid back games where I can just absorb the scenery, but this was just a huge mess.
Do not buy.

Demo 3D is a tablet game with a forgivable premise - Bridge constructor games meet Angry birds without the birds.   You set explosives on various premade structures and try not to hit red things and try to hit green and yellow things with the falling debris.
What's the problem then?  They didn't put a lot of effort into porting to PC.   The game controls all require "tapping".  There's no graphics or fidelity options - the graphics are at a fixed resolution, very low polygon for PC.
Lack of attention to PC specific configuration items and PC fidelity drag this game below the line, unfortunately.
This came very close to a thumbs up, and would certainly score modestly well if Steam gave us a more gradiated choice.  Here's hoping they decide to review their approach and take PC gaming seriously for their next offering.

So as not to seem like I'm mindlessly bashing the title I'll put some things I found troublesome.
1. User interface. Tooltips stay up and show the wrong item, even after you exit the inventory. The clicking buttons are not easy to see. Text is quite often layted over top of already existing text making it impossible to read quickly. Things that need explaining and tool tips don't have them when you want them (skill up items only pop up when you have points to spend). When receiving loot there is no indicator as to what you got. Other assorted quirks like not being able to craft items listed in the workbench even though you have all the ingredients.
2. Gameplay. Crafting is very imbalanced, basic need items require many resources and resources are few and far between, unless you happen to find the never ending spawn spots. When using your power attack via the right mouse button there is no way to cancel the ridiculously long animation which has the potential to make your loot vulnerable to others trying to steal it.
3 Building. Managed to get a Hammer of Build but was not able to place any foundation. There was  no indicator as to why I couldn't. Not sure if it's because I didn't have a foundation but none of the other piece previews worked.
That said I get that it's in early access but this was absolutely abysmal to play. I hope Route 66 gets this going because the idea seemed pretty neat. In the meantime I can't recommend this unless you are absolutely sure you know it's basically broken at this point.

Things I like about the game:
- The game is very cheap compared to similar games.

- You may have more than one hero, but the price increases significantly for each one. You may hoard, but it will cost you.
- Unit prices increase for every one you hire of each type. You can't just spam the best units.
- You have to choose which unit types you want, because you can only use half of them in each game.
- Your hero can only use a limited number of each unit tier at any one time, with fewer of the higher tiers.
- Building everything in your home town takes alot of time and gold. I still haven't managed to do it.
Things I dont like:
- Lack of helpful tooltips makes some things hard to understand. Like how the size of a population will affect the game. It's hard to win a game when the game doesn't tell you how things work.
- The heroes say "I will easily defeat them", but then he dies and\or loses several units in auto-combat.
- The combat AI is awful, sending archers and healers to the front row all the time.
- Not enough abilities available for each hero type.
- Unit animations are poorly timed (they deal damage and then they hit)
- I'm swimming in mana, without trying at all.
- Heroes are unbalanced. The scout and the warrior are one man armies, while the wizard can only cast 2 attacks through a whole battle in the beginning...
- Some province populations will hate you and rebel. You dont have a clue why, because the game doesn't tell you.
- Too little focus on magic, spells are too few and not very interesting.
- There's no combat log.

Eador: Masters of the Broken World is a great game if you have a lot of time to spend, and do not mind a slow progression curve. Presenting you with a strategy game set in a detailed world broken up into multiple shards, you can spend your time gathering land and power to eventually find one of many endings.
It is a big game, full of strategic decisions and plenty of things you can explore, find, and control. It is one of the largest games in scale that I have seen so far, which is both good and bad. Good, because, of course. That's more game for you to play in, and bad because all that scale takes a lot of time to get through. So much time that you may not have enough in your schedule to make good progress in it - I have over 80 hours in it, and I have not yet completed the campaign. As much as I like the scale, the shattered vibrant world, the astral mechanics and the immersive soundtrack, it has issues that it doesn't need to have.
The world in Eador is based on shards, with each shard being a whole new map to explore and conquer, and every one you conquer brings you a new building or advantage you can take along to the next. You gain astral energy based on how much of the world is in your possession, and how many people worship you, the astral spirit/master controlling the place. The problem here is that every single shard has you build up your forces from practically nothing. You can spend energy to bring some basics, but it is never really enough to skip through the early game and expensive. Plus, who knows what else you may want your energy for? Eador plays much more like several similar skirmish maps than a long unified campaign. Yet, there is throughout it all a large storyline, from world to world, where you can spend time talking to the other masters or decide to engage them, change things that have long term effects far past the one world you're in, or otherwise find out more about the game's world.
While in the game itself, there are a lot of random and semi-random events as well. The world feels as if it is actually a world, rather than just a game through these. The soundtrack is very well done, and it is easy enough to forget about time and spend several hours to take over another shard and advance past it.
But it has issues, as mentioned. It is imperfect, with occasional crashes and some balance issues making it very difficult to progress at times, as well as some design decisions, whether intentional or not, leading to some choices being just plain better than others. Out of all this, the worst of it is when your opponent gets a random event that allows them to have a guard dragon, while you are still in the earliest levels. There is no way to defeat a dragon at that point without a lot of grinding experience on your hero and luck.
The opposing AI is rather poor, and at times does not seem to even understand the basics of gameplay, which is sad as you will be spending a lot of time beating on said AI. Both the other masters and the neutrals tend to be like that, sadly. The battles being on a tiny, simplistic map that shows that combat is not the game's strong point.
But you're likely not buying this for the combat. If you're buying Eador, you're doing it for the strategy, the long term plans, the vibrant world, and all the good things it has. Try to not let its faults get to you, and you will be able to spend litterally days on it without any regret. But if you do not have time, patience, or are not that much into strategy and similar 4X games, you may not enjoy it. For those who do enjoy those things, here's for you.

Chernobyl Commando is one of those "budget" shooters that have you shoot through bazillion bad guys on your way to the objective, which usually just leads to another level. Other than the subject matter, it shows no innovation at all, and made no attempt to distinguish itself from the field. With that said, it is a decent FPS, but merely adequate.
The story is simple: you are Russian special forces and you're fighting the terrorists who went into Chernobyl attempting to obtain radioactive material to be sold to the highest bidder. Russians had the place surrounded, with gunships and planes overhead, but the ground situation is chaotic that bandits roam freely, and it's up to you and sometimes, your buddy Feodor, and sometimes, some allied units, to blast your way through the bad guys with variety of weapons... PDW submachine gun, AK-74 (or 47, can't tell), Saiga shotgun (with a scope?!), Dragunov sniper rifle, pistol (with silencer), sniper rifle (with silencer), and some grenades. Sometimes you get to ride in a technical and use a turret gun. At other times you get to play static gunner as you use a mounted LMG to mow down enemies attempting to retake your position. There's no lean, but there is crouch. This is a modern shooter so if you rest a moment from getting hit your HP will be restored. However, that's not possible on the "gunner" sequences.
Any way, the story takes a turn later and let's say you'll get some glasnost help in a certain Middle Eastern country. But the mechanics doesn't change... You do what you do best... shoot hostiles.
Given the preponderance of scoped weapons you are meant to engage the enemy at range, and they don't really rush you on easy, so you can basically take a few hits, and hit them when they pop out and change positions. On the other hand, it's amazing how they can hit you with a piddly SMG from 100 meters away. Which is very annoying. Also, the game does often hide enemies behind foliage, forcing you to spot the muzzle flash, and that is quite realistic.
Given that this is taking place in Ukraine, next to Russia, the lack of RPG is inexplicable. It's guns, guns, and more guns. And nothing but guns. And you are carrying way too many guns, really.
Graphics are actually quite decent, and the enemies are animated properly with good amount of polygons, though below the standard like MW or BF series. And it does support high resolution as I was able to run in 1680x1050 with no problems. There are also variety of graphics option to make sure you get the optimum frame rate. There are occasional kill cams but it seems enemies almost always die the same way. At least they usually die appropriately. If there were prone, they simply fall flat on their face when shot dead (In some games if you kill a prone enemy they pop back up, did a spin, THEN fall dead. This is NOT one of them).
The sound is actually quite good, with the various guns sounding "appropriate" except the shotgun, which sounds like a slightly thumpier regular gun.
The levels are a typical "rat maze" one way through, which appears wide open but you are prompted to return to mission area and you have like 5 seconds to step back in or DIE. Really.
The game did suffered one significant glitch. In the 2nd to final level the ground shown through and the vehicles were spinning like tops. Must be some memory corruption. Then the game crashed. However, reloading the checkpoint worked and there were no issues resuming the game. The checkpoints are quite appropriately placed, neither too long nor too short.
On easiest level I finished the entire game in 2 hours, and I played relatively slowly, instead of running forward and blazing through enemies. I think I had to reload ONCE when I screwed up one of those static gun position levels. But one easiest, it's a quick game. I imagine on higher difficulty levels it can be a bit more unforgiving.
All in all, Chernobyl Commando is a budget shooter albeit a "modern" one, and it's not bad, but it's very very mediocre. If you need something simple to occupy your time, and try something from the Russian / Ukranian perspective instead of the Western perspective this is not a bad game to try. However, there are better shooters out there, that are more exciting to play, better pacing, and so on and so forth, and are of even better value than this budget shooter.

If only there were a middle ground between "recommend" and "don't".
Another samey low budget shooter from a small-scale independent polish developer named Silden.
If you've played Manhunter (inexplicably renamed from its original title: Sniper: The Manhunter. Maybe too similar to City Interactive's many many "Sniper: [whatever]" games?) you'll notice a ton of reused assets to the point of absurdity. All the guns from Manhunter are there with only the arm textures changed, with one exception: The AK looking gun with the white camo and scope. While in Manhunter this had a 30 round mag and was essentially the best gun in the game, here it has only 10 rounds, the accuracy of someone with severe parkinsons holding a pistol gangster style, and takes many more bullets to do anything.
The sniping mechanics have been dropped (steady aiming, getting the "this is where your shot lands" dot, wind & bullet drop) and there's not much reason for there being 3-4 sniper rifles(!) in your inventory at the same time. The Dragunov becomes the best weapon in the game since it's got a faster fire rate than the suppresed AWP-like and is the most accurate shooter in the game, though the Barret you get when you leave the titular location (more on that later) may also count. So you're mostly left with the suppresed Walther P99 (technically your best non-sniper weapon, believe it or not), the AK-(47? 74? M? whatever) that's a disgrace to the AK in accuracy AND power, and the MP7 to deal with your absurd collection of soldiers (in very different armors), civilians with guns, gas mask dudes, and later turban dudes.
For about half the game, you get to "explore" (read: stay along a narrow linear path with no markers and make sure you simultaneously hit every star waypoint the way they intend you to and don't stray from the path or you'll be punished) the place listed in the title: Chernobyl NPP area. Expect this to involve "go to this place, shoot 50 dudes that show up out of nowhere, sometimes visibly spawning in, then do some stationary or mobile turret sections where 50 more dudes will show up, repeat". The one change-up here is later in this section some more heavily armored guys show up that take even more shots (that will miss most of the time) to put down.
For the second half, due to a vague statement or two (there's more story in the "About This Game" section on steam than in the game as a whole; most dialogue is basically "there are enemies ahead be careful, time to be serious, let's go")  you're in... Iraq, shooting terrorists in plain clothes that do much more damage than anybody in the Chernobyl area despite having the same ♥♥♥♥♥♥ weapons and less armor. Many fewer turret sections thankfully, this time mostly on hummers with much more accurate guns.
When you finish the game, you're treated to a long cutscene where you and your driver are invisible (seriously? There's very clearly a world model for "you" considering the main menu, and there's no reason the driver shouldn't be there) and the credits roll... and the game just closes when the credits hit the end. Like it became self aware and just gave up on existing. The AI, animations, and mission scripting are exactly the same as in Manhunter; not worth really mentioning.
Visually, it's a slight improvement from prior Silden titles I guess? I mean, some models look like they're pretty surprisingly high-poly for a game with no AA options, but shadowmap resolution is still (estimating) like 256 and the draw distance for them is just as bad.
Time for the real fun: The bugs. Much like Manhunter, you will occasionally need to restart your game after moving to the next level because the game will drop the framerate to unplayably slow, which can cause some hilarity if the level starts in a vehicle. It's even worse when going to the SECOND LEVEL, as the silos and buildings in the area? They all turn into some weird set of flat black rectangles.
In general it can be fun to run through in 2 hours on easy mode after dropping less money on it in a sale than what a fast food meal will cost you. Maybe someday Silden will get enough cash and attention to join modern City Interactive and Techland in the ranks of Polish developers that have the resources to make a much better title.

Game is really weird and has the ability to induce vomiting. First off, the game doesn't have any backstory and is just a person mind blowing balls out of their head against demons (I guess). Secondly, the game has multiple quirks and bugs. If you were to go and mash a bunch of buttons in a corner, the game would send you to the menu. I even closed the game, reopened it and got all the achievements. I have no problem with that, but it sucks when the game has to bug for you to even earn an achievement.

How not to design a game.
To the developer's credit, the art is very nice for what I think they were going for, the animations are good, the sound design is good if we ignore how repetitive it is ( all music is exactly the same, I keep hearing "This world is mine" every few seconds). I'll even ignore the oversized characters and hitboxes, the slow movement of the player character, and the unintuitive controls.
Even then, the game is horrible.
First up is the player's attacks. All of your attacks home in on the nearest enemy, and nearly all of your attacks are just a stream of mutlicolored lights (you can add triangles to it using a powerup- these do a ton of damage and are practically needed for most bosses). But, the "homing on nearest enemy" bit means that your attacks will ignore the boss if any of its endless stream of minions come between you and it. This serves only to frustrate you and prolong the boss battle.
Next is the enemy design. Scroll through the screenshots for the game and see if you can find an orangish-red guy that looks like Satan. Remember what he looks like, because touching him transports you bakc to the previous screen (that means that you have to beat the previous boss before you can attempt the current boss again- repeat for every time he touches you.) and he isn't just fast-moving, but also invincible- you can only wait for him to go off screen. He's just the tip too- there's also a boss that instantaneously teleports around the screen (no warning, no chance to get out of his way, only a ton of damage if you touch him), a boss that will randomly start moving extremely quickly, bosses that are only vulnerable to specific attacks, and bosses that seem to move in and out of the background. Oh, and every enemy projectile homes in on you. All of them.
Finally there is the general clutter. It's normal for a bullet hell to fill the screen with bullets, but this one likes to go a step further and fill the screen with fast moving enemies that occasionally blend in with the background (4th level is filled with enemies that just fly around the area extremely quickly and are hard to distinguish from one another. I got an achivement for killing a boss in this area that I don't even remember seeing), and you'll sometimes find that enemies attacks blend in with the background (5th or 6th boss-I lost count- has two attacks. One is a blue orb, the other is a stream of blood-red teardrops. The background of the level is blood red with some black on the sides. Anyone else see a problem here?).
The icing for this, though, is the developer. The base game is very low on content (based on the achievements, I had two or three bosses/ levels left after 30 minutes of playtime) so the dev releases two DLCs that are the same price as the main game- which is acceptable if they have the same amount of content as the base game (I couldn't get through them, but based on the steam achievements, they do not). Then however, the dev releases the Redux DLC, also for the same price as the base game, and it is basically an update. That's all it is, an update for the projectile behaviour and enemy AI, as well as a new UI. I think you can understand why that shouldn't be a DLC.

The Renegades of Orion 2.0 is perhaps one of the most creative and yet terrible single screen shoot'em ups out there. Most shmups have you as a space vessel, but you are some piece of 80s rock metal album cover artwork sprang to life. I would have preferred a more traditional route, but if you're going to be weird, go so far over the top that you end up in space.
Your goal is to destroy bosses, but the real challenge to the game are terrible controls, poor design choices and giant hit boxes. The arrow keys control move you around in 8 directions, but you are so slow and sluggish. Enemies can move in a full 360 degrees and just aim at you. Under normal circumstances, this is never an issue, but you and the enemies are each so large that its tough to maneuver to avoid them.
The only real attack here is eye lasers that halt you so there's a fight or flight thing going on, but never both at once. You need to get to a corner of the screen, shoot then move as enemies pile on you. When you move there is a chance that your eye lasers will move with you like if you move north, the lasers will move north.
There are other attacks, but the seem cumbersome and complicated. They require two keys and your attack key to work and even then your eye lasers shoot at the nearest small enemy, so there's never a reason to use anything else. Think of that as the game's balance. When you're being rushed head on, your attack does the same thing. If you go to the top of the screen where your head is above the screen and then shoot, nothing happens. The eye lasers are made up of tiny weak projectiles that launch every frame.
The keybinds are bizare. H for save, G for load. F for fullscreen I can understand in a way. The rest is just spacebar and shift.... to pause! When I press F12 to take a screenshot in Steam, a chrome extension for developer tools pops up. That's an interesting feature. I was never expecting that.
The game starts with you one on one facing a boss who summons demons to hover at you. Even from the first moments of gameplay there are issues. At the end of the boss there is a glitch that seems to fire off the same sound effect each frame. Most developers would have the sound once, but whatever.I also took note that at the bottom of the screen you have a giant health meter at the bottom and the boss health meter is a small number in the right corner.
I would say this is someone's first game, but I can also say its trying to be terrible on purpose. Its amazing this game can be 2.0, because as it stands now its cumbersome, tough and over complicated. The Renegades of Orion 2.0 is a valuable way to learn game design at its smallest levels. You have a simple game here and yet everything goes wrong with it.
Perhaps the biggest sin of Renegades is that its just dull and uninspiring. You can laugh at how bad the game is, but beyond that, there's no reason to push on.
On top of the bare bones content of "just play" there is paid downloadable content. There's just not that much of a game here. Its more of an oddity than something that could be confused for entertainment or fun. I was done after a minute of playing, but for review purposes, I had to push on.
The game can be salvaged with some sort of score system to make it more of an arcade game. As a single screen shooter, there just needs to be something that's more engaging that lets me feel like I'm in control rather than fighting a tough game.
Thank you to my friend Blanka for giving me Renegades of Orion 2.0. Hey even if I dislike it, I still thank you for it.

What I love most about Paradox games is the amount of detail, and depth to game mechanics, and HOI is no exception. While most would not consider it as complex as it's predecessor, it's still worth the purchase.
As with any other Paradox title, you play as any country starting in either 1936, or 1939. Playing in 1936 lets you build up your military and industry as you see fit, whereas 1939 lets you get right into the fighting. I played most of my early hours as a Brazil, which allowed me to engage in war, learn why it's generally a bad idea to attack Democratic nations when World Tension is high, and learn to keep units well supplied.
The only real issue I have with the game is the fact that at times, a 5 year old mental patient would play better than the AI. The worst offender is when units will leave their capital completely unguarded.
I also feel the AI sucks at directly building up against your arsenal. For instance, as Germany, by 1939, I have far more planes than France and the UK combined. This means, I can generally sink the British fleet in a short time with torpedo planes. The AI doesn't seem to care about defending against naval invasions either, which makes taking London by 1940 a piece of cake.
Overall, the game is great, but the AI needs some serious work. Good buy for 40, better buy on sale.

Very enjoyable game. Those who say it's extremely confusing, didn't play the tutorials. Which you should almost always do considering some games give bonus currency or something for playing them through (wink wink, nudge nudge, devs ;)). With that said, there are some things that could/should be added/fixed. The devs have heard enough about the UI, I think they know it needs some patching. So glossing over that. There's almost no control over the helicopters (and I know they're adding joystick support, but not everyone has one). Vehicle part deletion; it's a serious pain the way it's set up. Wrapping this up, the game is still amazing. With one of the most in-depth vehicle creation systems out there combined with a good physics system, multiplayer/single player offers hours pleasure.

This Game has MASSIVE potential if the devs know what they're doing.
I would hold off at this point though, as making vehicles is slow, and based on trial and error. That, and the only things you can make end up looking like dune buggies, even blimps.
The UI needs serious work, and remapping controlls is an absolute nightmare.
But besides that, this game is unique and fun. It is aiming for a realitively untouched genre and so far handles it quite well. The tools are simple enough for a beginner, but complex enough for people who want to fine tune things down to the fiftieth decimal and create extreme, realistic things.
I just hope that this does not end up like starbound, which ceased development right after being put up and was left in alpha for a shamefully long time, with only a few fun things to do. If these developers could NOT do that, it would be great.
Unless you cannot resist the idea of making your own space rocket submarine blimp that looks like dune buggy, you might just want to hold off on this one.
EDIT (Half a year later):
The dev team working on this is amazing! They listen to all forms of ideas and recommendations, applying as much as they can at an unbelievable pace. I remeber recommending them to add panels to make the vehicles look more realistic. Sure enough, just look at it now in the screenshots. They added it. This is truly a great early acess game that promises so much, while delivering at the same time. It sets the standard for how an early access game should be managed. If you enjoy racing, simulation games, building and sandbox games, this game will be the magnum opus of your Steam library!

I had a few issues with this game when I first started, this is why I gave it the thumbs down (for now)!
You can eventually work your way through the tute (not easy as they don't explain things very well), but after that it says to go out side and take the vehicle for a ride.
Problem is, you have to actually go up to a console inside the garage, (no idea why the vehicles are not inside the garage) and tell it you want to go outside, once outside, there is no vehicle, you have to press i to get a list of vehicles, then press i again to stop displaying the list of available vehicles, then point up in the air and press left mouse button to throw the vehicle in the air (again, no idea why you would do this), and then chase the vehicle as it will most likely start rolling away, no hand brake. Once you finally get a vehicle (remember to press x to start the motor), it is very hard to control it, there does not appear to be a button to press for brake, also it says to press page up and page down to zoom in and out, nothing happens. Not being able to zoom out a little makes it hard to see where your going. Editing vehicles is a little daunting at first, being unsure which parts fit with what, the tute vehicle requires a motor (when putting this in, it would be handy if the default angle of the motor would be suitable to put it in with out having to rotate it first), which I gave it, but when I went out side, it did not have a motor or even a left front wheel. Going to quick edit, it had a motor so you can not give it another, it also had all of the wheels, then switching to tune it had no motor or wheel (wtf). They could make this game a little more user friendly. Maybe add to the tute a highlighting function that lets you know where to place the parts that it is telling you to install!
Controlling the ground vehicles is very hard, because the camera is doining its own thing, so not controllable by the user. Most of the time is will go behind the vehicle, so long as you are going in a straight line, so it is not too bad. What is bad, is that the angle of the camera is not high enough off the ground behind the vehicle, so you will have trouble seeing where you are going when going over hills. It would be much better to provide an option for the user to have some controll over the camera.
Controlling the vehicle is also rather hard, especially at speed, it has major oversteer problems at speed, as well as the camera problem already mentioned, of not seeing where your going when going over hills.
There does not seem to be much to do while driving, collecting objects and going over ramps. I have not progressed to air travel at this time, so don't know what there is to do up in the sky.
At present they need to make it more user friendly, they are actively working on it and answering comments left here so I remain hopeful that this will end up being a really good game!!!

When I began playing Hell Yeah! I was not sure if I could enjoy an action platformer that looks like Mario Bros. from the 1980s. It looks like an interactive cartoon movie that requires plenty of jumping and jumping skill are required to advance in this game. I do not play many action platformers. After playing the first zone for a little bit, I felt like I could slowly enjoy this game.
The basic theme of the game centers around Ash, the protagonist rabbit. He is the rabbit prince of hell who finds out that photos of him romancing with a rubber duck could be made public on the Hellternet, hell’s version of the internet. There are 100 monsters who saw the photos, leaving Ash with one choice: kill them all. The story takes place across 10 zones, but there are restricted parts of zones so that you can defeat a certain number of monsters so that doors can explode to give you access to more of the zone.
The zones are diverse enough and rendered in 2D environments. Zones include a casino, ruins, museum, volcano, a spaceship, etc. While there is a lot of jumping, you will face monsters very frequently. Monsters are of varying personalities. Some indicate that they are bored, some are hanging out with friends, and some are downright nasty. Each monster requires a strategy that is not straightforward. You must study the environment to understand the strategy that is required to defeat each monster. Many of these monsters are much larger than you are. You move around with a jetpack and drill to navigate spikes, walls, and various traps. The drill can be used to kill bugs, but they usually are no good against the largest monsters. For example, you must figure out how you can lure a monster to an area where slime can be dropped on him for the kill. The ten zones are graphically colorful and eye candy in 2D. It looks like a kiddie game with a sense of humor.
Defeating each monster usually leads to a minigame that must be completed properly to finish him/her off. Since there are way less minigames than monsters, they get repetitive. One minigame requires you to answer a trivia question and another requires you to powerlift a barbell so that your rabbit become large enough to kick the monster through a goal net, resulting in gibs that splash all over the screen.
When you are out of the game you can visit The Island, a private property of Ash that is used to enslave every monster you defeated. The benefit of every monster working on The Island is that they will give you gifts such as more health, more cash, and surprise items. They work in the harbor, the mines, the lab, and the manor. Some monsters will show unhappiness or anger, so they must be sent to the beach or the tower to take away their unhappiness or anger. You can zoom into the beach to see defeated monsters play a game of volleyball, which I found amusing.
As you explore the zones, there are plenty of coins and jewelry to collect and they are important for buying items from the stores. Items include upgrades for your firearms and various skins for customizing Ash. Skins include hats and bike outfits. Upgrades to the drill occur throughout the game, but they can only happen by progressing through the story. There is a lot of backtracking in the game. when you finish one of the later zones you will realize that you must return to zone 1 to defeat more monsters so that you can continue to open later zones in the end. This backtracking can feel like a little bit of a drag, but there is a teleport system to make your backtracking less tedious while you analyze the teleport system’s simple map.
The control scheme I used for this game was WASD for directions and the mouse for firing weapons. The jumping can be awkward and frustrating, especially when wall jumping. Other times a slight mistake in a jump can lead to instant death. I got used to the mouse/keyboard scheme with enough practice, but some may end up preferring to use a controller. The jumping gets more frustrating in parts of zones where you lose access to all your weapons and jetpack.
The weapons in the game are your basic ones such as a revolver, shotgun, grenades, rockets, flamethrower. There are a few unusual ones like a holy water. However, I did not find much variation in how much damage they do. The ammo does not actually run out since they only require recharging to fire again.
I found Hell Yeah! to be more fun than I thought it would be. Despite the sometimes-frustrating jumps, especially where Ash had no weapons or jetpack, I enjoyed the gameplay enough after adapting to the mouse/keyboard scheme. I also enjoyed the variety of settings in each zone, especially in the casino and in the spaceship while shooting asteroids, bugs, and monsters. Hell Yeah! is not a classic action platformer game, but it is a decent one by Sega and Arkedo Studio.
My Score: 7/10

Being a fan of the Mitsubishi A6M series of planes, but wanting something more modern and flexible than MSFT's Combat Flight Simulator 2, I had heard a lot of good things of this piece of software, so I decided to go ahead and buy it.
But the thing is that it doesn't seem to run on modern computers. I'm using a Windows 10 64 bit HP laptop -which I would guess it is up to the requirements of a 10+ year old program- and, when launching the game, it shows me a nice image stating the title, along with a nice render of some planes. And then promptly gets stuck in 50% of loading the files.
Oh, but that's not all! It also brings my computer to a screeching halt, making even the action of moving the mouse pointer a slow chore. If that wasn't bad enough, it also screws up the display of my monitor, creating a series of black lines from the middle of the screen to the right border, which come increasingly thick as they reach the righternmost part of the display.
I tried the regular fixes mentioned in this games discussion -running it in Windows XP SP2 compatibility mode, with admin rights and without some graphic options (which were disabled from the get-go, to begin with)- but no matter what I tried, I had the same results everytime, forcing me to restart my computer at least 5 times in the span of half an hour.
As I mentioned to the Steam representative when I claimed my refund: If the developers don't issue a patch/fix for this problem, it would be better for Steam to pull this from the store, since, as time goes by, it will become less and less compatible with newer computers, but many people will still hear great things about this game and will purchase it to try it out, only to become disappointed some minutes later.
-Commanderraf

This game has become a solid entry into the "4x" genre at this point. You conquer the Eador world shard by shard. Each shard you conquer allows you to build a little bit better buildings.  The combat is turn based and is done very well. The variety of monsters, creatures you will face is also very nice. I am a little over 16 hours into the game and I am on my 4th shard and to be honest it is getting a bit repetetive at this point. There is no hero carry over from shard to shard so after you conquer a shard you then recruit a new hero for the next. I think this is where the game falls a bit. You spend hours working through a shard, building your main provicence and adding a couple of smaller buildings to the conquered provinces all the while leveling up your hero. This is honestly quite a bit of work and takes grinding to beat the shard. However once you beat the shard , you lose all your progress and your hero. You essentially start the next shard at ground zero. Albeit you have access to a little bit better buildings but you do the same thing again. Start your hero at 0 and work on beating that shard.
This is a fun game and at this point of its life plays solid- however I do not see myself logging 60 hours due to the repeat process on each shard.
Things I think would make this game more enjoyable for longer play:
Carry over your hero and make the next shard a level harder. This way you feel you are building towards something as you play through. Right now on shard 4 I stopped because I have a level 0 Warrior and he just croaked on 3 imps with 4 barbarians with him. It is frustrating considering on shard 3 I grinded my Mage to a great level and was enjoying the game. Then .... he is gone once the shard is defeated.
Reduce the amount of searching in each province. To get to 100% per province takes quite a bit of time and is very repetetive. I find myself at this point in the game rolling my eyes when I hit nothing encountered 3x in a row and it becomes a click fest to see what you will find.
Add more heroes if you plan on keeping the new hero per shard. They are quite generic and there is no real customization you can do to make the new hero on the next shard feel different.
Right now you only have 4 to choose. I have already used all 4 and I am on my 4th shard. From what I read this game can reach 20+ shards per playthrough.
The good :
Pretty game. Graphics are solid.
Combat is quite fun. I do like the movement points and I do like the challenge as the fights are not easy.
The variety of monsters,creatures encountered is very large.
Once you get the hang of city building with the wheel its pretty slick. I found myself realy enjoying the building aspect.
All in all .. this a solid 4x entry ....however if you are like me and enjoy customization of your characters and buidling your characters over the course of the game you will find this quite repetetive and almost a chore when you hit the next shard. (notice my frequest use of the word repetetive)
I would give it 7/10 based on solid gameplay, graphics,combat but it falls a bit due to lack of hero diversity, growth, and customization.

is an excellent adventure that offers a large amount of replayability and overall striking design.
The most apparent thing about
would be its mastery of atmosphere. The Empire of the Isles is presented with an impressive amount of detailed backstory, with other cultures, practices, and life in general making a consistent appearance. Furthermore, the city of Dunwall is stark and bleak, featuring fantastic art direction and level design to set a despairing tone. There’s little hope at all in Dunwall, but the mystery of how such a once grand city came to ruin is intriguing enough in of itself.
The gameplay is just about a perfect example of 'easy to use, hard to master'. There's enough abilities in this game that, if one were inclined, one could literally teleport past near every obstacle. However,  its much more rewarding to blend together abilities to in general have more fun - abilities that grant you the capability to stop time or take control of animals/humans can be combined in a variety of ways with the detailed and well thought out level design to make each playthrough unique. This really is where
shine, and a quick Youtube search could make the case of why this is so stronger than any paragraph can.
is very much worth a buy. There’s something here for everyone, and once you start it’s hard to stay away.

TLDR: Excellent Metroidvania platform/exploration game.
This game will leave you frustrated, puzzled, slapping-your-forehead, cheering, frowning, determined, exasperated and--in the end--smiling. In other words, it is damn near perfect.
I won't get into the plot or substance of the game, but the story is clever and weaves a wonderful mystery that you unravel as you explore new areas. This mystery is something that the original Metroid gave you, but Super Metroid (as a rehash) did not. With a new world, and a new story, this takes the best gameplay elements of the Metroidvania genre, adds a few of its own and takes off.
The humor and design of the game are very self-aware. For instance, an item lets you "glitch" through walls as was famously possible on older SNES titles. The main character constantly challenges the plausibility of his situation and injects just the right amount of humor into a bizarre mystery.
Play this! If you have investigated enough to see this review, you will LOVE it!

This game is a triumph of style and design. It wears its inspiration on its sleeve, but, in my opinion, largely improves on the originator. The weapon variety and movement upgrades in this game are some of the most satisfying I've ever seen in a Metroidvania, and the atmosphere, look of the game and graphics are pitch-perfect and genuinely stick with you. The combat, especially in boss encounters, can become frenetic and quite challenging, but make no mistake, this game's strength is exploration. And the story, as basic as it is, is genuinely engaging.
Simply put, this game accomplishes everything it sets out to do, and more. Some may criticize it for feeling too close to what it's inspired by, but in my view its quality easily transcends the source, placing it as its own respectable addition to the genre. The fact that a single person made this entire game makes it all the more impressive.
If you like Metroid, Contra, exploration, and strange sci-fi settings, you will love this game. One of the best I've played in a long time.

This one has grabbed me. It's not so much a game as a great kit for building things and trying them out in an expansive world. In fact, it's the closest thing I've found to an actual sandbox game. On the upside, the tools are easy to use and there are enough parts at this point to build a wide range of wacky contraptions. The world is simple, but it's attractive enough to enjoy, and it provides a good sense of space and motion as you invariably crash into it - repeatedly. The physics are solid and flexible enough to give you feedback on your design choices, but on the downside, they aren't realistic feeling. Just like any driving/flying game, it's a compromise. Once you stop trying to make it behave like the real world, it turns into a lot of fun. I'm experiencing some graphical flickering here and there, but I'm sure that will get straightened out. The devs are actively updating and involved in the forum discussions. There is no free build mode. You have to gather orbs to pay for parts, but it's easy enough to get a full kit of parts pretty quickly. There is apparently a way to get around the orb gathering, but I'm not smart enough to figure out the hints on the forums and I got tired of standing around in the pyramid with a dumb look on my face. :) Anyway, if you like to build and test and basically fiddle around with mechanical systems, this game will keep you entertained for many hours.
