Even though I love sports, I cannot stand playing Football, never mind playing Football games. I saw BloodBowl was on sale on Steam, but didn’t buy it as I’m not a huge fan of turn-based. I saw Mutant Football League and immediately thought of NFL Blitz for the N64. Little did I know I would hear some very interesting use of the English language and become comfortable with completely breaking, but following the rules of Football.
The
is actually really rock solid. It definitely follows the beautiful theme that NFL Blitz delivered by keeping a football game quick and intense. The game is complimented by the fact the delivery is made in the devs creativity and dedication to the whacky theme. It goes far as impacting the entire world of football, from the stadiums, to the play field, to the players, and especially to the rules of the game. MFL literally takes the entire experience to the next level and doesn’t cut any corners along the way. Menus are polished and neatly organized. There is a season mode available for players in which options can be customized. For example, you could choose to have players revived after every game if they die during the game. Yes, your players can technically die - or are absent – during the game should you get a few knuckle sandwiches to the noggin and bone shackling tackles. Your health will slowly decrease and you can run out of players for certain positions. If you run out of quarterbacks, then you’ll lose the game - plain and simple. Choosing a play in-game is extremely easy on offence and defense. It’s quick to navigate and the game plan is illustrated in a way for anyone to understand. Should you change your mind during a play, you can call-up a mini-menu to quickly change the game plan before snapping the ball.
Even if you’re a n00b at football, you’ll have a good chance learning the rules and strategies that come along with the sport. There is a n00b friendly feature when the player holds RT on either defense or offence, the chosen play is illustrated on the field. My friend who has no idea about football really appreciated this feature and maybe even taught him a thing or two about the sport. He also liked the back-to-back play feature as he didn’t like always choosing a play. I also really appreciate the fact you can customize a bit of the play (before snapping the ball of course). The player that you are moving before the snap generally has two positions to choose from. Of course if you’re impatient like me, you can snap the ball while the player is between those two final positions to, you know, not only change the play up, but keep the opponent guessing. The
in-game are varied just enough to complicate tactics. There are two sort of tackles that the player can do which consist of diving for an opponent or straight just going through an opponent. There are two different hit buttons : one is a little slower and more devastating while the other is quicker, but delivers a smaller impact. One appreciated feature is jumping and one amazing feature is attacking while being on offence. If players are jumping your way to take you down, you can hit that counter-attack button to shrug them off your shoulders and to the ground. This game is definitely unpredictable, but feels fairly balanced at all times. The fairness of the game is sometimes comparable to Mario Party turned on with bonuses; you don’t know who the heck will randomly open a box with a star. You will definitely have to know the game inside and out to have a solid advantage.
Calling the plays can be absolutely ridiculous at times. The regular plays are very efficient in what they do, but there is this thing called “dirty tricks” in MFL. The
of the game certainly compliment the catastrophic potential of dirty tricks (and the game in general). The x-factor, the shazpooz, the whazah, the qu’est-ce-que c’est, the spicey meat-ah-ball of this game is directly related to what you want to do and your strategic approach. Say the other team is low on quarter-backs, you can choose a “dirty trick” play and straight up terminate the quarter-back before the ball is properly snapped. The quarter-back does have a chance to defend, but the player better be quick on their toes to run! Another dirty trick involves the quarter-back pulling out a shotgun while running to get a first down. If you run out of bullets, why not take steroids on the field to run through the defense? Well apparently its encouraged in the MFL! So is bribing the referee. If you think you’re going to miss the run and want a second chance to go for a hail mary, a dirty trick can definitely buy you a penalty. Can the defense do something like that you ask? Well of course! Say the offense bribed the referee for a penalty against, you can choose to take out the crooked official! These are some examples of the insane ways that the gameplay is directly impacted by small tweaks to the rules and strategies – it was done in an excellent fashion! I love how the game is consistent in nailing the details. Dirty tricks can sometimes be sidetracked thanks to the randomness (or dangers) of the stadium. Definitely keep an eye out for any holes in the field as they may contain spikes. Getting slammed too hard on the ice may throw your character right through.
I should give a notable nomination for the
. The commentating in game is absolutely wonderful and the commentators themselves are quite the characters. It definitely reminds me of the intensity NFL Blitz has with a touch of “pourquoi”? In other words, the commentating is the cherry on top to complete the wonderful compliment cake that is this game. I hope that the devs definitely consider updating the commentary! Concerning dialogue, the players aren’t much for words. They sort of have their own language and will babble something out during a very brief cut-scene. The attention to detail to sound seems quite accurate as you will hear players crash through glass or fall into water.
Overall, a pretty solid game and would definitely recommend a purchase on sale. The non-stop carnage even after the whistle makes this an action packed game. The play is not over even though the whistle has blown. That’s what I like most about the game; there is always some thinking involved even though everything is colorful on the TV. If you are a football fan or just a casual gamer, you definitely will get a tackle out of this game! Heh.

Gah. Aethestically, this game is mesmerizing. Functionally, its feels like a mess.
What do I mean by that? There's no denying that this alien world has a very distinct artistry to it, and from a purely cosmetic standpoint it really, really works. What is this place? What's with these giant talking heads? Only the bare minimum makes sense, and from a Metroidvania perspective it does a great deal towards driving curiousity in the world around you. Axiom's Verge's amibiguity flat out captivated me; I wanted to know more.
And yet, that same amibiguity turned out to be a double-edged sword. You might think a strange, alien world would be filled with meaningful landmarks, but that just doesn't seem to be the case. The world as a whole just feels like a hodge-podge of random terrain that goes from "weird green-looking stuff" to "weird blue-looking stuff." Its nice eye-candy in the moment, but its make for terrible navigation. Getting a power-up essentially had me going, "Oh great, I wonder which forsaken dead end this thing hooks up with." Exploration can quickly devolve into aimless wandering as you travel half-way across the map just to find a health fragment (and subsequently pick another dead end to check out.) The poking around feels more like a mandatory exercise than a fun sidequest.
The cryptic nature of the world carries over into some of its powerups. It probably sounds cool on paper to run through walls, but again, which walls? Generic Wall #31 probably isn't a very good landmark to use for hiding secrets. You also hack enemies to produce all sorts of funky effects, like them being able to suddenly break seemingly random tiles for no obvious reason. And why can I hack only one out of five different pools of similar-looking acid? These moments of discovery feel less like "Aha!" moments and more like, "Oh, OK. That just happened, I guess." moments. Its wildly infuriating to feel like the world is just stringing you around, rewarding dumb luck rather than intelligent observation.
If that wasn't enough, combat is by and large boring. Early enemies are often placed in very exploitable positions, whereas later on enemies get really "homing" happy. The bosses, on the other hand, tend to be massive rinse-and-repeat affairs where you can, quite literally, stand and/or jump in place while mashing the fire button. Their patterns are often dreadfully predictable, and combat seems to favor raw damage output over finesse by a long shot. Combat can definitely end up adding to the tedium of randomly running to and fro.
Ultimately, its feels frustrating to have this incredible world held at arms length by obtuse mechanics. I can't say I've played anything quite like Axiom Verge and a part of me wants to keep absorbing its eccentric wonders, but I've found myself losing patience with all the wild goose chasing. The game more or less sells out completely to the cryptic dimension of Metroidvanias, for better or for worse.

My review became a mini guide so here is the overview and I will post more details in the comments.
Good:
- Very deep 4X game mechanics (with a focus on battles)
- Great turn based battle system (focus on tactics and not luck)
- Good RPG elements regarding the hero/unit development
- Many different units to hire and fight (most or all of the enemy units can also be hired if you are lucky to get an offer)
- Polished graphics and menus
- Nice humor (you can either play a good or evil “god” and the evil options are really funny to read)
Mixed:
- Not many armies to control or cities to build up so micro management doesn’t get out of hand
- Hard to learn even harder to master
- Endless playtime (if you can stand it - might be good for players who rather want to play in doses instead of one huge map/battle)
Bad:
- Tedious game mechanics
- Monotonous game play (most of the time you spend doing the same over and over again until you finally see/find/unlock something new)
- Easy to get stuck in “dead ends” (as long as you haven’t learned how to avoid them or have the patience to wait (for lucky random events or gaining gold/experience over time) or reload/restart)
- Still some bugs (Happened once that an enemy unit was not removed from battlefield and I had to reload the fight)
So what to expect from the game?
I expected another Fallen Enchantress/Warlock - MotA clone but this game plays quite different. There are the same features in place but they are used in a different manner. Think of starting one of the mentioned games. Build/take over your first cities on an isolated island and form your armies, then, when you are ready to conquer the next island: you have to start over.
This is basically happening in Eador. You conquer a "shard" where you face 1-2 enemies (at the first shards) and as soon as you conquered it you lose (mostly) everything you had earned the last hours. The shards do work on a greater scale though. They unlock new buildings/units and give some mild benefits to the starting condition of the next shard. I also can only speak for the first shards because even though I played 16 hours I'm still on my second shard! (+ the good tutorial that took me 3 hours alone) According to the forums there are 80!! shards to conquer - go figure the playtime you need to beat the game. Though I have to say I always fought my battles and didn’t auto resolve them because I’m a control freak and don’t trust the AI so you can decrease playtime a lot by automated battles.
I also don't want to complain about a long playtime but the simple problem here is: motivation. I think it would have been much better to only have like 20 shards but instead increase the rewards you get for conquering each shard and thus give a better feeling of actual progress.
Which leads to the real problem here, because having an extrapolated playtime of 400 hours and making only small steps on your way from shard to shard don't has to be bad in general, but the real issue is: The start of each shard is tedious and often frustrating.
You start with you major city, the only one you can really build up (and if you lose it to an enemy it's game over). Even conquered enemy cities are just better "provinces".
So now you can start constructing buildings from different categories that either increase income, mood, get you access to certain military units, spells or items. You also have to hire a hero because there are no armies without heroes! So the heroes are the real stars of the game and they are significantly better than every other units you get (at least in early game). You can choose from 4 different classes: Warrior, Scout, Commander and Wizard.
The problem is: The hero alone is not able to win most of the fights even right at the start of the game. You need either supporting units, spells or items to make him capable of conquering the provinces around your city. More units sounds like a good idea but they cost money and upkeep and the AI tends to attack the weak units first so they most likely get killed fast. Also when you buy units you don't have much gold left to build up your city. So what happened to me in the first level was that I started with a warrior (because he was great in the tutorial), build up the city and tried to conquer the provinces around me.
When you attack you get a nice text that estimates the outcome of the battle. It also tells you how many units you spotted and which kind of units they are. It is still a little vague because when you spot 8 units of militia and bowmen it makes a great difference if there are 1 or 6 bowmen and you won't know that. So despite the text I at least started every fight and would have lost all of them (tried - failed - reloaded). So my only chance to finally progress in the game would have been to use another (great but overused) feature: Exploring.
Every province (or tile) has a level of exploration. You can send your heroes to explore the tile which will give them experience (very important, but very slow), lets them find locations (most of the time fights that are often too hard to win but bring very important loot and gold/ you can also find shops with special items or units to hire) and expands the province for the population (lowers effects of overpopulation).
So back to my problem: It would have taken ages until I got strong enough to finally start conquering the provinces so I restarted the shard and chose the scout hero. The reason is that ranged combat is a little overpower and the scout alone can win some battles as long as the enemy doesn’t have too many ranged units himself or too strong and fast melee units. I guess you can also use the wizard for that matter (not tried yet) but if you go for a melee character I suggest to invest in spell granting buildings (especially magic missile) so that he can deal some harm from a distance.
So with the scout I was finally able to gain some ground and get the game going. Eventually I was able to hire a second hero (which makes sense because just 1 army to cover ~30 tiles is difficult, especially when the enemy starts attacking).
Which leads to 2 more problems:
First, when you hire a new hero midgame he is starting at level 1. You might have some items and spells available to give him or perhaps even can give him the supporting units from your experienced hero (but then this hero is significantly weaker) but all the easy fights are already done by your experienced hero so there is no (comfortable) way to level him up and make him actually useful. You can only explore and trial and error random fights.
Second: The enemy is really annoying. He often has several heroes (more than you have) and can take every province by just moving on that tile as long as you didn't buy any guards there. The point is that those guards cost money and all they bring is defend the province against a possible hero attack (later on you get access to better units that have more benefits like auto exploring the province or even increasing the income of that province (still less than their upkeep though)). So when you start taking provinces you don’t want to spend your money on hiring guards but rather want to wait until you have an actual frontline. But when you finally have one it usually consists of 4-5 tiles per enemy.

Portal is a game that I heard about for the first time from the famous Valve's Orange Box. Apart from that I never knew what the game was about, until the day that I could finally try it came. It blew my mind. Let's see why.
I believe that this is one of the best points of the game. The subtlety and brilliance narrative is something that I personally loved. GLaDOS is the only character in the game but yet she alone manages to keep the player hooked with her great personality and humor. At the same time, we can observe the scenarios and speculate about the story that took place before the player took control of Chell.
The gameplay is also one of the main points of Portal. As the name implies, portals are the core mechanics of the game and we will use them to overcome multiple puzzles and progress the story. Since the game used Half-Life 2 as base for its development, the mechanics and physics are quite polished.
There isn't much progress since Half-Life 2 in technical terms but the artistic style is minimalist but iconic. I think the game in general looks good but didn't make any kind of jump or impact like Half-Life 2 or its episodes did, it just only borrows elements of these.
The music doesn't have much resemblance to its sequel but I still think it's excellent. It's different since it has a more atmospheric and peaceful approach, one really feels alone within the walls of Aperture Science. As for the sound effects, there are quite a few that are recycled from Half-Life 2 so there's not much I can say about it. They're OK. But what I must say is that the voice actress of GLaDOS, Ellen McLain, did an excellent job. She definitely made GLaDOS a charismatic character.
In conclusion, I think that being the beginning of a famous franchise like this should be played with no doubt, even if it differs a little from what comes next. It may have some unpolished points here and there but in general it's a very solid and entertaining game, a must for the fans of the Half-Life / Portal saga.

Not sure if it's worth the full price, but if you're really into platformers this is a fun little diversion.
PROS:
* Mechanically sound, controls are fluid, at least with an XB controller. Haven't and don't intend to try with KB/M. Hitboxes are solid, almost everything is made obvious to the player, it functions as advertised. Mostly. Some of the jump physics are a little weird, but usually more in your favor than against.
* Joyfully nostalgic platforming. In many ways, I'm reminded of Jazz Jackrabbit, and if I didn't know any better, this game is paying some homage to it. The floaty jumping mechanics, aiming, variety of weapons, goofy humor, and the protagonist (anti-hero?) is, well, also a rabbit.
* Weaves quick time events and platforming pretty seamlessly (though some of the animations could use to be shorter). The animations for beating said events are over-the-top and fun to watch, but mostly only for the first time.
NEUTRAL:
* Deaths are very forgiving. This is kinda cool since you'll likely Sonic-the-Hedgehog-style your way into some traps getting caught up in the action. Fortunately, the game gives you a neat function to zoom out (and simultaneously pause) with the right bumper on the controller, dunno what it is for KB/M, but it's a nice feature to let you formulate your next move.
* No variety in difficulty. It doesn't really need it though I guess, the difficulty is pretty balanced.
* Fourth-wall-breaking, light-hearted and occasionally raunchy humor. It mostly falls flat to me, but that's subjective so I can't knock it. It's like Disgaea level humor, if it were just one-liners and no voice acting.
CONS:
* As a result of the first two neutral points above, replay value is practically non-existent.
* So much happening on screen that we see two issues: first, it's often difficult to tell what's an enemy, a trap, or a piece of the foreground/background, unless you're frequently stopping to take in the scenery. Second, there are framerate stutters, but they're infrequent and don't really hinder gameplay *too* much unless you're making a precision jump at the time.
To conclude, might be worth picking up on sale for platforming nostalgia. It's not bad, but I don't think it's justified at full price.

Of Kings and Men is an interesting game, with decent combat mechanics reminiscent of Mount and Blade and honed to a more refined form of parry-and-swing fighting. Is it perfect? No. Is it bad? Not at all, as a matter of fact, the game so far has proven to be very promising, but I mean that in the most positive way possible.
I think the twelve dollars I payed for the game was worth it, I even think that twenty five may be worth it at it's original price, but during this sale I do think that the game is a good buy. There is a learning curve, but if you played a lot of multiplayer M&B you already have a lot of the muscle memory required.
The bad parts of the game is the current low population and the UIs and menus being clunky and unappealing. I believe that with a bit of spitshine and after a few more promotional boosts, this game can return to the population required to play the game to the fullest. (it was once 1.2k~ peak, and now a 70~ people peak)
However, unless things have changed by the time you read this, do not expect massive and epic battles right now, because 70 people spread across different regional servers will not be netting you more than 4v4s or 6v6s at the moment. With the current sale, though, I'm hoping that by the end of this week we'll find that the game has a decent population again.

I'd been flying for the better part of an hour over endless, shimmering blue waves before they came into sight. At first I thought it might be just a trick of my brain, as I had been straining my eyes toward the horizon for a long time. But no, it's not my imagination, there are the faintest shadows against the sky in the hazy blue distance. First just a few, then more, and as I fly closer they elongate and begin to take shape. A squadron of heavy bombers, at least 20 of them by looks of it, and they are on their way to drop a hundred thousand pounds of high explosives on our airbase. Well, not if I have anything to say about it.
I pull back on the stick, climbing above the scatted, puffy-white stratus clouds and putting the incoming bombers a few thousand feet further below me. I let them come sliding underneath, and then I roll left and dive. The Gs push me back into my seat and I feel the blood rush from my head but I modulate my dive to avoid losing consciousness. In what feels like a matter of a few heartbeats I drop out of the clouds behind the squadron and get the tail-most bomber in my sights. The tailgunner has seen me and he opens fire, but its too late. A short burst from my cannons sets their right engine on fire. Another burst and the wing snaps like a twig in a gale, the bomber pitches sharply up and then topples over to the left. Thus begins their death spiral down into the sea below, a trail of black smoke highlighting the bomber's final path. I see a few white parachutes open along that trail of smoke but the helpless bomber crew no longer interest me. I'm getting near enough to the next bomber that their gunners start to open up, and white phosphorous tracer rounds are streaking past my cockpit glass. Cool, calm, collected... I feel the exhilaration of the kill but I ride the adrenaline smoothly. My hand rests lightly on the stick, my feet adjust the rudder ever-so-gently, and the swaying of the plane around me is like an extension of my arms and legs. The second bomber's left engine is in my sights and I squeeze the trigger....
10/10 Would stalk enemy bombers again.

Axiom Verge does the Metroid formula perfectly, allowing you to explore the world at your discretion and exploring ever further into a surrealistic alien world of isolation.
With an immersive soundtrack, beautiful visuals, and fresh ideas on old concepts, Axiom Verge will present challenge and interest to anyone who enjoys exploration-based gameplay as they solve the mystery of just what happened to Trace, the talkative protagonist we know little about out the gate.
The moments in which you're given to get to know the characters are given just enough time to learn small pieces of information about the world and just who Trace is.
I'd describe the art direction of Axiom Verge "NES Metroid if its tilesets didn't suck," but it's more like somewhere between Cave Story and NES Metroid. The games assets are generally beautiful but the lack of clarity of depth can be seldomly problematic.
All in all, I'd say this game is a must-have for any Metroid or late Castlevania fan on any system they can access it on. This game is a beautiful and fresh take on that game's formula.

It's worth every award it's ever been given. A superb entry in the metroidvania genre with most of its cues being taken from the first half of that tag. It pays its due respects to the 2D Metroid games of old while having its own identity with grotesque cyborgs, glitch-centric gameplay, and giant lady heads.
The pixel art and soundtrack both speak for themselves. The weapons have pleanty of variety to keep things fun. Enemies are well executed, and bosses keep getting tougher as the game goes on. You may have to experiment to see what works and what doesn't on certain enemies; but the game never punishes you for trial and error.
Don't feel shy about consulting a walkthrough if you get lost. Because this map is HUGE, with countless nooks and crannies full of secrets and upgrades. My only greivence is that there are bonus levels in the game which only appear randomly with each playthrough; meaning you could play this game 5 times over and still not experience everything. Seems like a needless restriction.
Aside from that, this game is a joy to play from start to finish. The fact that 1 guy made this game is incredible. If you're a Metroid fan who feels like they've been cheated by Nintendo for too long and you haven't played this game yet, pick it up. If you're cheap like I am, you can get this game half-off during sales.

Gawd, I've never "turned" on a game this quickly.
I played and enjoyed Eador Genesis. So when this came out I was excited. It's essentially the same game with much prettier graphics. It look great, the interface is better and I enjoyed it for a while. I really give them props on some of the art - it's some of the best out there. The quests can be fun and there's a great balance between enhancing your own territories and going after new ones. Then two problems hit me:
1. It's repetitive. Very repetitive. You start on a shard, build up, conquer the enemy and start all over again from scratch on a different shard. Rinse and repeat. That's not very compelling gameplay. They would have done much better with a faster paced, more open gameplay style.
I could forgive that. After all, it's okay for a while. What I can't forgive is flaw #2.
2. This "strategy" game is nothing of the sort for one reason - the AI cheats and will give it's side resources that are comparable to yours even if you should vastly outproduce them. So the whole game becomes an illusion because you aren't really "playing" the other side, you're playing against a bunch of foes that are generated directly in response to your own force. If you found a way to find a million gold in the game, rest assured the AI would have similar resources the next turn even if they were down to one or two territories left. As a result, the game is fundamentally broken in a way that will never be fixed. It's not a strategy game at that point because the AI doesn't need to play with any strategy.
I figured this out when I saw the AI pushing units it could not possibly create with only one city left. After some exploration and some help unravling the back end, we found that's the way it works. So there is no real "AI". It's like playing Civilization if the AI could just give itself cities and armies out of thin air every turn.
That ruined the game for me. Oh, it still has bugs and the gameplay is also still repetitive. But it's knowing how badly the AI can cheat that was the deal killer. It's lazy and insulting to the players. As such, Eador sadly gets two thumbs down from me.

So...I'm not the kind of person that is particularly fond of multiplayer games. Not only am I not a particularly competetive person, but I also sometimes find it frustrating how in some games, the progression system doesn't allow you to rank up while fighting agianst bots or whatnot.
However, BRINK allows me to still play the game despite me being all by my lonesome, and even better, allows me to rank up and get better gear. Granted, that's not the ONLY reason I like the game, but it was a pretty big selling point for me.
Anyway, I also like the gunplay, the variety in guns and attachments, how bots can be pretty tricky if you're not prepared, and the variety of 'Scenarios' you can play through in each map. This game is genuinely fun, whether you're playing with others or not.
One greivance I did have at first was the Challenges, however. Due to the tricky AI I mentioned earlier, the first mission 'Be Objective' was absolute hell. The first run wasn't...too bad, but the second run had me dying left and right and retrying a few more times than I'd like to admit. I got through it eventually, but I thought I'd give a heads up since the challenges award new gun parts. Otherwise, the rest of the challenges are much less frustrating, but can still put up a fight.
Overall, I like this game. I wouldn't see too many people besides myself playing it for more than 3-4 hours, but I'd say it's worth a shot. It is free now, after all :P

If you are new to Guacamelee! in general, look further down for a general review. Following is a comparison of versions.
When I first saw this, I thought it was a moneygrab. It is absolutely not. The Super Turbo Championchip Edition improves so much on Gold Edition that they are almost incomperable. The most notable additions are:
- The chicken bomb
- Rebalancing of the enemies in just about every area and stat rebalancing of enemies
- The fighting system got rebuffed and everything feels much, much smoother
- A new 'super' type mode you can initiate after doing lots of combos
- New story additions and a new boss
All in all, the game feels much fuller.
Now for a general review of Guacamelee!
Guacamelee! is a metroidvania that really knows how to mix its genres. While the basic mechanics of platforming and fighting are both there, the fighting has a good amount of depth to it without becoming overly complex. After playing for a while, combos seemlessly stream out into an arena of destruction... and it feels really good. In Guacamelee! I can punch and upper cut an enemy into the air, headbut them, body slam them, and then grab them to suplex them into the ground to knock other enemies off balance only to start another combo. And it doesn't require dozens of hours to learn. On top of the fighting system, there are many, many upgrades to find and buy. Search a large world for upgrades, find the good ending, complete some challenges, unlock some sweet costumes, turn into a chicken! Okay, that last one was a little different than the rest, but you get the idea.
TL;DR
Guacamelee! STCE is the best edition. The game is a metroidvania with more depth to fighting. Lots of upgrades. Chickens. Worth every penny.

Sidescrolling beat 'em up/platformer with Metroid style exploration. The game has a unique Mexican theme, with you playing as a Luchador Mexican wrestler dude, on a mission to rescue 'El Presidentes' daughter from skeletons, a guy with his head permenantly on fire and several other bad guys. The game doesn't take itself seriously and has a pretty funny story and set of characters.
The combat and exploration of this game is where it really shines though. If you know 2D Metroid or Castlevania, and even Dark Souls to an extent (with the shortcuts and linking world), its just like that in its exploration and level design. The combat is awesome, you can chain different style of attacks and throws together and its a lot of fun making huge combos, which happens often as the game regularly throws tonnes of enemies at you. I was really surprised how much I enjoyed the combat.
The game also has a really good looking and clean unique art style, that thankfully steps away from the common "pixelate everything" art style most indie games use. Animation is also pretty nice and feels responsive as ♥♥♥♥.
Overall I definitely recommend!

I just finished this game on co-op and I gotta say it's some of the most fun I've had in a long time. It took us about 7 hours to beat even with the two of us. You pretty much play as a super-hero luchador in a beat-em-up style game trying to save your princess. There is tons of secrets, in which you don't unlock the 'true ending' unless you find them all. You can also unlock different costumes which gives you different benefits and you can upgrade your skills. I played most of the game with the Diablo suit which kind of made it like hard mode even on easy.
I gotta say this game really did remind me of the old-school games and some of the music even sounded alot like Mario and other games. Enemies were decently hard to beat without being too difficult, but keep in mind I did have another player helping me. Storyline is decent and there is tons of humor in the game also. It's kinda like they took everything people love about indie games and put it into this game.
Co-op design is fairly decent but the camera kinda sucks as it will only follow player one instead of expanding. Every time you die you have a timer to wait to come back and when you do you're a little orb that floats around until your teammate releases you. I felt this made the co-op fair without being too much struggle. Pretty much a fun co-op experience that adds mild difficulty to great teamwork gameplay. Coordinating certain platforming can be incredibly hectic though and we usually just let one person do all the platforming at the hard parts because it was too hard with two people to do.
Co-op is also somewhat buggy... I have a screenshot where instead of dying, me and my buddy just have 3 copies of ourselves each...
I will probably replay the hell out of this game until I unlock all of the achievements. I can't really say too much bad about the game in all honestly so I would have to give the game somewhere around a 4.5/5.

HELL YES. I absolutely love this game. It really was just so much fun to play. The style, the music, the puzzles, the combat, I dig it. So much.
So Guacamelee is an action platformer. The level designs are really cool, in the smart platform design sense and in the 'aw yeah this place looks bangin' sense. The levels weren't exactly hard (I don't know if this or just the combat changes in hard mode though), but mixed with the combat, it was fast-paced, kept you on your toes, utilized all your powers, and generally makes you feel awesome while playing.
But aside from the actual platforming aspect, I think the combat is where it's at. I don't know much about pro-wrestlers, but I sure as hell felt like one. Every so often, you get a new power, and you incorporate those new powers into progressing through the levels and for creating some new killer combos. When you get all the new powers, you pretty much feel like a god. At least I felt that way. Was nice. Very nice. Punch enemy into air, follow them, 1-2-3 combo, slap them back down, follow with a body slam, pick them back up, throw them to the left, roll to the left, HEAD BASH THEM INTO OBLIVION. Yes I love the combat and one day I hope to become the master of all the Guacamelee combos and to make the Combo Chicken proud of me.
Simply put, the music is amazing. I actually found myself shaking my body to the music while practicing my pro-wrestling ways. I don't know how to really describe it, but the music really added that extra 'unf'. Especially the boss theme. I totally would have welcome any 3rd/4th/5th boss phases if it meant I could listen to this music and kick♥♥♥♥♥at the same time.
When I look at the graphics, the word that comes to mind is charming. Also beautiful and simple. And crisp for some reason. I think besides that, I'm just becoming a fan of this style of art, something that I also see in works like The Book of Life (movie) and Grim Fandango.
Not much else to say other than this game was just as much a pleasure to look at as it was to fulfill my unknown pro-wrestler dreams.
So yeah. Sweet game. I look forward to starting hard mode (re-re-replayability !!!) one of these days when my backlog isn't clawing at me.
Guacamelee doesn't take itself too seriously which allows for some really funny moments. Also, references. References everywhere. All in all, I had a blast playing it and -looks straight into the camera with a generic smile and gives a thumbs up- you will too! Did I mention you can transform into a chicken at will.

I started playing this game Febuary of this year (2017) and as of posting this review I have nearly 700 hours in the game. What enticed me to this game is the Millenium Dawn mod (As of this review my opinion on that mod has changed.) But even besides that mod the modding community is absolutely amazing. The mechanics and UI are challenging to learn at first but after a while will know them like the back of your hand. Even though playing as Germany or the US at first is aw great idea to get the bearings of the game, but playing as a minor such as the Peoples Republic Of China or Bulgaria, Yugoslavia (Especially with the Death Or Dishonor DLC) is great fun, Especially with mods such as The Road To 56 which gives these countries focus trees. The game is challenging, Not as challenging as say Europa Universalis 4 but it is much much more intuitive and the mechanics and al the moving parts work better than said games. That being said I have some gripes about Paradoxes DLC policy, but I will leave seperate reviews on the DLCs for that matter. This is an excellent grand strategy game and Paradox have been regularly been updating the game, With an update coming out early next year on the horizon. I wholeheartedly recommend to anyone looking for a new experience and maybe coming from Civilization or another Paradox game. Although the 40$ price tag is high for what it offers right now, Pick it up on the Christmas sale or another sale.

Thanks, SEGA.

In the spirit of joining my fellow SEGA Nerds teammates, I decided to join the Annual SEGA Horror Fest with a review. While I may not be the most appropriate person to talk about Halloween, since we don’t celebrate it in my country, I tried to choose a title that’s more related to our “Día de los Muertos” (Day of the Dead), our national holiday that embraces our joy for life, the cult and nostalgia for our departed ones and also… to poke fun at death.
Precisely, that’s what Arkedo’s Hell Yeah! Wrath of the Dead Rabbit does, poke fun at death, hell, and some other spooky things on the way. While French developers, Arkedo, might be long gone as a studio after a financial bankruptcy (should I dedicate a Mexican Día de los Muertos “Ofrenda” perhaps?), they certainly made games that were appreciated in a special way by some people (like Nervous Brickdown or Big Bang Mini for the Ninty DS).
A RESURRECTION FOR A PLATFORMER?
For a start Hell Yeah! is a platformer, a genre that many thought dead but that’s been slowly coming back thanks to the necromancy of retro gaming. You control Ash, hell’s current underworld ruler, who is trying to hunt down some of his minions that are threatening him with releasing compromising photos to the public. As fun and weird as the plot sounds this translates into comedic and bizarre interruptions or mini games that appear as you progress though mazes in the underground, perhaps this is a double edge sword, cause while some of us SEGA fans might fall into the gag and follow by, some others might get desperate trying to know what’s going on, because the game is not very intuitive in explaining these “on the go” mechanics. For example, some bosses require to aim and shoot as a mini game, but some people might not get how to do it, cause the game does not do a very good job on explaining so or that it is part of a gag.
For most, the game has a lot of fun to offer, but also requires to master some skill, since the controls require you to switch between sticks to aim for certain parts or to zoom out the screen to aim and hit some enemies.
SOMETHING FOR THE SEGA FANS
The game has a lot of fanservice for the average SEGA fans. As you progress in the game you unlock SEGA Character themed add-ons like JSR or Shinobi hats or items, you can also equip your attacking wheel with more weapons or features. There are also other fun hubs like your own island were you send your defeated enemies and punish them as it must due!
A KILLER OST AND VISUALS TO DIE FOR
There are 2 things that outstand in this game, its vector based visuals & character designs and its amazing OST. The vector artwork shines so well in this game and allows you to enjoy the aesthetics no matter the resolution, specially in PC, Arkedo did a great job. The OST is something to enjoy on its own, even if you don’t buy the game you can still download this awesome score, it has something for almost everyone, from lullabies to hardcore punk, and every tune fits perfectly in the game.
SUMMARY
This game is fun and enjoyable, but might not be appropriate for the narrow minded player. While its true that pretty visuals and a good OST are not all in a game, the title lacks of some areas to be polished like a more polished gameplay and controls.
Pros:
+ Amazing visuals and OST
+ Fanservice for the SEGA fans
+ Fun times and fart-type jokes
Cons:
– Not for everyone
– Requires control skill
– Lacks of explanation for some mechanics

I received this game as apart of some bundle awhile ago and just started playing it because the trailers looked promising.
However, I quickly found that this wasn't the case at all.  This game is devoid of any meaningful/humorous dialogue, and is instead full of overly-done, excessive WarioWare-esqe "minigames" one has to do after killing each of the 100 or so minibosses.  The platforming isn't anything special and actually comes with issues (no invulnerability frames after getting hit, meaning you can get "stuck" and knocked into an unfavorable death if you hit one enemy and get pushed into a corner/another enemy.
The dialogue tries to be too witty and breaks the fourth wall too often, making it rather painful to go through.  The game as a whole feels too "edgy" and the unique aesthetic/"appeal" of the game gets old fast, due to the game shoving excessive blood and gore down your throat in order to progress.  Hell Yeah! also tries to be a simplistic Metroidvania game, but fails to do so.  You're left walking around a map, just going from one end to the other killing minibosses in order to progress to the next world to do... exactly the same thing again.
This game looked really promising, but the gameplay doesn't change much from when you first start the game.  Good concept that unfortunately was not executed nearly as well as it could have been, but rather turned into a repetitive, simplistic platformer made challenging only by the location of save spots and hitboxes/environmental limitations.

Hell Yeah! is a holy mess. There's good ideas, but their burried in clunky controls and hit detection, repetitiveness, and overall a feeling of "too much". Too much redundent weapons, too much forced bargin bin mini games, too much juvenile humor, too much unskippable cutscenes and shoddy dialogue, too much color and objects bursting on the screen at all times making it hard to see. Despite all this, the pace is unbearably slow.
The execution lets down any potential the game really had. There's a separate side game called The Island, where you have defeated enemies work for you for cash, health, or items, but the rewards are minor and uninteresting, and the system itself is a boring distraction.
Hell Yeah! shoots for the stars and misses all 1,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000 of them.

While I haven't finished the current content quite yet, what's there so far is quite promising. I've been a danmaku shmup enthusiast for ages and, while I usually tend to prefer having a tiny hitbox, no shields, and one-hit death, the way this game integrates the shields, health, and movement speed into passive mechanics you can choose between is definitely intriguing, especially when paired with the ability to combine a wide variety of shot types.
The pacing could use some work, with the difficulty being very slow to ramp up (especially for someone already comfortable navigating through curtains of bullets) and with some of the levels feeling like they drag on for a bit longer than is welcome. Because the pacing is already being worked on, though, it's very likely this will be ironed out before its final release. There doesn't appear to be any storytelling to speak of in the game, which made it challenging for me to stay engaged, but there is the potential that later on, the gameplay will be enough of a challenge to entertain me all on ts own.
For a game so recently on the Early Access stage, it shows a great deal of promise.

Let me start off by saying that I've been playing all types of strategy games for nearly 25 years.
This game has potential.  I found myself trying to figure out how to reach the higher level content once I managed to level my hero up.  Many of the quests were extremely hard at the beginning stages of the game and added to the frustration of leveling up.  Basic units are no match to even the most beginning level "monsters".
The economy is unbalanced.   Unit maintenance is very high in relation to the amount of coin that you bring in from provinces.  Building costs are low which allows for quick building.   This will allow you to access units for purchase fairly quickly.  However, it doesn't seem to matter that much because there is a logistical issue with your hero only being able to hold 4 troop types at lower levels.  Even after leveling up to level 4, a hero still can only hold 4 troop types.  It is very difficult to level your units and keep your favorite units around.  Combat is unbalanced.
I'm not sure if it's a bug, but my garrison was transferred to another province when an uprising occured in that province.  I would expect the garrison to stand and fight.
The loot part of the game was very cool at first.  But there's no originality to the items.  Many of them are common low level items that don't help out too much.  Most of the game is loot based with low drop rates.
There are several bugs that cause the game to freeze/crash in the middle of the game.  This is not a huge issue though considering the game saves every 2 seconds.
If this game got some balance tweeks, item updates, bug fixes it would be a much more fun game to play.  It feels like the developers wanted to portray the look and feel of a 4x strategy game with all of the bells and whistles , but forgot the underlying basic game mechanics.

It's hard to play a game over 100 hours and then not recommend it.  And yet, I can't.  I wan't to - but I can't.

Specifically, the size of the 'shards' and the mechanics of the shards hurt the overall game.  Because of this, you won't even use most of the best units/buildings/etc.  In essence, you've got all this outstanding content that never comes into play bacause of the mechanics of the 'meta-game'.

Highly recommend to all fans of fantasy, strategy, and tactics games. Plenty of unique units and buildings, heroes and units gain levels and you can customize their growth, explore the terrain to find new locations and upgrades, manage resources, and increase your own power by conquering other worlds/shards. The campaign does a good job of introducing you to more intricate tactics and developments as you progress. One downside is that with each new shard/map you start over somewhat, but things still manage to stay interesting through new units and buildings, new opponents, and randomized events.

Axiom Verge delivers everything I expected and wanted from it.  This game looks and plays like the spiritual successor of Super Metroid, which is probably the primary selling point for at least half of the people buying it.  As video graphic technology accelerated, the 2D platformer style that was the bedrock of early console games has mostly been abandoned.  That makes new titles for fans of that style always welcome, as long as they're well executed.
If you have played the early Metroid games, then this game will feel incredibly familiar, like a homebrew bootleg port.  I say that in a good way.  The bubble blocks, lava pits, save nodes and doorway portals are all here, scattered around an unforgiving planet inhabited by insects, robots, biomechanical ghouls and vampiric monsters resembling creatures from the watery abyss.  The map is a complex labyrinth of pitfalls and hidden chambers and the soundtrack adeptly reflects the haunting atmosphere of the game.  This game knows exactly what it's trying to emulate and hits the mark perfectly.
Fortunately, Axiom Verge comes with enough unique twists on its mentor to deliver a fresh experience.  The full arsenal of weaponry is far more extensive and diverse than Metroid, triple the amount of various beam weapons that you might expect.  This provides a variety of options to eliminate your foes and I found most of them to be useful throughout all portions of the game.  Also, rather than using a "Morph Ball" to find and access smaller tunnels, this game provides you with a tiny drone to navigate those areas instead.  Like Metroid, you'll find various tools, such as a grappling hook, to traverse the rooms.  You'll also find powerups for your weapons and your drone that will eventually allow you to access areas you couldn't before, although the manner in which you eventually reach those areas is slightly different than it would be in Metroid.  The most unique tool is the Address Disruptor, which allows you to 'glitch' the enemies and environment.  This allows you to materialize hidden blocks or morph enemies into a different form with different behavior patterns.  Lastly, there are five separate entrances to 'secret worlds' that are randomly generated in different locations for each game, allowing you to gain additional powerups and secret weapons, if you can find them.  This makes the game slightly different each time you play it.
This game easily makes it onto my top five list of favorite platformers.  Aside from a few frustrating learning moments with the controls for some of the tools and one level with a very obnoxious music theme that sounds like a singing robot (Lower Kur), I loved everything about it.

For a cheap game Paradise Island isn't all that bad. There are much worse games out there for a similar price, but also much better games as well. Paradise Island follows the story of the ghost of someone trapped on the island. In order to escape they must collect 70 apples and 70 shells, like some tedious Easter egg hunt. To be honest the being a ghost part is probably not true. It's just the fact that you can pass through most of the terrain, including trees, some walls and most ladders. Not to mention all of the wildlife seems to ignore you.
Graphically the game is fairly beautiful. Golden sandy beaches, clear turquoise seas and lush green trees and plants. There are several landmarks dotted around the island too. Including a large Buddha statue, a small lighthouse and a few other places to note. Travelling from landmark to landmark can be fairly exciting and gives the game something of interest to aim for. But after a while you lose interest. The island, for the most part, looks very samey in places. The same rock formations dot opposite ends of the coast, along with several small boats washed up on the shore. Pointless books sit scattered around the island on pedestals talking about some pointless nonsense that, to be quite honest, no one really cares about.
For the most part Paradise is an interesting, if not short lived, walking sim. While collecting the shells and apples dotted around can be fairly exciting, it does get boring very quickly. To be honest, if you want a decent walking sim with a generous amount of freedom, then I'd go for something else. The vanishing of Ethan Carter is a fairly good example, or if you want a game set on island as well, then Salt is a better option.
With a cheap price tag, Paradise Island is worth a go, even for a few minutes, but if you want something that lasts longer, and is more enjoyable I suggest looking elsewhere. Good Day!

I've been asking, hoping, praying, pleading, begging, and moaning for this game to get remade for for a decade. Now that it's here, it's like having an old family member in the house. DO YOU LIKE BLOOD, VIOLENCE, CARNAGE, STUPID HUMOR AND... TACTICS?!!
I know, one of the things I listed is not like the others. But that is the best way to describe
. You have your violence and humor taken from Blood Bowl and then you have your real-time gameplay from the NFL. The game functions similarily to those NFL games made by other companies which is rather odd considering Mutant Football League is a game with a wacky setting. This was a surprise to me. A pleasant one after a while but at first I got a little desperate over the gameplay.
I'll start with the ugly. The tutorial in the game is rather heplful but presented in a weird way. This was one of the main reasons why it was quite hard for me to get into the game and actually review it. I started playing the game in the Practice matches which are freely customizable matches with to Achievement progress awarded. I was absolutely confused by what the controls were and did not understand why the Tutorial tips weren't showing up even though I had them on. Well, I try the buttons and finally managed to get a simple hang of the game. Then I tried the official mods which aren't Practice mathces anymore and there I could access the Tutorial tips. This was rather odd that the developers thought people would go and play the normal game modes straight away and never though that some people might start from the Practice mode. Not a big problem for most part but for me it really was going to affect my review if I wouldn't have just went on and played the game.
Now that we have that under the way I can actually talk about the game. As I said earlier the closest thing that comes to my mind is just your basic NFL game combined with interesting elements. There are different kind of
that are out of place from your usual NFL game and will usually give you different kind of advantages, like bribing the referee or gaining a shotgun or just simply using a not-so-legal passing method. They might now always work as the referee may not like them. And the Dirty Tricks are the absolute best thing the game has to offer. It really spices up the gameplay.
Even though you have the Dirty Tricks system in place you still need to rely on the actual football tactics. This might not be the most desirable design choice for everyone as this game seems like a arcade game rather than actual football game. The game is well executed though. It is not bad but just a bit confusing considering the setting and the art style.
Mutant Football League is a great game and I really do think it is fun to play. You'll just need to get the hand of the controls because all the controls are vital. Definetly a great game for American football fans and definetly worth checking out even as a game.

Im not big into writing reviews, so ill get to the point on the subject of "Of Kings And Men".
when i got the game about a week or two when it first launched its Early Access  i had tons of fun with the combat system as it fed my hunger for a more indepth medieval combat multiplayer game.
The State Of The Game-
The game is completely playable even at the launch of the game but it was still clear the game will require more work before you could even call it a done deal. The Combat seems to work as it was intended with archery needing some work with the aiming, but still works. (current aiming system has quite the learning curve, with tracking the arrow/bolts being difficult.)
As of now the game has quite the weapon selection, ranging form several Arming swords, hand and a half swords, two handed swords, Axes, blunt/maces, Polearms, pikes/spears, bows, and crossbows alongside a selection of shields that will continue to grow.
with the game taking place in a medieval time period we of course have a selection of different armor and parts that complete the medieval soldier and also ever expanding.
Being a Media artist and Animator myself, I take more interest in the Aesthetic part of the development since I have a far more of an Understanding in the matter.
The Animations still need alot of work as there are many secondary animations for the players character that are missing that makes the character seem less organic for Ex. The Movement is missing alot of secondary action that takes place while bearing arms like swords and bows that will have a negative impact on personality if not addressed, but i have seen some changes to animations that have improved on that issue quite a bit.
with the Aesthetic part of development taking more focus later after the core parts of the game is closer to finished. content for the game comes out as fast as possible. since the game is still pretty early in development most of the focus is on the more complicated side of the games development it will seem a bit slow. The developers do have a test server that the Early access community partakes in active testing for new implementations for game modes, game mechanics, new weapons, armor, character customization, and maps.
Now we all know what comes with purchacing an Early Access and i feel some people forget that the warning that comes with an Early Access shouldn't be taken lightly. Most of us hate waiting and i understand that, but proper development of a game takes time as many trial and error will be in the path from beginning and even after the end.
In conclusion, i do recommend the game to people who wish the help the developers financially support the development of this game, as the world we live in, money is unfotunatly important for funding projects especially projects as expensive as game design. I hope this review helps with seeing the game in a perspective that Early Access Projects should be looked at, and as many people of the OKAM community including myself hope to see this game flourish as the game starts to take its true form. I bid the Developers fair winds and calm seas in their Journey through the road map ahead and don't give up.

Type of recommendation:  If you love the turn based HoMaM games or possibly King's Bounty but want something more complex, you may enjoy this game. I played this game years ago, when it first came out, and had very fond memories of it.
Seeing this finally in F2P gave me a stiffy, as I'm finally able to enjoy it again online with friends.
ABOUT THE GAME:
It's fast paced, it's fun.
The guns are enjoyable to use, and pretty well balanced overall. Some guns are considered best-in-class, but you can be very successful using everything else as long as it fits into your playstyle.
The customisation options are simple and easy, and allow for small modifications to personnalise each gun to your playstyle.
The playable classes are basic, but each class played to its strength can be deadly. Medic, Soldier and Engineer synergize well in a 3-man fireteam.
Operative is a bit more solo-oriented, as you'll often be roaming around on your own, hacking stuff and abusing your ennemies' back sides thanks to your disguise ability.
Character customisation is mostly cosmetic, appart from the Body Type which will affect the way you can move around the map :
- A light body will allow you to climb, wall-jump and go everywhere quickly, but you're limited to snipers, SMGs and sidearms.
- Medium is pretty much the same mobility-wize, but you won't be able to wall-jump, and as a result you can't reach some places. You can use every weapon but the biggest ones.
- Heavy is closer to the usual FPS gameplay, as your character is the slowest and heaviest, and can't climb for cheets, but can carry the biggest guns as a trade-off.
Mix and match body type, class and guns to find the best combinations.
I personnaly play a light body Medic/Operative, and a heavy body Soldier/Engineer.
The art-style is very well done in my opinion, and the game didn't age too badly as a result.
The character faces and guns are top-notch.
I whole-heartedly recommend this game, that I personnaly consider a little gem.
Give it a try it's free, and currently populated. Fingers crossed, it will stay active for a while!

I'll keep this short (I'll try to anyway).  The game has a fun premise.  You build a boat out of various blocks and objects, then sail around a map full of nodes laid out like a sheet of graph paper, attacking other boats, recruiting crew, taking on bounties, and pillaging islands, all while the game gets increasingly difficult (and also drops better loot) the further outward you move from the center.  Between the semi-random events, RPG leveling and character customizing, tons of weapons, and even boss fights, you have plenty to keep you busy.  I quite enjoyed the game part of the time.
However..  the game is bug ridden, has some questionable gameplay, and some of the GUI stuff is pretty terrible.  A couple examples, if a crew member gets pushed to the edge of a ship or island but doesn't quite fall off into the water, the game thinks he's falling and disables them.  Enemies even ignore them, so that crew member is effectively now a statue and unable to fight or even get back to your boat.  Another example, if you happen to attack an enemy crew member that's carrying a bomb to one of his cannons (or blow up their cannon or the route to it), he will abandon loading the cannon but continue to carry the bomb, which can cause them to board your ship with said bomb.  Upon killing him, he drops it and it detonates in your ship, killing or nearly killing everything in the area (including your crew that was trying to fight him).  If more than 1 enemy do this at once, then on top of killing your crew and animals near the blast, they also blow a giant hole in your boat in the chain reaction, and there's not much you can do about it other than not using cannons yourself and not retreating if you board the enemy and shoot their gunners.
Bugs/mechanics aside, the GUI's themselves punish you.  If you collect too many weapons, it becomes really difficult to look through them and see what you want to equip, because you can't use your scroll wheel and can't sort the items (or I was unable to figure out how to in 40 hours of gameplay).  Attempting to mousewheel scroll will close the inventory and switch characters instead.  You're forced to scroll through your inventory 1 line at a time by clicking on a fake scroll bar button, and if you equip or consume anything in the list, it resets the scroll back up to the top.  Worse, if you go to a shop and try to sell weapons while having a whole bunch of them (it doesn't take long to stockpile random junk weapons), you are greeted with massive lag spikes every single time you sell a single weapon shifting the other items up, making it take a very long time to sell that extra gear.  To work around this, you end up having to make extra shop stops to make sure you don't have too many weapons at once (every 3-5 fights once you're fighting large ships).
In-game documentation on what various stats do is also very limited.  You have stats like Strength, Vitality, Agility, Dexterty, Luck, etc, but you aren't told what they do.  Some are somewhat self explanetory and you can watch and see what stats they increase.  But some things such as movement speed, aren't listed.  Vitality reduces movement speed while Agility increases it.  There are also tooltip issues, such as some items not having a tooltip at all, and weapons having very limited tooltip information when you go to buy them, forcing you to buy 1 and see what it's stats are.
It just feels very rough, as if it's still in beta and has all kinds of issues that need fixed or optimized.  But to my knowledge, the devs have moved on to other projects, so these issues may never be fixed.  Keep this in mind if you choose to give it a try, and SAVE OFTEN.  Save scum if you have to, just in case a game breaking bug nukes your playthrough.

As someone who plays a lot of Paradox games and holds them in quite high esteem I find myself not really liking HOI IV. Despite the pretty steep learning curve the game quickly becomes repetative and the warscore system is completely indecipherable - nations only tangentally involved with your conflict can claim territory on the other side of the world because of how the game lumps all conflicts together larger wars and hours of progress can be obliterated pretty swiftly.
The AI is poor as well, often sending large armies to starve, freeze, or dehydrate in the siberian wilderness or sahara desert. The friendly AI is guilty of this as well, so it's better to micromanage your army instead of giving it to the computer. Despite the huge number of nations, they all play pretty similarly and games can turn into huge grinding slogs where no progress is made for hours, and air power is usually an ancilliary element at best.
However, HOI isn't awful, and there is some fun to be had recreating the war or forging your own alternate histories, but it is much shallower than advertised and paradox has taken to releasing fixes in paid DLC, which is pretty low even for them. If your really interested in the second world war then there are probably worse ways to spend your money, but i'd recommend Stellaris or Crusader Kings 2 over HOI, both are (to me at least) more repeatable and interesting games.

*NOTE: REVIEW CONTAINS SPOILERS!*
This is another one of those times where I wish there was a 'meh' rating for games. I like the aesthetic of this game a lot, the music, the weapons, they're all cool, but overall I didn't enjoy my time with Axiom Verge that much. To begin with there is a lot of backtracking in this game, and while there are a few shortcuts you can expect to tread the same ground quite often and it isn't fun to do so due to how movement works. *spoilers* The way you traverse in the game horizontally becomes all about teleporting, you can never have a higher base movement speed like the old Metroid games so I was always just double tapping as much as I could to move as fast as I could. This is annoying and I should have looked in the options to see if I could rebind it. In addition it's pretty easy to not know where you need to go next so you're just wandering around, you don't always immediately use the ability you just unlocked to put you back on the right trail, which while a minor nitpick can be annoying.
My other main gripe is the spike in difficult near the end where enemies just become death dealing bullet sponges. I assume this is to balance out for people who went through and collected a majority of the powerups but I didn't and it made the last few sections extremely frustrating with many enemies taking up to 1/8th of your health in a single volley while taking many hits to kill. I also only used a couple of the weapons in the game, it doesn't feel like you HAVE to use the other ones so why bother? I ended up cheesing many enemies by turning into the droid and just running past them, then teleporting to my drone to avoid them, or gaming them by just running the drone into them and getting off one hit at a time before it died. This to me is not fun, but when you're on a sliver of health (or more in some cases) and the checkpoint is a ways away why risk it?
Overall it felt okay, movement didn't feel as good as I would have like and was finicky, and some of the combat was downright annoying (weird spikes in boss difficulty then being super easy, or enemies that did more damage than the bosses did). Overall it's worth picking up on a sale depending on whether you really like Metroid games and can overlook these faults. If not I would recommend avoiding it as it can be a very frustrating experience at points.

Axiom Verge is an amazing Metroidvania game, it is very reminiscent of Super Metroid in appearance tone and gameplay, but it has a very large set of it's own unique mechanics that work really well. The story is pretty good for a platformer and the music and art suits the game very well, the only issue is that the default keyboard controls aren't very good, and although you can rebind them I'd still strongly reccomend using a controller. If you have enjoyed one of the 2D Metroid games then you will almost certainly love Axiom Verge.

I can full heartedly suggest and recommend the game for those into a meaningful storyline, interesting plot development, and unique branching routes.

This game has everything a good World War 2 dogfight game should have, and everything that its closest modern competitor, War Thunder, doesn't have. First, it has good controller compatibility (using outside mods, but still). Another thing that I cannot emphasize enough on, is the career. You can select from any country that had a flying airplane (and was important), and you can create your pilot, select your rank, earn rewards, and rank up. It's all pretty crazy. Now, I can't rate the multiplayer due to the fact that I haven't tried it, so I'm going to skip to the mission builders. Now, there are two kinds of mission builders, quick and full. Now, think of quick as sort of your instant action, you select your opponents, select your plane, select the number, select the map, and play. There is a couple additional features, like the mission type or the altitude, but those aren't as important. Then there is the full mission builder, the spot that I've spent the majority of my time in. You can select from a huge number of maps, then deploy the planes, artillery, boats, buildings, trains, bunkers, cars, motorcycles, etc. The list goes on. You then deploy waypoints and ya'll battle it out. It truely is amazing, for an early 2000s game, like 2001 or something is when it came out. This comes with a bunch of DLCs and additional content for only $10.
Graphics
Aged very well. They are not bad, they are in the middle, but they still look fine for when it was made.

Probably 10 years ago, I was heavily invested in the IL-2 franchise, with both "Aces" and "Forgotten Battles" expansions, and later the "Pacific Fighters" module. It just BARELY ran on my cheap, office desktop, and i had issues with the CPU overheating because of this game, but I played anyway because it was AMAZING. I had always been a fan of the WW2 flight sims from Microsoft, but this was a cut above. I really felt like I was IN the plane, not on a simulator.
I had heard a lot of people saying that 1946 wouldnt work on Win 10. Recently, I heard a large number of people had success getting it to run. Since I hadn't enjoyed the game in 6-8 years, I dropped my $10 on trying it - and was blown away by how well it held up! See, I had just bought IL-2 Battle of Stalingrad a week prior, and was (still am) in love with it. However, I loved reading about all the old planes as a youngster, and to be able to fly 229 of the most famous, and the most obscure, aircraft of the era is like a dream come true.
The only gripe some may have are the interior visuals - they look very dated. They are, however, immersive, and entirely 3d, so It isn't unplayable. The exterior visuals really hold up well. If you compare it to BoS or Even "Rise of Flight" you can tell it's a bit older, but it still looks good. The worst textures come from ground units - tanks, jeeps, AA positions, all look like theyre from the 1990's, but since you won't see them for more than a second, I really don't notice.
If you're a Win 10 user, thinking about trying the more expensive BoS, maybe give this a try - I find myself playing it more than its hotter, newer sibling.

I am a long time player of this game, since its release on August 25 2016. I had the opportunity to experience the servers at double/triple full capacity and have followed the game intimately using videography and by attending community events and talking with developers personally.
My hours played on this game is inaccurate as I had lost over 400 counted hours before the December 12 2016 patch (last patch the old development team released). This means that I have an unhealthy amount of hours invested into this game.
The thing that I really enjoy about this game is how close it is to fighting in a real battle without harming yourself physically.

^^^ is a link of my opinion on the game.
I come from a background of high intensity competition (athletic) and traditional martial arts. And no other game I have played in many years of gaming comes close to Of Kings And Men in capturing that thrill and exhiliration.
The game is extremely difficult to learn without guidance, but can be taught consistently to new players well enough for them to develop their playstyle.
Favourite parts of the game :
Combat -
The combat is the fastest paced I have experienced for PVP and one that makes a solid attempt in promoting teamwork. I've played competitive SMITE, SWTOR, Age OF Wushu, Mabinogi and this game provides the hardest heart thumping, breathless fist pumping, and outright feeling of satisfaction when it comes to PVP gaming.
It features a fluid 8-directional stance definition which means that a fight/battle can change its flow by the breadth of a change in direction when fighting. The direction of a sword swing is also dependent on the point of view a player takes as the swing is released.
- If looking up, you will aim for the head, if down you aim for the shins / feet - This makes for a near infinite set of dimensions for where a swing can be released, the arc it can follow, and where it can strike.  The point of contact on which part of the arc of the swing it occurs also determines its effectiveness as a strike.
You can do feints, use footwork to determine distance (dodging striking), and block and attack all in one smooth moment without disruption aside from your own inability to determine the strike coming at you. This includes arrows/bolts to the back of your head in the middle of a fight.
Raid Mode -
Much of this game mode is an ode to the military understanding of Sun Tzu (author of the art of war) and the different types of ground found in battle. This makes it like a real live chess game, with definitive results for on the fly decisions.
Real Time Strategy cannot be better depicted than through this game mode from my experiences of watching it develop through early testing phases, to first live release.
An attacker's choices determines their spawn rate, time left, and method of winning. You can either out smart your opponent, out play them, or out number them. While defenders have methods for using advantageous ground through well designed maps.
I have seen raids last from 12 minutes
(one clan did a blitzkrieg up the torturous path successfully securing the west wall of the castle where their hoard began to dissiminate from distracting the defenders and pile in through this critical holding point)
up to 26 minutes depending on the play style
(another clan with attempted to reduce the number of lost troops by increasing the time through capturing objectives. their plan was thwarted by an assasin who targeted their commander over and over)
Hold Your Ground -
A popular single player/ multiplayer co-op where you can practice footwork/blocking, working as a team, and in the future maybe even more. With previously announced plans for innovating the game modes' map, it can create a more immersive experience when playing the game. I personally tested this game mode from trial to completion and have found the benefits of it for both blocking and working agains many enemies at once to be very effective
Clans -
The game recently featured in game clan systems that allows a player to join an active clan lead by someone who has retired. This feels appropriate as back in the day, you had to make a name for yourself before others would follow you / you earn "the right"
Clans have the option to upload custom heraldry which is displayed on all armors that have a cloth material in the game.
When properly organized, clans can come together with other clans and swiftly create events / battles amongst them to have fun for hours to come.
In the upcoming game mode De Re Militari, each player will be a vassal under their clan's banner. While being able to uphold the name and herald, players are able to act completely free thereby creating a live player based diplomacy. Clan leaders will have to decide to rule by order , fear, or abundance
Developer communication -
The current team of developers are basically realizing a dream game. Together they gather and analyze community feedback, often implementing with quick application and sometimes even outright putting player ideas directly into the game. More so lately than before as well, there is consistent and dependable release of information about the game on a weekly basis.
Graphics -
I've seen the coding process of maps, and to see how the artists and coders can work to create such organic landscapes is very impressive. You can also see how clouds move across the moonlit sky as it causes the glimmer off the edge of a glaive's blade to resonate to the pace of the winds.
Sounds -
From what I know, all sounds in the game are currently done by 2 main developers. Just 2. For those who know the dificulty of engineering/recording/mastering... 2 guys do all of that for this game.
Each sound is satisfying, now that they are layered with both ambient, environment, and personal soundscapes. Strikes imply the weight behind them and effectiveness over the armor, with distinct sounds for each armor type including helmets (headshots, head strike)
Creative Freedom -
For people that like role play, this game really can't get much better. It is a very "law less " land that it doesn't have many parameters of how the game SHOULD be played. Instead it provides a space for a community to come together and enjoy a thrilling gaming experience.
