Within a few days, Guacamelee went from a cool demo I played for a few minutes to one of my favorite games of all time that I was putting hours into every night.
How I got to that point is simple: its FANTASTIC. A beat-em-up/platformer/metroidvania/whatever sounds like a lot but it doesnt feel like much in-game, where you can do pretty much whatever you want most of the time. You can explore, you can beat things into a pulp, you can throw a bunch of chickens into a wall--you can even BE a chicken! The learning curve builds up perfectly from familiar platforming and simple combos to nearly DMC-level battles and quite literally the single-hardest platforming section I have ever seen (and beaten). And do I even need to mention how beautiful the backgrounds and level design is?? It forced me to stop playing and just stare on some occasions. My screencap folder for this game is INSANE.
I have not played the Gold edition at all but if you're new to Guac like I was, this is the version I would recommend, hands down. If you're looking to upgrade from Gold, I'd still say go for it because I love it that much. I do know one of the new areas in this version is one of the largest in the game and gives a nice twist to the plot that I enjoyed, but that's something that either matters to you or not. I would especially sugest getting the soundtrack bundle of either version (I regret not getting it myself) simply because its amazing in the way it conbines the sounds of a retro sidescroller with traditional Mexican music.
The co-op is another thing I've yet to try, especially since 4-player is exclusive to this version, but everything I've seen of 2-player looked good. It definitely makes arenas easier, but I wouldn't do any especially challenging platforming on anything but single player. That stuff is hard enough to do alone sometimes, let alone trying to catch up when your partner is ahead. But if you just wanna screw with your friends, then go right ahead.
Some rumblings I've heard involve people saying the use of Mexican folklore here is racist, and as a Mexican with personal ties to that folklore, I heartily disagree. Yeah, its weird that a Canadian studio made an essentially Mexican game. But personally? It's not near the worst I've seen in terms of using sterotypes. And the accuracy and respect present in the style and lore of this game more than make up for that kind of stuff. It seriously feels like a love letter to a part of my culture that I hardly ever get to see in ANY media, let alone games, and we need more of it. I need to be able to walk up to another NPC singing "Cielito Lindo" at the top of their lungs for no reason.
I'm THISCLOSE to fully completing the game (damn El Infierno challenges) but I'd definitely say I've gotten my money's worth out of it and more. My first playthrough went a bit longer than the average because I wanted the happy ending and that involves basically another playthrough worth of work. If 14.99 isn't that cool to you, its been on sale a lot in the short time I've had it so just stick it on the wishlist and be a little patient. It'll be worth it :)

A stunning arcade re-skin of the popular match-3/shmup mashup series with good production value.  Now it looks like Tempest, sounds like Blade Runner, and plays like Galaga.  Quite intense stuff, unlike anything you would usually associate with the brand.
It still banks on the 3 matches -> powerup mechanic, and there is only one play mode which is score attack through ~50 levels.  While levels differ only in marching patterns of neon marbles, plenty of variety comes from whopping 25 kinds of powerups you gradually unlock.
It's mindless fun to pull off combo, pick them up and trigger spectacular vector-shatters and sound effects in bullet time, easily enough to hold interest for ~2 hours of one playthrough (which can be suspended/resumed anytime.)  Regular powerups are instant RNG, but supers can be deployed at discretion, so some forward-thinking is called for as well.
Extra point for the dubstep music which ebbs and flows with the gameplay.  Bonus stages, secret levels, and epic boss battles wrap up a lean and mean package.
4 difficulty settings with separate Steam leaderboards inject much-needed speed boost (if nothing else,) but I won't suggest serious score runs because of obvious balancing issues.  Achievements are supported as well.
A bit thin on the content, nevertheless what's in there is a sublime arcade experience to zone out to.  Highly recommended if vector is your kind of retro.

For a game which basically screams at its users to use a controller, it is a shame that controller support is not shipped out of the box.  I'm running a mac and tried both an xbox one controller and a ps4 controller with appropriate driver support, and neither worked with Axiom Verge.  Ultimately I found a link to a tool I could use to manually map each button to the specification the game uses, then copy that specification into a text file which controlled which controllers the game would recognized.  After this, the game worked, but I realized I could get it on console for the same price and without ever having to fight this battle again, so I returned the game.
The game itself is awesome - I highly recommend picking it up on console.  It works great with a ps4 controller on the ps4, and I presume it works similarly awesomely on the xbox one with an xbox one controller there.  But I cannot recommend buying it on steam.
For those who are determined, or have no other option, the config tool is called "SDL2 Gamepad Tool by General Arcade", and the file to locate within the game is called "gamecontrollerdb.txt".  I found the tool did not handle analog shoulder buttons well, so you may be in for a bumpy ride.

Short answer: If you remember and loved Mutant League Football back in the day you'll love Mutant Football League. It's a great and unique game and an excellent refinement to what was a great concept to further skill over raw violence while never forgetting that a little good old fashioned quarterback slaughter is a perfectly viable way to victory. You will learn to despise the Nuked London Hatriots and Ghoulian Metalman as much as any team in any sports game ever.
Longer answer: It's more Blitz than Madden, a faster, more violent game than Blood Bowl and I can finally stop having a Genesis emulator for the old Mutant League games. MFL is more complex than you may think at first glance, requiring you to rotate your players to keep them alive, avoid deadly saw blades on the field, and learn just the right time to bribe the ever helpful Ed Hockaloogie thanks to a vastly improved system dictating when the refs will act on bribes making things just a little less predictable. Adding the ability to resurrect fallen players adds another layer of strategy to season or playoff modes. Personally I was a bigger fan of Mutant League Hockey than football, but this is an excellent improvement and refinement to the concept that became a cult classic in the 90s. I may think that imitating the names of real players so closely isn't that helpful when it results in Sickardo Blewis or Arson Emblamer, but its all part of the fun and there is a lot of fun to be had here. There seems to be a committment by the devs to continue improving the game, adding new races and possibly a franchise/story mode and I'm excited to see how the game progresses from here. But where it is now it is certainly worth the $25 in my opinion.
Also the Midway Mutants have a player named Ditkadonis which is just fantastic.
Just like the old days.  Awesome.

My whole life I've been looking for something that can rekindle my love of Metroid. Yes, there have been good 2D Metroidvania out there like Ori & the Blind Forest, but those... are not Metroid.
Enter Axiom Verge.
If you ever liked Metroid, and ever want to experience that kind of adventure again, then Axiom Verge is for you. It simply delivers on all front. Beautiful alien environment, winding paths with tons of secret, getting stronger as you progress, amazing lonely soundtrack. I booted up this game for the first time, and as I started playing, it reminds me of those feelings that I have when I played Super Metroid back then :')

Simply put, Metroid should have been this good.
The story is excellent, the controls are mechanically sound, and the weapons are rewarding and versatile.   There are lots of ways to work around puzzles, so you're not always repeating the same thing.
The game, however, is MERCILESS in its explanation of what to do next.   Like Metroid on the NES, you will be expected to EXPLORE and REMEMBER locations of things you haven't yet done.   Backtracking is essential in this game, as new tools and codeframes will unlock entire new areas.
A great game for the price, I hope this developer keeps it up!

This is a terrible game.
The game itself is a horrible mish-mash.  Even simple things like the sound and music sliders are done poorly (this is in unity, and they are clearly not getting the slider value from the saved preferences when they load the scene).   I couldn't figure out whether "Star Game" is a typo or just a really bad name for playing.
The power-ups, such as they are, are mostly random, and all last for just a short period of time.  This is a good thing, because power-ups can be negative as well as positive, like slowing down your ship for 30 seconds, or making you unable to fire for 30 seconds.
The objects on the screen are huge compared to the play area, which means that it is really easy to hit and to be hit.  Also, enemy shots often appear to have faint particle trails attached to them, without any actual image for the projectile.  This means you can't see many of the enemy bullets that are coming at you.  That is devastating for a bullet hell type game.
Also, the art is all over the place in terms of quality.  Either they have an artist that is really not very good, or they bought assets from a variety of places, and then just threw them all together without thinking if it made for a visually coherent experience.  Speaking of visual incoherence, your ship is set up in a side scrolling mode, but the particles in the background come straight at you as if they were purchased for a flight simulator.
All in all the whole thing just does not work.  The game is needlessly difficult due to randomly bad powerups and invisible bullets.  The art is a mess.  The options don't work right.  They didn't even put an intro graphic in the unity launch screen.
I assume this is someone's first attempt at a game.  Don't waste your money on it.

You are the only human at an all-pigeon school. The game starts off by having you romance different pigeons - like how a traditional otome game would. Many routes were similar to anime or otome archetypes such as the yandere, the introvert, the outgoing flirt, the arrogant student... it brought about laughs and occasionally some sniffling. I am an avid gamer of dating sims and this one seemed to be poking fun at all of them, which I loved!
As you progress on, you unlock the BBL route; which is the true end. It explains everything about the school, you, and the pigeons. I couldn't stop reading once I started. The whole story is incredibly deep and not what it seemed at the beginning. It's difficult to say why I absolutely loved it without spoiling much of the story but you start to get attached to all the characters; both the good and the bad ones.
I urge everybirdie to give this game a try. In my opinion, it's still worth it even when not on sale.

Before Undertale, where the main idea of the game is that you never have to kill a single soul, there was Dishonored.
--SPOILERS--
Dishonored knew that more than anyone, and while Undertale is still an enjoyable game with a great message of it's own, Dishonored carried a certain weight to it from the very first opening sequence. Your Empress and lover was killed in front of your eyes, the Princess who you consider to be your daughter was taken without a chance to get her back. I don't write reviews often, but I am writing this one because I feel this game is getting a bad reputation that it doesn't deserve. I'm Reccomending it, but please see the last paragraph.
Positive stuff:
This game, if nothing else, has an amazing combat system that I've never seen before. I think they stepped it up from the 'Mount and Blade' style combat. It has more to it than Mount and Blade did. I always felt that if there was ever a version of Mount and Blade that didn't have the stategy aspect and instead focused only on my player controlled character I would find myself in the 'Shut up and take my money' group. This game really does have that potential in it. The combat system and gameplay are awesome. Even in many of the Negative reviews, people say this is good.
Also, it's beautiful. I'm personally very impressed with the graphics... I'm probably easily impressed, but I really would say that it looks good.
The ugly negative:
There really isn't a community. When it had a community, there were some really fun, big fights. Basic arena stuff, nothing terribly special, but very few things in Early Access are... However, there isn't a community. So the only thing you really get to do is fight bots. This lets you test out the combat system, but does not let you really enjoy the game.
Some things to consider:
Many of the reviews I have read have gone on and on about broken promises from the devs... I've got a couple EA games in my library that, well, have stopped... you know, the kind of thing where there hasn't been any news in 7+ months, nothing actually happening... This isn't one of them. I see the devs posting news, working on this and that. Maybe they're not where they said they would be, but seriously, I've had to delay plans to make a damn sandwich because some ate the last of the cheese... There are abosolutely updates happening, and they're good. I'm not the guy who looks at the schedule that gets posted I don't know where and gets mad that it hasn't happened yet. I'm happy its not an abandoned project and updates and news are happening, and pretty regularly at that.
It is important to note that, at the time of this review, is has a 45% overall reccomended rate, and a 7% recent reccomended rate. I bought this game a while ago, but I will say that no matter how good a game looks, I wouldn't buy it with those stats... Honestly, I wouldn't even get far enough to read this review. But if you did, this game has potential I simply don't see anywhere else (and I do look), so I hope it doesn't die.
This game isn't ready, but that's why it's in Early Access. It's probably not following it's original plan, but I think that's ok. It is something that you're not going to find elsewhere. You should not jump into this and expect to find awesome battles with hundres of people, but you could one day. And lastly, the devs are working, changes are happening, and this could be an amazing game.

Ah, Brink. Where to even begin? Great game which after release in 2011 was a victim of hate-train and because of that (and numerous bugs) it was dead after few months. The game was made by Splash Damage, developer who made a FPS legend, "Wolfenstein:Enemy Territory, and team objective FPS in Quake universum "Enemy Territory: Quake Wars". Brink was suppose to be successor of these games and in my opinion the deserved succesor it was. Great story, unique aesthetic, objectives that make teamwork essential, really good audio work and visuals. So why it failed?
The release was rushed by Bethesda and there were multiple gamebreaking bugs at the beginning, one of worse was horrible stuttering on AMD cards/CPUs. While it was ultimately fixed, the reputation of flop did enough damage to make the game dead after just few months. It was premature born baby, that didn't had any chance to shine, which is shame - I was hyped, preordered it, even bought some cosmetic addons, and then I terrified watch as the game I loved was dying and ultimately there were maybe ~100 people play it in rush hours. And now, maybe as some sort of gift, it's Free to Play, but without any sort of microtransactions or "Pay to Win" system. Just a solid FPS that you can play for free, and I definitely reccomend to do so.
So why "Brink" is great?
For me, the main reason is story - the game take place in postapocalyptic world, after seal level raised, and where floods and droughts in mainland changed the world order into chaos. The supposedly last stand was the Ark - artifical, mobile island which first was a econovelty for celebrities, techhippies and scientists. After the world ends it become a target of migration for countless boats and by that it change to duality social system of rich elite in the Arc itself, and so called "guests" in newly built swimming slums.
Two sides of conflict are security forces and members of Resistance, and while there are no unique weapons or mechanics for both sides, the story is of course much different. I really don't want to spoiler the story, but as you play you will realise that there are no good guys in this game and the story itself is really great - what's unique there is no single player and you discover the plot just by playing multi, which is great in my opinion. However, there's lack of proper singleplayer in the game, so called single is just a multi but with mediocre bots, and unless you are really good that can make impossible to finish some of the maps.
The class system is similar to Wolfenstein:ET or Quake Wars, if you don't know these games - it's something like Team Fortress 2, but only with 4 classes, which are: medic, soldier, engineer and covert operative (spy). There are objectives to do maps, which canbe completed only by one of the class, i.e. destrying a gate needs a soldier and his explosives, hacking objective needs a covert etc, healing a escort needs a medic etc. Soldier, medic and engineer are straighforward and they don't need explaining, covert however have ability to disguise himself as enemy, which is really fun system and something that most FPSes lack these days.
Another great thing is weapon customization - for every weapon you can unlock different parts as you progress with character xp levels, and some by completing challanges - why I like the system it might not be liked by everyone. Challanges are quite hard, and rewards (drum barrel i.e.) can be gamechanging, so it leads to situation when good players are even more deadly in-game thanks to new toys. On top of that, with gained xp levels you are awarded with new abilities - some are for all classes (more health etc), some are for specific classes, so when you play the game you end up with 4 characters, one for every class. That, added with weapons parts make veterans much stronger than new players, and that can be offputing at start. On the good side - it takes only few matches to level up to the point, where that difference is only slight.
What was advertised when the game was released, was a movement system, that suppose to be some hybrid, parkour mechanic where you can slide, do wallruns etc. While it works ingame, it hardly can be describe as "revolutionary" - its just a feature that you even stop noticing after few hours of playing the game. However, there is another customization option when it comes to that - the body types. There are three of those: heavy, medium and light, and the difference is number of hitpoints (heavy is tankest, light is squishiest), movement options (light can use some alternative routes while medium and heavy can't) and weapons available (light can use only SMGs, heavy can use miniguns etc). Any class can use any body type, and any weapon available for that body type, which leads to some interesting combinations.
Another unique feature when compared to other team based FPS, is the system, where using your class abilities use one of your recharchable supply points. I.e. in Battlefield as a medic you can spam your revive or medkit abilities without restriction, in Brink however, you have only few points, that when used, force you to wait ~30 seconds to recharge just one of the point. That system force you to prioritize what you are doing. Is it more worth to buff your teammate with health now, or would it be better to save that point in case someone would need revive? Is it better to use granade (that spends supply point), or to give your teammate ammo? That system force you to think and I love it, but again, it might be offputting for some people who just want mindless and fun game.
As I wrote, I love these game but there are some thing you might not like. Lack of proper singleplayer is one thing, the other is lack of tutorial of any kind. There are only some videos ingame that explain how to play, but to watch them you need to spend some times in menu, which many people won't. If you just went into to match straight away, you might be confused what to do, and a need to manaully pick objectives won't help that. While all the weapons have it's pros and cons, the SMGs are simply better then other weapons, unless you want to keep a distance to enemy, but in game with team objectives it's hard to keep that distance.
"Brink" nowadays are compared to the newest game of the same developer, "Dirty Bomb", which is F2P team based FPS - I have about 350 hours in that game, and 110 hours in the Brink - the DB is much more active, polished game but it's pure F2P, which mean currency, microtransactions and way simpler mechanic. Every class can do any objective, abilities have cooldown instead of supply points, and the game itself while really fun, is nowhere near "Brink" when it comes to tactic and making important decisions in the game. The biggest flaw however is shallow objectives. In the Brink I know exactly why Im repairing and escorting the objective, why Im hacking that safe, why Im destroying that bridge etc. It's important and I know why it's important - in DB I have no idea why I'm duing these things, I'm doing it just because I want to win, and sadly, immersion is broken by that. While I love both of these games, Brink will be always first in my heart, and it was really sad to watch that game die in 2011.
Right now Brink suddenly is free - I wont's say its "F2P", because its completely different system and that term would be confusing - it's just FPS that now is given for free and you lose nothing to try it, even if you won't like it. See you in game!

If you're skilled you won't even need to use Intenso mode, but some people struggled with the difficulty of the original game, so I don't begrudge its inclusion. The purported remixing of existing levels is also very slight - basically a few new chests have been added and some old ones relocated. It's a non-event.
Perhaps most worthless is the new power-up, the Pollo Bomb. Once you've obtained it, pressing B while in the form of a chicken will make you lay an egg that explodes after a second or so, delivering a ridiculously small amount of damage to nearby enemies. There is literally no situation in which a pollo bomb would be preferable to straight-up melee. It only really serves to break a few new types of barrier rocks, which typically lead to some of the 'remixed' sections.
If you're not going to be using the 4-player co-op, which I haven't tested, this really only leaves the two new areas as an incentive to buy the game. And they're good - nothing has been half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and they don't feel like they've been shoe-horned in. They fit in seamlessly on narrative, geographic and aesthetic levels. They offer an extra hour or two of fun gameplay. But that's all they offer.
So ultimately, if you don't own any version of Guacamelee at all, buying this one is a no-brainer - it has the most content, and is the must customisable to your ability as a gamer. However, if you already own Gold, you need to ask yourself how much 2 hours of gameplay is worth to you, because that's the only thing of substance STCE offers over Gold. To market it as a completely separate game really does seem like a cash-grab, as I see no reason this couldn't have been sold as relatively inexpensive DLC.

Guacamelee is one of the best games I've ever played. I put it right next to Cave Story in my list of favorite indie games.
Guacamelee is a Metroidvania 2D-sidescrolling action game. Here are my personal highlights:
-Pacing and level design are both fantastic. The game introduces new powerups and abilities at a constant steady pace, which keeps the game feeling fresh the whole way through. Every powerup you unlock opens up new areas in past locations you've already visited, with new goodies to discover in each.
-Combat is fun and easy enough to understand. It's pure melee action and rewards you for chaining combos of different moves. It gives you full freedom to pull off different combos of all sorts.
-Art style is stylish, gorgeous, and makes good use of Mesoamerican cultural references/imagery in a respectful manner.
-The soundtrack fits all of the different (Mexican) environments perfectly. I don't think the developers (in Canada) had a single person of Mexican descent on their team when they made this game... but I can tell they did their homework on Mexican culture.
-Lots of clever easter eggs and references to other games like Metroid, Mario, Zelda, and other indie games. It was fun spotting them all.
I didn't really find anything to fault the game for, other than that it never recognized my USB gamepad, so I had to play it with my keyboard. It was still enjoyable despite that though. If you have a Xbox 360 controller (I don't, mine's a generic USB pad) you likely won't have this problem.
I definitely recommend this game! It deserves every bit of praise it gets. I sadly never got to try out the 2-4 player co-op multiplayer, but I imagine that would only have made it even more enjoyable.

This game appears to have been inspired by Total War. The top down map view certainly resembles the campaign map in the Total War series. Anyone familiar with Total War's battle map will find this game's battle map familiar as well. Economy has been streamlined to manage the Kingdom rather than province.
The RPG part of this game comes in when you are allowed to configure King Arthur's Knights. They level up through gaining experience through battle or resolving quests. Upon leveling up, the Round Table Knights are given one point to distribute to their general skills and are allowed to learn one spell. The Knights can also gain experience and abilities through events.
There is also a moral and religious alignment system in place, allowing players to be either tyrannical or righteous and Christian or Old Faith. Affiliation confers abilities, so players are encouraged to be consistent.
Quests are text based, but suprisingly fun and dependent on the Knight performing the quest.

Good alternative to Total War, if you enjoy added RPG elements and some text-based quests: which always helps to break up the game and keep it entertaining.
Protip: Select easy mode, anything beyond easymode is ♥♥♥♥ing torture.

As long as the game goes, it's ok. I like turn based games, and Eador didn't disappoint me. But on behalf of all Linux gamers, I have a problem. Steam should not call this a Linux game, yes it runs, but it is not playable. It has some really nasty graphical glitches in Wine.
There was some really good moves made to port few attractive games like CivV to linux, which plays natively and not in emulator (I know Wine is not an emulator...). My point is, if you do use linux icon, at least put some notion of it being played in Wine in system requirements portion.

Similiar to Warlocks, Fallen Enchantress and good old Master of Magic, Eador is all about battling in a fantasy worlds with heroes and armies. While you spread your influence for gathering resources you shouldn't think you're the only one doing the same.
As it is quite typical 4X game, there are few things that makes it work quite well - if you are about to invest some time to learn the game mechanics. That's the only drawback: construction (i.e. building up land) is more complicated, because you have capital region and "provinces" - and they don't develop the same way. Once you have built up buildings in your capital region you unlock more buildings for regions. And you can have only 3 buildings up on any given province, which doesn't make sense, but it forces you to prioritise. Luckily, you can tear buildings down on provinces. I wish there was a way to do the same on capital region, because you can have only 4 types of unit recruitment buildings.
That restriction is horrible. At the beginning you need some first tier "barracks" in order to muster up your initial army to get you going anywhere. The beginning is quite rough even on lower difficulties. However, on later stages you wish you could have more variety of higher-end troops, but the cap limit won't allow you to do just that. What's even more painful, some "garrison" troops, which are different from standard troops, require also certain "barracks"-types, so you need to do some research. Later on, you get hold on that, though.
Tactical battles are like from Fallen Enchantress. They can be very hard at first, but when taking full advantage of the terrain and vegetation it is possible. I am finding the very beginning quite hard on 2nd lowest difficulty level, though I haven't played but a couple of campaign maps. Like in Fallen Enchantress, you equip your hero, while troops get automatically geared up. Both heroes and troops gain levels and when they do, you can choose an upgrade for the victorious one. And when the leader gets level-ups, you can occasionally have more unlocked slots for more troops.
Balance on economics work quite well. Gold is scarce, but if you do spare provinces' guards you are asking for trouble. On frontiers they won't save you much against enemy troops, but fortification gives you more time to get in aid with your armies. But these fortresses cost dearly. But you still need guards and pay for their upkeep, because there are plenty of events you get randomly attacked on one of your provinces. These events vary though, and some are helpful. However, the events can occur a lot. It isn't unprecendented to have got four events on your regions at the beginning of your turn.
Graphics and sounds are okayish - nothing too brilliant, but they do their job.
Definitely worth picking-up on your game library if you're into Master of Magic and/or Fallen Enchantress - especially on this summer sale. 75 per cent off is not too shabby.

I played several games of the Luxor franchise and, I must say, this is looks more different than any of the other games. Luxor Evolved has bright, neon graphics with a very dark background whereas other Luxor games have been based on Egyptian architecture. This game appears to pay tribute to 1980s arcade classics such as Asteroids, Berserk, and Pac-Man.
The basics of the gameplay remain the same: you are a scarab at the bottom of the screen shooting spheres that correspond to the colors being pushed by the evil scarabs in an attempt to breach the pyramid. If they do breach the pyramid, you lose a life. What is different about breaching the pyramid from previous Luxor games is that the spheres will move back and you will have to shoot them down again. Previous Luxor games simple rushed the spheres into the pyramid upon breaching the pyramid. In Luxor Evolved the spheres will be rushed past you into the pyramid only after losing all your lives. Making three consecutive matches of spheres will throw up a powerup in the air that you must catch to gain some advantage such as reversing the horizontal movement of the spheres, turning a group of spheres into one color, or stopping the spheres temporarily to give you time to shoot them with less stress.
The neon lights are accompanied by a retro soundtrack. I think the soundtrack is not very diverse, but still entertaining enough to keep from being boring. As in previous Luxor games, you will find bonus items after destroying a scarab and your scarab gobbles it up in a Pac-Man like manner. There are bonus rounds that require you to take out spheres flying in patterns using your throwing knives. Secret levels are very interesting, but must be unlocked by collecting a fixed number of treasures, including fruits and coins. Survival levels test your ability to withstand several scarabs moving spheres toward the end of the pyramid within a set time. Another new type of level is the boss level. Boss fights require you to shoot spheres into the sphere chains circling the boss’ eye. In the meantime, the boss is attacking with rows of spheres below the aforementioned sphere chain. All of this action is occurring while listening to the techno soundtrack.
If you are a fan of Luxor games, you will be surprised by the dark background and neon colors presented by Luxor Evolved. However, you will be familiar with the chain reactions that look quite dazzling when a string of three or more spheres are eliminated. I found it quite entertaining to see secret levels showing a Pac-Man like maze and a Berserk inspired background. In my opinion, however, the Luxor games presenting Egyptian hieroglyphics were aesthetically better looking than Luxor Evolved. I first played this game in the Hard difficulty mode and I finished it after 8+ levels. It was unique and a laugh out loud (lol) moment to be able to continue shooting spheres when the closing credits were running. Scarabs were still moving rows of marbles when the game was over and the credits were running.
I think that Luxor Evolved is a fun game for those who enjoy arcade classics that have been remade in modern times. It is a game that will be entertaining for a few hours, but I do not view it as a puzzle game with a high replay value.
My Score: 7/10

Oh what to say about this game... It could be worse, but it certainly could be a whole lot better.
Pros:
+ Price is cheap, even when not on sale, which is a good thing for such a small arcade game.
+ I have to admit I do like the ship design and graphics, they remind me of old sci-fi games I'd play back in the day.
+ There is a story and background info. If you click on the media button you can can get some information on all of the ships you encounter in the game.
+ The ability to choose your own ship, although it can get a little confusing (I'll get into that later.)
+ There are a variety of ships to fight and powerups to collect.
+ Local highscores.
+ Semi-expensive trading cards.
+ The people who work on it seem to update it quite often, so at least they're comitted to making the game better.
Sidegrade things (I don't know what they're called.)
= Music is meh. Could be better, could be worse.
= The overall graphics. It's a Unity game.
= Controls are okay.
= Controller support. I haven't tested it out yet so I'm not sure if the controls are terrible or not so that's why I'm only putting it as a sidegrade.
Cons:
- Some things are really confusing. Like the ship selection screen. The first two stats make enough sense. Speed and Health. But then there's attack. Attack is a 100% on the first ship, but on the second and third ship it's either -20 or +20. What does that even mean? Same thing for the next stat, damage. And that being said what is the difference between attack and damage? Another thing that was very confusing for a while was the fact that those blue electricity orbs that fly at your ship are actually XP points, not an attack. There are a few other instances of this throughout the game.
- The difficulty. This game is way too hard (For me at least.) Because the ships are so huge. The screen of your computer is only so big and so it makes it amazingly hard to dodge attacks, especially with multiple ships coming for you.
- The game has a story, but I really can't understand the cutscenes because: A: The illustrtations are way too dark, to see, and honestly, they aren't that bad themselves. And B: The weird sound effect that the voice has makes it really hard to understand as well.
- These weird solar system things come flying at you (They kind of look like the antigravity powerups from Marble Blast Gold come to think of it.) and they seem to always have a different effect, which really doesn't make too much sense.
- The background is a static image of some generic sci-fi scene that does not scroll whatsoever.
- Grammar errors. Now I understand that Steam is used by people all around the world and that some devs who make their game in a non-native language to them might make a few mistakes, but this game just has way too many. Some examples are. "GO SLOW" or "STAR GAME" or "HORIZONTAL FREEZED."
- Animation and movement of the ship is very bad. My ship seems to constantly have some orange thing on the front jumping around in different colors, and the movement has no momentum at all; you can zip around unrealistically without starting off going a bit slower.
- The text used gets annoying after 30 seconds and then you just feel dyslexic.
- Probably something else I forgot.
TL;DR
Overall, I don't recommend this game. Again, it could be worse, but it could be so much better. I must say I kind of like the classic shoot 'em up flash game feel, but still not a great game. Pick it up on sale, test it out, and make some trading card profit.

Axiom Verge may very well be the most interesting indie metroidvania of recent years. It’s not most groundbreaking and you can spot where the game’s roots are easily. Still, every element of the game is done competently and is tuned to fit in the whole system. You can’t overlook the fact that whole game was done solely by Tom Happ. Sometimes whole teams fail to not put average pieces in the way of really great ones.
At first glance the game is an undeniable copycat of Super Metroid (perhaps any 2D metroidvania centered around shooting is) with all the foundation taken straight of it: the isolation feeling, save point system, health replenishment particles that some of the dead enemies leave behind, and the eerie vibe of psychedelic 80s sci-fi.
So it goes like this. You are “the scientist” named Trace, there’s an explosion in your lab. You are awaken in the alien world and contacted by Elsenova who is giant war machine representing “species” of Rusalki. They are at war with Athetos a mad scientist destroying space-time. More accurately speaking they lost the war and now you are their last chance. But that are the bits of the story from later on, for now all the instructions you get are “There is a gun in the next room” and “You must go, now”.
So you get out and start exploring. Enemies hit hard encouraging slow and methodical approach. Learning attack patterns and using distance to your advantage keeps you from restarting back at egg-shaped rebirth chamber. You make your way to the next rebirth chamber. You find few upgrades in the process and a new gun, which has a different firing mechanic (making it a highly situational weapon). And then you get to the boss; the slow and tense rhythm fades away.
It all just goes nuts. Boss fights are punctuated with delirious high-tempo electronic music and filled with adrenaline up to the brim. The screen is traced with enemy shots. You dodge and jump. You keep firing. Precision, speed and reaction will get you through first few bosses. Pattern-learning and staying focused will pick up after that. Bosses will have phases with tricky moves and more deadly attacks. You avoid damage and keep shooting watching how your enemy slowly turns red. All of this just turns itself into red pulsating blur.
The rhythm slows down again. You proceed further to keep on exploring. This is a simple loop of going through building up tension to climax points and back to calm concentration. You’ll collect more items, more weapons. You’ll meet NPCs. Piecemeal storytelling: cryptic dialogues and ciphered messages. Backstory takes significant effort to uncover itself. Same for some of the most powerful weapons.
Somewhere around the middle of the game Axiom Verge suddenly plays homage to Blaster Master repeating one of its key mechanics in reverse. Trace is granted an ability to launch a miniature remote-controlled drone to explore narrow spaces. Most innovative though is the Address Disruptor. The Glitch Gun. You fire it in a cone in front of Trace and it lets you pass through inaccessible wall (by evaporating them). Or it changes the properties of your enemy. Or it materialises a platform hanging in the air. It glitches. Magic happens.
The game’s most amazing secret though is its very well hidden procedurall-generated dungeons system. The existence of such a system within the game is what defines its author’s dedication to traditions of the genre. It’s this little details like a special mode for speedruns with some thought put into it that make a metroidvanian labyrinth interesting to explore, not just pass by.

This is probably one of my favourite games of all time.. Wait no scratch that. It's definitely one of my favourite games of all time. Hatoful Boyfriend is the epic tale of a hunter-gatherer girl who must go on the adventure of a life time.
At first glance, most people have assumed this game is just a silly game about dating pigeons, but if you've actually finished the whole thing you know it's so much more than that. Not only is it filled with a rich history, wonderfully refreshing characters, and a compelling original story, but it knows how to have fun.  I've played quite a few visual novels and dating sims, and I can say that even after you've only played two or three, they can get repetitive fast. No matter how much you like them, it's easy to notice how similar they all are with most characters only existing to fullfill their specific trope. Stories are made as a background for what the game is really about: dating. Hatoful Boyfriend isn't like that. Hatoful Boyfriend takes all the tropes from your average Otome Games and flips them of their heads making a refreshing change in the genre. Have you ever wondered why you'll fail in so many games if you don't date any of the guys? Hatoful Boyfriend explains it. All the characters have strong personalities and they don't feel so stale and one-dimensional. Sure, there's the shy quiet one and the obnoxious popular type, but there's so much more to it than that and every replay doesn't feel like a waste of time as you're actually learning more and more about the world they live in.
Every tiny detail with each of the endings makes you more and more curious as to what the ♥♥♥♥ is going on. The humour and absolute strangeness will bring you in, but the complex storytelling and interesting characters will keep you playing until the end. These pigeons aren't here just to be weird and make sales. They exist for a reason. They exist for a fully devoloped and well thought out reason and it's absolutely worth buying and playing to find out what that reason is first hand. I promise you'll be pleasantly surprised.

If you've played the original MFL, then you know that this remake does it extreme justice. It has all the blood, gore, and violence that you'd want out of a game like this, with suprisingly very good game mechanics that helps you get your violent and football fix all in one.

I never played Mutant League Football (was a Nintendo kid growing up), but I did play the Blitz games throughout the console generations and always enjoyed the violent brutality in them, so when I saw this pop up, it was almost entirely an impulse buy.
I wasn't disappointed. The game has a lot of entertainment value, with jabs at the NFL, its players, scandals, etc., and the over-the-top brutality of MLF and Blitz. Beyond that, it's actually a solid football game, something Steam was lacking, and there are enough options to edit to play the game in a relatively "normal" fashion, if you'd prefer a more basic football game, but doing so does neuter this game. Part of what makes this game fun is the gameplay of football, but also trying your best to absolutely slaughter and kill your opponents. You can, afterall, win the game if your opponent has to forfeit due to  a lack of teammates for certain positions.
The humor is there, the violence is present, and the devs have signaled they'll be releasing a lot of additional content in the future. This is a warm welcome as it addresses my one gripe with the game: there's not a whole lot in it at the moment. You have your basic exhibition (play now), season mode and playoff mode. The incentive to play these lies with the football teams themselves - you have to accomplish certain goals in the different modes in order to unlock all the teams. There are 18 in total, but only 9 start unlocked, and obviously not all NFL teams are lampooned. So this means, you need to have a strong interest in unlocking all 9 teams, as there is currently (but has been confirmed they are planning on including) no team edit, no team creation, no franchise, no story, etc.,. For someone like myself, whose hometown team is NOT in this game, I had to pick the most relatable team to play the season mode with, and the other teams I unlocked, I had no interest in.
Because of this, at 11 hours of gameplay, I've played exhibition mode, beat season mode and playoff mode and have no interest in playing another 20-something games to unlock the last team needed. So the planned additions the developer has - including creation and story modes, also new kills and new races - will most assuredly keep me playing this game more when they come out. As it stands, even right now I definitely feel I got my money's worth out of it, so if you're looking for an outrageous, extreme take on football, check this out.
(To note: there IS an online multiplayer, but I haven't bothered with it, so I can't tell you how well the servers are)

A simple, casual platformer with clean controls, good humor, but little difficulty and some minor level design problems. Although the level design looks like a Metroidvania game, this is more of a mask as there are almost no collectibles and you don't gain any new abilities that change access in the old levels (aside from a generic progression system of "upgraded drill").
PROS:
-Great art / animations
-Soundtrack was amusing
-Locations were varied and entertaining
-Controls are clean
-3 different "forms" throughout the game but controls are consistently good for them all.
NETURALS:
-Ship/Submarine mode was a bit shallow. Mainly just mazes.
-"The Island" seems pointless. Throughout my playthrough I was awarded $100 1 time. Not sure if I should have checked it more or not but I don't see the point.
CONS:
-Cannot skip dialogue scenes (not that many but still).
-"Missions" are very poorly designed. Many of them say to "race to the goal" but there are no markers or identifiers as to where the goal is!
-VERY easy.
-Although the game looks like a Metroidvania game, it has very few collectibles (1 per game zone, like 8 or 9 total) and the levels simply "unlock" as you progress. There is no use of newly found abilities (there are none) to access old areas aside from a "drill upgrade" that lets you go through stronger colored rock. Very generic progression in the level design masked as Metroidvania.

The Chaos system solidifies the very nature of what story-driven games have strived for since their creation: a sense that your actions in gameplay change the world in meaningful ways.
The Chaos system is the way that your gameplay choices, mostly your death count and how you neutralize specific targets, changes specific things in the game from that level on, such as dialogue and visual changes. If you play with a lot of enemy kills, the world itself will become bleaker and more cynical. These changes are so perfectly integrated that it'll take a couple playthroughs to get a sense of how much this system changes the world around you. The end level is completely made over depending on your Chaos, more than any other action game I've played.
I can't imagine that essentially doubling your work knowing that only a fraction of the player base would take the time to notice was an easy choice, but I love that they did it.
Its setting is the richest game setting that I've ever played, hands down. Everything down to the physical setting, people, and books are all in service to painting an amazingly rich and brutal world. Every scrap of supplemental material found in the game has subtext relating to the setting. The world, even at the lowest Chaos level, is cynical and depressing.
People often criticise the story, but I can't think of why. Perhaps in their mind, any story that doesn't try to pretentiously deconstruct video game conventions and instead focuses on a small-scale, tightly wound plot is simplistic drivel, but I think that this plot is one of the best I've played because of its sublety. It's amazingly written and voice acted, and it's confident enough to not hit you over the head with some background mysteries (a couple of which the second one simply lays out the answers to without nuance).

I already tried this game some years back at a free weekend, and quite liked it although I found it a little confusing at first glance, but somehow I didn´t purchase and all but forgot about it. Now I found it F2P, and thought I´d give it another try. I spent the last 1,5 days grinding to get a medium, heavy and light for both Security and Resistance.  I must say, i am very pleasantly surprised.
Graphics are very nice, very smooth, lighting is especially good. Artwork and visual appearance, model and character style (faces, clothing) are top notch, and blend seamlessly with stunning locations and map textures, giving an overall plausible feel although story, locations and characters tend to lean towards caricatures, but it all fits and thus the game has a little twinkle in the eye, without losing its seriousness.
Seriousness and story:  The background story is grim and gritty, and well narrated. It may have a little less depth than Skyrim or Morrowind, but is very coherent in comparison to other shooters, and  is delivered adequately for a fast-paced action shooter. It is also quite intricate, and in its outlines eerily prophetic for a game launched in 2011, what with the major headlines of the last 6 years. As you progress, you learn more about the background and start to wonder, who the good guys really are. Imho, it doesn´t need to fear comparison to extant action movies ( think "District Nine" or "Enemy of the State"). Playing the campaign missions alternating on the resistance and security side makes you really want to proceed, to get to know what´s actually going on. The pre-battle cutscenes are very well made, with smooth animations, plausible dialogue and good voice acting.
Gameplay is very fluent imho, generally fast paced, but with enough retarding elements (reload, objectives, in-battle customization, ect.) to prevent ultra-speed-rushing. It can get hectic around important objectives, where efficient, fluent teamplay is paramount. I can not corroborate the clunkyness other reviewers complain about. I felt the movement is very smooth and adequate, transitions from sprint to crouch, reload animations, shouldering the weapon, activating objectives, vaulting obstacles feel quite fluent, once you learned to time your buttons right, so there is some kind of learning curve here to get really proficient, levelling your character is not all it takes, there is more to it. For examples, not timing  a jump right might have you crashing into a wall and spend a second sprawling on the floor, and objectives do not auto-activate once you are near, you need to look at them and manually activate, which I like. Makes the gameplay more tactical. Furthermore, the challenges provide advanced training for things like that,t and also provide additional customization options as reward.
Customization options for both character and weapons are extensive and very well designed, but still bear a certain console-feel. You need to change menu-levels frequently. Skill system is basic, but adequate.
The only bummer for me is the AI in single play, where a mission can get quite challenging simply because your NPC teammates are thick as a brick, do anything but focus on objectives and exhibit abysmal timing in their actions. A serious lack of commitment to the common cause is what it feels like sometimes. But they are pretty good shots, and the enemy team tends to be tactically imaginative enough to prevent boredom.
What else is there to say?
Give it a try, it´s certainly worth it, and definitely a keeper for me.

Imagine you took Metroid, Final Fight and Lucha Libre and put it in a blender, then you poured that all over the sexiest person you can think of and made love to him/her for 24 hours straight. Then after you are done, you are given a billion dollars, the title of King of the World, and a back rub. That's Guacamelee in a hyperbole enfused nutshell.
In all seriousness, Guacamelee has precision platforming; challenging, old school, pattern based combat; addictive music; actual funny humor; and its a friggin Metroidvania. Plus its gorgeous... It is quite possibly the best game (of the retro-esque platform/combat style) that I've played in years. Definately the best Metroidvania since Monster Tale on the DS, its secrets are not super hard to find, but the skill required to get 100% more than makes up for the slightly easy to find items, and many of the abilities make the back and forth nature of this type of game much less tedious, as almost all of them are movement based in one way or another. There is nothing that I can complain about this game, except maybe that there are no sequels yet, or maybe that its only about 12 hours long for a 100% play through.

Thankfully for the world, the game actually does exist, and it's brilliant.
It's kinda nice to have a game with themes that come from somewhere other than Japan or the United States, even if nothing in Guacamelee should be taken seriously, vis-a-vis the reality of life in Central America. All of the stages and characters are beautifully crafted in a slightly demented sort of way, the fighting flows wonderfully, and the upgrade system is easy to use.
As for differences between Super Turbo Championship Edition and Gold Edition, there is a new boss, a few new regular enemies, two new stages, a few new music tracks, a new special power, and a heavily revised "Hard Mode" - which is many orders of magnitude more diffcult in STCE than it was in the Gold Edition.
In all, I honestly can't think of anything bad to say about the game... Like... At all.

Hmm..
Naturally when you're looking to buy a game, you want to get the latest and greatest version. It should have all the extra content, bug-fixes, and so on. However, the possibility exists that the newest verson could be inferior in some ways. Game-design is a constant and always finicky, and nobody ever seems to be satisfied with its results. So things get changed, and changed again, sometimes they're even changed back to their original state. It's a constantly confusing nightmare, and for what? In the end it all comes down to preference.
Forgive me, I love to ramble.
STCE is on paper*, the superior version of Guacamelee! Let's look at some of the facts:
Two brand-new areas to explore!
A new boss-fight!
Intenso!
Multiple save-slots!
New enemies!
Every foe has a visible health-meter!
etc!
If you're hankering for more Guacamelee, then definitely grab this! The new areas are great. They make the world a bit richer, and are fleshed out with plenty of secrets and fighting/platforming to be had. I also like the little changes such as costumes being unlocked via silver coins. The biggest deal is that the controller-issue I had with Guaca-Gold is fixed, making this by default the superior version for me.
BUT!
STCE is a different game, and it can be considered inferior in a way. The controversial addition is Intenso! It's the "shock gloves"** of Guacamelee. Once you fill a meter you can become a superpowered luchadore by pressing L3+R3. Once you purchase all of the upgrades you're practically invincible. Guaca-Gold wasn't a difficult game, so having the ability to cheese the rare moments of challenge makes things a bit too easy. Keep in mind that this ability is optional. Most of the time I forgot I even had it.
The new enemies are quaint. For the most part they're reskins that can move faster, hit (much) harder, and will sometimes teleport to get out of danger. Aside from nega-chupacabras doing tons of damage with their sword-stab, they're not a threat. There are also some flying fish in one of the new areas. They remind me of enemies from the Saturn version of Symphony of the Night. They only showed up in one area, and behaved in a similar manner. If it's a reference, then I applaud drinkbox for their attention to obscurity.
If you haven't played Guacamelee before, IMO it's best to go straight to this version. It's more convenient, since the original version doesn't have multiple save-slots. Having the most content is a definite plus as well. You might feel the urge to go back to Guaca-Gold for its original "true" level of difficulty but eh...I wouldn't recommend it. Most of Guacamelee's challenge is in a couple of boss-fights, and the optional areas like El Infierno. For the most part you're the awesome skull-cracking luchadore on a fun adventure. If you want a difficult Metroidvania, consider Valdis Story: Abyssal City (also on Steam).
Mostly though I'm just really happy and relieved that the controller issue I had with Guaca-Gold is fixed in this game. It's the main reason I'll probably never go back to the earlier version (though I have a fair number of achievements I should get).
*What is it with "on paper"? I use that phrase way too often.
**The gloves from Batman: Arkham Origins. Punch through any defense, combo count boost, makes things so easy.

Luxor is normally a casual game. There are these snakes of coloured balls, you need to shoot matching coloured balls to make them disappear, before they get to where they want to go. Same thing as "Zuma", except that instead of your player being rooted to the spot and rotating to aim your gun, your gun can move left and right along the bottom of the screen, and always shoots straight up. So - to me, it feels like Zuma crossed with Space Invaders.
This version has nice retro-futuristic arcade graphics, good fast pace, it has a feeling of needing high skill while not actually being that difficult to play, a feeling of progression as you earn new power-ups - and they gain levels, and it has boss levels (yes really!).
It really feels like an arcade game, when I was expecting something more like a mobile app. Which is a nice surprise!
I don't know if this is too obscure of a way of explaining, but it's a bit like the difference between "Space Invaders" and "Space Invaders: Infinity Gene". I guess that's why it's called "Evolved". :)

This was a really fun game much like the original Metroid game.  It is an open world game where you gradually find power ups that open up new parts of the world and allows you to go back and find items that you couldn't acquire before.  In the beginning it doesn't have much of a storyline, but as you go on, the storyline develops and becomes much more interesting.
The game does some pretty neat things with the physics of the game too.  It gives you items that allows you to hack the world around you so that you can teleport through walls, and destroy parts of the world around you.  It also gives you an item to transform certain enemies into different versions of themselves, rendering them either harmless, bigger so they are easier to hit, or helping you reach areas you couldn't before or killing previously unkillable enemies.
The one thing I didn't like about the game is how many weapons the game gives you.  I found 9 weapons and only about 3 of them were useful for killing enemies.  When I looked up a guide I saw that there were at least another 5 - 6 weapons that I didnt find.  Other than that, I had no complaint with the game.  The boss fights were fun and challenging, the storyline was interesting, and the gameplay overall was very enjoyable.  I would certainly play it again.
If you enjoyed super metroid on SNES, you'll love this game.

Guacamelee! Super Turbo Championship Edition is the remake of Guacamelee! Gold Edition.  On it's own it is a fantastic throw-back to Metroid-style platforming, exploration, and "weapon" upgrades that aid combat, mobility, and access to new areas (the weapons being your fists, btw).  It is a remarkable well put together game of roughly the same length as Super Metroid, perhaps a tad shorter.
A solid 10/10 if you're into number rankings. Definitely worth the money, and the time and effort you'll put into getting 100% and playing hardcore mode.
The caveat:
If you already own Gold Edition, I'm not sure this is worth the entry price.  I had and completed Gold Edition shortly after it came out last year.  Not wanting to spend money on this remake without knowing what made it different I finagled myself a copy through trading.  For those who have Gold Edition and are curious, the biggest CHANGE is enemy behavior.  It is slightly more difficult to scum your special attacks ad nauseum.  Another change is that costumes cost a second "silver" currency which is much more rare than the gold.  And the additions amount to 3 new areas with a total extra ~2 hours of gameplay (depending on your play style).  The other addition, which I never found necessary to use is a Turbo mode which makes Juan faster and more powerful for a limited amount of time. And finally you can drop an egg bomb as a chicken.
Are these changes and additions worth $5 to someone who already owns and has played Gold Edition?  Well, that's entirely subjective.  In retrospect I'm glad I didn't spend the money for the remake, but I am glad I got to play it.  I truly love this game, and if it was made 20 years ago I think people would still be hype about it today.
tl;dr
Guacamelee! Super Turbo Championship Edition is worth every penny to a Guacamelee noobie, and is a crapshoot if you've got Gold Edition.
Enjoy!

Luxor has always been towards the runty end of casual, what with taking the least interesting bits from Breakout and Puzzloop and not even really trying to do anything vaguely interesting with anything it does take from. It always, always felt like a bit of a "yeah, I want a marble blaster but totally not Zuma honest guv" thing.
And yet here we are with a vector reimagining of the game, somewhere in the region of Dark Castle Software or Sokurah's house styles and very, very pretty it is too. Yeah, I'm easy and I'm easily sold on things which glow. I can't say I actually imagined for a second it'd be any good but it is good and I'm not sure I know how to parse that. Sure, it's easy. it's tremendously easy and the difficulty curve is pretty much close to non existent but it's satisfying so that's OK, I think.
It is, still, Luxor at its heart. You have a bat that you move across the bottom of the screen to fire the appropriate coloured marble at the marble snake thing that makes its way down the screen. But I dunno, whilst the formula remains the same, the stark neon glow, the great sound effects, the classic arcade bonus rooms, it's like someone really took the time to try and make it work as best they good and then make it pretty too.
I like it. I like it a lot and it surprised me. It's perhaps trying too hard to straddle the casual divide but who cares when you've got neon exploding marbles all over the shop? Did I mention the bonus stages are great btw? The bonus stages are great.
The fast paced action of Luxor Evoled sure makes it stand out from the other luxor titles, but the graphical style reminds me of Asteroids. Too bad there's no sequil to this game.

I can be shallow sometimes. Luxor Evolved first got my attention with its unusual retro vector look, imitating arcade classics like Asteroids, Tempest, and Black Widow. Earlier Luxor games had an offputting sort of Egypt kitsch, but Evolved nicely ties the scarabs and pyramids into stylish, colorful vectors.
It's not entirely skin deep, either. Evolved still follows the basic Luxor design, with the player shooting colored marbles from the bottom of the screen at a train of marbles twisting across the screen, trying to match them three or more at a time before they can reach their destination. But the tempo of play is dramatically faster than other games in the genre, power-ups have more dramatic effects, and visual effects are exaggerated, all helping to create a genuine feel of arcade mayhem.
The bosses have a clever design that creates tension by forcing the player to manage matches in several places at once. Secret levels are cute homages to arcade games from the early 80s. It even encourages a one-credit clear by disabling high scores if you choose to continue after losing your last life.
Luxor Evolved is certainly a casual matching game in genre, but it's got enough arcade trappings that it might grab you where similar games failed. Check it out.

If you're an animal lover of any variety, you'll love it.

What did we get here from the old box of games? IL-2 Sturmovik: 1946 it is!
IL-2 Sturmovik: 1946 is a classic WWII plane simulator with many planes to fly. If you'd ever like a classic dogfight with a friend, this game is good. It is also a good game for stuff like LAN-parties as it can host servers on LAN-only.
This game might be really old, but it is just an absolute gem. It works on new computers (tested on Windows 10 and a gaming PC bought in the beginning of 2015, works perfectly fine in Full HD resolution). The game can literally work on any calculator you own as it is like 10 years old.
Don't let that fool you though, this is quite a good plane simulator. To start up your plane, you need to do a lot of stuff before going into the skies. Physics can be as realistic as you want them to be. Unrealistic physics are the most fun, since can bounce into the sea and still fly, but realism mode changes all that except graphics-wise.
Conclusion:
+ Both realistic and unrealistic can be amazing in their own ways
+ Runs basically on any computer that uses Steam
+ Compatible with new screens
+ Hilarious glitches
+ Great choice of WWII planes and even prototypes
+ Great for LAN-parties
- Quite an old game
- Graphics are not the best in the world
- Unrealistic mode glitches are fun, but sometimes not fun for your opponents
- Render problems at some points (just check my oil lake pictures, that is meant to be a river and a lake)
I CAN recommend this game to anyone who likes their plane simulators, but not everybody will like this ancient gem. I'll leave it up to you, as I DO have more positive points than negative ones, but the negative ones are more significant.

If you like games with fluid controls, the ability to skip cutscenes, non-cheap deaths and interesting character interaction, you definitely are playing the wrong damn game if you pick this horrible title up.
It's trying to be a 2-D Metroidvania style platformer with areas you can go back to eventually, and lots of random abilities to let you go wherever you want, but the controls are god awful. Either you use a pair of sticks (Yes BOTH sticks) to move yourself (The Left Stick) and aim your guns (The Right Stick) which means you'll often be either not moving to avoid hits, or you'll be moving and not firing, or you use the keyboard and mouse to move/attack, which I haven't tried yet but it sounds about as logical as a rabbit ruling hell and losing his seat of power to bathing with a rubber duck.
The opening cutscene doesn't actually run properly, with audio issues galore and sounding like the teacher from the Charlie Brown movies trying to tell a story, while the visuals are static and chopping at best. My machine must not exceed the necessary minimums enough, but even then, there's no reason for it to have no way to go below 1024 x 720 while playing. And there are monsters who can kill you almost instantly, and you have to muddle through their taunting dialouge over and over again. Speaking of which, the respawn time for the monsters is about as long as it takes for them to disappear from the screen's view, so be prepared to kill the same three guys over and over again as you move four inches forward.
Not only are the controls pretty bad for the gunplay, but there are sections that require you to use your circular blade to dig through the ground. THis would be fine if it weren't finicky at best, holding down the right trigger while shifting the stick around to dig can sometimes leave you in stupid positions or not breaking the blocks you want to, but then we get to the jumping. The jump button is a simple press/hold of A, but the height you'll hit is RANDOM. Sometimes you go high, sometimes you go low. BUt often times, you just go straight into spikes, into an enemy you don't want to touch, or under a falling block that kills you. Oh, and Spikes are instant death. For no reason other than to screw you over.
All in all, I didn't pay anything for this game, and I want my money back. Don't waste your time on this steaming turd. Sega, you can and should have done better.

This game really got me from the beginning - I even put Fallout 4 aside for two weeks, just to play and finish Axiom Verge. It is a clever mix of Metroid and Turrican and the setting also reminds me a bit to Kabuki Quantum Fighter. But don't get me wrong - it is definitely not a clone. It has a unique story, look and feel and somehow captures the all the positive things from the classic games I've mentioned before. I especially enjoyed the upgrades and new weapons. And if you think you know everything about a certain map you might be surprised by new secrets the next you come back with more powerful gear. The soundtrack also contributes to the great retro experience.

Now, I never played any Metroid games, or anyother medtroid-vania type games before, so this was first real "introduction"t to the genre. And, well, this game is truly something.
Exploration is, as you would expect, a massive part of this game, so making an interesting world to explore is crucial. Axiom Verge hits that right on the head - each and every area has its own unique (and very well made) visuals, soundtrack and enemies. Finding and exploring each of the diverse and colourful worlds was one of my favourite parts of this game.
The progression of this game is great. you will come upon something, play around with it for a bit, then realise you can't do anything with it and move on. Later, you will come across an item and think, "maybe I can use this to get past that thing I found earlier." You can backtrack to past areas and find find optional stat upgrades and notes, whick give you some backstory.
The story is presented very well - the further you progress, the more is revealed is revealed about the protagonist, the antagonist, the "Rusalki" race, and why and how you are in the strange world of the game. However, the story is, at its core, pretty straightforward.
The combat of this game is nothing to really write home about, but it isn't really terrible either. the enemy design is nice and varied and balanced for the most part, but combat can sometimes feel a bit clunky, especially against faster melee enemies.
The bosses are quite the same - they're challenging enough, but they're all quite unoriginally designed and pretty forgettable.
But overall, Axiom Verge is an absolutely phenomenal game, and I don't think it got the recognition it deserved, especially being developed by a single man. As of when i'm wriring this, the steam christmas sales are inevitably drawing near, so hopefully you'll be able able to pick it up at a discount. But even if you don't get this game at a discount, I would strongly recommend you pick this game up.

Really, Axiom Verge has been praised to the high heavens. Some reviews are so effusive that you'd think it was even better than its obvious inspiration, Metroid. Looking at Metacritic, the PS4 version is only sitting at 84, and it's definitely better than that. So let's dive in, shall we?
First of all, I don't want to hit much in the way of the story. What's here is pretty minimalisitic, and very intriguing, but in the end it doesn't feel like there's much of a resolution to anything. It's left ambiguous, probably intentionally. I don't know if there might be a sequel coming down the pike or not, but the story is certainly rife for exploring more. And finishing the game either under the 4-hour mark or getting 80%+ on items and map coverage leaves you with a scene that's decidedly cliffhanger-ish. I intentionally avoided almost all information about the game until I finished it the first time. The only thing I looked up was how many weapons there were. If you don't want to read about all the powerups and weapons, avert your eyes now!
Yeah, there are a bunch of those. You have a ridiculous array of death-dealing instruments. And the more you explore, the more you're going to find. The default weapon is very much base Metroid. You can get a triple shot, reflecting shot, the Kilver which is a short-range shotgun-style weapon, standard stuff like that, but there's some oddball weapons, too. The Voranj sends lightning blasts out in a huge pattern, but is weak. The lightning gun is crazy overpowered, locking on to an enemy and continuously hitting until they're dead. There's a weapon that feels distinctly like a multi-directional Diskarmor from Rygar. One particularly devious bit of puzzling will see you snag a Flamethrower, and that thing is really powerful in certain areas. There are 23 weapons in total, although three of them are super-secret weapons that you can only find in glitched secret worlds, and there is only one of them generated per save file. I ended up with the Heat Seeker, a really powerful homing shot that is actually even more powerful than the lightning gun.
There are also many powerups for your weapons, and for traversal methods. You can snag range, size, and power upgrades for your weapons, although sometimes they don't apply to certain ones. You'll also find the standard health upgrades. Then there are the cool ways to get around. Sure, you get some standard stuff like the high jump, and you get a drill that takes the place of bombs. But eventually, you'll get some more interesting stuff like a lab coat that lets you "glitch" through walls. This will upgrade a few times through the game. You also have a glitch gun that can affect the environment and enemies. It's certainly an interesting conceit, because a few puzzles rely on glitching enemies to achieve your goals, and it also lends to a sort of "is this really happening" vibe.
Small gaps are also fun. We all know about Samus' ability to roll up for small passages. Well, Trace can't do that. Instead, he gets a remote drone that he can use to navigate the passages. Eventually, you'll get the ability to throw that further, which also pairs with one of the last abilities, being able to warp to where the drone is. Wild stuff, that. There's also a shout-out to Bionic Commando with a biological-looking grappling hook, and the physics behave almost just like the NES game. Cool stuff!
I like a lot of the look of the game, but some of it bothers me as well. The game clearly shoots for a sort of biological horror / H.R. Giger-style look, and it largely succeeds. My only real gripe is that while the game is tile-based, it looks too tile-based. A lot of platformers attempt to hide this a little better, including Metroid, and this one doesn't do that quite as well. It's still solid, though, because the alien vibe is always there, the creatures are monstrous and well-designed, and everything just feels... wrong, but in the way that the designer intended. That couples with the soundtrack, a thumping, pulsing, heavy-bass score that goes really well with the sort of biological/mechanical motif.
With all those weapons, you'd think combat was great, and eventually it gets there, but enemies feel very bullet-spongey early on, especially if you haven't explored well and gotten a few weapon powerups. This gets better, but the game overall feels a bit more combat-focused than a Super Metroid, where atmosphere is king and most enemies are felled pretty rapidly. This game feels much more like if Super Metroid had held quite a bit closer to the original game than it did.
I mentioned the secret glitched worlds earlier, and those are pretty slick, too. You'll always find two powerups in them. You'll know you're close to one when the screen starts to get a strong CRT scanline effect with some distortion. Apparently the location of these is randomized from game to game, and the layouts are as well. No drill-wall secrets, though, so just get your stuff and get out!
Overall, I really, really enjoyed my time with the game. I know a game has its hooks in when the first thing I want to do when I get home is play the game, so this totally succeeds on that front. If you've got a strong hankering for a Metroid game, and you've blown through AM2R, this is a worthy competitor. Play it. You may love it more than I did.  It doesn't dethrone Super Metroid or Metroid: Zero Mission, but it's certainly quality entertainment, and stronger than most Metroid-likes out there.

When Stellar 2D was originally released, there was a massive bug. The main menu was always prominently displayed, even while playing the game. This menu took up probably half the screen, so most players had no idea what was going on. Before long, the developed issued a patch that fixed this problem.
Unfortunately, that just makes Stellar 2D's other massive faults easier to discover. This is a survival-based 2D shooter, only you can never really tell what's going on. As is typical of the genre, you have to fly around and dodge bullets. Problem is, the bullets are hard to see, and their hit-boxes are impossible to determine. Most of the time, you only survive thanks to RNG sending lots of armor and shield refills your way.
While you're trying to figure that mess out, certain tri-colored powerups will fly on-screen. Usually these items are bad news; they cause you to stop shooting, fly very slowly, or become unable to move in certain directions. Supposedly this is a "risk vs reward" setup. So I have to ask: Where is the reward? There's a 5% chance I'll get something good, or at least something that won't lead to death. The odds aren't worth it, so I have to try and dodge those powerdowns, as well as the practically invisible bullets. Awful controls, terrible graphics, and decent music round out this package.
I think I liked this game better back when it still had the main menu bug.
It's as if Frankenstein's monster had a goiter. The goiter was removed, but that still leaves a creature that should not exist.
