Mutant Football League is the spiritual successor to the 1993 Genesis game of--just about the--same name. It's a 7-on-7 American style football game featuring teams of monsters battling it out for gory gridion supremacy in an "after the bomb" world.
"Gory? Football is violent, but not THAT violent", you say? Ah, but it turns out trolls, skeletons, and robots are more cavalier about possible concussions or, uh, dismemberment, than real-life footballers. Indeed, in the Mutant Football League scooping up a diva wide receiver and breaking him in half with a move normally seen in professional wrestling isn't unsportsmanlike, it's the norm!
Even if you're not the type to willfully command your players to murder their opponents, players still must contend with the environmental hazards of the various fields: land mines, buzzsaws, pits of molten lava, sandworms, and more. If fatalities run high, you might have to play without a running back, or with half an offensive line. Lose enough players, and you might even have to forfeit the game.
MFL offers a fairly standard assortment of game modes: play now; a 13 game season with an eight team playoff; a playoff mode; practice; and online play. Online mode has random matchmaking, or the option to create a password protected room.
There are 18 teams playing for a chance to win the Mayhem Bowl, three: the Galaxy Chaos, Orcs of Hazzard, and Tokyo Terminators, are wholly original, and made up entirely of speedy aliens, bruising orcs and trolls, and versatile robots, respectively. The other fifteen are parodies of real NFL teams, including many of their players, such as the Nuked London Hatriots and their unsettlingly handsome skeleton quarterback, Bomb Shady; or the New Yuck Tyrants and their ridiculously coiffed--and ridiculously fast--demon receiver, O'Hell Wreckem Jr. These teams strengths and weaknesses correspond quite well to the current (2017) NFL season.
Teams have decent sized playbooks to choose from that are reminiscient of their real counterparts, with roughly half a dozen or so formations with a handful of plays each. You also have access to Dirty Tricks -- two per half for offense and defense. Plays like Strawberry Fields, where you lace whatever undead drink with hallucinogenic drugs, which reverses your inputs if used on a human, or makes the computer act erratically; or giving your running back a chainsaw for one play, with which he can literally cut a swathe through an enemy offensive line. Each team has a different handful of tricks they can use, and every team can bribe the referee, giving him a chance to make blatantly bad calls in your favor until he is either bribed in return by the opponent, or murdered (which is one of the few ways to definitely incur a penalty in this game. Say what you will about zebras, but they protect their own!) Finally, during half-time a Smash TV style minigame (think top-down twin-stick shooter) will play where you, armed with a gun, try to survive for 30 seconds against a hoard of zombie referees. Scoring 500 points and keeping your brains firmly inside your skull will grant you a Resurrection Dirty Trick you can use in the second half to bring back one dead player.
During the action all the basic functions are here: switching control of a defending player mid-play, dives, spins, jukes, leaps. You can call time-outs and audibles, and make substitutions to get specialized players on the field for certain tasks, or just to let a character heal a bit between plays (players have lifebars that greatly recharge between plays.)
Gameplay options include typical fare like changing the quarter time from one through fifteen minutes, and gameplay speed to either slower, normal, fast, or fastest. If you really just want to play Madden you can turn Dirty Tricks off, you can also turn incrase or decrease the damage players take, and even play with deaths turned off altogether. Difficulty has five settings, and begins to play competently on normal.
As for the audio/visual, I always find it best to let people make up their own mind by looking at some gameplay footage, since everyone's got different expectations of what constitutes good graphics or art design. This is a game by a small indie team, so expectations need to be kept realistic. Regardless, I think the graphics, and particularly the art style, are quite good, staying true to the designs of the old genesis game, and brought cartoonishly to life in 3D.
On sound, each team has their own theme song, which is a nice touch, and the in-game music is generally pretty appropriate for football; all horns, guitars, and bombast -- very NFL films. I really like the commentary, a two person (but three head) group headed up by the nostalgia bomb that is Tim Kitzrow of  NFL Blitz and NBA Jam fame, providing delightfully antagonistic play-by-play, and remarkably crass banter. This stuff is definitely unsafe for the ears of minors, or the politically correct. An option does exist to turn off the mature language, if you like your cartoonish blood and gore without potty humor. For what it's worth, I think they've provided some USDA Choice potty humor.
So, finally, how do I feel about it, and where do I think the game could be better. There's a surprising amount of strategy that goes into playing around your opponent's potentially game-changing Dirty Tricks, and the parody teams do a great job of invoking their real-life counterparts, all the while being imbued with a newly quirkly charm. As someone who enjoys AAA sports games for management, but finds them too slow for playing actual matches, I think this game has it just right, playing a slightly simplified game tuned for speed and ease of use, not unlike how major sports titles used to play back in the 16-bit era.
There are definitely some annoyances, some of which I'm sure will be addressed in upcoming patches. Buzzsaws are way too brutal an environmental hazard in their current state, and playing in any stadium featuring them over the course of a whole season presents a brutal home court disadvantage, because they routintely kill multiple players every kick-off, and heaven help you if you find the line of scrimmage overlapping their tracks. Also, playing on higher difficulties reduces the amount of Resurrections you get between games, but since player deaths are often outside of your control this doesn't feel like something you can overcome with any level of skill. I LIKE that this happens; I enjoy a bit of random misfortune in my games, but it shouldn't completely tank my season all by itself. Lastly, half of the teams need to be unlocked by fulfilling certain requirements first. None of the requirements are particularly difficult, but some are definitely time consuming, and I could see this being frustrating for fans of those teams.
I have confidence that the developers want to make this a spectacular game; Michael Mendheim's been trying to get this game made for years, so it's clearly a passion project, and I think this game has the potential to be a truly great football game if they're able to continue adding to it. A story mode of sorts would be great, considering the colorful cast of characters and post-apocalyptic setting, and obviously the remaining 15 NFL teams seem like an almost mandatory future addition. But even in its current state it's just a blast to play, and considering the dearth of football titles on the PC, any fan of the sport should at least give it a look. There's a demo available for the skeptical, so there's no reason not to try your hand at a little mutant mutilation!

The biggest mistake of my life was taking this game as a joke. I think that was probably the case for most of the players.
When I first learned of this vn I played the free version that was available thinking it was going to be a silly game and I ended up feeling sad and almost crying about my pigeon boyfriend, I was quite surprised. I did not expect a pigeon dating sim of all things to make experience such a sentiment. Unfortunately I did not keep playing.
Fast forward around 2 years later and while I was thinking about buying it during Steam’s Holiday sale it was gifted to me by a friend. I played a different route and had a lot fun, it was lighthearted and entertaining but again after that I forgot about it. The two routes I had experienced were entertaining and lasted about an hour but it wasn’t something to keep me going and encouraging me to play it all in one sit through.
Now…Today….I decided to see the rest.
I started with the pigeon Okosan that was obviously a joke even his “Human” avatar was still a pigeon and it was quite a silly route. While I kept playing some strange information was mentioned about events happening at the school. It didn’t really go into much detail just students gossiping about the mysteries of the school, talking about the mad scientist doctor, simple things like that. The more I played although somewhat repetitive these small snippets of information were given out and you gain some superficial knowledge about these events during specific routes. The way it was presented was slightly unexpected due to what I thought the nature of the game would be but it still retained some humorous and silly aspects.
Then it happened… I started yet another new game to keep seeing the remaining achievements/endings and was presented with a choice that wasn’t there before.
I was not prepared for what was waiting for me.
This was BBL what I assume to be the True Route and was quite a twist and change in atmosphere. Honestly I think this is where the game truly shines, I wouldn’t like to spoil anything but it basically explains the whole story around the school, how birds became intelligent, why a single human was studying in an all pigeon school, etc. and it does a good job of bringing the normal route stories together.
If I were to describe BBL in detail you probably wouldn’t believe me, I mean, it’s just a silly bird game poking fun at visual novels right?
I thought this was pretty amazing; the way the game presented itself with pink hearts, silly premise of dating birds, and the introduction of Okosan the pudding loving pigeon. There’s was just nothing to indicate the serious grim tale that would unfold (or maybe there was if I had payed attention to the archives oops). It caught me so off-guard and just had me hooked for hours.
I truly recommend this, for me it was a very enjoyable and rewarding experience.  If you don’t want to pay $10 then pick it up during a sale.

Hoi4 is satisfying and does a lot of things right but it has big flaws too
The gameplay can feel like watching paint dry, especially in the early game. I suppose it’s part of the experience so its not a huge deal. Hoi4 is much more ”strategic” than other strategy games i’ve played, there are tons of things to keep track of, such as, research, national focuses, manpower, world tension and so much more. There are lots of alternate history routes to go down for many countries. But some, like germany, russia, italy and japan are sort of forced down a chosen path. Sure, you could play democratic germany but what then is there to kick off the war in europe? Most smaller nations usually have a choice to go  democratic, communist or fascist, which can change up history singificantly and spawn new and fascinating scenarios, like rebuilding austria-hungary for example. But since the biggest powers are almost forced to fit a certain role, this leaves a lot to be asked in terms of alt-history. Over all, the alt-history potential is great, but could be a whole lot better. Now let’s move on to the gameplay. For starters, the AI is a joke, it likes to spam put massive amounts of bad units instead going for a better army in general, now this would make some sense for some countries like china and russia, problem is all the AIs do it to the point where it even starts to bog down your pcs performance. It starts wars it cant win, which results in absolutely disgusting amounts of border gore. Due to all the small bordering countries it didn’t kill off as they should and sometimes they can even just march in and grab land with no opposition, despite being the ones who were ”attacked”. And hand-holding your (ai) allies is almost guaranteed to occur due to your allies starting fights they can’t win. I would watch some  Let’s plays before buying to get a  good idea of how things work. I would also suggest waiting for a sale if you’re looking to buy it. Definately wait for sale if buying dlc too.

text:
Spoiler Warning: Axiom Verge is good, but ultimately not that great. The developer was amazing in how he was able to get all of it done himself, but it shows, and brings down the game.
Positives:
The way new mechanics of the "glitching" and drone are what really make Axiom Verge unique, and a welcome improvement on Metroid-like mechanics. The weapons have a good variety of behaviors.
The art has a distinct style to it, which is understandable from only one developer worked on this.
The universe has a lot of room for development and I would love to see more.
Negatives:
The world does not flow in a very organic or progressive way. The areas have little sense of connection, and although one or two weapons are useful for opening areas, this quickly goes out the window. The game plays a lot closer to Metroid II (the very linear Gameboy version) compared to a newer Metroidvania game, for most of the game. Only at the end where one is getting the last few skills or items do you need more than what was immediately made available or have to go to a previous part of the map to advance the game.
The world is very tight, which is the most important aspect of what the game does poorly. It's all action all the time, with very little of the map being relevant story-wise, and very little of the story coming out in the gameplay or environment. Never during play did I think "I really like this room/level" because it was beautiful or the way it fit the moment. Additionally, there's usually only a few new enemies per area or less, and these will be what you see in that area. After a while the game gets into re-coloring a few enemies, which is a little jarring because they're seemingly only used for some obnoxious difficulty in certain locations/battles.
The story at first was very interesting, but it doesn't get developed beyond an absolute minimum required to make the game go through a handful of plot points. There's also some glaring plotholes, like somehow you're in a computer environment (hacking and glitching) but also on an alien planet, and in a decayed civilization, and it just doesn't come together. Only at the very end does the final location mostly make sense given the plot. The lack of coherency between the world, story, and gameplay is the biggest problem with Axiom Verge.
The controls could've used a little work. The grapple mechanic is hilariously bad. I was really surprised at how poorly it controls given the author borrowing so heavily from Metroid. The grapple is pretty quickly superceded so it's not that bad, but it stands out the most. The weapon quick-select is also confusing, and the weirdness of how it behaves disrupts the combat considering how many guns you can get. The controller seems to have some deadzone (maybe 15%) but the lack of the option can make dashing and menu controls difficult with analog joysticks.
On the guns, there's not much of a difference between them in practice. Most enemies move too erratically to be fought by some weapons, and a number of the guns have pitiful range or pitiful damage, both of which gets you killed. Eventually you get upgrades for both range and damage, but this just makes the "useful" guns even better. Combat is pretty boring too, with enemies never being stunnable or blockable, having no weapon-specific behavior, etc, so it just comes down to spamming enough bullets. Many of the later enemies just dive right at you with near-unavoidable hits. The glitching helps make this more interesting, but late-game you end up just taking damage if you want to glitch (it takes time and might only slow them down), or take damage if you run straight in, so there's not much of a benefit.
On the art, most of the art time went seems like it went into the backgrounds, and not enough on enemies. The world has have plenty of art, which could've been used in more rooms, and even something like rotating tiles would stretched out the existing art. More enemies! What I would've given for just more space with more enemies. All the enemies even have only a few frames of animation, so it's not like more would've been that problematic. The art itself is more of a NES/GBC feel than SNES/GBA, and the visual crowding in a lot of places detracts from the detail and what could've been a simplicity of art.
Late game-item hunting is a pain, because some items are hid behind foreground and you can't tell where anything is. Games used to get around this by having some hint-mechanic (noises, x-ray), and it's annoying Axiom Verge didn't inherit that.
Overall:
For a game from a single developer, Axiom Verge is amazing. It brings some new mechanics to the table for other platformers to play with and take hints from. While the gameplay shines, the story and feeling of the game suffer immensely. I would absolutely only recommend it if you really really like the basic mechanics of Metroidvania games, because mechanics are all it does well.

I've done three characters' routes so far, so perhaps it isn't accurate to judge the game with only this short amount of time, but I felt the need to explain some issues I have with it now, because of the lack serious critical reviews that accentuate some of the flaws of the game.
*I understand this is somewhat of a "joke game" but I want there to be an honest review out there for anyone expecting more*
- There is no option to scroll back to text you just read through
- Saves frequently glitch out so that text is never displayed when you load them, rendering them useless.
- Sometimes steam will not register that you completed a route, and won't give the proper achievement.
- The skip button does not stop at unread text, which would be more of a problem if any new text got added until the last few lines of each route. Events barely change based on your choices, if at all.
- While the characters are interesting, they are given no time to be fleshed out in their routes because scenes start and end so quickly. You get maybe ten lines of text, often times less, in scenes like the festival or sports event. The difference between a good endign and a bad ending for the routes that have multiple ones is a small bit of extra text at the very end.
- A lot of the jokes fall flat, referencing anime tropes, etc. which was probably intentional given that the game is meant for the shock value. I can give this a pass because it is trying to recreate a stereotypical date sim.
- The stat-raising element is pointless and makes an otherwise mind-numbingly simple game frustrating to solve without a walkthrough. Example: for some reason, not hinted at anywhere, you can only get
if you

- Some of the character portraits are blurry on larger resolutions. The audio is pretty good aside from some low quality sound effects and at least one music track I recognize as most likely stock music.
I really like the over-the-top personalities and I think they really could've hit it out of the park if they were given more time to develop. Once you've gone through the game one time you can skip through every bit of in-between dialogue that isn't character specific, leaving around 20 minutes of actual gameplay per route.
It's times like these where I wish you could select an option between "no" and "yes" in steam reviews because, for what the game is, it's very cute. When it's shocking, it's shocking. when it's funny, it's funny. Perhaps the game improves in the final route (I already feel things bubbling under the surface) but the lack of comforts of a typical visual novel and general lack of functionality make it REALLY uncomfortable to drudge through the game several times over, despite how short it really is.

Hands down the greatest attraction and calibre in this game come from its papercraft art style. It's fun to look at, humorous both in writing and art, and the story itself is better than most arcade games in general, let alone indie-arcade.
Gameplay can be a frustrating or challenging aspect of Derrick, depending on how you view it. It follows the trend of mechanics-as-game (i.e. qwop) where trying to play the game IS the game. While Derrick is not extreme enough to be placed in that category, learning to use the mechanics to play the game will be a good portion of initial gameplay.
The arcade environment as well is different, as the levels seemingly will encourage you to explore, yet the timer is short enough that you can't stray too far from the main path - though that brings me to my next point.
There isn't a clear main path.
Most timed arcade games will have a very narrow or fixed path for the character to go (like endless runner games), but the basic game mode will not. This can be frustrating if you're looking to explore the level further vs run through to get a good time.
Having said all this, because the game is so different, I hesistate to categorize these as negatives because once you adjust or set these expectations in mind, it's actually a quite enjoyable and challenging game.
For retail I probably would pass, but on sale and as a collector of unique games, definitely worth picking up and playing at some point.

I loved BRINK way back, and I still love Brink. Now that it's gone Free to Play, people are finally playing online again.
The game was hyped as hell back in the day, but quickly died. It was a shame, because it was a brave new IP in a world full of cynical consumers and franchises that should have died long ago.
BRINK is a fast-paced, parkour-styled, objective and class-based shooter with lots of flair and lots of style. Character customization is kick♥♥♥♥♥ as are all the weapons you can play with. Some weapon classes feel more or less the same, and some weapons are only available to certain character frames (light/medium/heavy). The options of frames and classes makes for interesting, varied playstyles. As a light frame, you're restriced to light weapons (pistols, SMGs, etc), but you can move in ways no other frame can, giving you plenty of ambush and escape-points. The medium frame has access to all but the heavy weapons, and you can jump/slide over most objects. The heavy has access to all weapons, like a kick♥♥♥♥♥heavy revolver-fed shotgun, a grenade-machine gun, and even a goddamn minigun. On the other hand, the heavy can't climb any of the objects in the world.
The maps are pretty big, and at first somewhat confusing. Take some time just free-running through the maps, knowing the maps well can be vital at times. If you don't, you'll get really frustrated when the other team pins you down.
There's a drawback to the PC version though. It's free now, and that's great, but if you're running really new hardware, you'll crash a lot. If you run it on circa 2010 hardware, you're in the green. BUT, you'll be disconnected a lot. For some reason the servers will kick anyone at any time because it "failed to authorize" a player.
Then again, it's free. It's a great shooter, for free, with no pay2win stuff whatsoever. I'd say go for it. If it doesn't work, so what? Just uninstall and move on. You'll potentially have an absolute blast.

The original Guacamelee! is one of my favorite "Indie" games that I own, and I was extremely excited when I heard that the Super Tubo Championship Edition came to PC. I purchased it immediately and just finished my Normal playthrough.
Guacamelee!: Super Turbo Championship Edition adds a good amount of extra content, in the form of new levels, new enemies scattered throughout the game, a new boss, and new abilities. It's a "Metroidvania" style 2D action game, but instead of a bounty hunter or vampire hunter, you play as Guacamelee!, a luchador fighting his way through both the land of the living and the dead to rescue his love.
The Good:
*Unique art style drawing from Mexican folklore, specifically the "Day of the Dead"
*Great music and environments
*Tight controls
*Clever, rarely frustrating platforming sections
*Fun combat, with a mix of combo-based striking and grappling
*Simple story with humor and references to classic games all over every stage of the game
The Bad:
*Can't remap controls on a controller. This is a minor gripe, because the controls make sense, except for the new "Intenso" mode, which requires pressing LS and RS simultaneously on a gamepad. This is annoying, especially considering that RB and RT are both mapped to the same function, and either could have been switched to Intenso mode.
*Game is short. I wanted it to last longer. There is replayability in a Hard mode unlock and a challenge guantlet of sorts, with lots of hidden items to go back and find for 100% completion. But even with the added content, I beat the game in 9 hours (not 100%), with a considerable amount of backtracking and exploration.
*The new Intenso mode makes combat far too easy on Normal playthrough. Entering Intenso mode lets you just wail on anything until it runs out, forgoing combos and dodging entirely.
Overall, I'd highly recommend this game. As an owner of the original Guacamelee!, I received the upgrade at a discount (67% off, or $5). I had no issues replaying the game from scratch, because it's fun. I'd be less likely to recommend the upgrade to existing Guacamelee! owners at $15, because there's not THAT much new content. For new owners, however, $15 is absolutely worth it, even with the short length of the game. You'll want to get 100% completion, and then tackle Hard mode if you still haven't had enough.

Although picking a side does not matter too much as the same character can be used for Both Story playthroughs. They will just have different cosmetics for each side. I've come to enjoy the stories of both sides as it tells an Interesting story and really gets you into the next mission.. or at least the first three days of a story do. After the first 3 days, you'll be hitting your head off your Keyboard as a Difficulty spikes hits and you start to realize you'll just be playing basically the same thing, but with a fresh coat of Visuals and little gameplay change. Overall and despite my problems, I rate the story as the Highlight of this game.
(I must warn that Day 6 of the Security story "Launch day" is nearly Impossible to complete in solo. GET FRIENDS FOR THAT MISSION)
GAMEPLAY:
I'll say it right now, You'll really get a Dirty Bomb feel when you play this game. The gameplay and looks of the game really make it seem like it's a Dirty Bomb rip-off, despite coming out before Dirty Bomb. You'll spawn in after watching a Introduction to the Mission, and then its running to your objective hoping you don't get picked off by that one Bot that seems really good at standing in narrow corners with a shotgun. You'll arrive at the objective and pray that your A.I (or player) teamates can keep you alive while you repair/build as an Engineer, plant bombs as a Soldier and Hack things as a operator. The A.I can do the Objective too, But sometimes they just don't want to and plan to end their lives by running at the enemie head on. If they do attempt the Objective, you really gotta protect them as they will stand still like ducks and basically wait to die. Protecting is harder then it sounds as Enemy A.I will target the class that can complete objectives, meaning you will have to be Literal meatshield for the repairing/bomb planting/hacking/ or building teamate. It's not any easier when you attempt the Objective as Teamates forget how to aim, or decide its a good time to run off and do other unimportant things around the map.
COMBAT:
The Guns:
As Tony the Tiger likes to say: "They're grrrrrreat!"
The guns in Brink all feel and play well most of the time. They look nice too. Although (in my opinion) the Revolutionist have the best looking guns. It seems the people of the ARK really like Automatic weapons such as Assault rifles and SMGs cause there is alot of those in this game. They are the guns that really shine in this game. On the other less liked hand is Shotguns and Semi-rifles. Shotguns feel very Inconsistent. They have pretty good range, despite being shotguns and can put anyone down from close to Medium range. Sometimes even long range if you are lucky with the spread. That's not even the worse part. Sometimes the shotgun seems to really lack in damage when the enemy is right in front of you. You could Shoot a bad guy standing RIGHT in front of you, and ethier kill him, or bring his health down to half. He'll then gladly turn around and One shot you with his very own shotgun. As for Semi-rifles, they ultimatly don't feel that well tuned. Despite seeming as the most accurate guns, You'll find yourself missing more shots then you hit. And when a shot does hit, the damage never feels worth it. Honestly, any Assault rifle replaces the Semi-rifles as a better weapon to use. Pistols feel nice to use, but share the same problems as Semi-rifles. I don't really include that as a downside cause Pistols are suppose to be weak. At least in game sense.
Melee:
You get one source of melee and thats whacking your enemies with the butt of your gun. It's a really Unreliable Melee as it's best use is knocking someone back and throwing off their aim. However, your lucky if you can even get that close to a target and you'll be even luckier if the Melee actually hits and you won't be on the ground begging for a Revive. Melee is best used against other players as A.I will easily shoot you down, wether the Melee connects or not.
Grenades:
Every class gets Grenades, But you'll quickly learn that they aren't so great. Sometimes, they feel great and deal good amounts of damage while knocking enemies down and screwing up their aim. On other times, it feels like you threw a rock and the Enemy shrugs off the small damage and proceeds to fill you with holes. I highly recommend using a gun that can get a Grenade Launcher added on as this makes Grenades much more Reliable. (but lowers the throwing range)
GUN CUSTOMIZATION
As the trailer shows, you can customize your guns with a couple different add-ons. These don't alter the gun too much, but they help and you'll find Gunfights to be much more Enjoyable with a sight or grenade launcher on your side. The challenges to unlock these add-ons aren't even that hard, meaning you'll be rocking a sweet gun in no-time as long as you know what you are doing.
CHARACTER CUSTOMIZATION
Another Highlight of the game. I was rather glad to see the Offers this game gave in terms of Customization. It's actually rare for two players to look absoultly the same. I've spent alot of my time in this game just deciding the best outfit for my next misson. However, character Customization is not without faults. My biggest nitpick is the lack of females in the game. There are no female characters at all. None in the story. The only hint of females is from Audio logs you obtain while playing the game. For a game that prizes itself on great Character Customization, it's pretty ♥♥♥♥ing damning that the game does not Support Female models and the Develops never added any in the (6?)+ years that this game has been released for. But, I must agree that the Character Customization is great, and people will love tricking out their Security soldier, or Revolutionist to the max.
As I, and many others have said, Brink is a good game. It has a great concept, but was just executed poorly. With the right love and Support, Maybe Brink can grow to be something great in the crowded First person shooter genre. Then again, it did just go Free-To-Play. so maybe not.
Although with everything I wrote here, I do urge others to try the game for themsleves. It's worth a play.

Guacamelee is awesome. It's got impressive art style, gameplay is tight and music is great.
The best part of it is combat system. It's fluid and fast. You combine regular kicks and special moves into spectacular combos, finishing of enemies with piledrivers, throws and slams. Dodging is easy, so combat in this game is more about fun then frustrating challenge(unless you'll go for OPTIONAL stuff to get achievments).
Platforming gets gradualy more difficult and more creative as you learn new moves, but it won't be a problem(unless you'll go for OPTIONAL stuff to get achievments).
The world is huge and different, all areas are themed. Exploring it and finding hidden chests with upgrades is fun. Sometimes to get to the chest you'll have to beat platforming puzzles, sometimes combat challenges. There're also some side quest, which are mostly there for comedy reasons. Guys at Drinkbox generaly have a good sense of humor. You'll find a lot of references to your favourite indie and childhood games.
The plot is simple, yet characters are different and weird(in a good way). Every big area ends with a boss fight of sort. I don't know, the game is generaly crafted so well, I'd call it a masterpiece. Go get it!
PS. I've beaten Gold Edition and now replaying this version on a Hard Mode.

SO, got that out of my system.

Axiom Verge is a beautifully crafted experience that seems to have come into existence as a result of its creator's love for Super Metroid. Yes, that's right, creator is singular! A single individual, Thomas Happ, created all the art, music, story, dialogue, code, and all the other miscellaneous required elements of a game. While I don't think that's something that can be factored into a review necessarily, I will say that I find that incredibly impressive. I find myself inspired!
If you enjoyed Super Metroid, you would probably find this a lot of fun. The mechanics are similar in terms of movement, exploration, and progression. It's a truly solid 2d side-scrolling platformer.
The game opens to a small sequence featuring a scientist performing an experiment. Something goes wrong, and the building they're in collapses. This scientist is revealed to be the player, as the focus shifts to the same man awakening in an alien room, having been enclosed in an egg-like machine. A voice speaks out to you from an unknown origin, and it names you: "Trace".
After some initial dialogue, the game sets you loose to complete your initial objectives and get yourself comfortable with how the game operates. As you complete your objectives and explore the dangerous paths from point to point, you'll reveal more about the strangely organic alien world. Are the machines biological, or is the life here machine-based? What are the implications of some of the characters' appearances and motivations? It will be revealed to you in time, as you fight your way through a hostile planet to find your purpose here.
The movement of your player is vitally important in a game like this. You need to be able to interface very strongly with the game to accurately control your player and the weapon(s) they may be using to interact with the environment and fight the aggressively hostile enemies. Patience is a virtue here, as with other games like Super Metroid, where being brazen and reckless will result in your quick death. Watching how your foes move and respond and predicting their actions will benefit you greatly.
The controls themselves are simple, and very responsive. Once you understand the functions of the inputs, you can often use them to their full potential immediately.
The progression in this game comes in the form of items and weapons, which I'll refer to jointly as 'tools'. These tools will help you remove enemies blocking your path, eliminate obstacles in your way, and create new weaknesses in the environment and foes for you to exploit more easily. You're offered large areas to explore, but there is one correct route that will yield you a new tool. This new tool will demonstrate its utility to you immediately, and you'll remember an area you thought was impassable. It may no longer be!
The first time I played this game, I found it performed exceedingly well at surprising me with new mobility upgrades. I had been mentally noting locations that I might be able to come back to with new tools, but some of the tools so fundamentally changed how I navigate the environments that I was caught by surprise several times and needed to revisit some areas to see if there was a new path present. There often was.
The environment created by the developer in this game is excellent. Each zone has a unique feel to it, matching its purpose in the game world, and each room within has a carefully designed atmosphere within the zone.
The fact that it was all made by a single person becomes clear over time, as the thematic elements of each zone become unified in the music, tile art, and background art alike. The soundtrack immediately became one of my favorite game soundtracks in recent history, particularly the songs that play when
and
. I'm listening to the soundtrack now, actually! And not just because I'm writing this review :)
If you, like me, are prone to getting tunnel vision in games like this, where you hyper-focus on the mechanical elements and grow somewhat blind to the actual audiovisual elements presented... I highly encourage you to periodically 'stop and smell the roses' by listening to the music and examining the background art in some of the rooms as you move about. It's worth it!
Axiom Verge is mechanically challenging. Even on its lower difficulty settings, bosses are not a trivial matter. But, this game is in no way unfair! I find that the distinction between fairness and difficulty is an incredibly important one to make, and while this game may be difficult, it is not unfair. You always have the ability to analyse an enemy and find its weakness. You always have the ability to be patient and careful in your movement to evade incoming attacks. I find that I'm sometimes an impatient gamer, and most of the times I died while fighting enemies in this game, it was purely due to my recklessness, or my greed demanding I take another few shots at the boss before it enters its firing phase.
This game has difficulty options present when you start the game. I almost universally select 'Normal' and enjoy a single playthrough at the 'average' difficulty, so I don't drown out the story or environmental elements with the mechanical complexity in a game. After I finished my 'Normal' playthrough of Axiom Verge, though, I immediately went again for a 'Hard' run. I had enjoyed exploring the environment so much in 'Normal' that I had obtained 100% of the tools available. I tried going through in 'Hard' while getting as few tools as possible, and it was a significant challenge initially. I later felt like I had an excellent mastery of the controls as a result.
Technically, this game is very solid. I experienced no obvious instances of the game malfunctioning or causing me to lose progress or resources by failure of the medium. Pretty much all errors were mine.
I wish to make a special note about this game that may be considered a spoiler. I'll enclose it in spoiler tags here for you to look at later. If you find the game may be malfunctioning in some way or are concerned that your computer is not running it properly,
Performance-wise, I had no problems running it. It's a very graphically simple game with no 3D elements to speak of, as I can recall. I think any relatively modern non-gaming computer could probably run this game with no trouble.
This has to be one of my favorite games in my collection. I really enjoyed playing through it not once, but twice, and experiencing the challenges it offered. I thought it was difficult initially, but grew much easier over time as I got used to the play style and the controls.
I would highly recommend this game to anybody who had fun with Super Metroid or similar games (Cave Story might apply!). I'm incredibly impressed with Thomas Happ, and very glad he decided to put his time and effort into this experience. Thanks!

Though it has different gadgets and a different world/story, this is Metroid in all but name. But that's not a bad thing at all. In fact, it does everything you'd expect from a great Metroid game: wide open exploration of a weird alien planet, an assortment of an usual weapons and gadgets, challenging but not impossible boss battles. It's all here. Definitely recommend.

I started playing Quacamelee! Gold Edition, and though I really liked the gameplay mechanics, I wasn't a big fan of the theme at first. I also have a long queue of unplayed games I've been trying to get through, and so I set it down for a while. And then a while became a freaking long time.
So I saw GSTCE come out, and thought to myself, hey that game was a lot of fun, here's the perfect excuse to go back. So I picked it up, and this time I couldn't put it down (still haven't as the game is running while I write this). You have a pretty simple set of combat moves (basic atttacks, direction strong/bonus attacks, a set of meters), but some very complex combo abilities emerge. Additionally, the evolving moveset unlocks new areas in the game similar to Super Metroid (can't speak for later ones, never had interest in a first person Metroid).
The control scheme feels super tight and rock solid. Often, you play platformers, and the controls will feel sluggish, or delayed. Or the inertia when moving feels 'off'. But not here. The game throws tons of crazy challenges at you (especially inferno levels or tree top), but I always felt like it was my fault I was dieing and not due to the game asking more out of you than its gameplay mechanics allowed for. They push you, but not too far. It feels really well balanced in this respect.
There is also something very satisfying about the combo system. From throws, to slams, to just straight up clobbering. Popups, juggles, it's got similarities to a capcom Vs game or maybe even a smash bros. It's one of those games where it's just really fun to turn on and beat the crap out of some things.
The game's art style, while seemingly simple and cartoony, is very rich, and contains a deceptive level of detail. The game has save points that you just walk past throughout the world, so you never have to stop the action. Similarly for starting up, menus, and cut scenes. These devs recognize necessary modern conveniences, and they got the biggest of them all right: let the player play the game and don't force them to watch/do crap that they don't want to!
If you own the original, this going to come down to what you think $5 is worth for a game. Do you measure it in terms of gameplay hours? Or do you measure it in terms of skilled labor hours put into it by a small indie game company? I chose the latter, picked the game up and have a blast ever since. If you're even a small fan of metroidvanias, I would recommend this game.

Guacamelee Gold Edition is one of my favorite games of all time, so I of course picked this one up. However, while it is all shiny and new, that doesn't mean this version is just a straight upgrade. For the most part, the new content is great. I love the new mini-towns, the music, the 2 massive new levels, and the visual updates, but that doesn't mean that every new addition was perfectly executed. My main problem with the game is the Intenso mechanic. It seems really cool at first, but it REALLY hindered the combat for me. One of my favorite parts of Guacamelee was how challenging and tight the combat was, but the Intenso meter ruins that whole feeling. Instead of being a really fluid and tense action/platformer, the Intenso meter just turns the whole thing into a spam fest. This is especially evident in the new arenas. While I like the new arena layout designs, Drinkbox just decided to flood them with enemies to create the illusion of difficulty, but because of how easy it is to use the Intenso, these arenas become a breeze, with no real satisfaction attacted to them. Overall I would still recommend this game, but it's hard for me to say whether you should pick Guacamelee Gold up instead. I think they are both great, but STCE didn't feel as challenging or rewarding to me at all.

Since I reviewed Gold Edition previously, I'm going to focus on the differences and new content here.  See my thoughts on why I enjoyed this game so much here
Super Turbo Championship Edition is essentially a significant content DLC on top of Gold Edition, but since it makes so many changes to the game it is sold as standalone with a discount for previous owners.  Loading up a Gold Edition savegame simply would not work so if you started the game in Gold Edition you will have to start over in this one.  It adds two new large areas with new gameplay mechanics, adds a bunch of new enemy types (elite versions of existing enemies with new abilities,) some new graphical effects (heat distortion and shadows,) a new rage mechanic for combat, pollo bombs!, and reworks all the fights in the game.  There may be other changes I can't think of at the moment.
While none of the new content is strictly necessary to enjoy the game, I found it well worth the $5 upgrade.  The new areas are a lot of fun and quite unique compared to the rest of the game and are integrated seamlessly with the story.  The INTENSO rage mechanic works well as a panic button letting you recover from a fight that's going badly, and that does become necessary.  The fight rework in addition to the new enemies makes the game significantly more difficult which I appreciated but others may not.  In some fights they went a bit too far though, covering the screen with enemies, removing all sense of strategy and turning the combat into a spamfest.
So which version should you buy?  I would definitely recommend this one, with the caveat that you may find it too difficult.

I love turn based strategy games.  This game looks and feels a lot like Heroes of Might & Magic, but it has some flaws that holds it down from it’s true potential.  I’m writing this review for the TBS fans that know what they are looking for, and noting the exact flaws that ruin the game.
There are four tiers of strength for your recruitable units.  Each recruitable unit can level up.  However, no matter what high level they attain, they are really no match for the next higher tier unit.  No units can be resurrected, which can be infuriating when your tier 1, level 10 infantry is eliminated by a tier 3, level 0 archer in one strike.  I tried to cycle through my troops by only using my low levels to fight low level battles, but then you realize that your higher tiers would rather benefit from the experience, as they will need all they can get when they have to take on tier 4 enemies.  On top of that, the opponent AI will always bee-line to your weakest and most exploitable units first.  Battles have to be sought out, but are abundant.  The problem is low level encounters are just as rare as high level encounters.  All encounters are preset, and you can choose when to take on the encounter.  You might find yourself scouring the lands trying to find goblins for your tier 1, level 0s to knock out, wasting many turns in the process.  The best way to level up your army is for them to see combat head on, which makes it tough to build up solid armies without losing a few in the process.  I found myself sometimes recruiting low levels as simple cannon fodder or bait.  No units have a ‘taunt’ ability, so no unit can be used for ‘tanking.’ This greatly hurts the whole point of playing as a warrior type CO, and puts heavy armor defense infantry in a tough spot.  Most units can run or fly circles around them.  Terrain does play a role in mobility and stat adjustments, but not so much that it becomes a game changer.  Battles ultimately end up being very lopsided, with little actual strategy.
If it wasn’t for the core of the strategy being flawed, it would be a fantastic gem.  The graphics are very pleasing to the eye.  The soundtrack is limited and repetitive like an old console game, but can be turned off.  The interface may look intimidating at first, but it is simply spread out and unconsolidated, which doesn’t affect gameplay.  I only recommend it to those with a tremendous amount of patience and time on their hands.  Expect campaigns to take many hours at a time, and anticipate never being able to take on many battles due to the limits of what army you can develop.  In short, expect disappointment, but do your best with what you have.

Eador is the first strategy game I've really been able to sink my teeth into. And that's saying something, because I seem like the kind of person to enjoy strategy games...
The reason for this is because the game remains paletable throughout. I think the thing that typically drives me away from strategy games a few hours in is that, once you start to amass resources and turn those resources into troops, etc., there's so much to take care of at any one time that it's too easy to lose track of anything or
thing.
Eador isn't like that. While you can
get a gigantic army, colossal empire, and a mountain of resources, the buildup to that is very slow and easy to take in. Your armies are led by heroes, which cost exponentially more for each successive one, and each hero only starts with the capacity to have three units in its army (except for one, which starts with four slots). Over time, they'll level up and be able to lead more troops.
Essentially, this leads to a strategy game where the most important resource is time. Hard limits are set on just how much you can do in a single turn, so, rather than a game where the first guy to get a billion troops wins, you get a game where the guy to best optimize his time wins.
The campaign gets really drawn out, I switched to easy mode and still haven't gotten all that far.

I'm not going to beat around the bush here. This game is not good, and it is quite the example of false advertising. In fact, I'd rather go to Hell than be forced to play this game again.
This game appears to be targeted to the "I'm 14, I play Five Nights at Freddy's and I'm so edgy and random lolz rawr XD" crowd. Everything revolves around this motif. The protagonist is a cartoon skeleton rabbit that shoots his way through a Hell, flled with more cartoon animals. The artwork looks like doodles in a notebook, and the sound effects and music do not particularly fit with the theme and the concept. Listening to "The Crunge" or "D'yer Mak'er" on repeat for a few hours is a far more fitting soundtrack. At least the memebers of Led Zeppelin realized how ridculous these songs are, which maes them enjoyable. The game developers, however, lacked this self awareness. The unskippable and repititive dialogue (more on that in a moment) is filled with bad one liners and attempt to be funny. You know when an adult tries to be relatable and cool? This game does exactly that. In fact, I'm surprised that Hillary Clinton hasn't used it as part of her strategy to reach out to millenials (this is not a political post please don't attack me Valve mods).
The actual gameplay itself is marred by several serious flaws. The controls are incredibly awkward, and they somehow feel both stiff and slippery. It feels like someone coated the character in cold butter and threw him onto an ice skating rink. I know that WASD is not great for platformers, but it still is so strange. The rabbit has trouble dodging objects in mid air, which is something you need to be able to do well in order to advance in this game. He also seems to slide after you let go of the movement keys, which has gotten me killeed multiple times.
I tried using a controller, as the game promised controller support, but guess what? IT DIDN"T WORK. I even tried it with multiple controllers, so I am sure it is not a problem on my end. With a controller, I couldn't jump or shoot. These are the two things you need to be able to do in order to play the game. I tried remapping the buttons in the options, but it wouldn't let me. This false advertising irritates me, and I'm suprised at how many games keep doing it.
Speaking of options, the option menu is absolutely pitiful. There are two options from what I remember. These are very basic keyboard remapping (no controller for you, peasants) and the option to change the sound from stereo to mono. That's right, no opton for changing the graphics settings. The game runs at a constant 720p, and upscales to your resolution. It already looks strangely upscaled on my 1080p screen, so I'd hate to see it on a 1440p or 4K monitor.
The action in the game is very mediocre. You get to choose between a variety of weapons, such as a sawblade, a rocket launcher, grenades, and assault rifle, etc.. The only problem is, however, the game restricts weapons to specific enemies. This only raises the question: WHY EVEN HAVE WEAPON VARIETY IN THE FIRST PLACE?! It's a pitiful attempt at diversity and longevity that I cannot appreciate. The whole gimmick with the bosses is that once you defeat them, you get to play a minigame to watch a gory death animation. These come in two varieties. You get to mash a button, you you get to hit a button at just the right time. These animations are reallly just glorified quick-time events. The horse is dead far before this game stops beating it.
These issues are made even worse with the fact that there is no post hit invincibility. If this was just restricted to a certain game mode, I'd be fine with that. But, ths lack of protection makes the bad controls even worse. You can be bounced all around the map and quickly go from 250 to 0 in a matter of seconds. It is downright infuriating how cheap this game can be because of it.
The godawful cutscenes are another issue. I mentioned that they were repetitive and unskippable. I stopped paying attention because every dialogue feels the same. Ash is a teenage punk, and talks back to authority figure because he is so edgy. It gets old quick. Also, you can't skip them. You just have to mash the mouse in order to go through as quickly as possible. There isn't even voice acting. IT's just reading. I don't mind reading, but if I wanted to read, I would grab a book. Also if you die during a boss fight, which you most certainly will beause if the garbage controls. you will often be forced to go through the dialogue you just read again. This is so annoying, and I hate it when developers don't fix this issue. No one wants to read your stupid text bubbles again.
Overall, the game tries to be something that it's not. It tires to be a cool, edgy game with a unique feeling and concept, but it falls flat on its face with boorish storytelling and incompetent implementation. In fact, it eerily reminds me of Shadow The Hedghog. Both games star male animal protagonists that shoot and kill their way through dark, gritty, yet cartoony settings. They each have notoriously bad controls and serious game design issues. To give it that extra touch of cringe, both were published by none other than SEGA. You'd they they'd learn after their first try at such a game. Overall, I give it a 4/10. Maybe I'm just being too critical. After all, it is only a SEGA game that I got for free.
However, if you are one of those 14 year olds I was talking about...
10/10 edgiest game I've ever played

Hell Yeah! is... complicated. There's a large cast of enemies with unique (often disturbing) designs, each with their own little tidbits about them and name, there's very few repeats and recolors amongst them. The game itself is energetic, chaotic, and every stage will usually add something new to play with. On top of that the game plays well. The issue is that there's a lot of components in place that MAKE a great game it's just the execution ultimately makes Hell Yeah! mediocre, but still memorable enough to garner some sort of affinity - either postive or negative.
So let's start with the design. Hell Yeah!'s plot is essentially "compromising photos get out that undercut the ruthless and cruel nature of the Prince of Hell, Ash (which is you), 100 monsters saw it so 100 monsters (and the so-and-so who took those pictures) have to die, go get 'em tiger." As soon as you get into it, you'll notice how brightly colored and animated literally everything is. It's VERY difficult to pay attention to everything and Ash moves pretty quickly meaning you'll likely run into things. As nice as all the animated things are, the fact that the background is as alive as it is most of the time, it'll be difficult to spot the various traps and shots going your way. Meaning you'll die, a lot.
Ash attacks mostly through use of his giant saw-wheel-jetpack which can drill and shoot. You won't really be drilling much unless to kill simple enemies who get too close and to drill through certain rock formations. As soon as you hit zone 2, drilling enemies is overall a bad idea and is replaced by shooting them. Soon after that you realize that with the proper upgrades, you can have your guns drill much more effeciently for you (hint: buy the shotgun and missile upgrades, you'll rarely need the gun later in the game) meaning that drilling isn't that great. Same thing for a dash upgrade which requires you to stand completely still to charge before going forward a rather pitiful distance. Great for drilling certain structures but ultimately very niche and you won't be using it much because - again - missiles and missile type weapons are better for drilling. Finally, certain enemies can only be shot and killed from certain angles so you might be jumping and shooting a lot, which is hard given that you have to aim with the right stick (if you used a controller like I did, as the game recommends) and jump with the A button. Which is really awkward. Meaning you'll die, a lot.
Finally, the game is cluttered with somewhat invisible checkpoints at moments where the game decides it's important to save your progress. If you die, you lose everything you got from before you activated that checkpoint. Typically there's a checkpoint after killing one of the many monsters and through important stretches. But these are numerous enough to be useless at certain points and agrivating when they don't come up after particularly difficult stretches of a level (I'm looking at you underwater zone 3). So if you go through a long maze-like area, grab a lot of money which you need for upgrades and better weaponry, and then get killed by a boss or by the level itself and have to grab it again. Even better, the game will record how much health you had at the checkpoint, meaning that you can respawn in a difficult area only to be severely handicapped until you find a health station somewhere, often much too far away. As if to remedy this there are items you can purchase that will temporarily aid you and boost your survivability until death but these are even RARER so they're never really useful even when you find one of the few shops. Killing a monster also requires beating a short mini-game each and every time, some are difficult some aren't, and they all increase in difficulty as time goes on. There's enough variation that they aren't annoying features, but what is an annoying feature is that failing them recovers some of the monster's HP and takes away a scaled chunk of yours, depending on how far into the game you are. Meaning that you'll die- you catch my point yet?
Most of this review has been negative, but I don't want to take away the fact that I am recommending this game because despite these flaws it's still very entertaining and unique. Well, as long as you can tolerate the emo cute theme, I liked it so I was fine with it. There's a lot in here that makes it feel bloated, but still not to the point that undermines what this game does effectively. Exploration is encouraged and fun, yet restricted from a linear path that you HAVE to take. There's a little management game that you can play with defeated monsters in the background, but the rewards are pretty much worthless and there's very little interactive elements to it. Weapons are unique with their own abilities, but are typically beaten out by its upgrade or weapons you can buy from the shop. Levels and stages are unique so you can't guess what'll come next, but there's no real feeling of progression as every level is disconected. Defeating monsters is cathartic and a large majority of them are absolutely horrifying and wonderful, you can see the love put into them, but the minigames make some more annoying than difficult and pad out every fight.
Really every thing this game does right is hindered by another element. But it still tried to do these things and they almost worked, it's really really close. To me that's what matters and that's why I recommend it. Though more around the $10 mark than full price.

You know, I loved Metroid Fusion. But for as much as I liked it, it always felt like a missed opportunity.
After playing Super Metroid, I expected the sequel to be the same exploratory core implemented with different ideas. I wanted the next games to feature creative skillsets that would allow different ways to work around the maps. All Metroids needed exploration and progressive unlocking of sprawling maps, but not all of them needed Screw Attacks, Plasma Beams and Gravity Suits. Hopefully Nintendo would come up with different and innovative ways to reach ledges other than freezing enemies.
But alas, this was not meant to be. All Metroids feature mostly the same upgrades. It's boring. It makes them all feel like remakes, not sequels.

Metroid is dead... or is it? Axiom Verge captures the spirit of this classic 2D title perfectly while adding much needed tweaks to gameplay and setting the action in a bio-mechanical world reminiscent of the works of H.R.Giger. Oh, and the soundtrack is basically the greatest thing ever. Seriously.

Solid Metroidvania title.  Several powerups are very reminiscent of Samus' abilities, such as the ball and grappling hook.  I think this game strikes a good balance between hand-holding and actually having dialogue to drive a story.  Ending a little ambigious, but defintely gives you something to think about.  The wide variety of weapons promises a chance of replayability, but I tended to gravitate towards a couple weapon choices, as they just seemed better.
Strongly recommended for people who want to run around, blast enemies, and navigate terrain using a increasing set of abilities.

Axiom Verge has alot of in common with Nintendo's old title "Metroid" and the retro graphics style plays along just fine.
It's hard to believe that only 1 person, Tom Happ, has created Axiom Verge in such notably great quality. Excellent soundtracks, well designed levels, encounters and bosses. More than that, this sci-fi 2D platformer comes with a dystopian story and surreal settings that keep up a pleasant tension.
Open world exploration is fairly free in Axiom Verge. Quite some people might prefer to play the game with a walkthrough page. Yes, the game is considerably complex. Things that give the impression of a glitch reveal as part of the game mechanics with some very surprising moments.
I haven't found any major bug or error. Gameplay is very smooth and captivating, challenging. There was nothing that I could consider truely negative.
All in all, it's an amazing hommage to retro games and worth every minute playing - a "must have" for fans of the so called metroidvania genre.

IL-2 Sturmovik: 1946 is a game unlike many, and this can be for better or for worse. If you get this game, one of the first things that you will notice about it, is that it isn't exactly the easiest game to learn to like. The tutorials that are available to you do not put you at the controls of the aircraft you're being taught to fly, but rather make you watch another person fly it the way it's supposed to be flown. Really, the only true way you can learn to play the game is to start it up, and begin playing it immediatly. No tutorials, no help. Trust me, you will die. A lot.
I'm going to go ahead and tell you the things that you likely won't like about this game at first. 1: There are no "Real" tutorials that teach you how to play as I've said before, meaning the only way for you to learn to play the game is through jumping right in.
2: The controls and flight characteristics are very realistic, meaning that if you haven't played a Flight Simulator before, there are hundreds of ways that you can screw yourself over without actually getting into combat, such as putting yourself into a Flat Spin, Stalling Out, Ripping Your Wings, Overheating Your Engine, etc.
3: There can literally be a use for every single button on your keyboard, meaning that hitting one wrong button can mean instant death.
4: This game is unbelievably difficult to master in terms of everything, from flight controls to maneuvers to landing.
With all of these negativities said, it doesn't sound like a very fun game, now does it? That's where you're wrong. I believe that the people that made this game were absolute geniuses. This is the number one thing about this game - you need to be patient. You will die several times before actually learning to kill anything, but once you do learn, once the little mechanism inside your brain clicks with this game, it will be one of the most fun World War Two Flight Simulators you've ever played.
The Bottom Line is, this game isn't for people that give up easily. This game is for people who are patient, and people who are willing to learn. Do I recommend this game? Yes, yes I do, but only if you are willing to learn the complexities of it. If not, then don't waste your time with it.

is a (Now Free) team-based FPS created by Splash Damage, the same crew that brought us Wolfenstein Enemy Territory, Enemy Territory Quake Wars, and most recently Dirty Bomb. It's an objective based shooter that attempts to utilize the gameplay style of it's predecessors and it shows. Usually matches consist of "Attacking team, escort the tank" and "Defending team, stop the tank" sort of affairs much similar to Dirty Bomb, it's free to play successor (also on steam). Your team can set up ambush points, heal teammates as a medic, or just run and gun as a regular soldier.
The flow of the game is somewhat fast, with players being able to (sort of) parkour their way across maps. Speaking of the maps, i find them rather good. Factories, Waterfronts, Dark Urban maps set the stage for Brink's combat. But don't get too carried away, most of the servers i played had friendly fire enabled and boy howdy it can be very easy to accidentally blow up your teammates with a misguided grenade! Speaking of combat, it's
but if you've been keeping up with your shooters over the years, it's nothing special. I believe there's a few balance issues, very dodgy hitboxes and laggers that make you throw your computer across the planet in frustration. Oh and speaking of frustration, the game does have quite a few technical issues. Performance is all over the place, even on newer machines. "Campaign Coop" matches are locked at 30FPS (Why?!) but at least the multiplayer servers are unlocked.
That doesn't save you from the many bugs, glitches and oddities that can sometimes mar the experience for newcomers. Which reminds me, i played the game a bit during it's initial release hype and didn't bother with it until i recently heard it went free. So i thought i'd give it another shot.
+ Suprisingly decent graphics for it's age
+ Cinematic cutscenes in between rounds is neat
+ The large maps flow well and are rather interesting
+ Can be genuinely fun at times
+ Pretty spiffy character customization
+ Full of bugs, glitches and performance problems
+ Coop Campaign is locked at 30FPS
+ Art style isn't for everyone
+ Relatively low playerbase
+ Bullet Sponge health
Is the game terrible? No, not really. Is it flawed? Absolutely. Is it fun?
. But look at it this way, it's free and it can be a fun experience at times, if the community can get a good hold on it, who knows what the future could hold for the game. I respect Splash Damage for releasing the game to the fans rather than just discontinue it all-together. I wish more devs would think that way to be honest. Besides, i really can't put my finger on it but
really does have some kind of charm that's all it's own, even if it's broken as hell sometimes. So, if you're still interested go give it a shot. If you don't like it, uninstall it and go get Dirty Bomb! If you like it, have some fun every now and again, it really needs new people since the community has been dormant for a long time. Who knows, maybe i'll see you out there.

I am a Metroid player.  Metroid accompanied me through many long, lonely, and desolate hours...until I got a girlfriend.  And then, I often preferred Metroid to her.  I tried to continue the relationship, but the Super Nintendo version wasn't as good as the original, and neither were the Wii versions.
Axiom Verge is better than the original.
The dev is faithful, while being more complex and more fun.  The dev understands that exploration is a different pursuit than fetch questing.  The dev understands that exploring an alien world is about an immersive mood.  The most pleasing thing is that the game demands a freshness of mind that erodes after long hours of gaming.  When a game is limited to fetch quests, checking boxes, or grinding, you can go all night and make "progress".  In Axiom Verge, a tired mind misses the linkages between the protagonist's explanding capabilities and the demands of the in-game environment.
OVERWHELMINGLY POSITIVE

Despite the ongoing support, consistent patching, and free mini-DLC, Masters of the Broken World is still Masters of the Broken Game (hahaha, I'm so good). This is essentially the original Eador with some additional bells and whistles, but little expansion on the existing features.
There's really no reason to play this installment when the original Eador plays much more smoothly, actually works half the time, and isn't nearly as buggy. Even the interface in this game is more unfriendly, which is saying something when the original Eador's interface was just a mad collection of buttons.
Eventually, it might match up to its predecessor, but with the mods and stability offered in the original, there's really no reason to get Masters of the Broken World right now, especially since it costs more.

A very clever 4X that follows in the footsteps of King's Quest and Heroes of Might and Magic, but adds plenty of its own to the genre. The scale of the game is horrifying, it's taken me several days to beat my first randomly generated scenario out of what promises to be a 50-100 scenario long campaign.
There's a huge amount of content and plenty to do every turn, but it's presented in an efficient way and turns go quickly.
The game isn't exactly unpolished, but it has some splinters that could be sanded down. Expect a harmless crash every 24 hours or so. There's one bug that can hit fairly often and prevents kills from registering, especially on retaliatory hits and especially on slower combat speeds. It can be resolved without incident by autoresolving at the end of combat and almost always works in the player's favour, blocking its AI reenforcements and almost never occurs on the highest combat speed, which I would recommend using either way, because the second slowest is much too slow. There are very few games that I have logged in as much playtime on as the original Mutant League Football for the Genesis. I played this game for countless years, long after the Genesis was no longer the current console. To this day, that game holds a dear place in my heart. I was aware of the Kickstarter revival over the years, but didn't pay it much mind. Between the spotty track record of Kickstarter games even getting made, and my doubt that a remake could ever hold a candle to the original, I let it drift off my radar. To my shock, I randomly discovered yesterday that not only did the game officially get released, but that it surprisingly captures all the fun of the original. Even more surprising, as someone that very frequently plays all the modern Madden games, I was pleasantly surprised by how good the football feels. Obviously, it's not at the high-level of quality of the triple-A Madden games, but WOW was I blown away by how satisifying it still is, all while capturing the dirty plays and over-the-top violence that defined the original. In short, buy this damn game. I want to see more iterations of this, with even more polish and updated rosters. This is a fantastic budget title, that totally captures the magic of the original. It's Blood Bowl if Blood Bowl were a legit football simulator, and it's a bloody wonderful part of my childhood resurrected with care I honestly didn't expect.

This interactive tale falls short in a number of ways but flourishes in others. It certainly tugs at the heart strings, but in ways that are predictable (but sometimes that's not such a bad thing).
What really stands out to me is the surrealism, the metaphors for loneliness and escape, the parallelism between the boy and the bird both wanting to take flight. The artwork and transitions between scenes were beautifully crafted and will be what I remember most about this short experience down the road. I am also generally intrigued by games without dialogue, and I generally liked how the narrative was told without words.
That said, the narrative begins at a sluggish pace, so it feels like there's a lot to get to before the good stuff. I also found this game lagged a lot on my computer (despite my laptop being able to run more robust games without a hiccup). The ending was also dragged out a bit long in my opinion. All throughout I was hoping for more interaction, but I was spoonfed where to go and what to pick up, which kept me from full immersion and savouring each scene.
All in all, I would say this interactive animation was worth checking out. I'd recommend it on sale, though.

If you have played To The Moon, you're gonna find a rather similar experience in terms of quality over time. This game is a one hour experience that has nothing to do with To The Moon and tells its own story. A simple but engaging one. There's no dialogue, not many interactions and not a complex timeline as the other game; just a boy and a bird.

Some things to keep in mind before buying A Bird Story:
- The engine is terrible. Objects clearly meant to be round are stretched horizontally. Alt-tab will make the sound stop working. There's no gamepad support. When the camera pans around the screen jerks and studders. The mouse cursor moves really fast and it's intrusively large. The Steam overlay doesn't work.
- It's extremely slow-paced and focused on slice-of-life storytelling. It takes a long time before there is any sort of drama or conflict, and then it doesn't last long. It's not the kind of story that tries to get you invested in the outcome, but rather tries to draw you in with moodiness.
- 100% of the interactivity consists of obeying commands the game gives you, usually brief 'go fetch a thing' repeated ad nauseum. The result feels like an indie film that you passively watch but you have to do random chores to progress through.
- As such, don't try to disobey the signposted direction the game is funneling you toward. You will slowly crawl off and eventually hit an invisible wall, and then have to endure the tedium of walking all the way back to the one and only path.
If you're okay with all that, you may enjoy this game. The art is nice and the music is overly sappy but competently composed. It may be a good option if you're really into avant-garde narrative experience type stuff.

I have played this game before on the PS3 when i got at as a free game via Playstation Plus. I enjoyed my time immensly back then and felt like diving in again in this colorfull Metroidvania adventure about the bunny Prince of Hell Ash and his quest to destroy 100 monsters who saw emberassing photos of him. The plot is so unbelieveably simple and doesn't take itself seriously at all, which adds to the visuals aswell.
This time i also enjoyed my time with Hell Yeah, but not quite as much as when i used to back then 4 years ago when the game first released. The gameplay is smooth as butter, the gunplay is great and it feels great to explore the lands and be on the hunt for the next monster. Also the soundtrack is still really great, fits the levels fantastically and that one song in the Cute World is still stuck in my head because how catchy (yes i know it's cheesy as hell) it is.
However, there were two things that bugged me a little while playing the game and made me notice that the game feels a bit 'old' even if it just came out not to long ago. First of were the graphics, were it felt a bit...odd to me. Some of the animations are a bit too cheap, downright 2 frames animations and looked quite laughable at times (especially the Guitar killing thing where the hands stretch the Monster, that looked really awful). Otherwise you have some nicely drawn, whacky cartoony characters which are with a few exception all pretty well drawn. I generally like Ash's design alot.
Speaking off the finishers, these happen every time you kill one of the 100 Monsters you need to hunt down. Allthough there are many finishers with unique animations and how you perform them, they repeat themselfs  often and they get old rather quickly, with no option to skip. This can be pretty tiresome watching the same thing over and over again with no chance whatsoever. Most of these finishers are references to some pop culture media, which brings me to my next big point, the humor.
The humor is a mix of basic "lol gory and butts and cursing" and pop culture references. It really is nothing big, and even though it made me laugh alot back in the day, it didn't even really made me chuckle once on my new playthrough. It's just a shame because i thought the games humor would hold up a bit better after just 4 years of age. Luckily the gameplay and overworld art make up for it.
Still, i find Hell Yeah! a pleasurable experience and find it sad that the developers, Akedo Studio, disbanded in 2013, which also kills the hope for a sequel.
As for a recommendation, the game is pretty short and rather easy. After completion there is not much to do really, the unlockables are not worth it, the missions are lame and "The Island" is trash. So yeah, pick it up when it's on sale, for 5-7 bucks you will enjoy this little rabbit adventure.
