Its gameplay consists of the typical shootyshoot and platforming like many other metroidvania titles have although it's incredibly underwhelming in the metroidvania area since there is very little reason to go back to anything aside from the few points when you have to near the end of the game. There are some cosmetic gifts you can try to find and some simple side missions but they're not very rewarding themselves.
Playing with both a KB+M and a controller are both doable. During some segments though it's far more ideal to use the mouse for the faster aiming since for some reason using the right analog stick for these particular sections is incredibly slow whilst the mouse is as fast as you move it.
This game likes to emphasize about its loads of violence & gore but it's hard to take seriously since the entire game's animations look like something I'd see in a mobile game. With its groan-inducing humor and cartoony artstyle though I guess it shouldn't entirely be taken so.
The main goal throughout the game is just to platform your way through extremely standard maps to find and kill special monsters so you can unlock doors where you're to platform and kill more monsters so you can unlock more doors to do the same thing and eventually fight a boss, which itself is a part of the special monster pool. The special monsters are basically the keys to unlock doors when they're dead and for most of them it's an incredibly tedious process since the method for taking them down are usually either shoot them down or grind them down with your sawblade. Afterwards, as their HP reaches 0, you have to go through this Warioware-like minigame each time. If you fail the minigame you take loads of damage and they remain alive so you'd have to hit 'em a small bit
to get their HP down enough and do the minigame
where upon actual victory, you'll be treated to an unskippable slideshow-esque Adobe-Flash-like cutscene of a kill. Because there are loads of these special monsters in the game you'll encounter the same minigame and cutscene again and again, so even if you're a fan of the eye-rolling humor in the game they'll lose their appeal. As I got bored of seeing the minigame's reused cutscenes I tried alt+tabbing to another window for a bit and apparently it pauses the entire game sort of so the cutscene itself would just hang there until I went back to the game where it'd finally continue the little slideshow.
While much of these monsters are tedious to kill there are quite a few that get pretty clever in terms of finding the method of killing special monsters but these mostly appear at the later half of the game. At these times the game turns into a puzzle platformer sort of.
Nearly all weapons have unlimited ammo as they constantly recharge themselves. I never found myself using all of them since I didn't particularly need more than but a few.
If you're using a controller, trying to use the sawblade and a gun can get confusing. By default you press RT to drill with the sawblade but to shoot your guns you have to aim with the right analog stick and then press RT. I found myself drilling accidentally when I should shoot too many times.
For some wad of a reason anything that's even mostly off-screen is invincible. You can shoot in their direction but if you can't see them you can't hurt them no matter how big of a target they are. This becomes a serious problem against enemies that require you to move a lot to evade anything that'd hurt you. It's as if your fired projectiles disappear from the game as soon as they leave the screen.
Checkpoints aren't the best and are made a little worse plenty of times when they're right before a cutscene of sorts where characters speak. Each time you die at these times you'll have to go through the cutscene over and over again. You can't skip these dialogue things entirely so all you can do is mash NEXT until it's all over each time in case you'd rather not go through all that again, and even that's still slow.
It's a simple game overall with humor for the lowest common denominator but I definitely don't think it's $15 worth for little content.

There's really no way to write this review without mentioning Nintendo's "Metroid". While many games have spawned from the platforming exploration genre it defined, few have been as true and accurate of a love letter as Axiom Verge. This is not to say that Axiom Verge is a rip-off. Not by any means! If anything, it's a tribute that knows exactly what made Metroid great, and pays homage to those elements.
The title starts in typical fashion with an extremely large (and unforgiving) world/map that you can only access scraps of, at the game's beginning. Each navigation item acquired opens up more of the map, until eventually the player feels like a space ninja, with nothing out of their reach or bounds.
On the topic of navigation and exploration, Axiom Verge is much more true to its roots than many recent titles in the genre. There's no color coded doors or blocks. When you get an item that expands your ability to traverse the landscape, it's on YOU (the player) to figure out or remember where said item can be applied. While this can result in a bit of frustration and backtracking, I found it to feel a lot more satisfying.
As for other factors:
* The graphics are great (Pixel art, but with very intricate and detailed designs)
* Music is phenomenal (the game does a great job of capturing the feeling of isolation and an alien environment through the insturment choice and composition.)
* The story was really enjoyable for me (A lot of things are left unresolved, but done so tastefully as to keep the player thinking about it long after beating the game. Lots of great worldbuilding, and plenty of room for a hopeful sequel.)
* Gameplay in general is also great. (Fairly fast paced, good flow of enemy and platforming difficulty, with some real fun boss fights)
The best way I can really put it is that Axiom Verge is quite frankly the best "Metroid" game to come out in quite some time. (Not Metroidvania, Metroid. Thomas Happ is doing the genre better than Nintendo themselves at this point.) The elements of the Metroidvania genre (platforming, exploration, gatekeeping through items) are handled in a superb manner, and the game has enough personality to be memorable, standing apart on its own. For anyone who is remotely a fan of the genre (especially of the earlier NES and SNES titles) I can't recommend this title enough.

Only my child's insatiable love for Putt-Putt makes this mingame at all worthwhile, and even he got quickly bored of bouncing Pep at balloons.

The basis for this game is very simple: Putt-putt lost his balloons and it's up to him and his dog Pep to get them all back (by popping them?). Even with all of this game's simplicity it is fun to play.
The objective for each level is to use Putt-putt like a trampoline and bounce Pep around the screen until you pop all of the balloons, making sure not to let Pep fall to the ground! The balloons themselves come in a variety of types: normal colored balloons, balloon filled with candy (tasty, and they give extra points), trash (yuck, and they take away points), power ups (which can turn Pep into Super Pep, Putt-putt into a stretch limo, or a few other goodies), or balloons carrying paint buckets that can change Putt-putt's color. Every five rounds a space ship will appear and if Pep hits it you get to play a bonus round on the moon! The game does keep your current score and the highest score for anyone that has played it, so you can compete with others, or try to beat your highest score!
The game itself is pretty simple, but if the player is having difficulties, there is a junior help button that can be used to prevent the player from losing lives (and thus never lose the game) and also make it easier for Putt-putt to catch Pep. Additionally, this game comes with a mode that lets players create custom levels anyway they want. I like to occasionally play this game because of its game play, nice music, and fun atmosphere.

UPDATE 1/2016:
A lot of the bugs seem to be fixed, though a few might remain. I'm switching this to a *very cautious* thumbs up. (By the way, my hours in the game are exaggerated. One of the many bugs is that when the game crashed, it didn't end the process in the task manager. So, I once had the process running for a week straight, adding a couple hundred hours to my play time).
ORIGINAL REVIEW BELOW:
So many bugs! I really really want to enjoy this game. And for long stretches, I do enjoy it... and then a gamebreaking bug causes all of my progress to be lost. This happens over and over again. I keep coming back, so at its heart it is a good game. Every time there is a patch to fix a bug, several new bugs pop up in its place.
Most recently, they put out a big patch, calling it free DLC, and supposedly fixed bugs. It introduced an obvious, gamebreaking bug right up front that makes the game unplayable (enemy units won't die, they just sit on the battlefield at 0 health).
Here is a list of some other bugs I've encountered in previous builds, some of which may still be present (I don't know, since the game is unplayable on the first shard now)
1) I attacked another master, and won the final battle to take the shard. This results in a "game over" screen (this ruined my longest campaign, and even happened when I went to beat a different shard first, then returned to that master).
2) My provinces are invincible. An enemy master will defeat my guards at a province, then retreat the next turn, with the province still under my control and my guards at full health
3) I attack a province and end up in a mirror match, where I control both of my identical armies against one another. No matter which side wins, I both win and lose the battle.
4) Game freezing and crashing to desktop immediately after conquering a shard. It goes to the main astral screen, the conquered shard comes towards my shard, and the game crashes as soon as they merge.
5) The enemy AI completely forgetting to play the game. I once took over an entire master's shard with the enemy hero having never been beyond one hex of his capital. This was on a large map.
I cannot recommend this game in its current state. It's been a year of heartache for me, since I want to play through a campaign so badly, and I keep trying, but it's just getting worse.

For reasons largely pertaining to their huge set of teeth and the movie Jaws, humans have a bit of an irrational fear of sharks, with the common belief being held that they will devour you on sight. But rarely do we consider how the sharks must feel from this whole debacle. Derrick in particular is having a rather awful time, with the sea he inhabits being filled with pollution and his parents both being sucked up and put in a can. Understandably, he’s a tad upset and as a result is going on a worldwide quest to clear away these pesty humans and the toxic waste they’ve been chucking into the ocean. On paper you wouldn’t imagine this to be a cute scenario, which I suppose is somewhat ironic considering paper has such a large role in making it one.
Derrick the Deathfin is a game made entirely of paper, with origami characters, cardboard backgrounds, and cut out waves pasted together in an elaborate display of creativity and vibrant color. Take one look at the delightful art and it’s hard not to be immediately charmed, with the grooving soundtrack adding just the right overtone for such a wondrously enjoyable game. The hilariously self aware tips that pop up between levels and the stupendously horrible puns are just the delectable icing on the cake.
When you manage to get over the fantastic visual design, the actual game takes the form of something of an underwater platformer. Racing through levels you collect gems and hop out of the water through tires on your way to the finish line, with the catch being Derrick’s insatiable hunger that stands in for your health bar and requires you to continuously stuff your face with fish, birds, and the occasional stray child or else shrivel up and keel over. What makes this so enjoyable is how fast and fun it is to guide your deathfin through water, swimming with all the force and speed you’d expect of a shark, biting through everything in your path as they disappear in a comical “poof”. Unfortunately it’s also one of the games biggest issues.
As a giant predator there’s little in the way of danger on your journey to rid the waters of your foes (and anyone else who might stray into your path), but you’ll find a persistent enemy in the wild controls. Momentum plays a large role in movement in Derrick, but this becomes an issue in terms of controls as it’s incredibly easy to lose control and cause your character to flip out of control, often cutting you short of a jump or getting you stuck on the environment (a frustrating and consistent occurrence). This is all so terribly disappointing because when you can actually get a grip on the controls moving through the water feels terrific, but often this is easier said than done.
Surprisingly, the handful of time trial levels which do away with collectibles and send you flying through levels as fast as possible work far better with the often confounding controls, as without the need to control yourself with much of any precision they become almost completely a non issue. It’s too bad there are so few of these interspersed through the games 4 “worlds”, as they are a far better showcase of the best Derrick has to offer.
Even with a few controller qualms, there’s no way I could say I didn’t enjoy Derrick the Deathfin immensely. It’s imaginative, charming, and full of so much love and personality that I can’t help but want to pick it up and hug it (assuming you could do that to a game). The adventure is a brief one, clocking in at just about 2 hours, but if you fancy yourself a shark advocate or are just a fan of cute animals. eating other animals (?) there’s a lot to enjoy in this tale of adorable revenge.
PS: Don’t litter folks; respect the sharks!

This game is such a mess, and makes no sense. It's complicated enough to make a tutorial necessary, but whoever wrote the tutorial has no business EVER writing tutorials.
1) The instructions tell you to interact with things that are worded differently than in the instructions. This becomes a much large deal when it's part of a character sheet with tons of things to look through to guess at what they're taling about.
2) There's no logical flow. The instructions tell you to go to a vendor, then you do nothing with the vendor and instead build remotely on your ship with things that are alread in your inventory, and that the vendor doesn't sell anyways.
3) The movement instructions at the very beginning are clunky, not really defining how one click always does one thing, and the other does the same thing, but contexturally with different members.
4-5) There's (4) no backtracking to understand the context of an instruction; and (5) no tutorial protection to prevent you from having any possibility of proceeding.
EXAMPLE: You are fumbling with the movement instructions, since they're so unconventional. Once it dawns on you by trial and error, and you've figured that out, the tutorial has skipped ahead without you wanting it to or completing the previous thing. It's now asking you to interact with an object you have no idea how to interact with. You aren't sure how to interact with it. You assume since you were told to go to a vendor and they don't have the object, that you sell them the object. Then you figure out it was asking you to do something with the object, but you sold it, and can't buy it, so you have to restart a new game to proceed with the tutorial. And that's after you spent a lot of time ramdomizing your captains look. And even a patient person is getting beyond agitated at the game.
6) Almost impossible to do as instructed (with wartermellon and placement, because there's so much poop around, and you can't place on poop, but the tutorial has told you nothing at this point with how to deal with it).
7) Inconsisancy of logic.
In one scenario the tutorial asks you to go to a screen (vendor), and you'd suspect you are supposted to interact with it, but no you are not. In another screen, they ask you to go to a screen (skills) and now that you weren't supposed to interact with the last one (vendor), you assume you are not supposed to interact with the skill because you haven't been told to. But no, you'd be wrong again.
8) Text goes by too quickly when there's no interaction to do.
So your crew member that you upgraded suddenly attacks you. It flashes 2-3 screens of text up when this starts to happen, but there's no way to read them fast enough, so you have no idea of the lesson you were supposed to learn by that (or humor if there was no lesson). Then it abruptly says end of tutorial, and you are left sitting there having no idea what just happened nor the will to proceed after this series of insultingly frustrating blows.
For the record: I think the lesson was something about moral, or payment you need to provide the crew to keep them happy. But I don't know. If my assumption is correct, wouldn't it have been a heck of a lot more helpful for the tutorial to show you how to deal with moral (or at minimum mention it was an issue), instead of pranking you for being a noob because you didn't know something the game never mentioned?
I'm all for a briefer, more to the point tutorial that doesn't walk you through things agonizingly slowly. But what in the world is this mess? I've never experience such a frustrating start to a title that looked fun. The companies other game is one of the best ever (which has no effictive tutorial, which is better than this mess, but that game is more conventionally simple to get started in, and you can get away with it).
Maybe the game is good, but why would I want to continue playing at this point?!  I feel like the game has agonizingly pulled me through it's flaws, then slapped me for trying. Horrid experience. DON'T BUY!

I've never been a big fan of platformers or this genre Steam calls "Metroidvania", so I wasn't particularily intrested in playing this, but since I got it free with the a Sega bundle here on Steam back in February 2016, I figured I would put some time into it. I've played Sonic and Mario before so I have some expectations about the genre.
This stylish game has an amusing story about the prince of hell (who is a rabbit), who sets out to restore his dignity by killing 100 monsters after photos of him with a rubber duck in a bathtub were affecting his street cred.
The game runs flawlessly on my Windows 7 64 bit Core2Duo 1.87 Ghz, with a Geforce GT 430 1024 MB.
This game features Steam Cloud and Overlay Support, Achievements, and Leaderboards.
It does not have any cards.
I found the overall presentation and style of the game to be very good with decent music and sound effects, but I did not find the gameplay fun at any point during my 3 hours of playtime, and that is what matters the most.
As I mentioned, I've never been a fan of the genre, but I personally found this game to be rather boring.
Basically you run around a large (ish) map, collecting money and killing weak enemies while searching for the bosses that are your targets. You will often kill them in unique ways that feature a small mini game event. Once the enemies are killed, you can order then to do things for you in a seperate mini game such as collect coins or treasures. It's a unique feature for sure.
You then proceed through the door that only opens based on your current boss kill count and continue the process until you reach the stage boss. Sometimes you come across a store where you can buy customization skins for your character, or new weapon and health upgrades.
Unfortunatley, none of this felt fun to me.
There are not a lot of mobs to kill in the first couple chapters, there are a lot of annoying instant kill hazards, (though the game seems to have unlimited lives) and a lot of bosses to fight...but the whole process just feels like a chore to me.
I certainly don't feel this game is worth the full price of $16.99 CDN, so unless your a huge fan of the genre, I would avoid this game,
There are better games to spend your time on.

Axiom Verge is one of the higher quality Metroidvania games out there, but ultimately suffers from the result of being a one-man show.
While I generally like the gieger asthetic, I wish there was a bit more color variety, as you end up looking at a very monochromatic scene at all times and it's often not clear what is a platform or background decoration. This is the reason I put off buying it for so long, the art is like very early NES when they didn't understand how to make tiles correctly.
But the main thing I think needs improvement here is the game will take you about 12 hours to complete, of which 6 hours is wandering around being lost. This could have been mitigated with a fast travel system or something but constant aimless navigation gets old fast, and the game is much worse for it (you'll get sick of the fantastic music first). Even SOTN had a teleporter.
If you just want to play the good bits, I would recommend the text-only walkthrough somebody has a steam guide here. I resorted to this after I realized I was no longer having fun and wish I would have started with it.
That being said, it's clearly a labor of love by the developer. Which it turns out is just one guy, Tom Happ, who did all the art, programming, music, and level design. It's incredibly impressive that he pulled it off, it explains why so much of it seemed under-developed to me. That being said it is worth it if you can pick it up on sale.

The best Metroid style game available. Fascinating universe, compelling story, solid platforming with incredibly fun mechanics and great variety.

From the first boss fight to the last I crapped my balls each time. I recommend this for anyone who loves a good metroidvania style game. You will not be disappointed!

Made by Splash Damage (Quake, Wolfenstien) and a high quality, dressed up version of their Free to Play hit Enemy Territory; Brink is a game that failed horribley a a buy to play title. So badly that it's now free. Brink also paved the way for Titanfall's multiplayer based campaigns and parkour system. That's possibley why it's free now: To hook people that want to play something similar to Titanfall but free.
Unlocking wise, Brink is rather generous in letting you use almost any weapon in the game after quickly grinding through the eight "challenge" missions that are designed to teach you all of the objectives in the game, along with running you through a parkour course. From there, you unlock new abilities through simply mowing down enemies and winning missions.
Brink is a tale of warfare between far left and far right extremists. The left-wing Resistance, having been subjigated as a slave class for some time; has hatched a plan to clear a path to the airfields and escape to hopefully a better place. Meanwhile the right wing Security forces are completely innoculated against any idea of why the Resistance exists, and assume that because they are assaulting Security checkpoints they are trying to blow up the entire Ark; or in the case of the Security ide of the last Resistance mission: They litterally think that if the Resistance escapes that every other country is going to come steal their land and technology.
Gameplay wise, it's Enemy Territory combined with an intuitive objective system. Unlike in ET where you have to just follow people or use a map to fin objectives; in Brink you hold the middle mouse button which allows you to highlight which map objective you are persueing. In general, this is a mechanic that should be standard in objective based shooters yet remains fairly unique to Brink.
Unfortunatly, Brink suffers from terrible AI, which is who you will be fighting most of the time. They stand around like stormtroopers, and only seem to actually apply themselvs when facing a live player. They also tend to wave up, standing together for each grenade nuking.
Gunwise, almost everything is an Assault Rifle. There's only a few rifles, shotguns, or heavy weapons. While I appreciate the amount of spray and spray going on, the lack of a diverse shotgun selection is notable. They also have rather bizarre spread and almost no custimization. Which is unfortunate, because the ability to use iffernt typs of shotgun shells would of been a great feature.
I suggest this game for people that want a rather tightly designed shooter to group up with friends on. The maps are filled with cover, there are multiple playstyles, and the level design is thankfully extremely urban.

I used to own Brink years ago back when I played on the Playstation 3 and I was way younger then and couldn't really grasp the objectives concept of Brink. I wasn't big into shooters either so it ended up collecting dust however I never thought it was bad. Picking this up years later I'm really dissapointed by this in weird ways. I enjoy brink however it's just painfully unbalanced and broken because of how messed up the AI is. You can have some fun if you have 2 full teams, however if there's AI involved both teams are at a disadvantage. The AI is pretty dumb and overpowered at the same time. See they'll happily gun down a whole team, but they'll leave them in a revivable state so you have to finish them off. They'll rush in to revive you if you're down, but they won't actually help anyone else and it's more than likely you we're in a seriously dangerous area anyway. They go directly to the objective taking multiple routes and supporting like an online team might, handing out buffs and whatnot but when they get there the objective is swarmed by AI all trying to do one thing, while they manage to do it usually, they all die a few seconds after fanning out.
AI aside this really is a solid game but with the time gone by and the community a little bit quiet it's hard to do what YOU want to do. You can have some fun freeplay matches but the bulk of the content is ruined by the AI. You'll struggle to find a story mode match without organising one which is a shame as it's generally a pretty fun little campaign. However the challenge mode is the biggest problem, challenge mode is also very quiet but it holds all the weapon unlockables, if you ever want to customise your gun then you'll need to suffer through this.
Following on to the weapons from challenge mode, they're all pretty cool I suppose, nothing groundbreakingly original but pretty standard shooter guns. Some of the weapons base stats are fine and some are messed up completely so you'll want to customise them to make them a little more useful, but that requires struggling through challenge mode with a few good base weapons and that restricts that game even more! If you don't mind hip firing a sniper because it's more accurate that's fine or if you want to spray bullets down a hallway and hope for the best then this game is fine.
Overall this game was a product of it's time and that's all that can be said to try and redeem how badly it's actually aged. The graphics look dated, even for PS3 era and the game design itself is very drab. Character design feels like a bad caricaturist and the voicing is either too boring or too much. The setting is okay and the story is actually quite good, if not a bit cliche and basic but that can't hold up as a reason to actually play this. Realistically I had some fun when the AI didn't have a reason to be bonkers but that's not very often, between the auto deaths, stupid revives, terrible killability and generally getting lost and falling off stuff they're useless. I can't even reccomend you download this and try it for yourself. if you have 10-14 friends who also want to try this or played it when I came out you'll probably have a blast for free, if not just leave it, play something else.

Honestly, I'm not entirely sure whether this or Spore has the title of the "Worst Case of Wasted Potential" in gaming history. But in order to make this review accessible instead of sounding like a pretentious skrub, I'll start with a general summary of the game (honestly, there is so little of a story anyways that spoilers don't even really exist) and then compare the good with the bad.
Experience: I bought this game on 360 when it came out, had a blast, then forgot about it. So I rebought it a while back on PC after I had grown up and looked to see if it was how I remembered it was. The resulting dumpster fire was jarring, to say the least.
The Gist of Things:
-BRINK takes place on an enormous floating city called the Ark, which was an international project undertaken somewhere in the near future by all of the largest countries in order to provide a safe place for humans to take shelter and breed while the rest of the Earth was ravaged by some kind of ecological disaster (can't remember off the top of my head, because honestly the game spends so little on this cool premise in the first place that it doesn't remotely stick out). However, as they always manage to, society on the Ark sucks because the majority of the wealth on the island is concentrated in the hands of the few instead of evenly spread out (ala the French Revolution, even down to the percentages) and because of this there is an enormous amount of resentment from the underclasses (literally underclasses, since there's a giant tower in the middle of the Ark that extends like the phallus it is to screw over the workers) towards the high-rise dwelling scientists, politicians, and generally any semblance of law and order.
Things get worse when riots start happening under the leadership of some really charismatic schmuck named Chen, who for all intents and purposes does absolutely nothing for his faction (uniquely called The Resistance) while his kinsmen commit domestic terrorist actions and generally stir up lots of trouble. On the opposite side there is The Security (another original name that ironically enough suffers from the same problems that The Security from RAGE did, in that it makes no sense for them to exist and they royally suck at their jobs, making me think that the writers of this game and RAGE alike had no originality when it came to things like this), led by a police officer/unelected president of the Ark named Mokoena. Naturally these two leaders (Chen and Mokoena) hate each other for no real reason at all other than plot magic, forcing the two factions of The Resistance and The Security to duke it out in objective gameplay matches.
And I hope you liked that, cause that's basically the entire story, and that's not an exaggeration. The "campaign" (I use the term loosely because the campaign matches are copy-paste multiplayer maps with literally no difference between them) comprises The Resistance and The Security's continued efforts to become the most hated factions in all of fiction by doing nothing that makes any sense, such as The Resistance whining that nobody wants to join them after raiding and pillaging various Ark facilities, threatening (and then actually performing) a cruise missile attack on the giant tower in the middle of the Ark, and generally being rambunctious miscreants, while The Security furthers justifies this kind of nonsense by instituting martial law, unfair food/water rationing (even though everyone lives in a technological paradise because plot), and other such authoritarianism.
Why should you care? You shouldn't, because this isn't even a game like Doom or Wolfenstein where the story is non-existent because it doesn't need to be. This game's story is a terrible excuse for writing and even though it had a decent if not good premise, the execution was something that honestly takes away from the experience instead of being just unremarkable (like other Bethesda titles one could name)
Now that that wall of unreadable text is out of the way, let's get to the things you *should* care about.
General Gameplay:
BRINK is set up as a cooperative (i.e., not single player) FPS where the two teams fight each other while completing an objective (of varying nature) across a number of maps. You've seen it before in titles such as TF2 and Overwatch, and chances are you will regret ever thinking of those games while playing this one because you will hate your experience even more knowing how close this game was to being good.
How BRINK differs from the traditional arena groove is its focus (or more accurately, attempted focus) on rapid and fluid movement, meaningful and responsive gunplay, and ridiculous amount of creativity and replayability due to the sheer amount of detail players get to play around with. There are three body types (Small, Medium, and Large) that affect the physical abilities and weapons you can carry, as well as four classes (Soldier, Medic, Engineer, Operative) that all have markedly different abilities. Now how well did that go? Keep reading and you'll see.
The Good:
-Amazing character creation, millions of combinations and they (mostly) work really well
-The aesthetics of the game (because it definitely ain't realistic) are pretty good for 2011 standards
-Parkour is fun and innovative, even if disorienting and the controls kinda suck
-Level design is pretty good
-I'll say it again, the level of detail in the character creation is really good considering this is an arena shooter where you don't even see said character very often
-Music is kinda good I guess
The Bad:
-All characters in the game have an absurd amount of health and guns are generally useless at all distances other than point blank
-Characters can be revived from LITERALLY ANY form of damage because magic
-Unconscious characters (i.e., waiting to be revived) ALSO have way too much health and force the enemy team to spend time doing a finishing animation (nothing fancy, just a weapon butt) to kill them instead of wasting ammo
-Ammo itself is very scarce because it takes 2 clips (that is not an exaggeration for certain ARs) to kill someone
-Compared to character customization, gun customization is severely lacking
-Given that there are about 8 maps (2 in DLC, iirc) and incredibly little variance between them, there is next to no replay value in this game whatsoever
-Teams respawn in waves, so if you get sniped and nobody's around to revive you, you could be waiting up to *20* seconds to get back in the game
-As mentioned earlier, the story is mostly absent from the game and when it is present it sucks
-Most guns and their attachments can *only* be unlocked by finishing Challenges, which are tedious and easy-to-fail "activities" that exist solely to♥♥♥♥♥♥off the audience
-The levelling system in this game is incredibly poor. You gain a level, you get a perk. However, most of the perks are uselss in the skill trees for the classes and because you are restricted to a max of 20 perks (for 20 levels) you have to play four seperate characters to be efficient (i.e., remotely competent) in any of the classes because multiclassing is discouraged. This is compounded by the fact that levelling takes a very long time and the grind is very tedious (grinding, in an FPS? Really?), as well as the missions being both unfun and quite long (playing defense can last 30-45 minutes per match if your team sucks).
TL;DR: I would not recommend this game. However, if you look past its many flaws you might see something that could've been great if it hadn't made quite so many poor decisions. So if you actually decide to play this masochism simulator I would encourage you to play one character up to level 20, then uninstall the game and pretend you never experienced this.

First off: this game is fun. If you like HOMM/AoW style combat and empire development, this will be right up your alley. It's a bit simpler (units don't have many spells/skills and mainly boil down to melee/archer/mage/healer), but not simple. As is typical for these types of games, the combat gets repetitive.
Now, there's another Eador game, named Eador: Genesis. It's 99% the same game, but this one has (much) better graphics and some minor tweaks. However, MotBW also introduced some serious bugs, one of which is pretty game breaking. It's also a bit slower than ideal, especially on older systems. A lot of the gameplay revolves around reloading the game as a "go back in time" mechanic, mainly because of the inability to properly scout enemies and the impossibility to predict the actual strength of an army [unless you play the first or second difficulty, out of 7 or so].
Eador: Genesis is bug free and due to its age suffers no lag or delays. The "reload last turn" mechanic makes more sense there, but is also less forgiving than the full save/load in MotBW; to be hones it's much more interesting that way.
So my advice would be to pick up Eador: Genesis ($6 on
I believe) unless you REALLY like flashy graphics in a tactics game.

Being only 13 cents, I thought it would be worth the small risk. It wasn't. Some of the bugs described by other people have been fixed, but the game itself, while not exactly "broken" is still not exactly playable, either. It's hard to tell when you're taking damage, what caused it, and where you could have gone. Most enemy attacks come in the form of this sort of mist, which I can only assume is made up of particle effects, while your attacks are clear and straightforward. You get 3 lives (i think?) and the trend among the lives seems to go like this:
1) Die in first five seconds from an enemy that isn't even on screen yet, but is still shooting a continuous beam that covers 1/3 of the field of view.
2) Flood of pickups, most of which are bad to actually pick up but they look just like the good pickups. I'd chalk it up to chance but when 4/5 of the chances on this one buff/debuff pickup are debuffs and the one buff is so exaggerated it might as well be a debuff. Maybe that was the goal in the first place. Die from not being able to move properly thanks to pickup.
3) usually last a bit longer, but still get killed when 2 ships spawn offscreen at the same time, each one shooting a continuous particle stream covering a third of the screen.
Basically, There are enemies you can't kill because they are shooting a constant stream that covers 1/3 the FOV, The enemy ships can shoot you from offscreen, there's no real pattern to the attacks so there's no promise of a blind spot or way to defend yourself, and those are issues I discovered from the first three times I tried playing. Oh, yeah. the first time you start up the game, you can't skip the opening cutscene. Which I can take to mean that the game has no way of knowing whether or not it's been opened before. If this were a web game with that kind of problem, I'd forgive it. End of the day, I can't forgive it for being another game that gives the great Unity Engine a bad name just because there was some dev who doesn't know what he's doing. I'll probably let it run until I get all the trading cards, sell them on the market, then get my 13 cents refunded if I can.

This is a game that is about medival battles and personal interactions that create their own stories, their own rules, their own kingdoms. The idea is noteworthy though not fully realized, It is missing at least a medicum of lore and game mechanics that will keep this game from becoming a mass-slaughter of hackers and self-proclaimed bandits when it finally becomes decent enough for the public to take an interest in it once more (advice for developers: perhaps through a huge update and a sale? Maybe around summer and then another one during winter?)
So here are some unbiased positives and negatives of the current version of the game:
Pros:
1) The combat is unique and it works
2) Armour and weapons are superbly made (texture wise)
3) The environment is well crafted with good atmosphere
4) The graphics are great
5) Frequent updates
6) VERY, VERY good music selection (Very, very, very, very good)
7) Has a lot of promise
Cons:
1) Slightly buggy (the developers are thankfully working on that)
2) Not enough servers for decent multiplayer games (horrible ping for a multiplayer game)
3) Does not have a Singleplayer mode (unforgivable)
4) The Epic needs a lot of work
5) Very demanding on the PC (hopefully, lower-end pc's will be able to work with the game once it is at later stages in completion... hopefully)
The game would be decent - good even, if most of the bugs were fixed (they are working on it) and more servers were put up.
I believe that putting this game out as early-access was a mistake. They should have finished the game first, then released and updated based on feedback. But there is no use crying over spilt milk...
Overall, I would advise not to purchase the game at its current stage; however, do put it on your wishlists as when it is finally done - it will be worth checking out.
I recommend this game for the future.

The prince of hell (a skeleton rabbit with a cape) got photographed together with his rubber duck and is lampooned on the internet for it. The only reasonable reaction — of course — is to kill everyone who has seen those embarrassing pictures.
Developer Arkedo sets Hell Yeah's morbid humourous tone from the very start of the game. What follows is a surprisingly good 2D platformer.
On his journey to kill every single one of the 100 monsters fallen in disgrace, our hero rabbit visits various areas of hell, ranging from a casino to space. The game is packed with comic like brutality; exploding enemies, blood fountains and grotesque finishing moves.
On first sight, Hell Yeah seems like one of those gag games, that aim to be taken with a pinch of salt and don't really try to be good games at core. I'm talking about the likes of Brütal Legend or Goat Simulator; games that wouldn't be enjoyable, if their mechanics were stripped off their context. But after finishing Hell Yeah, I feel like I should give up on that prejudice towards gag games.
Hell Yeah takes typical platformer mechanics, like wall jumps, moving platforms and Donkey Kong Countryesque cannons, and combines them with guns, which can aim in 360 degrees, and a buzz saw. That core mechanic itself is functional — precise jumps were a bit tricky though, because there's next to no acceleration and only one movement speed (the directional input is binary and there is no run button).
Steady variety is what makes the game fun in the end. You can play on gambling machines in the casino. There's a part where you operate a submarine and you can shoot rainbows, that bounce off of walls, somewhere else.
Finishing moves are a source of variety too. The monsters don't have individual moves, but more than 25 different finishers are included in the game. They are occasionally really creative and particularly show of the games polished visuals. All of them start with a short quick-time-event or mini game, making them clearly more interesting than most games finishing moves, but bottom line, they still get old after you see the same animation the third time.
After finishing the game, I was positively surprised how much bang I got for the time invested. Every mechanic and idea is used for a short amount of time and then dropped for something entirely new. Take the rainbow gun I mentioned earlier. You get the gun play three or four different situations with it — which all require the gimmick, that shots bounce off walls — and then you never see it again.
On the other hand, the short innovation cycle leaves no room for any of the mechanics to grow complex, which again, fits the far from serious visual and narrative style of Hell Yeah.
It's a cool game. It cracks the jokes, shows off some crazy ideas and ends before it gets repetitiv. Play this with a friend and a few bottles of beer and I bet you have on or two great evenings.

I could say a bunch of stuff here about how I grew up in the '80s and this game is a nostalgia bomb for me. I could say a bunch of stuff about how it would have absolutely rocked the gaming world back then if the hardware could've supported it, with its sprawling worlds, titanic boss fights, multitudinous weaponry, and secrets aplenty.
I would be right in saying those things, but to do so would be to diminish it in today's world of first-person shooters, 3D graphics, and oversaturated retro genre.
The simple fact about this complex game: it is absolutely amazing, whether you grew up in the '80s or in the '00s. Everything about this game is fantastically done, from the faithful Metroid-style artwork to the haunting electronic soundtrack to the fascinating storyline to the sense of balance you get from every upgrade. Even the ending is satisfying and doesn't feel rushed. Nothing about the game feels tired or rehashed...just familiar, like visiting your childhood neighborhood for the first time in 30 years.
None of the 20 main weapons feels overpowered, even the ones you find late in the game, and every one caters to a certain play style. No enemy is frustratingly difficult to kill, though some of them are -very- challenging. The maps will challenge your sense of exploration even as you go back through them to net that elusive 100% item completion rank.
I can't say enough good about Axiom Verge, but I will say this:  Tom Happ, please keep making games, because you've crafted a masterpiece with this one, and I can't wait to see what's next.

Okay, I enjoy this game. I enjoy it alot. I have dumped alot of time into the game. If you like Strategy/RPG mix overall I think this game is something to look at. I won't hide the fact that the game is still buggy even after being out for a year, but the developers have been patching the game non-stop since it came out April 2013.
The Ugly:
Okay this game still has bugs, for some people game breaking bugs, and for others bugs that are iritating enough that can make it painful to play the game sometimes. The game was released last April almost completely unplayable, and over the past year it has improved for the major part. Yet I won't gloss over the fact that their is still alot wrong with the game.
The Bad:
The game probably is not all that balanced. Their are 4 tiers of units, and some T4 units could trample an entire army. Not all of the Hero classes are balanced. Their are 4 of them, but they all are playable. It will be nice to see what the game is like in the future.
The Good:
Did I mention patching? The developers still care about the game. They have been patching it a while, and still patch it.
There is alot in this game, alot of units, alot of choice. Alot of lore burried deep within a rough exterior. The game does not look half bad. The game is not fast paced, but is the type of game you can start playing, and come back between turns as you do something else, but will also keep you wanting to play "one more turn" when things are getting good or you near to beating another map. The developers have recently added a boat load of new units and spells, and have dropped hints are future expansion to the game.
Is the game, worth $19.99? Its a hard sell considering how buggy it can still be. I do thing its a hard sell, but I've enjoy the time I've dumped  into the game and I do appreciate the patches that have gone into it. The game has gotten good, and hopefully it will cotinue getting better.

To put plainly, it is possible for a country to demand control over a territory that it neither particpated in the conflict or was the origional belligerant.
Multiplayer is an entirely different mess that requires the playerbase to develop house rules to counter faults in the combat system, escelation of war, and game breaking bugs.  Most rules will ban a "space marine" divisions that exploits how the divsion stats are calculated to gain the river crossing benifits of marines and armor of heavy tank destroyers. To me this one is most frustrating because it seems that whomever is in charge of the balance of the game is asleep at the wheel.
Overall I don't think I've had a run through of a single or multiplayer game that I enjoyed. In single player the victories are hollow when you realize that the AI is unable to develop effective strategies to counter you. In multiplayer you are very likely to spend 2-3 hours playing "Bob the Builder" only for someone to quit, troll, or realize that the gulf of skill between teams is hilariously one sided.

I bought this for thirteen cents, because last time I bought a game for a handful of pennies it actually turned out well.
Not this time, though.
To start, the intro is a long, drawn out sequence of polygons materializing into the name of the developer. Naturally, it's unskippable or I wouldn't whinge about it. Every time you start up this game you spend 15 or so seconds watching digital paint dry so you can be reminded of who made it.
Once you reach the menu, you can change settings, get a description of the player ships, and "Star Game." "Star"-ing the game allows you to get a bit of understanding of the game's story in audio and comic format, but only a bit. The comic may or may not be well drawn. It's hard to tell, as it looks like it was passed through so many filters in photoshop it's almost nothing more than grimy blotches of paint split up into frames, and the voice-over is somewhat hard to understand.
After the comic, there is something that technically qualifies as gameplay. The ship controls don't feel very smooth or natural, enemies fire clouds of smoke that blend in with the background, and floating powerups may randomly speed you up, slow you down, or lock an axis of movement. As someone who's played a decent amount of shmups both on Steam and off, randomly screwing over the player or hitting him with things he cannot see are not generally considered good elements of gameplay in the genre.
Other than that, the enemies and powerups seem to be randomly placed, dying advances the level, and there aren't any animations for ship movement.
Keep my thirteen pennies, dev guy. Keep them, and when you're planning to release  your next game, ask the pennies, "Have I really made a complete product, or should I keep working?" They won't respond. Pennies can't talk. But in your heart, you'll know the answer.

As much as I like 2-D shoot ‘em ups, there isn’t much good I can say about Stellar 2D.
This game has potential to become a decent 2-D shooter, except the gameplay constantly works against you while playing the game. The ship is fairly hard to control in contrast to most 2-D shooters out there. Pressing up and left while shooting will cause the ship to ignore your input, making it harder to maneuver around enemy projectiles. Some of the bullets are difficult to see, particularly the linear bullets that are mildly faded. It’s not too big of problem, but I’ve died so many times not knowing what just hit my ship until the last second. The biggest problem I have with the enemy bullets is the sound it makes when the enemy ship fires one. The default audio level of the sound effect greatly contrasts the default audio level of the background music and you will constantly hear the same few sound effects every second. The red, blue, and green sphere thingy (Note: I don’t know its official name) is the most annoying mechanic in the game for me. Basically, its risk versus reward. You can either get a speed boost, power boost, or one of the major debuffs the game has to offer. These debuffs occur way more than it should and it destroys any chance you have at surviving. These debuffs include: no horizontal movement, no vertical movement, having your ship slow down, and worst of all, the inability to shoot. The inability to shoot not only allows you to become more susceptible to damage, it also hinders your progress towards making it to the next level. Finally, the bosses are a joke. No really, they only exist to randomly show up and die in less than three seconds.
As much as the bad stuff outweighs the good with this game, some of the good ideas this game has seems faintly innovative. I like the leniency of this game. The amount of HP it gives, the shield mechanic, and the rate the health packs spawns lends the game to a more casual audience. The amount of health the enemies have, make the gameplay fast-paced and mildly amusing compared to the average shoot ‘em up. The range upgrades makes the game somewhat enjoyable for me. Having an edge over your enemies when using this upgrade is satisfying to say the least. If I could say anything bad about it, it’s that you’re not able to pick up a better range upgrade until your current one runs out. That and the fact you can only keep it for a limited amount of time.
Overall, the game felt unsatisfying. With a decent idea, bad gameplay, and that unskippable logo sequence, I would recommend getting it only for the trading cards.

This is a great flight combat simulator, maybe the best out there.
The graphics are kind of outdated because its not a new game, but still good and rounded, the airplanes are very nice modelled, landscape are simple but cool, effects are not bad.  Panels and Hud are not special but you have lot of views to choose from.
The strong point of this game is when it comes to simulate the typical features of this kind of combat and this aviation era. You can see realistic aerodynamics, ballistic trajectory,  angle of attack stalls, overheat, spins ( you need to know how to proper get out or it will spin until hit the ground ), torque effect, potential energy, and much more.  The hitboxes and damage effect also works great.  You have a enormous variety of planes and targets to choose from, and every plane have their own characteristics.  There many other cool features.
The only downside for me is the campaign, because it´s take so many time and are not something that catch you and get you evolved, i just don´t feel like it is a campaign.   But i had a lot of fun doing custom missions, and multiplayer can be real exciting and challenging.
IL2 have a lot of option to setup the game more easy and friendly, but in cost of the realism of course, i´d rather play it "as real as it gets".

Wrath of the Dead Rabbit you play as the prince of hell, who was photographed secretly by paparazzi while bathing, now you go on a quest to find all 100 monsters in hell who have seen your nudes and exact revenge.  Gameplay wise I feel like it sits in a place in between platformer and twin stick shooter.
There are a variety of weapons and tools to use in your quest including but not limited to, Rocket launchers, mini guns, grenade launchers, giant buzsaws, shotguns, and lazers. After defeating each monster to finish it off you are brought into a variety of WarioWare type minigames to get that final hit. if you fail the boss heals a little and you have to do it again. While not complex the finishers were pretty fun, in my opinion.
The game has a lot of stuff in it to do, you've got customizations to collect, weapons to purchase, and even an island where you keep your monster friends who do jobs for you (slave labor). There are even side missions you can complete for extra rewards. While the game is not very long if oyu rush through it, it can be quite substantial if you try to collect everything and 100 percent it.
I recommend Hell Yea! Wrath of the Dead Rabbit to fans of platformers, adventure games, sidescroling shooters, and anyone who just likes and indie game with cheesy comedy.

Could have been good, but was plagued from the start with bad tutorials, confusing menus, and, amazingly enough, bugs during combat that would prevent progression.

The game has three tiers. On campaign level you conquer "shards" that give you new technologies and buildings, and compete with other NPCs. Each conquest happens on a map where you and your opponent have a castle, raise an army and fight for territories and resources. Finally, each fight happens on a tactical hex map.
Campaign level is little more than a sequence of missions. You have some choice on what to attack next, but it does not matter much. It is extremely long, and most will stop playing before end. After playing 200 hrs I am about halfway.
Arena level is fun, but NPC is not competitive - its just something to kill when you want the arena to end. The fun comes out of selecting a sequence of fights to level up your hero and your castle. Its somewhat similar to King's Bounty in play style - you pick fights, your hero levels up, you can now win harder fights, but there is no hurry to do something by set time.
The tactical fights are reasonably entertaining, units have various spefical abilities and immunities that you have to keep in mind, there are spells, tile bonuces, fatigue influence etc.
This would be a very good game, if not for bugs. Bugs! When I bought it a year ago, it was essentially unplayable, so I let it settle down for a while. Now it is somewhat better, but still, hourly crashes, NPC units endlessly going in circles, lockdowns, corrupted saves... when half of the challenge in a fight comes not from defeating an enemy, but from avoiding triggering the known bugs, the game definitely has quality problems... and if they didn't fix it by now I guess they never will.
So... I am not recommeding it because of bugs.

After two dozen restarts as nearly every faction with what felt like every strategy, I finally "finished" WWII in a historical path as the USA. A [truly] Grand Strategy game that lasts for only 12 years, with every hour as a single game turn. It feels like you can't really break the mould, but the possibility for immersion and role-play is all in the player which is status quo with Paradox titles. WWII games are a dime a dozen these days, and while some of the best or most fun focus on the first-person or squad-based combat - few embody the wide history-changing magnitude of the role the leaders of countries played during the era; Hearts of Iron has always been the Rock of the Marne in this regard.
HoI IV is an evolution for the series, breaking from the complex systems and micro-management of earlier titles to open the Grand Strategy up to more casual WWII players. In my opinion this is what the series needed and Paradox looks at the core systems and the role they play: production, battle plans, division design, land/naval/air war. Several systems are half-implemented or worse have a trivial impact on game-play: trade, diplomacy, and national unity. Some systems are outright missing that would be a surefire sell to this level of gameplay: intelligence, supply, chains of command. Hopefully like many main-line PDX titles these will be addressed through a steady stream of expansions, Free-LC, and regular release of 'overhaul' patches. I appreciate the approach to what seems like an 'endless life-cycle' for their games and hope that HOI4 gets the same treatment.
Since it's release, there have been patches that fixed the air war, the interface, and tuned the production systems. The AI is adequate - but low and behold I think there is no other game that has a more challenging task for an AI. Even Civilization could be a more simple AI than simulating the alternate history that titles such as Hearts of Iron allows you to explore.
Hearts of Iron isn't for everyone, but if Grand Strategy or armchair-generaling is your forte, the 4th edition will be a staple in your arsenal for several years with the dedication Paradox will give it. I recommend it, and also the soundtrack is epic to boot. I recommend "Land of the Rising Sun" for your playthrough.

So a lot fo people are complaining about bugs, personally I have not encountered any, that out of the way let's get into the review.
Pros
-Pirates, if you like pirates congratulations, this game has them
-Pets, I had a giant spider named Jeff the Spider God, he rode on my captain's head and bit people the captain was fighting
-Skill customization, sure it's pretty simple, but I like it well enough
-Ship customization, All else aside building your ship and customizing your flag can be pretty fun if you like that sort of thing, and if you don't just steal a ship from some pirates you murdered
Cons
-Swimming, you would think that choosing a life at sea would sort of require that they know how to swim. You would, apparently, be wrong. Just came back to the game after a decent while and forgot this fact and promptly lost every crew member to drowning.
-Knockback, Knockback in this game seems like it would be a good thing, have crew with melee weapons with good knockback and let your ranged crew sort it out from there. Unfortunately high knockback usually means you punch someone three miles and into the ocean, making them drown and losing you all the loot they may have had on them
-Micromanagement, Micromanaging your crew is a huge pain, particularly when you are already in combat, crew members on low health will continue fighting no matter how many times you try to make them run.
-No longer under active development. This con speaks for itself, and for some people can be a deal breaker. As of a few months ago the last update for Pixel Piracy came and went, the devs are working on a new game (Pixel Privateers) which will play similar to pixel piracy, but has a redesigned and more easily fixable game engine. It will also have multiplayer unlike Pixel Piracy, so if you want multiplayer then wait for Privateers to come out.
All in all I find this game really enjoyable and I eagerly await the release of the successor. The game for me runs perfectly fine, and is a good time waster if nothing else, though getting the game on a sale will probably be more appealing to most.

This is so close to being an amazing game that it causes me physical pain. It's that close, but there are a few crippling flaws that just ruin it. First, there's the combat. There are different ranks of creatures, one through four, one being weakest and four being most powerful. The problem with this is, after a certain point, anything below rank three will die in the first turn of battle because the enemy AI consists entirely of 'KILL WEAKEST CHARACTER'. The combat maps are tiny so forget any sort of strategy, mid and end game opponents can hit you anywhere you stand. Oh, and those opponents are almost always all one to nine monsters, plus nine to twelve wizards. There are three wizard types, and you will see up to a dozen in every single combat.
There are dragons in the game, and you can find them as random encounters. That isn't a problem. A single low level dragon can be beaten, but it's fairly tough unless you come loaded for end game critter hunting with high end, high level units. It's cool. You get an achievement. What isn't cool is that the dragons can spawn in groups of up to six, and all of them in the level 15 range. There might be worse groups out there, but this is literally what invaded one of my provinces in my current game. This isn't something you can fight. I also mean that Literally. You can not defeat these multiple dragon encounters. It isn't possible. You can build an arena in your home province and send heroes to battle in it to gain experience. Why am I mentioning this? because as soon as a hero reaches level ten, the enemy heroes you battle in the arena can also spawn with dragons as minions. It goes about as well as you'd expect.
On the plus side, your units can level up and improve their abilities, but it really doesn't matter, because a lvl 30 tier one unit will still be instagibbed by a lvl 1 tier four. And the upgrade system is utterly worthless as well. Why yes random number generator, I did want to improve my crossbowmans hand to hand skills for the fourth time in a row. No, he doesn't need better ranged attacks, he needs to be able to swing that butterknife he has like a man!
There are hundreds of items you can find, which is nice, but there's almost no storage space for them. You get a tiny little vault that can't be upgraded. It wouldn't be so bad but on the same screen you have access to the merchant window to sell stuff, and hey, if you guessed that had a scroll bar and infinite space in it, go get a cookie or something. You can build an artifact shop so you can buy artifacts, but unfortunately it doesn't cycle through different ones. You get the opportunity to buy three randomly chosen ones and it never changes for the rest of the game. Those three items are pretty much going to be terrible and I really want to chalk it up to being a bug that it doesn't refresh every so often, but it's been like that since release so probably it isn't.
There are four types of hero you can recruit, but you shouldn't bother getting anything but a warrior. The warrior is so much better than the other three it defies belief. Scouts can be useful for the rare encounters designed exclusively to kill warriors, but that's about it. Oh, and yeah, there are encounters designed from the ground up to murder warriors. packs of medusa will petrify you and then poison you, giant spiders will web you down and poison you, giant slugs will poison you if you hit them or vomit poison on you from a distance if you don't.
Edit: Okay, so I finally managed to grind a mage high enough to use a specific spell named 'white magic', and basically, it lets you break the game over your knee like a rotten twig. Two casts will clear virtually any combat encounter of critters, barring the two (the latest update may have added more) creatures who are magic immune. Once you get one cast per combat, better beleive that mage is going straight to lvl 30 since he can now effectively obliterate entire armies. Unconquerable foes turn instantly into big, meaty sacks of free XP. Just load up every unit slot with lvl 1 swordsmen, the enemy creatures/mages/whatever will go and kill them while your mage, free and unharmed, fires magic nukes that hit EVERYTHING ON THE MAP FOR MASSIVE DAMAGE. This is a well balanced, well implimented ability that reduces multiplayer combat to 'whoever goes first wins'. Casting it does a small amount of damage to the mage, but a couple of healers can fix it easily before any monsters that made it to turn two kill them for being a weaker, easier target than the wizard FIRING MAGICAL NUKES AT THEM.
Oh, and I hope you like really, really really loud TING! sounds, because the game plays one over and over at random for no reason I can discern.
Edit: I also hope you don't like loading saved games, because doing that while the game is running will cause the entire thing to crash. Not always, but often enough that I had to mention it.

A great homage to its predecessor on Sega back in the day. Gory, explosive gridiron football with punny fantasy characters and teams, cheesy but hilarious smack talk and commentary by the infamous Tim Kitzrow from the NFL Blitz series. It's a gloriuous mashup of old and new. If I had to compare, it's NFL Blitz meets fantasy characters with over-the-top gore.
Dev Support
Devs are awesome! Continued communication and consistent updates to improve and add new features. Can't stress enough how important and awesome this is for games these days.
Gameplay
What sets this game apart from other football games are the unique Dirty Tricks that you can call on both offense and defense that put a great spin on the standard game of pigskin. Not only that, the massive carnage you can deal out to your opponent's team can result in them having to rethink their strategy without any running backs or you could get a win by forfeit if they lose too many key players. This also adds an additional layer of strategy to the game that can result in a victory that would otherwise be a loss. I messed around in one game and was down by a few scores towards the end but narrowly won due to all the opponent's QBs dying. There's also a way to resurrect teammates before it's too late if you set those game options initially too, so it's not very easy to win by forfeit either.
Other nice features include lots of teams to choose from and more planned in the future. Season and playoff modes to setup tournaments with your friends or play on your own. Well designed stadiums with their own unique hazards like mines, ice holes, and giant worms to add to the carnage. Half-time "show" which is a mini-game that awards the winner a free Resurrection.
Controls
Standard game controls for running around, stiff arming, passing, etc. Controller and (customizable) keyboard support but I HIGHLY recommend a controller.
Graphics
Graphics are almost on par with most other sports games but animations and character design could use some more variety and improvement. I'm a sucker for variation as it can get old seeing the same animations, etc. Some of the wrestling-style tackles are incredibly satisfying to watch.
Sound
As mentioned before, the commentary by Tim always has me LOLing at the game even after hearing it many times. Great carnage from hits and explosions too. Good variety of songs for each team.
Singleplayer/Co-Op
The AI is pretty stout when playing against a similarly rated team, but the lower rated teams are no slouch either. They're pretty "smart" (see also cheat) :) about calling good plays and dirty tricks and good at time management. I haven't really played much Co-Op yet, but the option is there now for 1v1, 2v2, 4v4 so that's great if you have a group of friends to crowd around a screen and play. Great season and playoff modes as well as a practice mode. Needs a franchise mode for continued fun.
Multiplayer

Let me preface this with saying I have a GTX 1080 and an i7-7700k.
Here's how the story goes. I found out Brink went free to play and I remember seeing it when it came out and going "Eh, that seems like a good time waster game but I wouldn't spend $ on it." So I decided to waste some time. Downloaded the game, launched it, customized my character and decided to launch the first story mission so I could learn the combat. Before launching the mission I did my usual perusal of the options. I saw that the game would not allow me to put the resolution at 1080p and thought "Hmm....that's weird." So I left it in some weird resolution that was as close as I could get it and thought "No big deal, the menus look perfectly fine in this resolution." So then I launched said story mission, this is what followed:
I watched as I launched an offline solo mission and was told "Wait for joining" to which I stared confusedly at my screen for nearly 10 seconds before finally being introduced to a loading screen. Upon getting into the actual "match" (apparently the story mode is just AI matches with cutscenes in between them, no actual attempt at a campaign like map). Without being asked to select weapons or a class I was faced with a 10 second count down which puzzled me further (because I was expecting an actual offline story experience) and was finally given control of my character. I ran about 10 feet before my stomach dropped at the realization that this game was running at around 25fps. After running down a corridor in truly choppy fashion I was introduced to my first enemy where I emptied a clip into their face only to be left gazing upon the magic pixel floating above their head while I reloaded and was swiftly Tony Montana'ed by his friends.
Here's the good part, after dying I was told to wait for a medic. In which I watched my entire team slaughtered and had to wait about 20-30 seconds for a respawn. I respawned and walked five feet before th e game froze up harder than a no-damage Ninja Gaiden Ultimate Ninja difficulty run. I was forced to CTRL-SHIFT-ESC and close the game with task manager. Here I sit now realizing why this game has mixed reviews.

The store page describes this as polarizing, and well I guess that puts me in the negative side of the camp. I'm certainly no stranger to story driven products through Steam, but A Bird Story just doesn't feel engaging. It's a linear narrative conveyed entirely through RPGMaker visuals that tells the tale of a boy who comes across an injured bird and must learn how to let go, through bizarre sequences like flying on a paper aeroplane mixed in with normal scenes like life in a classroom.
While the premise holds value I just wasn't that interested in it. The tale woven feels lacks the depth I've come to expect from stories, and while the visuals were enough for me to gain an understanding of what was happening it sadly wasn't enough to make me want to know more. At times the pacing could be sluggish and a few instances where I felt the tone was inconsistent with the overall package. With only an hour of content to have even that amount padded out was disappointing. It's also a story that, as far as I can tell, you can't pause when the game is in one of its automatic sequences.
The player interaction is pretty limited as well. Mostly it's take boy from point A to point B, and if you try to wander off the path the game has set out it just blocks you off and forces you back. In some cases it's expecting literally one input to trigger the next thing, dressed up as player interaction. The one sequence that deviates slightly is just hunting around each screen for a nest before moving to the next one. I never got the point of any of it.

I've just finished the story right now at exactly 3 am in the morning, and I really feel like I have to give a review instead of going to sleep and coming back later. Well, A Bird Story is actually a very nice interactive story, and I say interactive story because it really is just an interactive story which some people tend to mistake for as a game. A Bird Story has a very limited "gameplay" (I say gameplay because I don't know what else to call it) which just includes walking around and pressing some arrow keys in order to move on with the story. The graphics/art can either be good or bad, depending on the player's taste. It also doesn't have that much of an interesting plot/story. So why did I recommend it? I did it because of the way it tells the story, which it actually does so well I got goosebumps when it ended and it did it without a single line of dialogue. True, the story may be a bit boring, bland, or mundane (or whatever synonyms you can think of) at times, but that's actually the beauty of it (in my opinion). These boring scenes (like looking out the window during class, getting creeped out by people in the elevator, wanting to play in the rain,  etc.) are what makes A Bird Story and its main character more relatable to the player. So if you're wondering whether this title is worth the money or not before buying it, I suggest you stop looking at this review right now and just experience it for yourself, or you could try grabbing it if it ever comes on a discount.
Note: The music is nice though

Mutant Football League is the definitive spiritual successor to the original Mutant League Football on the Sega Genesis.  If you're a fan of MLF or even NFL Blitz, you will love this game.
Designed by Michael Mendheim, creator of the original game, MFL boasts countless throwbacks to the Genesis classic while also bringing many new features to the table.  Yes, you can still kill players to knock them out of the game--permanently.  And yes, you can still bribe (and murder, if necessary) referees.  But there's more.  One of the most significant additions is a vile, vulgar, utterly hilarious commentary team voiced by none other than Tim Kitzrow, whose iconic work in such arcade games as NBA Jam and the aforementioned NFL Blitz speaks for itself.
If you've never played the Sega Genesis game and aren't sure what to expect, here's a quick rundown:
Mutant Football League is a violent, fast-paced, 7-on-7 American football game in which over a dozen teams comprised of skeletons, robots, superhumans, orcs, and aliens quite literally fight it out for victory.  Fields are littered with deadly hazards like mines and buzzsaws and teams can even call "Dirty Trick" plays like "Shotgun," which makes the quarterback whip out a literal shotgun.  There's also plenty of post-play fighting, so don't be surprised if a linebacker elbow-drops your star quarterback right to the morgue well after the whistle is blown!
Offline you can play against the AI in one of several different modes, ranging from a one-time exhibition game to a full-fledged 13-game season (playoffs included, if you qualify for them).  There's also local multiplayer/couch co-op, meaning you and up to three other people can play with or against one another.  Online play is currently limited to 1v1, but the developers hope to expand on it in the near future.
The game looks and feels surprisingly polished and is incredibly fun to play.  The controls are responsive and intuitive and the AI can put up one heck of a fight.  There's also a nice variety of teams and fields/stadiums.  Additionally, there are plenty of options that allow you to drastically alter the experience.  Don't like losing players permanently?  Turn on resurrection, and they'll be restored the very next down.  Don't like trick plays?  Turn them off, and you'll never be crushed by a gigantic defender ever again!  More content is also on the way, with demons and werewolves coming post-launch free of charge.  Mod tools are also planned, which is incredibly exciting for obvious reasons.
Bottom line:  As I said at the very beginning, if you're a fan of the original Mutant League Football or even NFL Blitz, you will love this game.  It is fast, and it is violent.  It will make you laugh, and probably even cry (losing a star player early in the game is never an easy pill to swallow).  But most of all, it will make you realize that it doesn't take a massive team with a ginormous budget to produce an outstanding football game that delivers hours upon hours of fun.
