I found this game to be quite fun. Definitely a more entertaining twist on football than some other football games, but then again, sports games aren't my forte and the last football games I played was on the playstation 2 and Nintendo 64, I will admit that. I still found it most entertaining and look forward to having fun with people on this game.
The dirty tricks are varied and interesting, and they help you get a win even if you are trailing by 16 points the the fourth quarter by slaughtering their quarterbacks. Scoring points is also made easier by bribing the ref, warp speed, or any other dirty trick, as well blocking any scoring runs or passes with dirty trick defensive plays to prevent yourself from having a Kentucky Wildcats vs Florida Gators situation. Aside from dirty tricks, you have attack plays that allow you to assault other players to help even the odds in your favor. You could also play an 'honest' game with no dirty tricks or assaults but where's the fun in that?
The AI has several difficulty settings to it, from easy to masochism. I tried it on the first three of five difficulties as of this review and found it to be pretty solid for the most part, although I will admit to nearly losing to average ai had it not been for dirty tricks since, again, sports games aren't my forte. Any bugs I ran into are taken care of in quick fashion and because of that, don't linger around.
There's multiplayer in the game so if you want to wreck some player's lives or get wrecked by players, there's that for hours of entertainment, just don't think let your ego get the best of you since dirty tricks, when played right, can make good and bad players equal like colt fireams in the old west. There's also co-op in case you want your friends or total strangers join in on giving out slaughterfests to ai or players.
Overall, I am having a most enjoyable time from this game. I would whole heartedly reccomend this to those who are looking for a twist on football, those who want a game that would be entertaining with others who are sober or drunk, those who want a sports game with lots of dark humor, or to use this game as a revenge fantasy against football teams that failed you or caused your favorite team to fail.

When I first played this game, I thought to myself, "cool. Another Metroidvania game. This could be fun to play sometimes I don't think I'll get too attached, though." The second time I played this game, I couldn't stop until I was done with it and then some. I went back and completed it, found all the items and secrets, delved into the numerous theories floating around the Internet. I needed more. The deeper I got into it, the more it took its place as my favorite video game that I've ever laid my hands on. I've never purchased a single game for every console that I own so fast before.
One of my favorite things about this game is just the artistical aspect of it all--the attacks are beautifully animated, and the environments all have their own feel for each area. The pixel art is well-crafted and isn't at all distracting from the action you're putting Trace through; in fact, it makes it that much more immersive when you're fighting off a boss at least 5 times the size of you. The fights are relatively simple, but each boss has its own weak point like the good old days, and you don't have to spend hours trying to figure out what to do to land a hit. Which is awesome. There are so many weapons scattered around, you can pick and choose your play style, and use the best weapon that you like most. Not every weapon is required to beat the game or certain enemies. The secrets scattered around the game definitely help add to the story events that lead up to Axiom Verge's story that you play through, and there were a lot of moments where I genuinely had to sit back and question the things that I was told in black and white. I've never played a game that kept me awake for 3 days continuously poring over information trying desperately to find out what actually happened in certain instances, and that's a damn good sign. Considering that this was crafted by Tom alone, this game shines in many ways, and if you grew up on the good old games like Metroid like I did, this will not only be a blast from the past, it'll keep you wanting a sequel in the future.
If you like Metroid, you will love this game. Tip: the music is great so buy the package deal to get the soundtrack at a super cheap price.

Do you like Metroid? Do you like platformers? Do you like awesome soundtracks?
If you answered no to all of the above, buy Axiom Verge. If you answered yes to any of the above, I assume you already own it.

One of my favorite games i've ever purchased. It presents a refreshing Metroidvania game in which you find numerous weapons that you can use in creative and fun ways. On top of it all plenty of secrets to find, with great difficulty levels, bosses, and story.

Overall: Axiom Verge is an excellent Metroidvania, worth the price of admission.  It feels more like Super Metroid than SotN, so if you're a bigger fan of the Metroid parts ofa  Metroidvania then Axiom Verge is right up your alley.
Pros:
* The story presentation is a nice change on the typical "save the the world" trope commonly seen in the Metroidvania genre.
* Your character controls very well.
* There are a plethora of powerups and weapons to be discovered.
* The world is large enough to feel "big" without being so large that navigation is time consuming.
Cons:
* Many of the weapons are not very useful, or are only useful in very specific circumstances.
* The environments have a sense of sameness after a while.
* The boss fights can feel a little gimmick-y.

Axiom Verge is a lovingly crafted "metroidvania"-style 2D action adventure; a genre that hasn't received a lot of love lately. It is set in a alien world and has a bunch of neat pixel art and great music.
It borrows gameplay elements from various old school games and even adds a few new tricks into the mix to really open up the movement possibilities  later in the game and make you re-think and see places you have already visited in a new light. It has minor flaws, such as some of the acquired weapons feel a bit useless compared to others and some areas are more memorable in design or have better music tracks, but nothing I would consider deal breaking.
Absolutely recommended if you can appreciate a game that gives you a vague idea where to go but doesn't hold hands all the time; one that is built around backtracking and exploration.
ps. Nominated this for the "I THOUGHT THIS GAME WAS COOL BEFORE IT WON AN AWARD" award.

While many of the serious bugs have been resolved a year later, a few game-breaking bugs do remain (albeit the ones listed above do not).
Gameplay balance remains an issue, and it inherently leads to a very grindy game.
So it remains a diamond in the rough.
---
After almost a year, this game remains a bug-ridden hellhole, with very little tactical or strategic balance at most levels of the gameplay. I'm almost tempted to say the bugs are worse now than they were a year ago.
Some bugs include:
- if more than one battle of any kind occurs on the map, no other battles can occur. They immediately auto-resolve with both sides being listed as dead despite not being dead.
- The AI cannot conquer any terrain where it has to fight player guards. Neither the guards will die nor will the province be conquered.
Some gameplay issues include:
- In campaign mode, it is entirely possible for the capitol of an AI to be guarded by 9 centaurs. Centaurs are powerful tier 2 units. If this occurs in the first or second mission, you have been given a near-impossible task, as the gameplay elements that allow you to defeat centaurs are not available until later in the game. You can, of course, surrender, and keep playing. This, and similar balance issues, remain a frustrating element of the game.
- Starting units are worthless and unless you follow certain strategies or know what you're doing, you're likely to be stuck in your home province for many, many turns.
All of this is incredibly sad, as the game's core concept is pretty great. The programming and game design, however, are lackluster and poor. A great game marred by poor design.

“Stellar 2D is a retro style space arcade game, it's a 2D game in a 3D world. With an addictive, fast paced, casual game-play style.”
This quote has some truth to it, but also some lies. Stellar 2D is a retro style space arcade game but it is NOT addictive. In fact, this game seems quite incomplete and quite bad at the moment. HOWEVER, there is some potential buried deep within Stellar 2D. The overall idea isn’t bad or original. It’s basically a bullet hell, casual space arcade game. Sounds like a fun game right? WRONG! Currently there are SO many problems that Stellar 2D isn’t fun.
-Random status effects prevent horizontal or vertical movement.
Like WTF! These effects are the most annoying part about Stellar 2D. These so called “power-ups” make this game unbearable.
-Virtually invisible bullets
These “bullets” (I use that term loosely) are practically invisible 99% of the time. It makes this game not fun and just bad, unless the idea was that in the future bullets (all except you’re bullets) are undetectable.
-Game’s Menu / HUD
Do NOT get me started about this menu or HUD. Although the developer had fixed SOME issues, it’s still s*** and visually unappealing. Like what’s up with the font?
-Graphics
The game’s graphics are s*** at best. The opening cut scene’s graphics was the worst that I’ve ever seen in a game…EVER! It’s just not good.
-Sound Effects
Gave me permanent, PERMANENT hearing damage, 11 / 10.
-Space Crafts
Many appear to be unoriginal and copied.
What also “bugs” me about Stellar 2D is that there are STILL bugs (see what I did there) in this game, mainly with the menu. On August 5th 2015, I launched Stellar 2D to find the audio disappeared the moment I clicked on the menu. Although (for this game) no sound is better than sound…this shouldn’t happen. Now I know the developers did fix some issues but still, COME ON! This would be understandable if this game was in early access, but it’s not!
My final comments on this game are, I’m glad I got it for $.15. At this stage, it’s really, REALLY not worth purchasing. However, I like the idea. If the developers can fix this game up then I’ll gladly change my review from negative to positive.
I really hope that this game will eventually meet my standards but as of now…it’s just painful.

Every birdie, it’s time for the one, the only, bird dating game. You, the only human at St. PigeoNation Institution, are now surrounded by tons of male single birds who are ready to mingle. I remember my first encounter with the quirky game to this day. I was sitting in a lounge with a friend who looked at me and asked if I had seen Cryaotic’s new video; when I said no, she pulled it up, and I’ve never been the same since.

Of course, after seeing Cry play the game, I wanted to experience the life of a bird dater myself, and purchased the game as soon as it went on sale (I’m cheap). This game has yet to disappoint me.

If you go into this dating simulator expecting quality, fluffy content with a wholesome, cute relationship with a bird, it won’t happen. The game isn’t completely stupid and the plot is really deep, but you’re not going to get any adorable CGs (Character Graphics) of your bird and protagonist cuddling.

Though it isn’t what you’d call a cute dating sim in the first place, this game definitely takes a whole new turn. This story gets DARK. If you finally choose your bird, you’ll probably end their route thinking, “What the ****?” I didn’t experience a single path where I wasn’t just perpetually shocked. Nothing could be as wild as a plot—which just goes absolutely crazy—played out by BIRDS.

To many, they are probably are just thrown off by the birds, the puns, and the fact that you’re the only human there. But once you get past that initial confusion, you’ll be thrown into the plot of St. PigeoNation’s students and teachers. The game coated the plot with silly bird puns and, well, the characters being birds, covering the intensity to come. The plot isn’t the most perfect thing in the world, but the thought that these are all birds pushes rationality out the window.

As the game continues, the world will get darker and darker, and on certain birdie paths, you’ll realize how unfortunate all these birdies are. While the plot and characters are all this game really has (the soundtrack is composed of various free music, including Christmas music), it really is worth the couple dollars it costs.


Pros
• Each bird has a canon human form
• Bird puns
• Each character has development and some quirk
• Unlockable special bird
• You’re dating birds
• Dark, interesting plot
Cons
• Bird puns
• You’re dating birds
• Soundtrack can get annoying after multiple playthroughs
• Plot has strange pacing at time

Overall, for the few dollars it costs, the game will provide plenty of laughs as you find yourself getting deep into the plot of St. PigeoNation. While I find the soundtrack annoying and tend to play without sound, it is a personal dislike that doesn’t take away from the gameplay and content that Hatoful Boyfriend provides. There is replayability trying to delve deeper into each of the birds and plots which make the game a really enjoyable buy for the price it was and the amount of content you can get from it.

I believe that Hatoful Boyfriend is a very comical, quirky game that is worth the five dollars it asks for (or less during sales)—if you’re interested, you should certainly give it a chance. I give the game an 8/10; small issues I have and my distaste for the music does get in the way of a higher score. Even after beating the game, I still have found myself pulling it up, showing to others, and playing paths again to remind myself of my birdie husbands.

Neptunia U is without a doubt one the weakest entries in the Neptunia series, but that is to be expected of a spin-off. This one (along with Megatagmention, which is very similar) was clearly made with Neptunia fans in mind. The plot revolves two reporters (based on Japanese news and magazines) and the goddesses of Hyperdimension Neptunia 1 and 2 (it is recommended that you play through both of those games before this one) completing quests. Things don't really pick up from there which is a real letdown considering how entertaining the stories in the mainline games have been. From the start, it is clear this is not a plot heavy game. On the bright side, the dialogue in cutscenes is as great as ever and new characters fit right in with the cast.
The game is a good way to kill some time, and all the characters have different moves and a different feel, giving you enough variety to find a character that you'll like. but because things can drag on and on and get repetitive (you'll spend most of the time defeating enemies in an arena), this game is hard to play for long periods. There isn't anything that can be considered complex or hard to learn and its mechanics are very well explained, so players should be able to learn very quickly.  The game's main gimmick, the Costume Break (clothes tear after taking too much damage) can a bit awkward, especially when considering the appearance and ages of some of the characters. If this is something that bothers you, "fanservice-free" outfits that don't tear are available as unlockables very early on.
My biggest complaint about the game lies in the Irregular Quest missions, which do not tell you what your objective is and then require you to lose the battle in order to receive a hint as to what that mission's objective is. This is seriously unneeded and just make things inconvient. Another major issue is that the game will constantly crash every 15 to 20 minutes on some computers. This can easily be fixed permanently with a bit of research, so I do not see it as something that should hurt your experience.
If you can get the game on sale (it's very low in price during Steam sales), I highly recommend it, as it is a great way to kill some time, but I would also avoid buying at full price due to it's simplicity.

Well, for starters -- this is a Neptunia game. If you don't know what that means in terms of setting and characters you should probably look at the main JRPG series first. This is a spinoff which isn't considered canon -- but it could very well be since it's not reshaping Gamindustri in any way.
Also, this is a Neptunia game, using IF's patented(?) technique of asset-reuse. It has considerably less story than the main games (if you can even call it a story -- I haven't finished the game yet).
On the positive side, the lack of story means fewer visual-novel style dialogues and much less childish brabbling. Compared to Re:Birth3, the visual novel parts are generally better -- all of them are voice acted, there can be more than 2 portraits on screen, and they move around a bit to indicate who's talking.
On the negative side, the lack of story also means considerably less Neptunia humor. The 4th wall is only getting a light beating, and there isn't much in terms of gaming or console references.
Gameplay is nothing special. This is an action game, so it's basically button mashing your light and heavy attacks along with combos thereof, moving around, possibly firing an SP skill every once in a while. You fill an EXE gauge by killing stuff which lets you go into HDD eventually which depletes the gauge over time, or when you fire your EXE skill -- which, contrary to the SP skills, very much feel like "press button to win", especially when you do it for the final boss.
You take 2 characters into battle that you can switch around; other characters do NOT gain experience so you need to use all your characters to level them. There is a Lily system, which provides some passive bonuses. The passive character heals over time, and gains points for SP/HDD faster.
Characters feel reasonably different, even Rom and Ram (although I do have to admit that I need to fire a heavy attack at the beginning to figure out which of the two I'm playing :-))
Missions aka quests are basically always of the "kill trashmobs first, then kill boss(es)" type. Locales are familiar, except that they are much more restrictive as the fights are arena-style.
Playable characters are the 4 main CPUs, the candidates, and 2 characters that I think have been created for this game (Dengekiko and Famitsu). As for the main story, no other characters appear, although there are a few "guest" appearances post game.
Talking about postgame, there will be a couple additional quests, and two additional game modes. The Gauntlet is just rubbish, while Neptral Tower is a grindfest of levels to beat.
Killing monsters will get you "medals" of the appropriate type, which can unlock equipment or stat upgrades. These upgrades are fixed and don't actually consume the medals -- so this is mostly an annoyance as they could have unlocked the stuff automatically when you hit the required number of medals.
The game certainly isn't difficult. I found combos to be generally complicated to pull off since it's hard to tell when to press the next button unless there's a signal move like "Hit X until the char dashes, then press Y". But that didn't hurt me at all, and for many characters I'd just spam attacks without paying too much attention to combos at all.
Although the game is solid enough, I can imagine that there are better games with this kind of gameplay, so the usual caveat applies: if you like to nep-nep your monsters instead of just bashing them, go for it. Maybe wait for a sale, though.
If you can't stand the main Neptunia series, then this game probably won't change your mind.

Its happens when I enter or exit boss doors, and when I enter new levels.  Thats the only bug I've encountered during my time with this game.  Overall, its a decent game, but with the constant crashes I cannot recommend it.

It was a Sunday in the winter of 2004. A record-breaking crowd was on hand to watch the Football League championship game. None could have known that this was soon to become the darkest day in history.
Butch Justice blazed across the field  for the winning touchdown, but before the glory could be felt by the multitudes, the earth began to rumble, growing more violent with each passing moment, until a 10.3 earthquake ripped the stadium from its foundations.
Noxious gases, thick with the stench of radioactive refuse, seeped into the air. Gallons of toxic liquid belched forth from the earth. Those unfortunate enough to come in contact with the poisonous fumes felt their skin boil... change... mutate.
The fortunate souls in the stadium who survived were no longer human beings. They were now mutants, forever transformed into hideous creatures with strength, speed, stamina, and agility far superior to any human.
Rising from the ashes of this devastating tragedy was the most exciting and dangerous sporting competition that the world has ever seen, known to all as... the MUTANT LEAGUE!
-Mutant League: The Movie
For the uninitiated, Mutant Football League is the spiritual successor to Mutant League Football, a post-apocalyptic Madden spinoff released in the year 1993 on Sega Genesis/Mega Drive. It was known for its remarkable violence. Players weren't just injured in MLF. They were obliterated, using nasty audibles (called Dirty Tricks in MFL), on-field hazards such as landmines, or plain old late hits. Even the refs can be killed (or, better yet, bribed and then killed by the other team). The popularity of Mutant League Football led to the release of Mutant League Hockey and even an animated series called Mutant League, yet never led to an official sequel from EA.
Mutant Football League, developed by a team led by Michael Mendheim, who created Mutant League Football, is essentially the same concept as the original: It's football with no holds barred in an "xtreme" nineties camp post-apocalyptic world, with teams of skeletons, robots, trolls, and aliens. Like its predecessor, it plays a lot like a more arcadey Madden, if Madden let you kill the opposing players after the play, turn one of your players into a giant, use deadly on-field hazards to your advantage, or fire a literal shotgun. It's absolutely nuts.
A new feature in Mutant Football League is in-game commentary. It's standard in sports games now, but wasn't yet possible in 1993. If you've played NFL Blitz or NBA Jam, you'll recognize the voice of the main commentator, Tim Kitzrow, who is joined by a mutant with two heads to add color. They're funny, and not always in a family friendly way. You can turn mature language off, but I don't think there's much point. This is not a particularly family friendly game in the first place, and the often crude commentary adds to the somewhat cheesy atmosphere of the game.
The game has eighteen teams, most of which are direct, non-trademark-infringing parodies of real NFL teams, which naturally consist of parody versions of real NFL players, such as "Airbourne Dodgers" of the "Grim Bay Attackers." Any of these teams can be played in a solo exhibition, season mode, playoffs, and online and offline head to head or co-op.
Summing up, Mutant League is extremely violent, fast, explosive, not particularly realistic, but a whole lot of fun for someone who has at least a passing interest in football and/or virtual dismemberment.

Axiom Verge is a beautifully crafted action adventure platformer that takes a lot of inspiration from the Metroid franchise while, at the same time, adding it's own unique flare to the genre. Through it's art direction, creature designs and music, the atmosphere is nailed creating an all around stunning experience and a lasting impression on the player. This game is addictive, and the game play is fun, but they have some serious file handling errors.  Their file handling errors manifest it two ways.  The first is that if you try to attack the wrong shard the game will crash during the first save event.  The second is that if you try to attack the wrong enemy on a shard and the game will freeze.   I don’t know what’s going on, but this is pretty basic stuff.  It is kind of surprising that they could create the graphics and gameplay that they have and yet still not even manage programing 101 file handling issues.
Here’s the use case that ruins the game for me.  I have three shards that I can attack.  Two of them will cause the game to crash during the first save event.  The third freezes every time I try to invade a territory controlled by the last of four enemies.  As such, there is now no way for me to even attempt to continue, let alone win, the game.  I guess that I could just kill off all of my heroes, dismiss all of my guards and troops, and then wait for the last enemy to conquer my castle, but who would want to do that?  Besides, there is no guarantee that surrendering this shard will allow for the creation of a shard that won’t crash.
It looks like this game will be really fun someday.  But until they fix there file handling issues it is just frustrating.  As such, I wouldn’t recommend buying it until after they fix these bugs.

I only felt the need to write a review because of all the people hating on this game. Not that I'm going to come out swinging in an attempt to defend it as it definitely has issues, but it has also been out for all of four days as of this post. Four days and the dev is already admitting to making some mistakes (start menu locking up and making the game unplayable) and better yet, taking steps to fix them. How many triple-A titles are chock full of bugs at launch requiring patches for the next few weeks? Pretty much every WoW xpac comes to mind among many other titles. I'm guessing that's forgivable because it's a big name developer, right? The game is a DOLLAR at base price... I work a minimum wage job part-time and find nearly that much in loose change on the floor when I sweep at night, how is anyone complaining about anything in this game? Especially since it's on sale for thirteen cents... that's not sitting between the cushions in your couch? It's far too loud, yes. Turn your system/headphone/speaker/whatever volume down if the in-game volume controls don't work. Game.exe seems weird? Really? Should they have named it stellar2d.exe instead? Do you remember any of the older games that started up in DOS as ______.exe and sat there while command lines popped up until it had finished doing its thing and the game finally started? There's more that I'd bash on but I'll just get to the review.
~~~~~~~
The game is quite simply a very low-end indie version of any side-scrolling shoorter you've ever played and this is visible in pretty much every aspect of the game. It seems very similar to the old shooters I played as a kid in the local arcade, R-Type for instance, though much less polished.
I can't comment on the Config window that pops up after launching the game as I set it to what I felt should be right the first time and never messed with it again and I don't play with a joystick, WASD works great.
The main menu is uncomplicated and features the usual selections though the sliders in Options are more difficult to manipulate than they should be while the font throughout the game is perhaps too stylized and the navigation arrows in some places aren't immediately obvious (the ones in the ship select screen particularly) and need some sort of contrasting border or perhaps not be neon blue. The Credits page (did anyone even bother checking that out?) points out just how much of an indie title this is, six people. That's counting the gal at the end who was responsible for the social media end of things and not credited with any sort of development. Something else I noticed, they're all the type of photos you'd see on someone's facebook page (except for David Webb's, totally lives in an 80s sitcom... ) My point is these are just a few people, probably all friends, who wanted to make something and share it with us.
As for gameplay, it's actually kinda challenging, for me at least, and it gets very frantic further in but is fun in its own way. I think the gameplay elements need to be a bit more clear, like the swirling blue cloud that starts to chase your ship around... what is it? It'd be cool if hitting a new power-up either reset the timer on your current one (assuming they're the same) or swapped to the new one. I feel that the traps, debuffs basically, are a bit too powerful or unclear. For instance the vertical/horizontal freezes and no shooting, they last far too long in my opinion. The no shooting one especially, that basically ends the game as the screen is swarmed with enemy ships long before it wears off.
There needs to be a cursor for menu navigation or have mouse movements change what items are selected as with tabbing through clickable things in a window. Just seems weird that you have to navigate with an invisible cusor.
The intro movie made me facepalm, I just... that voice, it's a good try though.
The ship designs for the most part are very interesting and I feel sensical in many cases. I'll probably use some of them as ideas for Space Engineers or my own artwork.
I love most of the backgrounds and in fact I'd have paid a dollar for a game that was simply dodging asteroids with high-res versions of the images used for the backgrounds (total space nut) though I'm not sure how I feel about images that are obviously from other games like seeing the Normandy from Mass Effect.
The music is kinda nice and if they released a twenty-five or even fifty cent DLC of the soundtrack I'd probably snag that too if the tracks were at least a few minutes long each or all mixed together to make a long-ish track that looped well.
I think the general backlash from many of the commenters could have been avoided if the game had been released as Early Access and therefore obviously a WiP and as it stands right now I think that's the only way this should even be on Steam since it is far from completed (glaring typo on the main screen for instance unless that's supposed to be Star since the game is Stellar 2D, stellar-star... har har?) But that also means that if they plan to do more with it such as general improvements maybe there will be more modes like a zen type mode with relaxing music or a super swarm mode featuring default gameplay but with a bazillion debuffs that last a fraction of a second just to mess with you...
Overall I can't sit and play for hours straight and I doubt this game will get more than a few hours of play total but for the price it's well worth it. It needs a ton of work but it's a decent attempt at producing a simple game so it gets a 3 or 4 out of 10 for execution but I'd add a point for the attempt and at the non-sale price of a buck, it gets another point or two for value so say an even 6/10. I definitely don't feel that I was ripped off, even if the developer made no more changes to the game and left it as is, it is playable and mildly entertaining. Not a bad way to kill ten or fifteen minutes before heading out the door. Recommended if for no other reason than as encouragement to an indie developer to try again.

To me, Dishonored is a real treat for anyone who enjoys having a great deal of freedom in the way they play through a game. If you want to run through each chapter murdering everyone who looks at you too long, go ahead. If you want to creep through the shadows undetected and take care of all your targets through non lethal means, you can do that too. Feel like possessing your enemies and making them have unfortunate "accidents" involving rats, go wild. Mix it up, be adventurous with any combination of powers and playstyles, each decision impacting the condition of the world around you. While the game is mostly linear, it offers a fair deal of replayability with the various different ways to complete each mission and the three different endings the game offers.
I'd highly recommend this game to anyone who is even considering it. The gameplay mechanics are enjoyable, the environment is visually appealing, and the story is fun to play with.
To add on to that, the Knife of Dunwall and Brigmore Witches DLCs are equally as impressive as the main game itself, offering a new playable character with their own powers and a truly immersive storyline that offers a different perspective on the main game. Do note that Brigmore Witches is a direct sequel to Knife of Dunwall, so be sure to get both if you want to experience the story as a whole.
I would also recommend playing these two DLCs if you plan on playing Dishonored 2 (trust me).
The other two DLCs are entirely optional non-story related content packs. One is a collection of time trials and challenges (which are fun, I will admit), and the other simply allows you to start the game with a little collection of gold and bone charms ect to give you a little headstart in the game.
All in all 10/10.

My hours are a bit wrong on this one, as i have previously owned the Disk version of il-2 Sturmovik: Forgotten battles and Pacific Fighters when they first came out.
My god is this game great. Whether its making your own Career as a fighter over Stalingrad, or making your own Insane missions in the great mission builder, this game is the best Combat Flight sim i have ever played.
Dynamic campaigns mean you'll never quite have the same mission twice (Although alot of the times you'll be doing the same thing depending on your aircrafts role, but in different locations against different amounts and types of enemys) while still getting in Historic battles such as Stalingrad, Berlin, or Midway (And everything between). If thats not your thing or you feel its too repeatative, then check out the mission editors.
Quick Mission Builder is an easy and fast way of making anything from Bombing missions to straight up massive dogfights. You simply just choose what aircraft you want to fly and how many squadmates and your Allies and Enemys, Pick the loadouts, skins, and countries. (You can fly an American plane as a German if you want) Then get into the action and deal with whatever you threw at yourself.
Full mission builder is a bit different.....and i mean alot different. You control every aspect of basically anything. Control weather, time, Cloud height and make buildings and objects. You want a plane to take off, fly to somewhere along a specific route and altitude? Done. You want to patrol something? Done. Do you want Tanks and AA guns on the ground supporting or making your own Ground offensive? Done! You can even position Static cameras for those moments you just want to sit back and watch the carnage. Blow up and damage cities with a simple slider and clicks. Hell you can make planes Kamikaze things if you do it right. One of my personal favorites is to make roughly 50 aircraft, Fighers, Bombers, whatever, and fly them straight it to a massive area filled with AA guns and just try to survive for as long as you can while watching♥♥♥♥♥♥get blown up.
All and all i would give it a 10 out of 10. This one completely missed the mark for me.
Like the much beloved previous work To The Moon, Bird Story boils down to how much creative and artistic license and leeway you're willing to give to the notion of storytelling through the RPG Maker software. To The Moon got you to forgive its shortcomings while Bird Story makes them more noticeable. I'm not one to compare apples to oranges or even apples to apples, but every way To The Moon worked is where Bird Story doesn't. Moon vied for time with cutesy humor and bread crumbs towards the story while Bird Story kills time with tedium in both story and gameplay. Where Moon delivered an engaging story that culminated into something and compensated for the game engine, Bird Story delivers next to none with nothing but the expected. And whether comparisons are fair or not it just plain doesn't work like it's predecessor somehow did. Lightning did not strike twice.
On its own two legs Bird Story, without any comparisons, is a dull story. Imaginative kid finds injured bird and cares for it. No twists or anything, that is just it. When that domino of story entertainment falls every other one does too. Beyond an interesting piano soundtrack for heavy eyes the art, particularly visuals, aren't special. Even within the confines of the RPG Maker realm. Bird Story did find one or two interesting ways to tell it's story within its medium, but it was very often repetitive and painstakingly slowly delivered. And finally the gameplay, there's just next to none. And yet its still tedious somehow.
Cute at times and another interesting take on RPG Maker, but dull dull dull. For me it just is not worth the short 1hr investment.

Probably the best Metroid game to come out in years.
Unlike most of Metroidvania games, Axiom Verge is most clearly influenced by Super Metroid: there is no RPG inspired system of progression where you grow stronger by continuously killing monsters and watching your numbers slowly increase. Instead, your character grows stronger and more versatile by finding tools, weapons and health upgrades scattered around the world, both in plain sight and hidden in the levels. The game is similar to Super Metroid in length, with Axiom Verge taking around 12 hours to beat on my first playthrough.
The game does a good job introducing a number of new weapons and tools that only make it more efficient to kill your enemies, but also make it faster to travel around the world. Some of these are inspired by Metroid (a small drone you can remote control) while others are a bit more interesting (a gun that can "glitch" enemies, causing their graphics to go nuts,  become vulnerable or start destroying their surroundings, among other effects). There is a nice line of progression to these powerups, giving them more uses as you progress through the game, allowing you to backtrack and find more secrets. There are a few bosses, ranging from smaller ones to ones that fill out the entire screen, giving them nice variety while giving a nice break from the constant exploration every now and then.
The game has a story, told with the few cutscenes in the game and log entries you can find scattered in the world. While the story isn't all that groundbreaking, it complements the game's atmosphere without being too overbearing; the game rarely stops your progress with a cutscene and never forces you to go through a certain path or arbitrarily locks places in the game due to not having gotten far enough in the story; the meat of the game is gameplay, and the narrative is really a secondary element rather than the main course.
If there is something to criticize here, it's that the regions in the game aren't as memorable as in other similar games, even if the H.R. Giger inspired graphics aren't bad at all.
If you've had an itch for a Metroid game, pick this game up. And while you're at it, try out AM2R too.

Easily the best "HOMM" type game I've played. HOMM is pretty much dead to me these days and I have no interest in the new version where you stack troops and faceroll boring maps for more story bits. I'm a bigger fan of the King's Bounty series but those are still largely about progression through troop stacks and a bit lacking in the grand scheme development. Eador however, is ALL about the development of your capital and all of the land around it. I was initially put off by the more story/objective driven campaign and didn't fully realize that this game did in fact have a sandbox mode, so I'm glad I gave it a second chance.
The thing that really sets it off is that you'll take over bigger plots of land, but will have to fully explore it, clear all of the dungeons within it and completely run the enemy forces out of it before you actually gain the land making fights a lot more thoughtful than just single tile-grabbing. This process may not even be possible until you level up a bit higher and come back As in just because you walked on a tile doesn't mean you fully own and control it.  You are also fighting not only all of the monsters around the map, but also the AI building their capitals as well. Not to mention there's actually things on the maps like rocks and hills that you can USE. I took out a bigger army due to great placement with ranged units and chokepoints. That would NEVER happen in HOMM.
Of course there's tons of tech tree type buildings and troops with upgrades and multiple classes of heros. It's your typical foray across a map, and the game itself does nothing brand new. It's just how it's glued together and operates that sets it apart. I picked this up for a fiver in a bundle at one point and I've seen it that low on a sale. If you like turn based strategy games you could do so much worse here for that price. It's another game that has 100's of hours potential going for it.

IL-2 Sturmovik has developed from an Eastern Front ww2 flght sim into an absolute monster! It's detailed, unforgiving at times, takes effort to get into, and has a steep learning curve. Despite, or because of all of that, it's an awesome game. Given it's pretty old now, most mid range systems will do well with this. The graphics were good for its time, and still hold up ok in the sky.
There's a huge online community of verteran players making all sorts of custom missions and skins for this game. Skins are easy to import.
These days there's plenty of action for the other fronts of WW2 as well, especially in the Pacific.
Damage is well modelled, flight characteristics have been well researched, with only a few glitches, and aircraft interiors are beautifully done. Oleg , the man who started all this, was insistent that no aircraft be imported until the cockpit was fully accurate.
I'd recommend this for someone who has an interest in flight from this era, and is willing to put in the hours to learn to fly adequately. I'd suggest starting not in your favorite aircraft, but something more forgiving like an IL-2 to learn to fly. Eventually you'll be able to handle other aircraft no problem. Landing is a big challenge, I've played over 2000 hours on this game back in its CD only days and I'm still  more nervous about landing than combat!
There's also some "what if?" aircraft included, hence the title 1946. They're fun, and make for an interesting experience, but don't add to the realism. There's some fascinating player made 1946 missions out there well worth playing.
This is not for the casual gamer. I can't stress this enough. This game demands your attention and your commitment. do so and it'll reward you. A number of real-life veterans have said this game captures the difficulty of ww2 air combat. Don't expect an easy ride.

Dishonored, a game where
There's a beautiful thing about games that let you choose your playstyle - because what is a game if not interactive?
In Dishonored you are always met with different ways of doing things and experimenting with different outcomes, which made it my favorite stealth game. It always makes sure there's different ways of getting to your objective; but doesn't hold your hand and make it obvious. It awards the careful planner and seeker of all things odd or shiny with safe routes and pride, but challenges even those people with occasional objectives that requires going out in the open. Were you to fight your way through a crowd of enemies, however, it makes sure to remind you there's a reason those hidden passages exist by completely pulverizing you.
But since Dishonored was made to easily tailor itself to your needs, there are lots of options to choose from in the skill trees, making those battles more fun and variated as you go, and helps keep your interest alive.
The game surrounds you with a pretty environment and perfect level design, with an amazing and unique art style.
Each level varies in quirks and style; some places feel warm and luxorious while others feel cold, dank and poor. Personally I believe it strengthens the moral choices you are faced with and helps you immerse in the story, helping you create an emotional bond with certain factions and/or people, which might even make you feel guilty for murdering... at times.
Basically, Dishonored kindly asks you if you want that cold "revenge dish" to be microwaved for a minute or two.
Because of its many choices, It becomes a very humane experience, if you allow it to be one.
Moving and Blinking around is so fluid, and feels so good. Great storyline too. Graphically unimpressive, but aesthetically fantastic. One of my favorite games.

Dishonored is a game where you play as a ex-Royal Bodyguard, Corvo Antanno, farmed for a crime that wasn't done by your hands, and you are given help from the inside to escape from a prison and after breaking out you are introduced to new allies and now have the freedom to decide on future targets' 2 or more possible horrible fates with potential fallout from each one. Magic system is good and let you have some choice in how you want to play.
What's good about this game is the fact you have some freedom on how you want to accomplish your missions either making the streets and buildings run red with blood, be it your mission's target, a guardsman or civilian, or sneak your way through the missions without shredding so much as a drop of blood and subjecting targets to horrible fates, or a mix of both. If you commited enough bloodshed, game more or less make future missions a little more difficult to fight or sneak around in with additional guardsmen and rats and every kill or chaos level do influence the future missions.
Characters in the game are well voiced and anyone around you, either a ally or a enemy, are influenced your chaos level and they may speak differently depending on what you do.
So overall, a must have game if you like action-stealth games with a dose of magic within the setting.

Great game. First off, it's a Hack and slash spinoff variant of the Turn Based JRPG main series, Hyperdimension Neptunia U: Action Unleashed. That being said, it's more for people who have played the main series, or for anyone who just really loves anime/manga. As the title may suggest, a deep story is most definitely not going to be found here, or anywhere within this franchise. Bear in mind, however, that does not mean the game is bad. On the contrary, actually, that's part of what gives this series, and this game, its charm. Just the random silliness and easy-going atmosphere of the game is enough to suck you in for hours, laughing along with whatever nonsensical shenanigans are going on.
Although very simple in principle, the game proves quite challenging if you just grinded one or two characters out and neglected all the others, as there are certain quests that require certain characters, giving the game a more full feeling than if you could just use the same two characters and beat the game in an hour or two.
The music is characteristic of the series, and the graphics are pretty good as well, even featuring a little improvement. The combat system is centered on combinations, but the different tiers of attacks are pretty parallel to those of the main series, which is comforting if you are new to Hack and Slash games.
All in all, it's pretty good. I'd personally pay full price for it, but that's just because I've been a fan of the series for years. That being said, if this is the first game in the franchise you're buying, either start with the main series, or pick this one up on sale.

Yes, it’s another one of those Steam indie gems. Truth be told, LOG the game can’t really disappoint if you weren’t expecting a lot to begin with. This is afterall, the Steam debut of developer/publisher RobotKSR and they had the courage to go for something bold from the get-go. That takes digital brass balls and their attempts at originality shall not go unnoticed by yours truly.
Players shall get to control and witness the wonderful adventures of an anthropomorphic (humanlike) log which goes on a rampage against those which cut him down along with his “brethren”. A partially motivated revenge tale, yet Log seems to fight mostly other trees and wildlife which seems to me a bit absurd but that’s this title’s logic, I guess. There’s barely a coherent plot here and the visual style isn’t helping at all. Don’t ask me why he’ll reach outer space and fight aliens or how is this going to save the forest, but let’s just assume that the entire game is a drug-fuelled cosmic trip into the unknown and proceed along those lines.
Unity Engine all the way. Still, I had guaranteed stability and proper 4K scaling. It seems quite fitting that I review today a creative indie title which makes good use of watercolor backgrounds and intentionally crude drawings at the same time. Make no mistake, Log the game’s visual style is not accidental or a last-ditch attempt from a developer who ran out of funds. I really dig this style. It has to be as ludicrous as the main plot in order to click in place and I’m certain that in a perfect gaming world (and if it was released several years ago) this type of platformer might have supplanted Super Meat Boy and other staples of indie side-scrolling platformers. Or not.
A soundtrack is present and repetitive. Not much going for the sound effects and no voice acting at all. Pure 2D platformer features and I wasn’t hoping for my ears to be overindulged by Log the game’s musical repertoire. No harm done, but definitely nothing special either.
Log the game features 10 levels of various length plus a minimalist B&W tutorial. Most of the gameplay revolves around Log’s struggles to jump from one platform to another. Why is that an issue? Well, you’ll have to upgrade him a bit until he’ll be able to jump (not to mention, double jumping) enough and stop falling to his death all the time. The first level’s animation involves a lumberjack’s truck from which Log has to jump. If players don’t follow through, they get stuck along with the truck which falls into a spiked trap. Genius level design over there, look it up on YouTube.
At least Log has customizable appearance, weapons and powers. The helmets and melee weapons seem purely cosmetic though. No extra armor/health or weapon damage seems to be implemented if you purchase newer and more expensive options with the in-game currency. It certainly won’t feel pointless collecting as many coins as you can. You’ll still be wacking a sword/axe or shooting infinite bullets which deal the exact damage, but those surreal landscapes sure benefit from character customization.
By the time you reach the later levels which feature some barebones 2D vehicular combat, chances are that you long since abandoned playing this game altogether. Pacing is a real issue in its case. Even I find it hard to press on, despite the promise of increasingly weirder foes and locations. There’s not enough motivation here and the clunky control scheme isn’t helping in any capacity. You'll be forgiven if you play the game in short sessions, in order to relax and cleanse your eyeballs.
Weird and psychedelic looks aside, LOG the game is slightly overpriced given how simple and repetitive its gameplay mechanics and sound selection can become. Also, the developer’s decision to launch this game without Steam Achievement support (I know that Trading Cards are now harder to implement, for newly released titles) is baffling to say the least. There are more than a few tweaks which would make  LOG, more enticing but my suggestion to the dev team is to start with a price cut, then a few Achievements.
+ Interesting visual style.
+ Shock humor value?
+ Sufficient gameplay variety through unlockables.
- No Steam Achievements nor Trading Cards.
- Simplistic premise and story.
- Limited sound selection.

If you're here in 2017, you probably know what this title entails, so really it's up to you to decide whether you want to buy a pigeon-dating visual novel. (No real gameplay here, other than clicking between, at maximum, 3 choices.)
It's well-written for what it is; the first "half" of it can border on tedium since you're essentially skipping through tons of texts the more endings that you get, and I'm not so sure I can say the second "half" is worth that tedium - just because by that point you're really reading through interactions, with little to no input on your behalf.
The coding in this game is a bit annoying - one example induces a soft-lock, if you save at the dialogue where you get to make your very own choice. (The result, when you save and reload, is a picture of a quail staring at you for eternity.)
Get the VN if you like VNs and subverting tropes, since for about $5 or so you get a pretty good deal - I enjoyed it for what it is. I won't recommend it for the casual player, though, since they won't get much out of the experience if they aren't dedicated to slog through the whole haul.

Hell Yeah! can be summed up as a tons of idea being jammed together, resulting in a bloody mess. It sorely lacks a design and quality control pass.
It really feels like the devs did a meeting, thought about all the things that might be cool to have in a game, put all of that in Hell Yeah, and then shipped it without actually checking that theses things would actually work.
Cool animated death scenes for bosses and mini-bosses ? Great ! Mandatory minigames/quick time events needed to trigger theses scenes ? Not cool.
Super colorful world with tons of details ? Awesome ! Busy background and color that mesh together making the action hard to figure out ? Bad.
A mode where you exploit your defeated enemies to gain treasures, like any respectable boss of Hell should ? Wow i never thought of that before, great stuff ! Having that mode be tied to real game time rather than ingame time when your game can be done in 2 play sessions ? Idea completely ruined.
I could go on an on about what works and what doesn't design wise, but i don't think that's really needed or interesting. Even basic guidelines like "don't put mandatory unskippable cutscenes after the checkpoints" are broken over and over again by this game, so going over every detail would just be a boring laundry list.
On the quality control aspect, the game somehow manages to have lag spikes even on powerful computers and the options menu is so bare bone that there is no way to change volume or cut music.
But, to be fair, when the game works, it can be pretty fun. And contrary to most games, it gets better as time goes on, thanks to all the cool weaponry you get. But there are just too many issues to really enjoy it.  On the whole it feels like either it was rushed to release, or there was a big failure on the design side.

Axiom Verge is, in my opinion, a great game for a few reasons:
1) Solid gameplay with tight controls
2) Mechanics are clever, yet practical--they will be familiar to fans of the genre
3) Story is present and interesting, but unintrusive--the focus remains on actually playing the game
4) Axiom Verge's artwork faithfully pays homage to the titles that inspired it
5) Soundtrack is fantastic
It amazes me that this entire work was made by only one man.  I thoroughly enjoyed my time playing Axiom Verge.  The only drawback I found was that, like the older games that inspired it, Axiom Verge suffers from a lack of replayability.  There is a hard mode and a speedrun mode for those who like to challenge themselves in that way and if you like the game for the game's sake, then there should be no problem.  However, if you are like me and are a bonus content/unlockables junkie, then it will be hard to find a reason to pick it up again after the first playthrough.  Nevertheless, I think Axiom Verge is a great game and would recommend it to fans of retro-style platformers.  If you can pick it up on sale, all the better!

In between, events take place that you must resolve in some way. For instance there is some wizard that resurrects some death people and you have to decide whether to fight the wizard, pay it off or ignore it (just making this one up as an example).
Fights bring you to a hexagonal field which is pretty much standard across TBS type of games and you have to fight the enemy with the army you have (pretty much like you have it in other TBS games like king's bounty).
Loads of fun and highly recommended.

I opened the game. I started a bombing sight tutorial, didn't listen and went strait into the game as a Ju87 Stuka against some Russian bomb targets. Going in, I didn't really know the controls, but I let the autopilot spend the 2 minutes it took to get to the targets. After a short 30 seconds, the other stukas had already dropped their payloads, I didn't know how to but I was told the mission was complete. I was still flying however.
We were then suddenly surprised to see a small fighter group of Ishaks close in on us from the ground. I thought this would be a good opportunity to learn a bit about the dogfighting. So, I dive in the mighty Stuka, hoping to boom and zoom a lowly Ishak.
After about 15 seconds, I got one on screen. I fought for a good while with my plane to stay on target, line the sights up, get in range, stay far enough away for the bullets to hit him, and also fight the speed of the Stuka in a dive. I then lined the Isak up and...
Fired. Miss. Again. Miss. AGAIN! Direct hit.
I heard the machine guns roar as bits of the Ishak's wing went flying by when I suddenly got about 500 messages from other pilots;
"Two is hit!"  "I down!"  "Need assistance..."
And then I was shot and my fuel tank exploded, shutting off my engine. I tried desperately to force the damned Stuka to the mainland and crash "safely", but to no avail. I bailed out at 300 metres and was shot by an enemy pilot. Real damn honorable.
10/10 would fail again.

I would not recommend
to those who think very traditionally about what "a game" must be like, because there isn't a lot of agency as a player or intricate gameplay. And I can understand some being potentially put off by that. But for what it is in fact attempting to be and is clearly advertised as - that is, an interactive short story, rather than a game in the traditional sense - it hits the mark
is an experience that I'm very glad I had. It's simple, yet thought-provoking. It's down to earth, yet injected with a healthy, enchanting dose of fantasy and imagination. It's deeply emotional, yet doesn't shy away from occasional comedic moments (which, by the way, really surprised me in getting some genuine laughs out of me). It uses absolutely zero words to convey a wonderfully executed, heartfelt story of childhood, friendship, and loss. The complete lack of words of any kind (aside from the end credits) makes this equally accessible to speakers of absolutely any language and those too young or otherwise impaired in reading ability, which I think is something pretty special.
At first glance the pixel art is tiny and the animations seem like they'll be limited, but the further I got into it, the more
impressed me with how much it could do in such a small space. Being a short story gives
the freedom to have many different bespoke character sprites for each and every small moment, making it feel alive the whole way through.
The music is also incredibly deserving of praise. It swelled into emotional crescendos and faded into silence or quiet at all the right moments. It's beautiful and I am strongly considering buying the soundtrack. Calling it
devoid of gameplay also wouldn't be a hundred percent fair; a simple thing like which arrow keys to press at which moments is sometimes used in adorable and inventive ways to keep the player feeling involved.
For anyone who doesn't need absolutely everything on Steam to be gameplay-heavy, and is at all interested in just settling down for about an hour and experiencing a charming story, I would definitely recommend
.

Before you start reading, I'd like to say that I do not hate the game. Yet, that does not mean I like it either. I like some aspects of it, but other than that, nothing.
First of all, the graphics and colors are nice - though a bit tiny -, and the music is really good, just like To The Moon. Though I liked it, I wasn't particularily amazed by To The Moon's story - compared to many reviews I've seen that claim that the game is really, really good, really immersive and heartbreaking/warming. But, considering it may be just my taste in this, I still respect that opinion about it.
However, it felt a bit ... empty. Some may say that it's the point of it, but, it really feels empty, in the story itself. It has a dreamy feeling about it - a good one a that, but only to tell a story we'd find in our everyday lives - and, let's be honest, a bit typical. That parallel makes it somewhat off and weird. It also keeps on guiding you here and there, without leaving much of a choice - which can be fine, if it was more intuitive. Sometimes, I was a bit clueless as to what to do at the moment. Also, whether or not you fail on some parts, the game itself fixes it. So no real challenge here, even if it's not what we'd seek in it in the first place.
Another point that left me a bit frustrated was the fact that we can't pause during the many scenes in which you can't do anything - so if you get distracted, you end up losing track of the story. It's a bit sad to get lost/be too slow in a game that not only guides you, but also is supposed to be really calm and slow...
So, in all honesty, this prequel - also, yes, the fact that it is a prequel to another game scares me about what's going to come out next ... - would've been really good, if only some parts weren't as disappointing as it is.
Still, I hope the main game will be better. I have hope.

This is one of my all-time favorite games, let that be said. Lots of hate for this game, complaints about performance issues I'm just not getting. I had this on the xbox 360, put in plenty of hours there too.
It's BRINK. Splash Damage's parkour shooter that never really took off, despite beautiful soundtrack, fantastic graphics, and the most customization options in a game to date (it set a world record at the time!) I've played through it quite a few times on console, and all the guns take is some getting used to. They feel weak, yes, but they behave like guns in that they're hard to control usually, which adds to the challenge. Whether you find this enjoyable or annoying, entirely up to preference. Also, there's the movement system. Again, takes some getting used to, but is worth it when you can effortlessly glide across terrain.
The story is very well done, and I'm disappointed there's not more to it. Well, one can always hope. The artstyle more than makes up for that, giving you plenty of an idea of what the ARK is like.
Overall, I totally recommend giving it a try. If you don't like it, you don't like it. That's fair.

The basic gameplay will mostly be familiar to fans of the Heroes of Might and Magic series: Hero units, backed by a recruitable army, explore the world and fight with each other. There are towns, equipable items, all that good stuff. However, where HoMM  tends to be fairly simple, Eador has enough depth to drown a whale. What you build, where you build it, and what you stock your army with can have huge consequences, and every turn has dozens of choices about how best to improve your situation. Add in random events, potentially dozens of battles per province, and a solid enemy AI and you've got a recipe for a huge time-sink.
Most 4x games become bogged down in the late game: Your strategy is set, you've built everything you need to, and now it's simply a matter of hitting "next turn" until you win. Eador's campaign averts this in a wonderful way: The maps are fairly small by 4x standards, but you have to complete dozens of them. The world has been split into shards, and your goal is to control as many of them as you can. That means that by the time you've reached the "just hit next" stage you'll have completed one shard and it'll be time to move on to the next, where you have to build up your forces all over again. That's not to say that beating a shard has no benefits: Each one you control grants you boosts to your income, troops, or abilities, so planning which ones to conquer in what order actually matters to an extent.
All-in-all an excellent strategy game that I'd highly recommend to HoMM or Disciples fans.

I can partially recommend this "game". It's an excellent simulator with a wide variety of aircraft and mission types, including carrier-based operations, and the price is great. It's difficult and you'll need to put in quite a few hours of practice before you can make successful bombing runs and shoot down other fighters, but it's fair.
However, there's really not much of a game here, there's essentially no story, and there's a lot of time spent doing rather tedious things. For example, I was playing a bomber campaign and so many missions went like this: 1) take off from the carrier and get in formation (a few minutes of fun), 2) fly in a straight line for 20 minutes (boring), 3) set up a bombing run and drop bombs (2-3 minutes of great excitement), 4) spend 20 minutes flying back (boring), 5) land on the carrier (a few minutes of fun). There's time compression, but it can't be safely set very high. Sometimes the mission generator mixes it up, but the vast majority of my time was spent uneventfully flying to and from the mission areas. I'm sure it's realistic, but it's not exciting or fun.
In summary, it's a great simulator that lets you do all kinds of military flying and the huge number of (mostly randomized) campaigns gives tremendous replay value, but after you get the hang of it most of your time will be spent feeling bored unless you actually enjoy flying in a straight line in formation for 30-60 minutes per mission.
I've heard that the multiplayer is decent but I don't believe there's any matchmaking so you'll have to find a community if you want to try it.

"Il-2 Sturmovik: 1946" originally began as an Eastern Front flight combat simulator which branched into Europe, The Pacific and then into the immediate Post-war Jet era. It has become a bit of a cult following with several loyal players continually playing, hosting, creating skins, missions and campaigns.
It is probably one of the longest running dedicated combat sims which though using a limited and dated engine, is still able to satisfyingly emulate the widest scope of aviation combat centered around World War 2 in varying difficulty levels and complexity. It has over 150 flyable aircraft from varying aspects of nearly all theaters of operations as well as associated maps. It includes pilot campaigns from nearly all sides, a quick mission builder and a full mission builder. But most of it's contemporary strengths come from beautifully made skins, missions, campaigns and utilities from it's many followers and fans that run the gamut of historical to flights of fantasy.
It's latest version is 4.12.2m (which is the latest steam version - No patching needed!) which has been officially updated by a group called Team Daidalos (rumor has it they are even working on 4.13!) has added flyable aircraft, tweaked graphics and sounds and additional mission building options and objects. (it even now has the option to add 3rd party "Online sounds" and still be a 'stock' game) It's multiplayer capability is via Hyperlobby where you can usually fly and/or host missions, join dedicated server maps, or get limited help from people there.
Besides the stock game, many have added one of the popular mods to add even more popular aircraft, different flight models, digitized sounds, improved graphics and mission building options and objects. (Most mods can be switched to stock easily via a simple program).
It has the added advantage of being able to run smoothly (A critical point in combat flight sims) on most older systems.

TL;DR: slow paced but gradualy exciting anime like and interesting tower defense concept.
It's a interesting tower defense concept and it really gives that "Defend the Earth!" anime vibe. The first time a boss showed up I got really excited, it almost makes me fell like I'm inside one of those giant robot against giant monster anime, but using a city instead of a robot.
But, just like anime goes, there is as much talking as there is fighting. The beginning of the game is really slow with all the characters introducing themselves. Also, after you get the hang of it the game becomes easy until you unlock new cities to play with increased difficulty, but this is good for those who are slow learners, and also help build up tension for when you finally unlock a stage where you begin to struggle and feel your blood pumping while trying to cope with the new enemies and new attack patterns that catch you off guard.
The voice acting is also not that bad but can get tiring after a while considering you will be hearing the same dialog over and over again while selecting options during the development stage of the city, but it is not much bad considering you will be constantly swaping squad members and only the currently active members talk to you during city planning, so you can simply swap that annoying girl with other member when can't handle hear her voice anymore.

It's really impressive how much I did not like this game. To the Moon is fantastic, and A Bird Story was just utterly lackluster in every respect.
The controls were a joke, very slow and always restricted for some reason. Even then, the interactive sequences were few and far between. This game was the epitome of "Press F to Pay Respects."
The story was absolutely terribly paced. I think I would have enjoyed this game a lot more if it kept a respectable pace and was over in 15-20 minutes, rather than dragging on for an interminable hour. Each scene was a little slower, a little longer than necessary, each fade a little deeper and darker. And then there were about twice as many scenes as necessary.
The entire game, really, was a really shallow, painful melodrama, with just a couple brief glimmers of characterization amid a sea of sap. The music, the visuals (all other characters were ghosts...?), the contrived interactions, everything was designed to wring as much emotion as it possibly could from the viewer, and it went way overboard. The only emotion I felt was frustration.
The only saving grace is that it was only an hour, albeit a very long hour. I really cannot recommend this game to anyone.
1/10

I don't think the main purpose of the game was to make you immensely upset as it progresses.
I think it's about capturing one's purest and most innocent intentions. Even if a bit selfish, And one completely special bond between two completely different living creatures. "A Bird Story", at least in my eyes, focuses entirely on that. And it does a great job at it.
How happy were you when you were little and you were able to enjoy the rain? To jump from one puddle to another? How happy were you when your parents were gone and you could jump on their bed or to simply make paper planes out of a sheet of paper and go around without a care in the world around your house? Well, we've all been there, we all lived our own special universe, we were all eager for the world.
About the game : It's short, it doesn't have much interaction and as it is written in the description it doesn't have a single dialogue. So what's so great about it? Well, it's simple - the setting, the intend behind it and the glorious soundtrack.
I don't think necessarily that this is a must-have or must-experience title, but I would recommend it for anyone that wants to experience something different for the span of an hour and a half. It had me smiling during a few moments. And smiles are definitely priceless.

Let me preface this review by saying I pre-ordered the game on XBox 360 at launch, so my hours on record don't reflect my true experience with the game.
I won't tell you that this game is good in a technical sense, because it totally isn't. The framerate will be terrible, you will have strange graphical issues and you may even encounter game breaking glitches.
The actual achievement in this game is the concept; the idea of The Ark and the opposing forces is interesting, and, if the game were executed correctly, it has great gameplay ideas. I personally like the art style as well; The customization options make your character(s) really come to life in this world. The problem is that concepts themselves don't translate to good gameplay, proper development and execution of those concepts do.
I wouldn't have recommended that you pay money for this game. The pros are hard to put up against the cons, and the cons killed this game on its release. Playing the small amount I did for the nostalgia, it still pains me to think of the potential the game had versus the end product. I remember regretfully returning the game for store credit maybe a month and a half after release, and have been wary of pre-orders since.
That being said, I recommend you give the game a try, especially since it's free. Maybe you will enjoy the environment and world the developers built as much as I did. Maybe sometime in the future the IP holders will consider revisiting the world and give us a good experience vaulting through the crates and corridors of The Ark.
TL;DR: Brave this garbage fest so that you might find the gems in the rough, rough gameplay. Plus it's free, what have you got to lose? (Don't lie, you were gonna play CS:GO today anyway, it's not like you're wasting too much of your time)

Despite being a bit dated, IL-2 Sturmovik: 1946 is still a top notch flight sim. The game had a number of substantial updates since its release, with the most recent being just last year (2013), though I'm not so certain if the game will see as much now with Battle of Stalingrad on the table. A plus in my book, some aircraft that have multiple crew stations can be manned by human players in multiplayer, so there's a possibility you can even get friends who don't care for flying to join in.
If you're looking for a solid World War 2 to 1946ish era flight sim, this is a safe pick and you especially can't really go wrong with it if you get it on sale. If you're new to the flight sim scene, I would suggest trying the A6M but be careful of your dive speed. If you excede 350mph, you could cause damage to the airframe --even to where the wings tear off...

Hellooo. I used to have IL-2 Forgotten Battles, but I decided to replace it with this. I have only played a little bit, but I think it is enough to write this review. Buying the thing was pretty simple but I had problems starting the game up. It was extremely frustrating but I submitted my problem to Steam Support, got an answer instantly,  followed the instructions that they gave me and it worked perfectly. IL-2 is of course getting old, but it has it's advantages. It plays very smoothly on my computer (A windows 7 that is kinda clogged with stuff that has built up over the years) and you get more options than newer sims. I thought this would be a good purchase instead of a newer one, since I get so many aircraft. IL-2 Sturmovik Battle of Stalingrad (recently released) is a great, high-end sim, but you can only fight with Russian and German planes and during the same time of year and the same location. This was a better option for me because I can fly what I feel like flying. Just today I reanacted Pearl Harbor, then I flew a 1944 USAAF mission over Europe. Also the game has language of course, and some noseart is a little, well, you know. But this can be fixed. You can switch off subtitles, and for languages that you can understand you can simply delete the "bad word" files. And nose art files you dont approve of can be deleted also. If my instructions arent very clear, I'm sure you can look up how to do it. Anyways, the aircraft selection is wonderful, you can fly aircraft from all the major powers, (some smaller countries too). You can fly alot of stuff from 1930s biplanes, P-51s, all the way up to late WW2 jets, including some wacky German experimental aircraft. Also, a very neat feature is that you can take a picture of your face and use it to make your own pilot! You can zoom in on your plane and it's you in the cockpit! I love it. You can create your own nose art and slogans too, along with entire paint jobs. But I dont know a whole lot about that besides adding art and text to the plane. So yeah, overall I would recommend it, it works for me. "You stay classy". *clicks tongue, puts on goggles, and flies away* Merry Christmas by the way. Hopefully you'll be getting something from steam. I'm probably going to get T-72 Balkans on Fire next.

Axiom Verge is the masterpiece of an individual who deeply loved Metroid and Castlevania. Retro game play is the calling card of AV, and the game play is spot on, with responsive controls and imaginative weapons. The intentional 'glitches' and classic pixel stylings harken back to the late 80's (16-bit era) when there was actually still a use for an imagination whilst playing video games. 2D platforming at its best, with lots of hidden areas, and nods to the original game (upon whose magnificent shoulders this giant stands) make this a wonderful gem of a game, with a price tag which won't blister your wallet! Axiom Verge is not perfect, for sure. Drilling straight down is a bit of a chore, but with so many motion options, there must come some compromise. I've only got about 4 hours (or so) of game play under my belt, so I won't even begin to try to write a complete review; for now, I'll say that I am very pleased with Axiom Verge as a whole, and look forward to many more hours of fun at the helm of this retro ship!!

So the Rabbit prince of Hell has been caught in an embarrassing situation with a rubber duck and the only thing that can make it better is vengeance, that and getting the incriminating pictures back and showing everyone who’s boss.
This game is many things, crazy, colourful, insane, fun, psychotic, confusing and frustrating. So let’s start off with the story, it’s silly and fantastical to the nth degree, I loved it. It’s so off the wall zany that I had a blast with it and the crazy characters both friend and foe. The many worlds of hell are super varied and imaginative from the neon night club to psychedelic dream world I loved every one of them.
One particularly favourite part of mine was the huge amount of fatalities there were when taking down the 100 individually created enemies. They are all unique and die in a huge variety of bloody messy cartoonish ways. The vast arsenal of pure destructive weaponry was also another highlight, not feeling the magnum switch out for the flame thrower or one of a half dozen missile launchers, my favourite is the shotgun a must buy when you play.
Not everything is great though, the controls are very tricky to master and even when you get the hang of them they still mess you up from time to time. The DLC missions on a keyboard or almost impossible and took me a few frustrated hours to complete. The in game dialogue is also much more miss than hit with no laughs at all from me the whole play through. The ingame options are also pretty much non-existent with no audio options or graphic changes of any type present.
That being said this game is a lot of fun and I would recommend giving it a go for a few hours of entertainment. If this is on sale pick it up and try not to think too hard as you splatter demons on mass on your one bunny crusade through hell.
One final note, I know I said it before but play with a gamepad, the keyboard is not good and will lead to a lot of frustration with the precision platforming in some sections and virtual missions.
