Well. Brink. 6 years later seeing it show up in Steam sales, I feel compelled to give it a positive review - with some caveats.
I love the work Splash Damage has done, I have played the game at their offices and had high hopes for it. The game sought to bring the same objective-based team play from Enemy Territory and Quake Wars (which I found terrific), make it more favorable towards console, sprinkle in some parkour and make a hit. It never quite made that.
For one thing, the maps were strongly tilted towards a few choke points and controls on PC felt very 'console-y' with a small field of view and context-aware 1Button. Nonetheless, I had quite some fun with it. Mobity is an important, concious choice; the objective based team play is there in all its glory and class fiddling is quite fun. It's been 6 years. Should give it a go. As should you, as it's free to play and you're reading a random review. Why not give it a shot instead?

It's a pretty short, cute visual novel that has a really great story buried under all the unlockable character endings. I was honestly surprised that this game made me feel things - I was just expecting weird goofy interactions and references through the whole thing. Replaying it for the different endings can get tiresome but thankfully they anticipated that and put in a fast-forward option that you can toggle during the introductions and mandatory scenes.

Bought it expecting lame puns and not much else. Seven hours later and I'm contemplating getting the DLC. How did this happen to me? How do you even review this game? Even without the bizarre premise, it isn't exactly your ordinary dating VN. Hatoful Boyfriend honestly deserves plaudits just for skirting the blender of meme-game shovelware with a setting like this, let alone producing a convincingly authentic VN with a twist.
Let's get it out of the way. Yes, you are a human at a school for birds. The only human. You'd expect this to be handwaved and rarely referred to, right? Bzzzt, wrong. The plot is actually far deeper than anticipated; the real cherry atop this game is the BBL route at the end, which radically alters the tone and veers in a far darker direction than the main game. Themes include: murder, suicide, rejection, dystopia, genocide and human experimentation. Yeah. Seriously grim at times, it manages to combine Sherlock and Under the Dome in fleshing out the main cast far beyond where the main game takes them.
Before all that, the main game is actually pretty pleasant. The...birds...are characterised surprisingly deftly, and avoiding the common VN pitfall of nailing one identifiable trait to a character and bludgeoning you over the head with it at every opportunity. These guys are genuinely sympathetic, and each route generally avoids too much repetition beyond the first semester. Your avatar is pretty funny, and seems to channeling her inner Mongol about half the time, as she studies in class and makes choices regarding the secret lives of birds. The foreshadowing for the final route is subtly done.
Even if the Bad Boys Love route didn't exist, I'd still be rating this positively...it's a solid VN, funny and polished. The end route only elevates Hatoful Boyfriend considerably above most peers, and was a refreshing departure from the usual themes in dating sims. A murder-mystery whodunnit tacked onto a game about romancing pigeons - why not?

As the Japanese march through China and the Germans to Poland; the United Kingdom prepares for war. Italy has completed their African campaign and look to Greece. Russia feels uneasy with Adolf Hitler. Spain is thrown into civil war and the United States waits... knowing that war is looming over the horizon. The story of WWII always ends the same, Hitler gone, a red Europe, and a new superpower. So, mix it up a bit! Lead the US into war with Canada and take their land! Control the German Reich and beat back the red Russians. The world is full of "what if's" and you can answer some. Change history for better or for worse. Lead any country where you see fit and take hold of history.

Somethings I really like about this game is that Paradox wasn't afraid of making one nation more powerful then another, the United Stated is stupid powerful, and it's something I admire because they are telling it how it was. The German Reich had no chance of standing up to the United States and they knew that. I will say movement of troops was a bit tricky at first, but once you learn it's not a problem at all, becomes second nature almost. I do also admire how they handle different government types too; like you can't just go on a rampage as the US because it's a republic and a republic like the United States isn't really an aggressor. Overall I feel Paradox has handled history very well this time, it's a great game and allows for people to learn about the war that took the most lives in history.

A mediocre side scrolling shooter with an uninteresting premise and bad visuals. Apparently, it's also only a tech demo of sorts, which the store page fails to mention.
Ship movement is floaty and not crisp whatsoever, it feels like you're constantly sliding on ice. This makes side scrolling shooters very irritating and unfun to play.
The visuals are amateur and weak, which wouldn't be a problem if the gameplay wasn't so bad. I should mention that background effects often move forward and overlap with the foreground, causing a confusing display and you can't ever really tell what's going on. Giant, obtrusive text blocks the screen every single time you collect a pickup, making things more annoying than they already were.
However, that shouldn't be a problem, since all you really have to do is move around and hold the spacebar without much thought, even if you can't see what's going on. After enough enemies die, you progress to a new background, and the process repeats until you encounter a boss enemy. Boss enemies also present no challenge, and every one I faced went down within a matter of seconds.
There are only two music tracks, from what I heard; the title screen and in-game track. If you spend more than 5 minutes playing this, you'll become very acquainted with the 10 second techno loop during the shooting segments.
Avoid this unless it's on sale and you want the trading cards, or you hate yourself.

After realizing my last review looked like complete sh!t, I've decided to re-do it and make it simple.
Pros:
-Great Aircraft Selection.
-Easy Controls, I used a mouse and keyboard, and still had a blast.
-Fantastic Damage Model, you can actually see bits and pieces, plus the pilot bailing out of his aircraft after you obliterate him.
-Engaging combat, the AI sure know how to get the blood flowing.
-Large map selection.
-Dynamic Campaign, which is very, very unique, you can play as someone in a certain rank, in a squadron, or work your way up, there's even a bit of RP elements, as you can change your picture, personally, I changed mine to a s3xy pin-up model, gotta give some lovin' to those hotties.
-Very well optimized, I never crashed once.
Cons:
-Somewhat dated graphics, however that's understandable, the game is like 11 years old, and there's mods to fix that issue.
-The AI can be really stupid at times, missing ground targets almost everytime, whether with a bomb, rocket or machine guns, or how big the target is, the AI can miss it completely if there's not enough planes attacking a target. They're better at carpet-bombing and torpedoeing.
-A few missing planes from the aircraft selection, I unfortunately didn't see any P-40Ms, or any F8F Bearcats, still a very wide selection, again, most of it can be fixed with mods.
To sum it up, with how many pros I gave this game, this game doesn't lack in anything really, it does it's job, an air combat sim. I found it hard to find any negatives, but if you've got the money, definately buy the game, it's well worth the price if you're a fan of WW2, and or aircraft.

"Developed solely by Thomas Happ." That's right. One man made everything there is to the game. The story, the art, the music, everything. Is it worth the price? Definitely. With at least 12 hours of base content and tons of secrets to discover, the game isn't going to get old anytime soon.
The story is, in my opinion, amazing. The art is great, and the cutscenes really stand out. The music is probably the best part of the game; no matter how bad things looked, the music always got my blood pumping for some old-school action. The mechanics do get repetitive at times, and I have a lot of issues with the way the Grappling Hook was implemented. I've also got some minor issues with the default keybindings, but they're nothing you can't change.
If you liked Metroid, you will like this game. If you loved Metroid, you'll probably love this game too, just like me. Even if you don't wish to play it as a nostalgia trip, play it to see what one man can accomplish with a good amount of experience in the game development industry and tons of free time. Notch, you say? Happ is where it's at, boy.

This is the 2D Metroid game we've wanted for years now. It harnesses what made Metroid great while giving it's own unique (and slightly randomized) spin on it.
The weapons are fun to experiment with and the "corruptor gun" can have surprising results if your experiment on enemies - like turning them into platforms, chain explosives or remote controlling them.
Be warned though - the backtracking does not hold your hand. Make notes if you think the 2-flags per area are not enough. Some times it's obvious what upgrade you'll need, but this game did surprise me a few times with what it brought to the table.
One other small downside is the lack of teleport option. There's only a central hub "tunnel". Which is even worse if you, like me, didn't try standing on the giant heads there, which act as vehicles.

This is a new record for the most racist and xenophobic you can be without saying a single slur. Let's go through the checklist: Russian stealing a superweapon? Yup. Sells it to a Middle Eastern warlord? Yup. Enemies running around yelling Arabic phrases at you? Yup.
Let's discuss what this game is. It's a third person shooter, in the same lines as Gears of War or Spec Ops: The Line. While those games implemented story tremendously, and had some intriguing and intense moments; this falls short. There's something a little weird about running through Libya shooting people while you play as "Pope." The sheer American-ness of it all was a little disappointing because it was done seriously. It wasn't tongue in cheek like Team America. It was done with a sense of legitimacy which detracted from the entire experience. The writing for the plot was as xenophobic as you'd expect (come on guys, the cold war has been over for 30 years. You don't need the obligatory Russian arms dealer); the dialogue feels like it was written by that girl out of the movie Paul (remember when she swears for the first time then just can't stop? Yeah, that's our protagonist in a nutshell) and there are more than a few moments where I found myself going "people have to be warned."
I found myself yelling at an Apache helicopter and all I could think was two simple things. Firstly, how did the pilot hear me through the canopy, over the arctic winds and the sound of the helicopter engine. Secondly, well done writers for not making it a Hind; you've at least showed you can avoid SOME stereotypes. Then I just found myself using a rocket launcher where the smoke obscures your view so you can't tell if you hit or missed. It was far too obtrusive and frankly made the section alot more difficult than it needed to be.
Then we can top that off with so many sections where you do the standard run from cover to cover to avoid a heavy machine guns dreadful maw. Except, the cover mechanics are broken and uninteresting. There was no rush or desire to push forward. I had to FORCE myself to go past it, especially because after getting close to the end of a minute long cover dash; it instant killed me with no warning because tank cannons; why not? Then I had to go all the way back to the start.
Now lets think about a very important aspect of third person games: animations. Quite simply, there's a bit of a lack of decent animations or bump mapping. You can punch or hit with your rifle butt to kill enemies instantly. They can also pretty much do the same to you. You can die in two punches but it takes nearly a full magazine to kill you on the hardest difficulty. Speaking of magazines, you'd think reloading would require you to remove the magazine from your gun and replace it with a loaded one? Nope. The magazine NEVER leaves the weapon. It remains there while you wave your hands in a reloading fashion.
From a game where you kill half a thousand or more indigenous peoples; you'd think there'd be a variation in guns. Nope. There's an M16, M249, AK47, SVD, M136-AT LAW (which they call an "RPG"), M1014 and a UMP. That's a total of 7 guns, between over 500 enemies. Not exactly varied. And they don't handle or sound good. The crosshairs don't change size, they just jolt when you fire. Then top that off with their lack of accuracy and inconsistent damage and you have for a shooter that lacks the fun of shooting.
All in all, this game is a colossal disappointment which I genuinely only completed in order to have all the achievements in a game. The story of Pope killing Arabic men to protect the freedom of America is one which I realised halfway through being told did not even need to exist. It's arguably the most disappointing third person shooter I've seen and actually proved something to me. I thought all Modern Military Shooters nowadays were just the same tired rehash about terrorists, Russians and "America! F**K YEAH!" but I was wrong. Somehow, there's something about the Call of Dutys and the Medal of Honors and the Battlefields that makes them at least decent, if not fun. This was a formulaic attempt to recreate those games and hope to do just as well. But it turns out, it's much like a home-made chilli or a savoury mince. You can't just look up the recipe online and everything's fine. If you take 50g of America, 2 tablespoons of Freedom, a pinch of Xenophobia and fry that with 400g of Questionable Views of Foreign Nations (add water and stolen superweapons to thin the sauce) it doesn't necessarily make a good game. This is what happens when you follow a formula to the letter. It lacks originality and character; which is pretty much essential for a good game.

First; some context to what I'm about to say. My mates and I who absolutely ADORED M&B: Warband saw this coming out and were like "Oh♥♥♥♥♥♥dude this is gonna be so ♥♥♥♥in epic!". Being an actual lord that can have control AND impact of the world as it progresses? Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥bricks on a ♥♥♥♥in stick, that sounded AWESOME. In the initial stages of the game, where only the deathmatch modes were available, the initial idea behind the game was well conceived. A world that resembled the M&B series BUT had tweaked world mechanics and systems, as well as more in-depth combat mechanics. The first 2 hours or so were fantastic, but beyond that things started going downhill. Many reasons are responsible for this.
(Holding down the mouse button places you in a stance to guard in a certain direction, directly related to the direction of your mouse movement. Releasing the button released an attack from the stance the user is currently in.)
- This mechanic is creative and somewhat succeeds at making the combat less button mashing and more strategy, but flops in the fact that certain weapons have RIDICULOUS reach, making the best strategy simply : Wait to parry a strike , then get a free hit as the enemy recoils from the impact.
- You might argue that this is a high level strategy, but any one who has even played this game for a decent period of time would beeline for the longswords or the scythes and just turn matches into this weird orgy ritual dance of people dancing around in weapons; NO one attacking in fear of opening themselves up to attck.
- A difference in location is supposed to offer differing bonuses or strategic advantages that are supposed to utilisted by those who know how. But in OKAM, this is dumbed down to a level where a change in location of the battle basically does  not even affect the outcome of the battle at ALL.
- another reason for this is the crappy design of the capture the flag modes, whereby people are supposed to used their wit and strategy to contest different points at opportune times. With OKAM's current system of "one point can be captured only AFTER the one preceeding it is captured." In a context of a medieval war sim, this system completely ruins the game by funneling everyone; archers, skirmishers and heavy warriors into ONE tiny area of the map for the weird staring orgies I mentioned above.
- The epic is a place that is best described as a persistent world, similar to the various warband multiplayer games. However, the developers managed to ♥♥♥♥ up so badly in so many ways that it is arguably the reason why the game lies in the forgotten corner now.
- The epic was the main attraction of the game for ♥♥♥♥s sake! It was what EVERYONE who bought this god-damn game wanted! They wanted to be able to play good-looking mount and blade with a consistent living world that adapts to the choices made by the players! Instead, the players got a huge pile of disappointment ranging from : The Epic releasing a whole 3 weeks after the original date; dubbed the "Epic Fail" by a online review. The content in The Epic is such a farcry from what was promised that many of the players just chose to forget about the game entirely. Last but not least is the alarming INDIFFERENCE the devs have toward the game : "The most anticipated part of our game isnt done yet? lets not tell our dedicated niche audience what's happening!". This infuriates me perhaps the most out of the other points. Why? because the community that came together to support the devs and purchase the beta of the game are rewarded not only with shoddy products, but a provider that doesn't even care about it's investors?
Shame on you devs, you abused the trust of this community and your dream is now a steamy pile of rubbish forever forgotten. I hope you learn from this and strive to do better, because after this MONUMENTAL letdown, I know the community WILL be smarter.
Thank you for reading

If you enjoy the old school Heroes of Might and Magic you'll like this game. It takes out some of the more frustrating resource management by reducing the types of resources from 6 to 2. Heroes feel a little underpowered in this game, but the four classes are pretty well balanced. The campaign mode adds a nice level of strategy. While each shard you conquer feels like its own world, and is a brief heroes of Might and Magic style game unto itself, the strategic brilliance is in how they link each conquest. As you conquer shards you obtain benefits and unlock technology that you can use in later conquests...for a price. The writing could use some polish, and it's difficult to pin down exactly, but it feels at times as though maybe a less than thorough job was done translating the game from another language. The real gold of this game is in its expanse. It is basically impossible to completely explore every shard, or at least would take a very long time, and the game does a nice job of providing you with new and different encounters. Do I want to try and forge an alliance with the elves on this shard or the halflings? Is it worth the time or should I just slaughter them all and take their lands? Should my hero spend his time hunting down that dragon that's plagueing my kingdom or should he pillage my enemy's domain? It's also nice to be confronted with actually insurmountable obstacles from time to time. No I can't explore this laborynth and kill it's minotaur at level one, but just because I can't face it, doesn't mean I can't see it. So many games have the "you'll get there when you're ready" mentality and it negatively affects suspension of disbelief.
The story is fairly generic fantasy, but Astral politics can be fun, and it's nice that the way you treat your subjects and those around you has a concrete effect on the way they interact with you. Do you value story over gameplay? Do you love games that stir up emotions? Have you loved To The Moon? If so... you might like this game, but there's a good chance it will leave you disappointed. It certainly didn't amaze me.
Right off the top: this game is short. Hell, you can probably play through the entire thing in little more than a single hour. This doesn't give you enough time to become attached to the characters or get emotionally invested in the story.
Another thing you might not expect: no dialogue. The game goes out of its way to tell the entire story with nothing but environments and visual metaphors and it certainly has some really good ideas on how to convey it. But some of the metaphors fall short of the point into obscurity and there's a limit on how complex a story you can tell this way. I'm still at loss on what actually happened at some points in the game. I wasn't shocked or surprised or touched in a deep way by anything I saw.
But what really kills this game is the interactivity, or to be more precise, the near-complete lack of it. The game is comprised of lengthy cut-scenes connected by brief and meaningless moments of interaction. It's 100% linear, no choices ever matter and all you're ever required to do is going from point A to point B and sometimes pressing the action button. It's mundane and pointless. It's anyone's guess why the game even bothers to give you control.
Overall, it's not all bad if you treat it like a (semi) interactive intro/trailer for an upcoming game, but on its own, this game doesn't have much to offer.

This game in one word:
I appear to be one of the few people who hasn't played To the Moon, so I can look at it with a fresh pair of eyes, not compairing it to the other one.
Generally, I don't like 'this type of game': a pixely 2D RPG-ish short with few possibilities. IMO the biggest downside of this game is the limited amount of actual gameplay. Most of it is animations, telling the story for you. Often I asked myself aloud 'do I get to play this movie, or...?'
But, the upsides! The artstyle is cute and reminded me of Braid and the music of Spirited Away. What grabbed my attention nearly immediately was the humour. How well the surreal visual comedy was implemented caught me by surprise and made me laugh out loud multiple times. The lack of dialogue doesn't bother me, on the contrary: I think that a story told through visuals and body language makes it way more creative, fun and personal.
I played it alone in the evening in a crappy mood, but this game made me smile a lot and by the end I just felt happy, and that is all that matters to me.
I would say, 4 dollars is a bit overpriced for people who don't expect much anyway, but it is definitely worth checking out during a sale. (Final thought: I wish the game allowed me to take screenshots, it has some beautiful moments)

Disclosure: Got the game for free during a recent Steam promotion.
What a shame.
This is a great concept and visual style, wrapped up in poor gameplay design.
Controls are floaty, making timing puzzles for pushing objects (thankfully rare) and precision platforming (not so rare) a nightmare.
Conversations with boss monsters are unskippable, and will repeat themselves on death. If you happen to be above an instakill spike pit when one triggers, good luck not falling in when you regain control.
Enemies will continue to shoot you during the boss kill animations, meaning it's entirely possible to die while killing one of the monsters and have to repeat the battle.
Instagib traps (spikes, acid-spraying monsters) have a habit of sitting juuuuust outside the camera, meaning many occasions of leaping to your doom with no warning.
Heals are few and far between. Have a clutch situation against a hard-fought boss? Better backtrack through the whole level to heal up, or else you'll be stuck one hit from death every time the following checkpoints load.
It's unfortunate, because the game does have its charm (maybe an over-reliance on flat attempts at zany humour, but charming nonetheless). I wanted to like it, as some really nice work went into designing the 100 bosses (at least visually - gameplay-wise not so much). But in the end, I only got through it out of dogged determination. Just shy of six hours, completed the game with all achievemens, and no desire to return to it.

As a title, "Blade Kitten" probably brings to mind a bunch of things. Very little of them positive. As a game, Blade Kitten brings to hand a bunch of things. A very different set of things that manage to be completely different from what was expected. And yet, very little of them positive.
To get the obvious out of the way: this is the most 2006 game to ever exist. It is a Saturday Morning Cartoon through and through, made by people who either read or made one too many How To Draw Manga books. It's of the "bounty hunter" variety with an emphasis on being slice of life - for roughly half the game there's not much of a plot beyond pursuing almost unrelated goals while the main character overreacts to having her... bounty hunting key stolen then deactivated by a longtime rival? I didn't read the comic, this didn't make any sense. Didn't need to.
Probably says something when the nearest entity they have to step in for death-defying character motivation near the end is a pet rat.
So none of this is particularly bad or good. If anything I'd say it's not aimless enough, I was enjoying it particularly well before it made the mistake of trying to have a plot. Certainly has its audience either way.
For the aesthetic, you've got your somewhat alien planet that's probably too human, with your somewhat human protagonist that's probably not alien enough. It looks fine when it's not applying some nasty filter; the environments, enemy designs and character costumes are all fairly interesting and apart from some really weak animations it's alright.
No, where this game completely falls apart is purely the gameplay. It's a mess.
"Floaty" is a term that's tossed out a lot and technically doesn't mean anything unless you subscribe to terms like "gamefeel". While I don't, I'd certainly describe everything in this game as floaty, and I'll attempt to define it for you without making too much of a mess of it.
It's a 2.5 action platformer with de-emphasized action and platforming. It's all mostly automated - just cling to a surface for your cat-like protagonist's claws to spring to action and just crawl around whatever. You've got a basic moveset that's short ranged attack, long ranged attack, slide, grab attack, and a slam attack. Also a midair and ground block so long as you still have stamina left, that old amazing mechanic that's always great and not annoying.
Everything is weakly animated, with little character follow and little indication that hits register other than particle effects and SFX. It takes way too long to perform any action, with grab attacks locking you into several second long animations that show nothing but static poses, and stamina itself regenerates at the snails' pace of 10-15 seconds for a full bar. Where every stamina-reducing action predictably halts it.
It's not like this is a tactical game about meter management - even then I'm heavily biased against it. In this game, you just chew through it to either abuse the slam attack to clear crowds or sprint for 2.5 seconds, and then spam light attack and jog while it recharges.
Platforming itself involves a whole bunch of waiting for way too late, or jumping across two or three platforms then just walking across the ceiling for way too long, and generally just takes too long and is ridiculously easy for how much time it demands.
This isn't a short game. Sure, you can run through it in 2 or so hours, but unless you do it'll be at least 5-6 hours for a first playthrough. It's a full-length indie game. And that's way too long for a game that doesn't have the novelty, pacing or patience to sustain it.
With a surplus of lackluster mechanics in love with empty levels, and an underwhelming narrative that leaves me with very little to recommend this on. I did like the complete overhaul that the alt costumes got and the general aesthetic, and while the pacing does pick up in Episode 2/Act 3 it's too little too late.
If you really want to see what's up with Blade Kitten here and get a fistful of 2006's nerd culture, then yeah it won't be the worst game you've played. But it just left me bored, and boredom is timeless.

This is the 2D Metroid game we've wanted for years now. It harnesses what made Metroid great while giving it's own unique (and slightly randomized) spin on it.
The weapons are fun to experiment with and the "corruptor gun" can have surprising results if your experiment on enemies - like turning them into platforms, chain explosives or remote controlling them.
Be warned though - the backtracking does not hold your hand. Make notes if you think the 2-flags per area are not enough. Some times it's obvious what upgrade you'll need, but this game did surprise me a few times with what it brought to the table.
One other small downside is the lack of teleport option. There's only a central hub "tunnel". Which is even worse if you, like me, didn't try standing on the giant heads there, which act as vehicles.

It's an okay game. The concept of team-based ,objective-oriented FPS is really what makes Brink stands out from other shooters. However it was a missed shot, as almost everything in the game was rather badly executed
-The campaign is fairly interesting in terms of gameplay. 2 sides go against each other, and you get to replay missions from different perspective . However, the story is bland due to the promising lore not being explored and explained enough to make you care.
-Parkour system feels really clunky. I can't describe it exactly but you can feel it through the gameplay
-Gunplay is unpolished. Recoils can spread like fireworks on the 4th of July. I wouldn't complain about the recoil but this is a fast-paced shooter and it's all about fast movement and precision.
Gunplay in multiplayer is even worse as the hit registration is frustratingly messed up.
However, The best thing that redeemed Brink for me was the Progression system and customization. You can unlock various weapons, mods, skills and outfits from leveling up or completing certain challenges. It really provides a good amount of gametime which doesn't feel like a grind fest.
The customization system undoubtedly put almost every shooters nowadays to shame.
I'd only recommend this game as it is now "free" on the Steam Store. If you'd like to play a better version of Brink, i suggest you checking out Dirty Bomb. It was made by the same developer.

Pros:

Ultimately if you are a fan of the turn-based strategy genre then you probably won’t want to miss out. But until Snowbird either adds in a whole new raft of features (multiplayer options, alternate ways to conquer shards) then for the sake of pretty graphics it’s hard to imagine why you would pay upwards of £20 for an identical remake of a game that is still available for £2 - especially in a genre where graphics are less than a secondary concern.  The amount of bugs and crashes I experienced as well as the constant repetitiveness makes this a hard game to recommend but at the same time I have enjoyed the game and how exceptionally well this game is put together beneath the surface.  Juggling multiple management systems and tieing them to karma, story and making the whole experience fluid is not something to dismiss on a whim, however that already appeared to be present in the original game, so the question remains: what value has Snowbird Games really brought to Eador?  That is a question I struggle to answer, even after 98 hours.
A (now) solid turn based strategy game that stands shoulder to shoulder with many others but perhaps not quite matching the immersion that the Heroes of Might and Magic series provided.  What it lacks in story and frills it more than makes up for with in depth mechanics and gameplay however it is difficult to see anyone who is pressed for time or ambivalent about this genre sticking with Eador beyond the first few hours - especially when the tutorial alone took me 6 hours because I hadn’t realised there was no need to explore everywhere to 100%!  It’s a shame as the game really comes alive after the first few hours of invading a shard when you get the tier 3 and 4 creatures involved to take on the larger encounters in the game.

I one word,
excels at being "heartwarming".
This is more of a personal tale interconnected with the game
rather than a formal review of the game in itself.
Snow doesn't fall where I live. If ever Brazil was known for falling snow, it was in the southernmost region of the land and nowhere else. May the 18th arrived, late and dressed in white, to be the exception. An inexplicable climate anomaly happened to one, and only one, neighborhood in the vast city of São Paulo: mine.
I was running down the street from school, panting and freezing. It was far too cold for my usual garbs, cars were filling the streets in chaotic traffic and the various trees that surrounded me had shed their leaves in silent prayer after so long without rain — and no doubt after the strength of the falling hail hit them like rocks.
Out the corner of my eye I saw it: a bird buried deep in chunks of melting ice. It struggled to free itself, its little chest heaving in a show of effort. Without thinking twice, I halted on my tracks, knelt down in the ice and leaves, and took the poor trembling thing in my hands.
It felt like holding a tiny feathered heart, one that could stop beating at any second, lest I look away for a single heartbeat.
At that point I was less than 5 minutes away from my home, but that swift time saw itself doubled once I was forced to walk in a more tactful manner in order to not jolts the poor thing around.
Arriving at home felt like arriving at the emergency room of a hospital with a terminal patient dying in my arms. I ushered my mother to get a shoe box, stripped my father of his newspapers, turned the house upside-down for one of those old yellow light bulbs that grow hotter with time, found bundles of cotton and put it all together in a makeshift bed I'm all too proud of despite its hastiness in coming to life.
The bird looked like it was going to die. Its wet feathers were stuck to its tiny body like a furry dog after a long bath, making it look sickly and fragile. It was trembling and didn't even flinch away from human touch so shocked it must have been. My mother then said — and this I'll never forget:
"You know he's probably going to die, right?"
We found some recipes for home-made bird food, and fed it and watered it with a dropper. Eventually it eased its trembling under the warm light and the thermal isolation provided by the newspapers. We made holes in the shoebox and decided to leave it there overnight, with the lid closed lest the bird fly off and hit a window. I slept unsettled.
Morning arrived and mother ushered me downstairs, messy hair and all, to do the honors. We brought the shoebox to the backyard and I remember holding my breath as I slowly lifted the lid.
Witnessing it soar away was one of the happiest and warmest I've ever felt. The feeling persists.
, in its tenderness, managed to resurrect in me all these fond memories. Freebird Games have a charm in executing stories that by far exceed words and, in roughly one and a half hours,
brought me to relive from good friendships I've had and lost, to the one bird I saved during that unexpected hail storm.
I see no reason not to recommend this heartwarming game. Although some would argue its briefness is a weak point, I see it a strong one: Freebird Games knows for how long narrate a sweet tale without giving anyone cavities.
is a short endearing story whose only major fault, according its waiting crowd, is not being as good as
. Granted, it isn't, but that only goes so far as the script, in my humble opinion. The execution still sustains that signature whimsiness and tactfulness that few of us can only ever dream of achieving in any realm of our lives.
Tale about childhood. Tale about friendship. Tale about growing up. Name speaks for itself.

The soundtrack is amazing, the graphics are what you'd expect from Freebird Games, the story is short and simple, and the gameplay is... rather simple as well. Reviewing Global Ops: Commando Libya is like reviewing a trip to the dentist, if you enjoy a little pain then you'll enjoy playing this game.
Your mission is to take control of half a two man special "special" ops team as they make their way through 9 or so levels of corridor shooting one-dimensional gun play,  The action is experienced as a third-person cover shooter in that you must use the environment to avoid taking damage as you shoot the hordes of dumb ai controlled enemy soldiers.  You must run through various locations that are distinctly the same, moving from cover to cover, avoiding a barrage of shots that do not easily kill you (at least on regular difficulty) until you get to the end of the level.
There is barely any variation to the core gameplay.  In some sections you must avoid lethal fire from tanks, helicopters or hvg. machine gun emplacements [that you cannot destroy,] or the like, while picking up ammo and grenades from fallen enemies, until you find conveniently placed weapons at the end of a level section.  There are a few locations that require you to use some sort of heavy weapon to destroy a boss (helicopter, tank etc)
Graphics are nothing better than okay, while music if fine.  The overall look and feel of the game is that it is something from the 1990s - probably due to the game engine being used.  Story and voice-overs though are bad, really bad.  I mean the stuff of bargain basements, not legend.  Truly the narrative is something out of a Hollywood Z-list action movie.  While the voice acting is just as bad.  Your AI controlled buddy is practically useless, getting lost most of the time or moving out of position into the area ahead where the enemies are pouring from but, without actually killing anyone.  Though he does chip in with the odd kill from time to time.
If you are wondering if there is anything positive about the game its probably that you can use numerous guns, even if there is little to differenciate them apart.  Weapons include: UMP-45 SMG, M16+M203 grenade launcher, the latter of which doesnt work, AK-47, M1014 shotgun, frag grenades, M249 light machinegun, the Draguov SVD sniper rifle and M136 anti-tank/vehicle launcher.
I still cant believe I am recommending it.  You maybe asking why... and how.  The thing is despite all the negative aspects of the game, it actually feels fun to play.  Yes the story is pants.  The audio amateurish.  Gameplay is basic but, if played in short bursts it can be mildly enjoyable in an old-skool kind of way.  I found myself smiling as my AI buddy and me took on hundreds of cliche enemies ala Rambo style.  I guess if you played games twenty years ago this may remind you of the titles of the same franchise and bring a smile of nostalgia to your face.
Overall though I would only recommend getting this in a sale.  Its definitely a guilty pleasure.  Though the game is over quite quickly and is nothing special.  The ending is maybe worth getting too also. If you dont play it, you wont miss much.  However Im off to replay this on hard.  Pope if you're reading this... read a dictionary and learn to count past 10, you dumb s-o-b!

Global Ops: Commando Libya is one of those games where they try to cash in on a "theme", but ended up being "overtaken by events". The plot is as generic as can be: some bad guys found a nuke, and some tinpot dictator wants to buy it (for what, exactly?) and the good guys have to hunt it down. The plot's pretty interchangeable, and the things you can do in this game? They try to do a bit of Call of Duty type game where you get both third-person and rail shooter sequences, but not that interesting overall.
To be honest, graphics are not that bad, but the result is you can't really tell where the ammo and such are. Also, while I like a commando who's properly armed (an assault rifle, AND a LMG? Please) the enemies are hilarious... As they are armed with... Apache gunships? and Blackhawk choppers? Shouldn't it be Hind gunships instead? Also, right at the beginning, they are showing an Antonov An-255 Mriya, pretending to be a B-52?!  This game is a generic shooter that was hastily put together to take advantage of the death of Moammar Ghadaffi.
With that said, the game is below average. The levels are kinda... meh, feels like MOH redux (the EA revamp) but with clear levels instead of lots of up and down slopes and hints of "uneven" terrain. There are ways to flank the enemy... sometimes.
You are limited to two weapons and grenades, but then, there only are like, well, M-16, AK-47 (or 74, can't tell), Dragunov sniper rifle, shotgun, UMP (submachinegun), and rocket launcher. There are attempts to make a cover shooter, as "space" is context sensitive enough to let you slide into cover and peek out and so on. Occasionally you get to use a mounted weapon, but that's about it.
You do have a shadow... I mean a fellow shooter, who will tell you the obvious stuff like "turn right here!" or "let's go through that warehouse!" but he's actually impervious to damage. At least he will occasionally kill an enemy. However, he gets stuck on the weirdest things, then materialize out of thin air. AND he doesn't shoot the enemies that comes between you and him... and the Enemies mostly ignore him too! However, you have to follow him around, since there is no map, no nav marker, nothing. Only by following him will the plot advance. If you lost sight of him, well, good luck, but generally the game is a rat maze... single path. It will open a path for you if it appears you have nowhere to go.
Enemies... Heh, you get everything from generic "towelheads" to generic "balaclava goons" generally armed with AK's, and only later you see some "red berets" (armed with UMPs? In Libya?)  and some security goons (wearing "suits") And they all sound the same and die the same... From a Russian renegade ship to deserts of Libya. And the random comments by your guys? Are just as bad, or perhaps, worse, as they seem to be written by some amateurs, who thought Rambo and Arnies are actually representative of US military, would write. And they *sound* that way too. "Don't f*** with Pope (call sign for your character)"... Yeah, right.
All in all, it's a cheaply made game, and at 2.50 it's... barely tolerable. You can find better games for that 2.50. And if it's any more, forget it.

-"Detailed graphics: fight in realistic settings from Greenland to Libya!"
They're completely mediocre. Boring and bland. And so many boring hues of brown terrain.
Well. That's me disputing the description. Onto the review.
Finished the game on toughest or whatever and got all the achivements so let's start this trainwreck of a review.
Let's start with the good. The graphics aren't terrible.
The achivements are all relitetively easy.
That's it. On to everything else. In otherwords.
THE BAD.
First for me is LAG. For some reason at least for me, It was horrifyingly laggy. everytime I tried to move the camera ended up with a huge lag spike. It finally fixed itself when I changed the affinity to two cores and back to eight while the game was open. Who knows if that fix will stick though.
(Update. It didn't. Seems like it's a texture issue. A very poor one.)
Facial animation. There is none. At all. If they speak it's a blank face. ALL THE TIME.
That brings me to the next point. Voice acting. It's HORRIBLE. They sound bored and not at all natural. And even though the game involves a russian and libyan in a cutscene they both speak english with really poor accents.
Weapons. They don't feel like they have ANY impact. It's like your shooting marshmallows. And on top of this the weapons themselves are kinda crappy for accuracy. Have an enemy a bit of a distance away? Be prepared to waste half your magazine hopeing that one of the bullets hit the enemy you're aiming straight at. Sniper isn't bad but obviously a pain in close quarters.
The story itself. Completely and utterly forgettable. Bland and boring.
A.I. - Utterly horrid. Half the time they just run past my ally and run to me. Sometimes they'll just APPEAR next to me. As you play harder difficulties the game doesn't make their AI any better. Just stronger weapons. That's it.
In game dialouge. It's like they got a bunch of teenagers to write it. Every other word is either a swear word or a ridiculously stupid joke. It's not even fun to listen to.
UPDATE
They didn't pay any attention to detail. There was one moment where I noticed that the character's head was the SAME height as the doorhandle. The couch nearby reached up to his waist. The turret gunners, if you get close to them you can tell that the character's are only standing there with their normal guns in their hands. There was no attempt to make it seem like they were holding it at all.
There was a few moments where enemies came in a car and the door opened and closed. No one came out or anything. The four enemies just appeared outside it.
There are some parts. The vehicle parts. They aren't nearly as good as some say. The enemies are hard to hit while moving and due to the lack of impact you don't know if you hit them. There is no on screen reticle while fireing in a vehicle aside from the first one. UPDATE.  When you're in a tank later you actually have a reticle.
Overall. This is a painful experience that I urge no one to attempt.

A game with a lot of potential, so perhaps I would recommend with a patch, but right now it seems to have a lot of little bugs. One particular one I have had happen to me on multiple occasions, you fight a battle and win but the hero dies after the battle for no reason I can see (during the battle he would have taken little or no damage).  The hero still shows on the map, and you can give him instructions, but he won't actually do them, so you check his status, and see it's because he's been stricken dead somehow.  Another is that during battle, even though I have auto-combat turned off, sometimes individual units will move or attack on thier own; it happens almost always after you have done something with another unit.  It's annoying and makes battle harder because you never know when a unit will decide to do thier own thing.

From the makers of To the Moon, comes a tale about a boy, his bird, and the connection between them.  This is a short one.  (I clocked in at just over an hour.)  It is also not intended to necessarily be a game, but more of an interactive experience.  There is no narration nor words on the screen.  And yet I found myself drawn in at how rich the story of this one is.  The animations are simplistic, yet they are beautiful.  Once in awhile it requires you to participate by doing this action or that, but for the most part you just watch as the story unfolds and carries you along for the ride, just like the paper airplane in the trailer.  If you are like me, and enjoy atmospheric games and are looking for an experience similar to its "counter-part" To the Moon, then I highly recommend giving this one a glance. This is a game where you HAVE TO:
- Watch the same "first encounter" animations over and over and over and over if you die and come back to the same creature again.
- Watch the same dialogues over and over and over and over if you die and come back to the same area again.
- Do the same things you just did over and over and over and over because the game uses a very spare checkpoint system.
- Watch the same "fatality" videos (which are very cool and funny at first) over and over and over for 101 times, until you get sick of them.
- Watch the ending credits, which is VERY long, until the very end.
The game starts as a very colorful and different type of platform game, and for the first few hours it's very fun and even addicting. But after a while, the spare checkpoints start to infuriate you as you die countless times in some of the places. Make no mistake, this game is HARD. It starts to get boring and the game feels like I chore. If it wasn't for my OCD for unfinished games, I'd have stopped playing this at about 50th or 60th creature. After that limit, the game gets very bland very fast.
There are some neat ideas though. "The Island" is a very fun addition to the game. It helps keep things interesting and fun for a while. The creatures are really funny and most of dialogue is above average in terms of creativity (there are some old, boring jokes and memes though).
Overall, I'd recommend this game only if you have a lot of patience and an insatiable hunger for platform games. Otherwise, stay away from this game for the sake of your sanity.

Wow, where do I even begin? I installed this to see how it was. Here I am, 13 hours later and I binged it. Played it in two 6-ish hour sittings because I couldn't stop for anything but falling asleep. There's a lot to talk about with this game, both good and bad.
This is the meat and potatoes of the game. This is what's going to keep you occupied for most of the time, so it's important that this works well. It does. I've found very few situations where I was annoyed or bored with the game. The shooting feels great and suitably difficult and kept fresh by the insane variety of weapons and tools at your disposal. I particularly enjoy that each weapon more or less seem to have a specific playstyle and enemy type in mind, which keeps you varying up as the game goes along. There were a few I simply didn't find useful at all, being the Nova (which you get very early),
and
. The only thing that stood out to me was the grappling hook. Yes, I'm spoiling that because the grappling hook exists in every Metroid game ever, so it's not a big deal. It doesn't act like other grappling hooks and that threw me off a lot and it took me about an hour of gameplay to get used to how it works and its quirks.
Enemy variety is good, although you keep crossing back through several areas multiple times, and this is where enemies can become very familiar after a while. There's also not really that many different types of enemies. You have wall crawlers, static sentries, chasing sentries and different kinds of flyers. But their art style, sound and attacks keep them from becoming stale regardless.
Bosses are suitably huge and while the first boss is a real pansy, they quickly become trickier and trickier to the point where you sometimes completely fail to understand how to beat it until you've tried different tactics.
Enemies are suitably difficult and as you ramp up in power with new weapons and strength, so do the enemies. I found that towards the very end of the game enemies became really difficult and I found myself dying a couple of times to certain rooms. This can frustrate some players, but I found it to be enough to simply press on. The game also allows you tools to explore ahead of you and deal with dangerous threats without really putting yourself in danger, on occasion. It's however incredibly easy to forget you have these tools.
I have rarely found a game that compels me to explore so much as this game. While the storyline is fairly straight forward in where you need to go and what to do, this opens up later in the game, but I never felt I was stuck wondering what to do. I always knew almost exactly where to go next to progress the story, and when I didn't feel like doing that or I got a new tool I felt the urge to go back to older areas and explore and see what new areas I could visit with the help of the new tools. It's absolutely awesome in that regard. It rewards exploration greatly. My only complaint would be that some puzzles were perhaps just a little bit
obtuse, requiring me to really use my head. When a game makes me take out my notebook and start deciphering messages, it's a good game.
I won't spoil any specific abilities you get in the game as I felt they were an incredibly refreshing array of abilities that I quite frankly haven't seen much in this kind of game. Usually what you get is the basic double jump and perhaps a dash and that's it. This game allows you to explore and manipulate the environment in such a way that you quite often forget just how much freedom you really have, and get stuck on a simple puzzle because you forgot you had this awesome ability that would let you pass this obstacle, because other games wouldn't have let you do that. It's definitely one of the games' great strengths, and also perhaps a weakness. Because, as I said, more than once I ran around lost because I forgot that the game allowed me to do things other games wouldn't and therefor I didn't think of them.
This is a matter of taste. Some people can't stand the SNES style graphics and I respect that. However, I found them to work excellently for this game, and overall I found most areas to be distinct and creative, matching with its enemies. I have nothing to complain about here. Everything looks crips and colorful and effects are nice and easy to digest.
Sounds were very distinct and I could quickly learn what meant what, which is a good thing from these types of games. Usually sounds can be confusing, but I found every sound to be familiar after a while, which meant new sounds stood out and made me stop and wonder what that was. Music was really great and I liked almost every track with few exceptions. It has a chiptuney electronic soundtrack that fits the graphics style and the dark story perfectly.
I grew up with the IBM 5150 and later the NES as my go to computer and console gaming as a child, so perhaps my expectations on a story are somewhat lower than others. Back then most games had a throwaway story, fitting on one page of the manual. It was all about the gameplay. This game surprised me with having a very Flashback-y style story with dialogue and I was really surprised to find myself being drawn in and wanting to know more. The world is simple, but crafted very well and the story is really very basic once you've seen it all. But the way the story is told keeps you guessing and wondering. On more than one occasion I admit to have been "mind blown" over how the story progressed. In spite of it being so it was still easy to follow and it really kept me wanting more.
The game has fullscreen and windowed mode, as well as graphics scaling to allow you leeway in the size of the window, should you go for windowed mode. Sound and music have separate sliders. Controls are rebindable for both controller and keyboard. The game allows you to use either a list or a selection wheel for weapons.
The game took about 13 hours from beginning to end from me and that was with a lot of exploration and running lost looking for secrets (yes there are secrets). I can easily see someone spending 20 hours on a single playthrough with sufficient exploration. But looking back at it I could probably have rushed through the main story in 4-6 hours if I wanted to. It's a great testament to the game that it kept me engrossed for so long in spite of being comparatively short.
I heartily recommend this game to anyone who likes weird, dark, sci-fi stories and platformers of old. It's not an easy game, nor is it forgiving. The puzzles take some real thought and it will put your platforming skills to test. But it's a great little game and when I see it was developed by a single man I am more than impressed.
Metroid is an Axiom verge clone.

The Metroid series may be dead, but its spirit lives on, and nowhere is that spirit stronger than in Axiom Verge. It has just the right amount of that familiar Metroid feel while also bringing plenty of new stuff to the table.
First, though, I want to get the handful of negatives I have out of the way. Since this is on a game site, I am rating this as a game. The first playthrough...actually the first SEVERAL playthroughs I could not even get through this. The main reason I bought this was because of how much fun I had with the similar looking "Long Live The Queen". But this isn't much like that at all. Once I committed to the story and had more petience I did make it through, reading everything. There just is barely any game here. I see this touted as a visual novel....well there really isn't much story either. Dialogue is so generic. It's mostly a lot of awkward pauses and people being rude to your character. Reminds me of your most people play tabletop roleplaying games and what they say to NPCs when they do.
The stats you have and build on....don't seem to do anything. You get to select what class you are taking as an elective a lot and each time that choice determines which of 3 stats go up (unlike the 18 that LLTQ has), But your stats really don't do anything. They need to DO something. THe elective choice really determines who you spend more time with. As each of the other characters in this seem to ONLY spend time in one place the entire game....thus making the world seem unrealistic.
I like that you CAN steer yourself toward relationships with certain people and that is easy enough to do. After one playthrough I got the hang of the goal...."end up with someone". But a lot of time that goal isn't actually finished. BUt at least they wrote an ending for each person and that is satisfying. And your choices DO have effects on other characters. That too is rewarding. But there really needs to be much more of a story. More weaving and intertwining of characters. Since there really is no gameplay there needs to be more goals. Other games add collection type of goals...like Batman even amidst the fighting, has riddles to solve and question marks to collect and plenty of achievements to do. This game needed more achievements and other little things to accomplish on a meta level to go along with the story and that would have easily produced more ideas for sidecontent. But as is almost all of the achievements are which endings you get...aka who you end up with at the end.
The bizarre idea of being at an all-bird school as a human is just so weird but cool and makes wyou want to just start dating birds. But that part of it is really underwhelming. The biggest problem is that almost all of the birds are white. So it's like...oh who's that bird? isn't that the other one? Haven't I met him before? Oh wait this is someone else. Is this a woman or a man? I have no idea. I thought my roommate was a girl. YOU CAN'T TELL! IT'S A BIRD.  Making things more complicated is that it uses all Japanese names. Why? It had no reason to. Maybe if the whole bird idea was dropped and it was just a human dating sim story, but there really is no reason for that. Because having Japanese names mames it harder to distinguish if it is a boy or a girl (I almost typed bird or a girl). I guess that's just picky since it is FOR anime fans so I could let that slide but it does complicate matters. The other thing that completely subverts the whooole bird idea is that it provides the option of giving you a portrait of each bird AS A HUMAN. It does this when you meet each one. WHY DOES IT DO THIS? This completely ruins the immersion of being in an allbird school. Why bother with birds then? The thing is....the dating birds thing is the ONLY hook this game has and then it ruins it with that idea. And even while it is breaking the bird immersion it does it poorly because not only do most of the birds appear white but their human potraits look mostly the same too. Thin anime characters with different colored hair. I only used that feature once and never again because it was so wrong for the story and the game.
I did like the characters and their simple stories. I wanted more from ALL of them. If you are going to make a dating sim...why not allow you to go on MORE THAN ONE DATE. Why not let you date multiple people. It's like once you go on one date, then you find out a brooding secret about each person and then that's the end. And therein lies the only actual satisfaction. Trying to get each ending. And it is fast enough to play through the entire game very quickly until you get to a part you haven't seen before. And this is the best gameplay feature. With the simple click of the mouse button (or keyboard type), you can skip through the current bit of dialogue that's scrolling on the screen. That is SO IMPORTANT. Great. So just multiple click through the parts you've seen before! Hold on! there's an even BETTER button. They have a fast forward button! Click it and it zooms through whole sections until you have to make a choice or until it reaches a new chapter. That is so WONDERFUL. They need to use this format to make another much longer and more intricate story because that gameplay suits this kind of game perfectly. However, the amount that it actually has to skip before you get to even your FIRST choice is VERY VERY telling on how few choices you actually have.

Achievements: All possible and easy-- though some require a painful level of grinding.  Through the course of the game, you'll probably have completed roughly 300 missions-- maybe less.  That many missions will have likely unlocked all accessories/gear that the game offers and maxed out every character's level.  The "Lily Lord" achievement requires the beating of an additional ~900 missions or more (45 pairings each requiring around 20 missions to max out).  It's just a bit too much of a grind considering there's nothing else to grind for-- item drops, levels, etc.
Pros/Cons:
+ Most text is voiced and the voice acting is great.
+ The artstyle is adorable.
+ Combat feels pretty fluid and satisfying.
+ The amount of fanservice is adjustable.
+ There are some fun unlockable abilities/items.
+ Each character feels fairly distinct in terms of combat.
- Every mission is way too alike.  Each quest, with very few exceptions, is essentially 'kill 100+ enemies' or 'kill 100+ enemies then a boss'.  There's no story behind each mission or any unique rewards for completing certain ones.
- Most missions can be completed by mashing the x button.  There's nothing challenging the player enough to deviate from that strategy.
- It's common for both characters to be defeated at once since the partner spawns in at the same location the first character just died with no invincibility frames.
- Though I did get 31 hours out of the game, most of that time was spent achievement grinding.  I'd say, rather generously, that the game's content took me around 10 hours to see.  I don't believe that warrants the $30 pricetag.
- Though some missions had maps with paths to navigate, the large majority were just simple arenas.
- Most bosses felt like oversized enemies and could be killed just as simply.
- It crashed a few times for me.
- There's no autosave.
Overall:
Hyperdimension Neptunia U: Action Unleashed gave me a good first impression.  I was charmed by the sequences of visual novel storytelling, and the combat was fluid and fun.  Sadly, though, the game just fell flat.  It felt as if I was just slaughtering foot soldiers in Dynasty Warriors again and again without any major changes or overarching purpose.  At first, I liked that mindlessness, but, for the price, I wanted more.  I wanted more customization, more story, more challenge, more reasons to keep on grinding.  I was not given these things.  With so many great features like the art and voice acting, Hyperdimension Neptunia U: Action Unleashed had so much potential.  Given its overly simple and repetitive nature, I cannot bring myself to recommend this game.  Perhaps bigger fans of the series can find something to redeem it, but I could not.

This game is, and always will be, the best WWII Flight Sim of the decade. The simulator has a myriad of options, features, possibilites, and systems. The fact that I can take off, set my radiator, propellor pitch, ask the tower for weather information, and then go off an shoot the ailerons off of a HE-111 is mindblowing to me.
PROS: Very realistic flight dynamics, dynamic procedurally-generated campaigns, realistic and pretty destruction models, accurate cockpits and aircraft, 100+ aircraft, huge living maps with towns, bases, roads, supply lines, and weather.
CONS: The lighting engine is nothing special, awful polka music in menus, forests are composed of 2D lie trees, your pilot might just get shot in the face immediately after takeoff, really poor and repetitive radio voice clips, unforgiving flight dynamics: DO NOT BUY THIS IF YOU ARE NOT FAMILIAR WITH REALISTIC FLIGHT SIMULATION.
The satisfaction you can get from lighting an A6M on fire over the pacific, or land on a carrier in terrible weather is something unmatched by any of the other games in the genre - and I've played most. Only in IL-2 could you spend a sortie hunting down and destroying enemy supply lines on your own accord, get your rudder blown off, and then safely land on a dirt road in Smolensk.
All in all, I've had this game on every PC since I've discovered it, and this is really something else if you're into aviation. As with most flight sims, it is a niche product; but I can tell you that if the glove fits, you won't regret buying it.

An innovative spin on the turn-based strategy genre. Compare to Heroes of Might and Magic or Disciples. You can also be as kind a ruler as you wish, or as evil a tyrant. Eador has some cons; a diplomacy system that is extremely limited and almost completely non-user firendly (I have yet to successfully forge an alliance with another master while on a shard). It also forgoes a totally pure RPG system like the Heroes series as heroes don't carry over between maps. So while you can level up to your hearts delight within a shard, all those experience points and high-powered items are lost once you beat it. Your deity character is also non-customizable and has little effect on actual gameplay. But besides these minor qualms fans of the TBS genre should pick this one up.

Blade Kitten is based off a Web comic of the same name and follows the adventures of bounty hunter and human/cat hybrid Kit Ballard on the planet of Hollow Wish. Kit's job is to track down local baddie Terra-Li, but she quickly gets involved in more sinister events involving the planetoid's various races. For a game that supposedly serves as an introduction to the universe of Blade Kitten (with more downloadable episodes slated for release), the game does a pretty poor job of setting up events. There's no real explanation as to who Kit is, what she can do, or why any of the action she's getting involved in actually matters. This is a pity because the character of Kit Ballard is quite appealing. The pink-haired protagonist sports sass and charm in equal amounts, and it's great to see a new, fun female character in gaming, even if she is bogged down in some narrative muddle.
While the cute Kit may initially draw you into Blade Kitten, the game's basic action platforming offering won't do much to hold you there. While the game's environments are in 3D, Kit navigates them purely in 2D, side-scrolling left or right to traverse the game's large levels. In terms of abilities, Kit has the acrobatic skills to climb almost any wall or ceiling and uses a sword as her main offensive weapon (Kit's sword--the darque blade--floats beside her like an obedient pet). Kit can also double-jump, block attacks, and sprint to quickly get past some obstacles. It can be fun to leap, slide, and climb around Hollow Wish as the acrobatic Kit, but this fun is fleeting for the most part because the platforming in Blade Kitten is quite basic. The majority of the game involves simple jumps from ledge to ledge or climbs up and down walls, so there's little here to really engage or involve you. Kit will occasionally have to ride a Star Wars tauntaun-like creature across environments, but even these are extremely linear events. There are only a few instances where timing or accuracy will matter--such as a level where you have to flee from a gigantic monster destroying a castle or the game's final, platform-destroying boss--but they're stretched out far too thinly throughout the game to offer any meaningful challenge.
The game's action offering is just as basic as its platforming. There are only a handful of different enemies in Blade Kitten, and most are easily defeated with a couple of simple sword swipes. You can get through the majority of the game spamming Kit's basic attack, with only one enemy type requiring any other strategy to defeat. Even the game's various bosses and minibosses are a cinch to overcome. Blade Kitten does offer obsessives plenty of hidden areas and loot to collect in out-of-reach places, but given that there's enough money to be found to buy most of the available upgrades even if you stick to a fairly linear path, there's little incentive to go wandering.
With a poorly told narrative, easy platforming, and dull enemies, there's little to propel you through Blade Kitten's 13 stages, which take about five or six hours to run through. At least Kit herself controls solidly, but there are some occasions when the game frustratingly glitches. Some instances are fleeting (such as when Kit inexplicably starts to move at a snail's pace), while others are more serious, requiring restarts of levels to fix (such as Kit getting trapped in the environment or getting stuck in walls).
Blade Kitten's strongest area is its visuals: The game's anime-inspired world is rendered brightly in a cel-shaded fashion, and it's great to look at the various environments Kit has to traverse. But even here there are issues. The world looks great, but it's sometimes difficult to differentiate what pieces of the environment are on Kit's plane (as opposed to what's in the foreground or background); thus, figuring out exactly what you can interact with leads to some confusion.
At its best, Blade Kitten is a decent distraction that features some pretty visuals and an appealing protagonist, but its gameplay is too shallow to make it an involving or memorable experience. Kit Ballard may be a fun character, but on the strength of Blade Kitten, there's little reason to look forward to what her future adventures have in store.

What can I even begin to say about this game? What can anyone say about this game? Is this even a game? I can't really tell much anymore.
So, if it isn't blatantly obvious by the big blue thumbs-up right over there to the left a little bit, I like this game. A lot. In fact, it has surpassed, to me, the likes of Undertale, Borderlands, and my previous favourite game in existence (Pokémon Mystery Dungeon: Explorers of Sky, which I would absolutely recommend you try via emulator if you haven't played it already), to reign supreme above them all, now sitting in my second-favourite spot overall as of August 2017.
Why?
Well, I'm glad you asked. That's what this "Review" feature on Steam is for. It's a really handy little thing.
So, first off, the short version for all of you who'd like to get a general consensus on my feelings about this game and why you should have bought it already, and then bought it for a friend or seven immediately afterwards, and for those who want to avoid knowing much about it. Trust me, you really do want to go into this game knowing as little as possible.
Hatoful Boyfriend is a dating simulation game about birds. Pigeons, to be exact. It has you play the only human girl in a school full of the things, and it's your job to get one of them to like you enough to have beautiful, mutated half-bird/half-human hybrid children a couple years down the line with.

Of course, you've got a wide selection to choose from. You have your typical tropes that can be found in most of these sort of visual novel-style games, such as the "best friend" character and the character who thinks they're above everyone else, but there's also some more varied personalities, including a creepy doctor and someone who thinks they live in a JRPG.
If you're a fan of these sorts of point-and-click narrative-driven experiences, then you'll adore Hatoful Boyfriend, as it both combines a legitimately enthralling narrative with a grand amount of humour, wit, and a tendency to subvert the tropes the genre is based on.
It plays great, it looks great, and if you find that you like the characters' personalities, which are the driving force of the experience, then there is not a doubt in my mind that you will find yourself having fun when going through, even if it's just for the first couple of routes you decide on. Which, by the way, there are a total of sixteen of spread out amongst the game. It's honestly pretty impressive.
Alright, now that that's out of the way, please play the game before reading any further. I'm dead serious. I do not spoil anything directly other than the personalities of each individual character and a couple other minor things, but I assure you that the experience is much better suited to play absolutely on your own. Go buy it right now, sit down, get a couple endings, and come back if you so choose.
Or just ignore me and keep reading. Whatever's your cup of tea.
Take this as a secondary line of caution even if you don't need one, but I cannot quite fit the full review on here. Instead, I've made a Google Document containing the rest of it.
If you really want to slog through all of my detailed opinions, you can do so here:
Long story short, though, buy this game. Just do it.

Were you expecting a punchline? There isn't one, and that pretty much sums up this game.
From the very start you're thrown into the game without guidance. Instead of a main menu, the game starts in a empty room with a bunch of pillars and a diagram that looks like a control scheme selector. Instead, that's the sole instructions you'll receive for the entirety of the game. It took me five minutes to figure out even the most basic action - stand next to a wall and press space to break through. Using this on one of the pillars does some sort of four-dimensional fold into the main maze.
The rest of the game seems to be wandering around the randomly generated maze collecting books. There's no positive feedback indicating that you're doing things correctly, or any sort of gauge to indicate progress - just a counter on how many books you've collected. When you die, you're "score" will be shown, compared to previous runs and then you get to start over in the pillar room.
From looking at the other reviews, apparently a lot of people enjoyed this. I was just not one of them. To me, it felt more like a tech demo than any sort of game.

illumine is truly a hidden gem of a game in a sea of mediocre (and sometimes just plain bad) games within the same price range. It's the perfect mix of Zen and panic and can seamlessly transition between the two in a moment's notice and without warning.
You play as (coming from an American who only knows enough Spanish to say "I don't speak Spanish," mind you) an inpronouncable symbol on a quest to collect books and "make friends" with letters of the English Alphabet. And by "make firends" I mean boop them so you have a higher Karma score when you die. We'll get to those bits later. But all the while, you're trying to avoid "A"s, "Я"s, zeroes, "M"s (or possibly "W"s), and perhaps other things that want you dead. Why do you need to collect the books? I couldn't tell you; I haven't beaten the game yet.
The graphics are simplistic to say the least, and really nothing to write home about. But for a game where you play as characters such as @, the simple visual style really works here.
As I mentioned, there is a Karma system in this game, which is used to (as far as I can tell) unlock new ways to play. You gain Karma by booping letters, putting out fires, freeing letters trapped in cages, and possibly other means. But in order to do that, you need to deal with possibly the biggest flaw of the game: enemies that will kill you in sometimes cheap and unfair ways. One-hit deaths abound in this game, and your biggest enemy is likely to be those zeroes hiding behind the wall you break that will kill you dead. Then, in true rouge-like fashion, you go back to square one. Another problem I sometimes had was that your character will occasionally break the wrong wall when you're in a corner. This has actually gotten me killed before.
But honestly, those are the only two problems I have with this game. It's challenging, it's addictive as heck, it's simple and easy to pick up and play, the soundtrack is great (and I would love to own the OST if possible for the excellent ambience), it's relaxing, and the price is more than reasonable. A lunch at Subway costs more than this game, so I would highly recommend you buy it, play it, die, and play it again. So you can repeat the process from step two all over again.

Well, this is an odd one. Gameplay is as follows-
You go through an actively generating world influenced by the walls you break. You attempt to find books whose locations are shown through waves of light and sound cues. As you do this, you avoid certain characters (literally letters/symbols) that are hostile while interacting with non-hositle characters. Each action you take makes progress towards a certain goal.
Progress in each one is shown after you die. Then you respawn, ready to continue.
The music starts as a simple beat, and everything around it adds to it. Your movement, the presence of enemies, interactions with characters, breaking walls...
The visuals are minimalistic, as seen in the preview.
Honestly, it's addictive but frustrating. Not in a bad way, it's just some deaths may seem unfair. I recently got this, and put  an hour into it in my first session. I would reccomend this to people who enjoy exploration and gradual discovery.
