Its not your typical pick a race, class, here are your abilities, now get to it game.  The shards you attempt to conquer, will add to your abilities and somewhat define and refiine your strategy.  The game has been a pleasant journey of discovery as it doesnt come with a manual (although you can find the manual through google translate if you need game info).  Shards of different gametypes, pieced together (ex: HoMM, Masters of Magic, Warlords, etc) and its friggen extensive.  I am over 40 hours in and not even halfway through.   Altogether, it works for me and if you like these kind of games, you should find this a unique experience as well.

In all its a minor annoyance in all the richness this game offers.
I have seen many gripes on the forums concerning this game, I have none here.  I guess you will either love it or hate it, but dont be swayed buy the naysayer if the above mentioned gametypes gave you some joy back in the day.  Eador:  Master of the Broken World is a worthy game.

Another unfortunate victim of a premature release. This game is an X-Com-esque turn-based tactical game that looks great on paper (and perhaps screenshots) but fails to provide a fun and consistent playfield.
My review is in video form here:
To recap it:
- Inconsistent flanking mechanic. (does it even exist?) The game does not provide you with sufficient or clear indications. In fact, it seems the AI gets to perform flanking shots, while the player does not (or perhaps it's just that the player's squad is so abysmal at aiming it merely gives you a small percentage boost).
- Wildly changing difficulty. Some maps will be short and easy to clear of enemies, others will make you scratch your head as to the logic of the level design. Case in point is a pirate mission in which you need to find and kill the pirate boss, which is hiding at the end of the map. Killing him left my squad roughly at half-health, at which point 4(!) dropships of pirate reinforcements arrived, each carrying 6 soldiers across the map. Yes, you've heard it. 24 extra enemies, while my squad is not only gravely wounded but also flanked due to not having cleaned up the pirate boss' henchmen yet.
- Wide open areas on maps where you're supposed to hurry and save prisoners fighting enemies. This forces you to either take extremely high damage while exposed or run around the map seeking cover while the prisoner AI decides to not shoot back at their attackers, even if they are completely exposed to an easy assault.
- Polish. There is a severe lack of it. The squad has no voices like in X-Com. This might seem like nitpicking but it was one of the bigger things that made you feel more involved and keeping your soldiers healthy, knowing they were actual 'people'. Here, they might as well simply be robots.
- Continuing polish problem - the UI looks like it belongs in an alpha. While it's functional, the base and world UI are very simplistic and boring while the in-combat UI is positively ugly.
- Unimaginative base building. There is no research and no decisions on what to build or where. If you want better tech, you will have to gather materials to upgrade your tech forge. This will instantly grant you the next level of tech. If you need more energy, you will upgrade the generator, for which you need to gather materials. All base building is instant, by the way, no time involved apart from gathering resources.
The bottom line is, this game fails to draw me in as a good substitute for X-Com, which is by far the superior product. Yes, the price of Shock Tactics is much lower as well (on release) but it's a game that should not have been released for at least 6-12 months.

Shock Tactics is the most infuriating and baffling game I've played so far this year.
The developer was inspired by XCOM and wanted to create a tactical turn based strategy game. I get that. XCOM 2 was actually my favourite game of last year.
The only things this game does right is the mechanics it took straight from XCOM. Everything that the developer tried to do themselves is in most circumstances terrible design decisions.
The map design features a huge amount of open areas that have no cover for your soldiers. Many of these areas require you to move through them in order to reach the end of the level, which opens up your characters to be shot. Often times the characters are shot by enemies that are either at extreme ranges which you can't fire at yourself, or by ones that suddenly appear during the enemy turn with no indication that they were there before.
Mechanics like that feel very cheap and make it irritating to even play the game.
There are mission objectives that involve the requirement to keep all your characters alive. That does not work in a game that relies heavily on RNG, as your entire attempt can result in a failure because the enemy got lucky and hit a critical on a 7% hit chance. That's fine if you can keep going through the level, but a failstate because of it is terrible.
I quickly learned in the game that attacking enemies on your turn is pointless, because anyone behind cover will have at best a 20% hit chance. The better option is to just put all of your characters on overwatch (yes, just like overwatch from XCOM) and let the AI blindly run out of their cover so your soldiers have a 70% hit chance.
That takes all the tactics out of the game. You just throw your soldiers in some cover and hit overwatch until you kill the enemy. The AI will always run out of cover by the way.
Speaking of AI, multiple times I've had the enemies just stop shooting at allied or player soldiers and instead run back and forth for their entire turns over and over. It's outright broken at some points and seems like the developer just gave them overpowered abilities to increase difficulty in the game.
The voice acting is some of the worst I've ever heard in a video game. It sounds like the developers voiced it themselves and aren't native English speakers. I'm not attacking the voice actors personally, but it's incredibly hard to listen to as the game constantly pronounces words and sentences in very odd ways.
Sounds in the game are sometimes extremely loud and then other times almost too quiet to hear. The transport landing almost made me deaf, but it took me 15 minutes to realize there was actually music playing in the game because it was so low.
Your characters don't talk in the game, which considering the voice acting might be a blessing. Instead everyone just grunts and sounds like a dog barking every time the get hit.
The menus are also terrible to use. They don't properly dictate what to do and sometimes just don't make sense. They look very basic and are actually off center in spots like the loading screen. They also spelled "version number" wrong at the main menu.
Does the game do anything well? It has different abilities for your soldiers to use and some neat ideas like the turn based overworld and base building.
Most of the abilities however are directly inspired from XCOM, which did all of them much better.
People are going to reply to this saying "give it a break it's an indie game". I disagree with that, being an indie game or developer doesn't excuse making a poor product that they were obviously not equipped to even attempt in the first place. This could have been a neat idea if they made a simple tactics game, maybe in a pixel art style and focused on doing a couple things well instead of doing everything mediocre.
If you like XCOM or turn based games, this will probably just make you angry while you play it.

You know how you've always wanted to play a demonic stygian rabbit prince with a buzz saw and missile launcher?  Now you can!  This is the strangest tale about a bunny in Hell since Matt Groening started drawing.
Hell Yeah! is a platformer (shooting type), which feels like a slight throwback to Sonic The Hedgehog in areas (especially a casino level).  I say slight because the similarities are superficial.  As a platformer, it is not the best, and far from the worst.  The design is good enough to be a fun game.
Where the game really shines, though, is the creativity of the design, but that is not without criticism.  You will quickly forget that you are in Hell, and there is no logic to the levels or encounters.  It's as though the designers put whatever was on the top of their heads and said "that's cool, do that".  It gives the design a random feel, overall.  I don't say that as a bad thing, but the Hell theme gets lost in the craziness of it all.  Awkward ideas like healing from blood showers become commonplace very quickly.
The game has a major overreliance on unlocks and minigames.  Fighting a monster opens a Mortal-Kombat-esque finishing movie, which is done by playing a minigame before performing the fatality.  These are very simple games that are extremely easy, often parodies of other games like Guitar Hero, but they are not always clearly explained and have very short timers.  There are sections of the game which require specific costumes to pass, which can be confusing when there are between 100-200 masks to go through.  There are sections of the game where gameplay changes entirely, with different vehicles or losing your wheel, these are practically minigames in themselves.  None of which are fully realized enough to be a full game.
The major sin of a bad platformer, of course, is poor controls.  Tight controls are what separates great games from bad ones.  This game has almost good controls, but the issues that it does have make the game frustrating, and are very apparent in the side-missions.  You continue to move after you stop moving sometimes, rolling off of ledges or into obstacles too easily.  The jetpack isn't always reliable, though when it works it is useful.  The worst problem is with getting hit.  Most classic platformers had the sense to give a player slight immunity after getting hit, not for easy playing but because the consequences for getting hit can be catastrophic.  This game sucks at that, and is a good example of why games like Mario were made like they were.  A single hit throws you back without control, where you can immediately get hit again and start bouncing around like a pinball with limited movement.  When this happens, you can still move, but the results can be unpredictable.  When one-hit-kill osbstacles are present, the game just becomes frustrating.
There are a variety of weapons and cosmetic unlocks for the game, which are accessed as rewards, or through the in-game shop (not real money, fortunately).  The guns are interesting, but you can pick one you like and use it for most of the game, there is not much reason to switch weapons around.  The shop quickly becomes irrelevant when you get enough money, which is plentiful, and you buy out the store.  At that point, you still collect money, but why bother?
For all of its faults, though, it is a fun platformer and an easy game to get 100% achievements on.  Not awfully difficult, and not awful.  It certainly is worth it just for the craziness of it.

Blade Kitten is a competent side-scroller--but not a particularly phenomenal one. While it plays amazingly smoothly, controlling protagonist Kit Ballard feels completely iffy; it never really feels like she's going where you want her to, but where it's most *convenient* for her. Jumping puzzles and combat really suffer as a result; you never really feel like you're doing more than mashing buttons.
Progress also greatly suffers when your upgrades are all unlocked from a menu. In-game cash is earned and spent in your Pause menu for health bonuses, new weapons, and even new costumes. It never feels like they matter much, however. In spite of all the doodads you can find in each level, it'll never really feel like it comes together.
And yet... this game still feels oddly pleasant. Climbing the walls and ceilings feels effortless--this alone makes exploration tons of fun. The strange alien locales also feel oddly inviting. The awkwardness does bring this game down heavily, but Blade Kitten is totally worth picking up if and when it's on sale.

Very unfortunate to recommend against purchasing this game. The developer put a lot of love and work into it, and even recommends and facilitates people downloading the game via torrent first before buying. He put forth a rather ambitious development schedule and stuck to it. People who are saying he abandoned the game are not STRICTLY correct.
That said, there are just too many game breaking bugs. The game was not left in a working state, and you will not be able to play it from start to finish without needing to load a save to avoid a bug. Most catastrophic from the state I currently see the game is pathfinding issues, specifically when landing on certain islands - this results in your characters either becoming stuck motionless on land until they are told to board the ship - at which point they dive into the ocean - or your captain becomes permanently immobilized on land. This is a very, very - very common bug, and you should expect it if you purchase this game.
While I certainly support a developers decision to move on, especially when they were clear about their  games' development timeline, and love that the developer encouraged people to download the game and try it before buying it - I simply cannot under any circumstances advocate leaving a game that people payed for in such a broken state.
Sadly, I do not recommend you purchase this game.

I want to enjoy this game. I truly do. I've spent a lot of time playing around with a few captains, even had a crew set to that of the Mass Effect group. (I got lucky with a few picks of crew mates and my starting captain it was a blast.) But I can not say that you should go out and buy this game.
What's to say about it? It's a cute idea of 2D art with a hint of side scrolling and it's cool to create your own ship and set up your own crew. But when you get down to the meat and bones of the game you start seeing issues.
Right off the bat, though not game play related the visiual is blinding like that of a thousand suns placed into one room. You need to tweak around the option menu to reduce the bloom as low as it can go, which in reality it makes no sense to have bloom at the highest setting to begin with. I just suggest messing around with the visiual option until you get it to where you can see things. The controls do take some getting use to. It kinda of feels like it's trying to be an RTS game when in reality it isn't, when you have to make sure everyone is in your little group or else one or two will be hanging back in the ship while the rest of you are attacking.
It's a tad annoying to have to go into the menu and hope you hit the right number that somehow picks all your crew so that you have no one left behind. I'm not sure if you have to do it all the time but with some of my play throughs anytime I got a new member I had to go into the menu hope I hit the right number and see if all my crew follows.
The directions aren't that clear either in how to do this. So there is a lot of trial and error. Next is the story, or lack there of. You're a captain who wants to prove that you're the best captain in the sea. And in order to do that you need to take down four other captains. Sounds a little boring huh? Well it is. Because once you see how tiny the map really is and the fights are easy with a fully upgraded ship, which should take you just a few hours at most to get a really good ship and steam roll past anything. You start to get bored with it.
Sail off.
Get into a fight.
Win said fight.
Go to an island with a tavern in it.
Hire more crew mates/buy better gear.
Repeat.
I know I'm being hard on this game but there is so much that could be done to make it better. Sadly though it seems the dev has left this game behind to collect dust. I just hope that in the future the dev learns from their mistakes from this game and can make a better one. There are other pirate games out there that deserve your attention. Pixel Piracy is not one of them.

I bought this game on sale, and I almost regret not buying it at full price. This game is awesome.
If you're curious about visual novels, but aren't really into the idea of playing a potentially NSFW dating sim (a.k.a. you're in the same boat as me), I recommend this highly to you. The concept of talking birds may be offputting to many, but I'm sure there have been cartoons and anime with stranger concepts. After a while, you'll likely stop caring that they're birds, and the script gently reminds you that you're a weird, freaky human through references to your hunter-gatherer instincts that you've honed through living in the wilderness.
Each of the characters is a wonderful spoof of typical dating sim tropes (the senpai, the foreign exchange snob, the best friend, the nerd, the athlete, etc.), and the routes vary from sad to whimsical to just plain EPIC. And once you're finished with the routes... well, you've only hit the tip of the iceberg. This is a game that rewards the faithful, and your reward is a story you'll never forget as everything you thought you knew gets thrown out the window and reassembled in a whole new light.
Trust me when I say you'll never look at pigeons the same way again.

The most honest review I can give is this (tl;dr will be below:
I'm a weeb. And I like hack and slash games. Games like Akibastrip or Senran Kagura usually end up being my favorite types of games to spend a summer on. So I did enjoy this.
But that being said, the characters aren't really too in-depth even on character models. There's not much to "collect" either. Kill hordes of enemies, they drop coins, and those coins offer upgrades, but that's really about it. As far as I can tell, there's not even a shop, and according to the progression screen, I played this game for 2 hours and I'm 15% done.
Also they talk. Forever. I don't even know what the plot's about at this point because it grew so boring and cumbersome that I started skipping dialogues. Remember: games like Senran and Akibastrip are my favorite. I don't skip dialogues often. But this one, once they start its like they never want to stop. If I had even speedred all the dialogue instead of skipping I'd probably be another hour or two longer in this game just from that.
Long story short, this is a simple time killer. Which is exactly what I wanted and also exactly what I expected. So I enjoyed it. But it's a surface game. There's not a lot of depth or progression as far as anything is concerned. I waited till the Steam summer sale to buy it for like $5 so it was definitely worth the money I spent on it, but I wouldn't recommend paying over 15 for it, let alone the full $30 price tag.
Tl;dr?
Pros: Weeby, hyperdimension neptunia characters, simple, hack and slash. Simple, casual fun with silly strip mechanics of AKibastrip or Senran Kagura games. You don't have to have played previous Hyperdimension games to keep up, but if you do it helps. Funny dialogue and humor, often breaks the 4th wall at times, lots of cultural references to other games and anime.
Cons: Lack of any depth given to characters, combat or plot, LOTS of talking that you're eventually going to just start skipping because it goes on forever.
Recommendation: Buy on sale if you like very simple hack and slash weeb games like Akibastrip or Senran Kagura, but I don't recommend any one buy it at full price. And I was REALLY hoping I wouldn't feel that way because these types of games are my favorite kinds but I honestly couldn't see myself feeling justified spending over $15 on this (and I have Senran Kagura Peach Beach Splash preordered for my ps4 currently).
Action packed and silliness you expect from the Neptunia franchise. I really recommend to pick this up while it's on sale!

I bought both the basic game and the Episode 2 DLC at a discount, and I find that the game overall is worth it. I like the art style very much. The characters seem interesting, though the main character is a little annoying at times, but unfortunately they're not explored much in the game storyline. As for the game itself, I like the variety of actions offered by the game mechanics. The level design also includes some decisions that reduces potential frustrations in this type of game. For example, in most places there's no "instant death" due to a jump miscalculation, and there's aiming aid for jumping in some of the narrower platforms. I feel that this, combined with some aspects of the game mechanics (e.g. ability to climb walls, health that regenerates after a while) encourage exploration.
There are some parts of the game that can be improved though. For starter, movement constantly feel as if the player character is on the verge of sliding. Enemies and early levels feel repetitive, and towards the end of Episode 2 there's a sudden increase of instant death possibilities, which is IMHO an annoying change. I also don't really like the way boss fights are implemented, with only one "correct" way to cause damage. I hope these aspects can be improved in future games in this series.

I got the main game free, but I paid for Episode 2 and the other bits. Well, here goes...
To start, it's not a very complicated game, but it isn't too simplistic either. It has a really nice balance that works for the world, allowing you to appreciate everything. It really seems to draw on older sidescrolling games, which is a lot of great fun if you enjoy those like I do!  Sadly it's only recently I've truly been able to appreciate the game and really play it, as I finally have a computer that isn't total crap.
The characters are funny, quirky, and just overall really good. There's more to them than meets the eye when you first see them. I've got a bit of a crush on Kit, I must admit. It's not often I see a female lead, and less so one that really captures my interest for being just a really good character. Flirtatious, sarcastic, but also sympathetic, she really does come across as human (or Felion, rather? Haha) and not just a robot or there to show off 80 percent of her skin. But don't let that fool you, she's still sexy and she knows it! (worth noting: I am also very happy because unlike some games where I find the voice acting to be very wooden, this has a lot of "character" in it.)
The only thing that makes me sad is that the game overall is a bit shorter than I hoped. But that just means I really enjoyed it and I want more of it, so don't take that as a complaint, per se.
To conclude: It's a REALLY fun game, with some pretty great replay value, in my own humble opinion. Though I got this for free, if I could pay for it I would! It's worth the price, it really is.

Okay, controversial game!
We, xcom massive fans, have all been waiting for an alternative; something to keep us going after we finished for the 10th time the xcom 2 campaign, replayed xcom enemy within and waiting for Long War 1.3, right? :)
So what do we have here:
PROS:
- Decent graphics
- The environment can poison and kill you
- I like the idea of an explorable world map. Different sites come with slightly different missions and rewards
- The base construction is good enough. Not as satisfying as xcom though
- Interesting enemies so far
- The voices are not amazing but it's nice to have/hear your main character's voice
CONS:
- Far from amazing graphics
- The environment can poison and kill you (yes, I know, it's a pro as well) but there's no way of knowing exactly what's poisonous. And if all the plants are then we clearly don't have enough safe cover places
- The shot percentages seem to be the opposite of Xcom - 20% is pretty easy to get for both you and the enemy. I never missed anything over 80%
- No save during a mission. This can be a plus if you had the option to opt in or out. It's nice for a hardcore game but missions can take a while and if you have to quit the game during a mission, you already lost it.
Will try to keep updating this review as I go along... for me it's a definite positive! Yes, it's a far from perfect game but maybe the only real alternative to xcom (along with Xenonauts).
I think by promoting this game you also promote the genre.
PS: Also, let's not forget that this game is £13 at launch while XCOM2 was £40 - so it's not really fair to expect xcom like graphics and everything perfect. I hope the developers will keep supporting this game and make it better and better!

So far, not so good.  The gameplay is OK, but not great.  The UI could use some polish.  This I can expect from a small indie developer.
Edit: After quick feedback from the devs (Thanks, btw!) I was able to get this game... ahem... running.
Thoughts after the first mission.  The UI is still clunky.  The game is a resource hog.  Even on lowest settings, it maxes my CPU and GPU and uses 10 GB (!) of RAM.  So, maybe there is some optimization to be done.
Also, the AI is pretty much non-existent.  The one mission I was able to play had me tasked with keeping 3-4 "ally" units alive.  They just parked it across the map, flanked by the 3 or so enemies nearby.  They never reacted, tried for cover or fired back, and let themselves get masacred.  The time it took me to treck it across the wide open map, the 2 snipers in high cover were able to easily smoke my rookie squad.  All this on a mission with the lowest difficulty rating...

Shock Tactics is a low-budget clone of XCom 2. Weaker graphics, voice acting, enviroments, effects, UI, sounds, etc. But I'm generally OK with that. For example, I played a lot of Xenonauts, which also has poor presentation values, but the underlying gameplay was interesting. I found Shock Tactics to lack the tension and depth that either of those games have. The XCom series thrives on its careful balance between abilities, cover, technologies, etc. With Shock Tactics I felt all that really mattered was if I was in cover or not. If I was in cover, the enemies would waste all their shots on 1% attacks while my other units would just fire away. There are different unit types, but the abilities aren't that interesting, such as the sniper having a bonus to hit chance and one bullet instead of 3, but the same range and plays fundamentally similar.
I didn't play enough to write a long and detailed review, I just got bored and couldn't take it anymore.

While the RPG Game Maker graphics remain the gameplay and story telling is different. You witness a story about a boy and his pet, adventures and life decisions. What you have here is actually barely a game. It has minimal input from the player and even that is linear or irrelevant. The game tells you when you can move but takes away this ability without notifying you and that feels bad. Not a terrible experience but just really average. A pretty good Metroid inspired platformer developed completely by one person. Axiom Verge is probably the most successful indie Metroid style game outside ofCave Story. (I'm excluding other Metroidvanias as many of them focus or feature melee combat).
There's about 14hrs of content if your not a completionist on Hard difficulty (I completed it just under 14hrs with 95% of the map discored, 77% items, 36 deaths). Hard isn't terribly difficult, but there are some very cheap enemy placement and unfair-ish boss battles. There is an acheievement for not dying, but I find damage unavaoidable in many spots of the game.
The game is unique enough on it's own, interms of it's art style, soundtrack and item pickups. You'd probably expect the typical Double/Super Jumps, Morphball/Crawl powerup, Super bomb and flight upgrades, but many of the power ups are JUST different enough to be unique, even if the function is similar to most Metroidvania games. By the end of the game, I had too many weapons and it feels like Thomas Happ had to "fill in secret spots with items" and instead should have had some weapons be upgraded. It is as if he had fun making different weapon types and putting them in the game, versus thinking what should actually be in the game.
The story is also unique in comparison to Metroid, but I'm not convinced it's satisfying. (NOT A SPOILER) I'll just say that the ending either hints at a sequel or hints at more to come if you get a higher compeltion rate, but I didn't feel I earned a big story reward.
If you're a perfectionist/elitist when it comes to your came, you may not love Axiom Verge, and the newly released Metroid 2 Remake Project AM2R might be more your style, but this is still a solid game that outshines many games developed by more than one person.

Axiom Verge is a classic-style Metroidvania game (heavy on the "Metroid" part - as in, they could be long-lost twins). So, as someone whose list of top favorite games of all time contains Metroid and Super Metroid right up at the very top, you can probably guess how I felt about this… I loved it. The way I see it, if you're going to pay homage to the best, you may as well go all out, and do it right. And on that front, Axiom Verge does not disappoint. So if you’re a fan of those games (or the 2D Castlevanias, etc) then this is a no-brainer.
The game is extremely well-designed, looks great, has a good soundtrack, and plays well (for the most part). You can't ask for much else. I enjoyed the exploration, item collecting, boss battles, story, and the overall atmosphere of the game. My only small gripes have to do with the way a couple of the game mechanics work (or rather, don’t work) - specifically, the grapple tool and the dash/teleport ability were way too finicky and/or inconsistent to pull off, for my tastes. I'll concede that part of the issue is probably that I used the control stick on the controller rather than the D-pad for primary movement, which makes those abilities harder to reliably pull off, but in my opinion, that should have been accounted for as part of the design. In particular, the dash/teleport ability just didn’t work consistently enough for me, and made a few parts of the game extremely frustrating. But other than that, I really can't think of any other complaints.
All in all, this is about as good a game as one could possibly hope for in the classic Metroid style. It's a game I could/would have probably made myself, if I weren't too old and lazy now (or, like, had no job or family). So major kudos to the developer (just 1 guy) who not only had that technical know-how, but also the time, ambition, and dedication I lack, who actually followed through and made this. It's a very, very, impressive piece of work, and well worth checking out for anyone who is a fan of this genre, or classic-style 2D action-platformers in general.

This game is frustrating to no end. I really wanted to enjoy playing it, but just couldn't. It was enjoyable at first, but it quickly grew old and frustrating with all the bugs.
- Really bad tutorial. The tutorial literally "stops" like a quarter of the way in and just assumes that you understand the rest... I thought there would be more to it, but aparently that was it. I had to open up the help menu and read everything before even getting started because the tutorial literally teaches you next to nothing helpful.
- Swapping ships is cool, but you somehow can't transfer your loot from ship to ship??? I don't understand... You kill enemies from a ship, but you can't move your cargo over before switching ships. I tried a lot of things to transfer the cargo but failed. There might be a way, but if there was the tutorial never covered it and the UI doesn't indicate it.
- Your pirates ignoring your commands is so frustrating. It's a major pain getting them to attack the right targets and not to do stupid things on their own. Retreating from combat is literally impossible as the AI is a potato and your guys instantly die.
- If you enter combat with an enemy ship, you're forced to engage with it until you win. You initially have a 60% chance to flee combat at the start screen, but if you fail, YOU HAVE to fight NO MATTER WHAT - even if the enemy ship doesn't have cannons or attacks you... so dumb. I've instantly lost games because I accidentally sailed to the wrong location and was forced to fight enemies a lot stronger than me. I don't know why you can't escape combat after it's started - seems like lazy game design.
- Crew with the ability to clean your ship won't clean it unless they are part of your "Ship Crew" group... I spent hours in a game where my entire ship was filled with poop and was getting frustrated because nothing was being cleaned... Gee, I wish there was a tutorial or help menu to teach me these things.
- You can't give your crew specific orders (like clean the damn poop or shoot a cannon). This makes it really annoying since it feels like you have no control in the game whatsoever. You just have to hope the AI is smart enough not to screw you over in encounters.
- Knockback is extremely annoying since your crew can't swim initially. Now, it does seem like a somewhat interesting mechanic at first. However, getting half your crew instantly killed because of one enemy knocking everyone back is really stupid. I honestly wouldn't mind it so much IF YOUR CREW WOULD OBEY YOUR ORDERS AND RETREAT PROPERLY.
- In towns with taverns, your crew will jump on the land and eat/drink at the tavern costing you gold. This is actually pretty cool. However, it's really frustrating when you need to recall them back to the ship since you have to select all groups to move back to the ship and then physically click somewhere on the ship. Not only that, but if some crew are slow to come back to the ship, you can have others that will go BACK to the land... There seriously needs to be a SINGLE BUTTON that when you click it forces everyone on your ship.
- Sometimes looting ships can get really annoying since a lot of the loot is in jars/chests on the ship. Aparently only your captain character can loot items which is really stupid. And it seems like your captain is the only one that can dig for treasure.
- Speaking of treasure, the treasure maps suck in this game. It leads you to a location and it's just a regular island. When digging around the ground you won't find anything. So it seems like I must be doing something wrong? I actually wouldn't know if I did anything wrong since there's no tutorial to explain anything and the UI sucks at explaining things. I may have gotten the treasure, but with no message, it's very underwhelming. Doesn't really feel fun at all when it should be one of the most fun things to do in a pirate game.
- Leveling up your pirates is interesting at first, but eventually it becomes a major chore. I love leveling up characters in video games since it gives me more control and adds a bit of depth. However, since you can control 10+ pirates at a time, it's really annoying trying to manage all of their stats and skills. The main problem is that it's very easy for your pirates to die in the game (Combat, Cannon fire, Drowning, etc). It's really disheartening when a pirate you've leveled up 10 times gets killed off by something stupid. I really wish you could set it up to level a particular way and let it auto level.
- Cooking in the game seems like it's cool, but it ends up being implemented really poorly. Pirates are forced to cook some food before eating it (like fish you catch in the ocean). However, it seems like only the pirates with the cooking skill can eat the food... they don't even prepare the food for the rest of the crew...
- Aparently you can only put food on your ship when you're at a dock in town. So even if you're catching fish in the ocean with a fishing rod, you have to go back to town before you can place the food on your ship. Like what? That doesn't even make sense...
- Your ship never gets destroyed by cannonballs. Why? Because the stupid cannonballs kill off your entire crew before it even comes close to destroying your ship. Aparently you can automatically hit any part of a ship. There is no such thing as being protected inside the ship. And since you can't control your crew very well, you can end up grouping them together and getting them all massively injured by a single cannonball. Oh, and make sure your crew isn't standing near the edge of your ship since the cannonball will knock them into the water and auto-kill them...
---------------
The game had some positives, but I'm not even going to list them since it's clear this game is too frustrating to play. I really wanted this game to work since the premise is so awesome and they do a lot of things right. It's unfortunate that the bugs, lack of tutorial, poor UI, poor AI, and bad controls had to ruin it.
Not really worth getting, repetetive and boring.

Hyperdimension Neptunia U is definitly one of those games where prefrence is a big deal. For me, it just wasn't for me.
First thing I noticed when I first picked it up was the ENG audio. Luckily there is a JAP audio selection in the options menu as well as subtitles. The downside with this is that not everything is subbed. There were several sections in the game where you just had characters speak without subtitles. To me that's a bit annoying, but not a major complaint since their voices are all pretty great.
The battle system feels very repetitive and quite boring actually. You can pretty much grab a character, find one combo that doesn't have a huge idle time afterwards and just repeat. Of course this doesn't work for every stage, but I found this doable through most of it. The character interactions between the characters are great until about hour 8 where you're getting repeats every 20secs or so since it will take almost no time at all to get decent at this game. The real challenges don't come in until after the main story. That's when things get more intense, but even then there is just so little there.
The story itself isn't very memorable, but it is actually one of the things I like most about the game. It's cute, it's actually written very well, and the small talk between the major events at time are great. There are several refrences to games that came out around U's first release date and boy are they great little refrences. I honestly think this game would have done better as novel compared to a Hack n Slash genre based game.
I could go on to pick small things here and there, but here is my overall opinion.
It's a great game for Neptunia fans, but not a great game for Hack n Slash fanatics. I would not recommend this unless they were a Neptune fan.

This is the worst stealth game I have ever played.
Upon starting up the game, you are told that your name is "John 'mad' Doe." You are a freelance stealth operative who works around for the different countries during WW2.  It is then up to you to choose a country to work for and do what you do best, that is sabatoge of enemy bases. After choosing your country, you will be brought to a menu where you are given a briefing on your mission.  Here, you can customize John's loadout, equipment and even choose apropriate camoflauge for the mission.  You are then thrown into a giant open world map, with multiple routes to complete your objective. you are also sometimes given a set of more than capable AI teamates.  This is all very nice and well implemented, it's just to bad that they didn't focus more on the "game" part of this "game"
The amount of controls for this game are absolutely ludicrous.  You will probably end up having to rebind and memorize over 100 different keystrokes just to make the game playable.  After that, you will of course try and move to your objective. However, the developers of this game didn't understand the concept of a "stealth" game.  Any time you try and move john around, you might as well be playing the sound of a b-52 bomber over a boombox at full volume.  It is not remotely possible to sneak around in this game.  On top of this, if you try to turn John around to fast or make to sudden a move, he will fall over to the ground faster than a boombox playing the sounds of a b-52 at full volume being hurled out the back of a b-52.
You might be thinking now "Well if I can't get close to the enemy, I'll just take them out from far away."  That's just the problem.  Every weapon in the game has no silencer. You might as well be firing rockets, dropping bombs or shooting a .50 cal machine gun at them.  Finally, there is also no way to see how visible you are to enemies.  Since the maps or so open, you can literally be seen by an enemy miles away.
Overall this is a poor excuse for a stealth game.  Stay away from it, and instead look at better stealth games like the original thief.

My favourite WWII game. You can select to play as any country. There are even known countries inside occupied countries that you can play as. E.g. if you want to play as Egypt or Israel, then you play as Britain who have those areas in control and then free them as a state. You can select historical mode which manipulates the countries to act like they did in WWII, with agreements and opponents or you can simply leave it out and have complete chaos, which is funnier.
You can support any country's political party if they have the same ideology as you. So it is possible to play as e.g. Nazi Germany and turn the U.S. to fascist as well, who will most likely join your faction.
The game is really complex, terrain and weather might affect your troops, but it isn't that hard once you play with recommended division templates which can be found in guides. The game has an active mod community, I recommend a minor mod as a must have - Any mod that changes Hitler's Germany's flag to their actual one.
The only bad thing about the game is that they make DLC's that have quite small changes and could easily just be patches instead. This game makes me proud to be Swedish however.

I did encounter a couple of bugs: a cut scene failed to trigger for me, making me have to restart a section, and I also managed to fall through the world. the controls could be awkward at times, a sequence of buttons refusing to activate because I got the timing a split second off, or me not being able to tell the difference between traversable and non-traversable territory.  the final boss with its incredibly fiddly mechanic that didn't trigger half the time was a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ especially as it kept suddenly refusing to attack me, making it hard to bait. these bugs don't make it unplayable, just a bit irritating at times, and I think the good parts make up for it, especially as the game is cheap and constantly in sales.

The story is... there but doesn't always transition smoothly as you progress through the game. Not a bad story, but has a few plot holes that may go unnoticed in the first playthrough. The Episode 2 DLC wraps up the story very well, though.
Apparently, Blade Kitten was a comic before this game was made. Some parts are mentioned in this game regarding Kit's past but give little detail. I'm not sure what they're like though. I've read some of it after playing the game... seems to be alright.
I'd get this and the ep. 2 DLC in a bundle than separately, save you some money.

This is much smaller, less riveting, thought provoking etc as To the Moon, which I thought was truly excellent.
A Bird Story has no written story, just a story via pictures and animations.  The art style is very similar to that of To the Moon, and perhaps slightly more polished.  The story itself i found difficult to get engrossed in, but was cute, and really more of a cinematic.
Overall, don't look at this as anything like To the Moon.  Just a cute little story about a boy and a bird, it brings just a bit of happiness.

I loved To the Moon and recommend it for anyone who has ANY interest in story-driven narrative heavy games.
A Bird Story is NOT To the Moon. It's a mindless waste of time that tries to make itself feel special by telling a story without dialogue. In the end, no one cares about any of this, because of a lot of reasons.
Being without dialogue makes it extra hard to get invested - not impossible, just harder. Also the complete lack of any meaningful interaction with the game - everything is very slow and you really have zero input in the game at all - it may as well be pixel movie because the player input is tedious and completely irrelevant.
Also the lack of any real conflict makes you wonder why we should even care. There is no grand evil here, nor is there even a minor evil - there's really nothing that even makes the game partially investing emotionally. The closest thing you get is a "chase" sequence with some lightning that is as pointless as the rest of the game.
I literally couldn't recommend this game less. The fact I'm even writing this will hopefully make you, the consumer, realize that it's not worth your money - there are free stories or interactive games out there with more content and more compelling narratives than anything you'll find in this "game".
The saying "Do not judge a book by its cover" is quite applicable here, or maybe morph it to "do not judge a game by its play time"

Anyone who has ever loved metroidvanias owe it to themselves to check out this game.  In a world where we have endless rehashes or clones of the games that spawned this genre, Axiom Verge is a shining example of a reinvention of the style.  The graphical style is clearly inspired by Super Metroid and other 16-bit games from that era.
I have always had a problem with recent metroidvanias with the over-used style of "Get item A to get item B to get item C to get item D, etc" that makes it seem like you're seeing the same corridor hundreds of time as you pass back and forth through it.  If the metroidvania is done well, you don't notice that you're passing through the same area over and over again.  Axiom Verge doesn't over-use the same pathing, and even allows multiple paths in some instances.
The theming is beautiful and dark, while also keeping the game upbeat and moving forward.  The story is intriguing and always makes the player wonder what else there is.
Overall, a must-play for any metroidvania fan or for platformer fans in general.

At one point I actually liked this game, but now, it's garbage. Absolute trash. The devs behind this game have outright lied to everybody. They've failed to deliver on almost any of their promises, and now everybody's gone. You'll be lucky if you can find a handful of players to play against on any server not in Europe, and even then it's just the same people you'll see over and over again. Combat is broken to a point where it's almost beyond repair, and two-handed swords are the only weapons that work. One-handed swords won't make contact with your opponent almost ever, and for whatever reason they actually swing slower than larger, heavier weapons. Additionally, they have shorter reach, less damage, and you get stunned if the enemy hits your shield. Two-handers, on the other hand, dominate every aspect of the game, and there's no sign whatsoever that they will ever be balanced out or nerfed. Don't even get me started on archery. There's also a leveling system where you can level up your stats and skills, but the skill section doesn't actually even do anything and there are really a couple of viable builds you can go with if you want to be any good at all. Don't bother balancing stats, just stack all your points into weapon speed, and then either damage or health. I used to actually be pretty good at this game, so I know what I'm talking about when I say that THE DEVS HAVE BROKEN THEIR OWN GAME.

The Multiplayer servers have been dead for sometime now. Don't buy until people come back to the game unless if you like 2v2s on a map meant for at least 30v30. I hope this game does make a comeback though, I enjoyed the engaging and skill based melee gameplay but at it's current state, I would not buy it.

It looks great, it sounds great, its got entertaining brawling, loads of missions, and tons of rewards to earn for bashing more monsters. Stuff ranging from stat buffs that apply across all characters to new weapons and costumes. The combat is a (dumb) blast - its really just mashing out simple combos and dashing around groups of enemies, occasionally broken up by unleashing special moves and swapping characters, until you can transform and then really wreak some havoc on large groups of enemies and bosses - but it is very enjoyable. Sometimes you need more 'Fighting Force' than 'Bayonetta', you know?
The girls' playstyles are diverse enough and have just enough to learn that you'll have fun experimenting and getting better with each style the more you play. Plus there's enough enemy variety, and there are enough ways to power up, as the game goes on to keep it from getting too repetitive throughout the entire playtime, I think (though the level designs are very simplistic). Its just really well done - the animations are great, knockbacks and hitstuns feel perfect, and there's loads of great Visual FX to provide rewarding feedback to everything you do. All the while, you're fighting to tunes that sound straight out of a Playstation-era Mega Man X title (there's a lot of great stuff here; catchy melodies, good arrangements, high energy stuff. Classic Japanese video game music with a "cyber" veneer).

If you're worried about it getting pervy - especially since this game, that heavily advertises its "costume breaking", features lots of characters who are, after all, little girls - fear not! You can adjust... well, everything that may grate. You want to give them unbreakable outfits? Go for it. Wanna mute the voices**? On a character-by-character basis, even. Conversation/dialogue scenes lasting too long? Skip'em. There's a solid amount of "quality-of-life" refinements here, which is great. This is definitely a good "podcast game" - just something to mindlessly play while doing something else, so adjusting your experience a bit is welcome. Just make sure to head into the Options and the SETUP menu (on the World Map screen) to dig into all this stuff as soon as possible. Otherwise you'll miss out on some stuff that would really up your enjoyment of the title early on, including leveling up your characters via the Medal system.
( ** - to be clear, the voice acting is great. The script is generally pretty cute and funny, while the English cast are matched well to their characters and crushes every line. The problem is just that the voices get so repetitive in stages that you're going to want to mute them before the first one is over. Literally, they have to announce every special move they do, as well as throw out the same 3 or 4 quips every few seconds. The dialogue scenes are good, but the in-game just gets too obnoxious.  )
Basically, if you're looking for a fun, flashy time beating the crap out of loads of enemies - one that's still satisfying-to-play and simple-to-grasp (but not AS simplistic as something like arena brawlers Croixleur Sigma or Mitsurugi Kamui Hikae) - this absolutely gets the job done. Its the modern equivalent of a Streets of Rage-type experience, with vibrant candy colors and magical anime girls: sometimes that's all you need ;)

If Hyperdimension Neptunia U: Action Unleashed taught me anything about the beat ’em up genre, it’s the importance of audio-visual feedback.
What makes the button mashing madness of 1-vs-100 styled games so satisfying is the spectacle of dashing armies of enemies like leaves in the wind, typically to the tune of roaring rock music complemented by the screams of your fallen foes. Meaty sound effects, kick♥♥♥♥♥music, spirited voice acting, and violent, deleterious, larger-than-life attacks are all necessary ingredients for a rousing musou-like experience.
Hyperdimension Neptunia U: Action Unleashed, developed by Tamsoft, the creators of the Senran Kagurafranchise, perfectly highlights the importance of the individual elements that go into a stellar action game. Unfortunately, it highlights them not by being an example of what can be achieved when they come together, but by demonstrating how insipid a game becomes when they do not.
In a world far removed from our own, the console wars waged by hardcore gamers is personified with anime aesthetics and a heavy infusion of moe. Video game consoles and developers take the form of technicolor waifus in a land that is a surreal parody of the gaming landscape: Gamindustri.
From the outset, Neptunia U makes it clear that the game is non-canon, and the story is of little consequence to the overarching plot of the series. The cast of cutesy consoles have been called to defend Gamindustri from a growing monster threat that threatens each of their respective realms, and that’s about as deep as the story gets. The game clearly couldn’t care less about spinning a compelling narrative, instead focusing on the goofy interactions of its characters to fill out the space. Neptunia U never takes itself seriously for even a second, demolishing the fourth wall in the first few moments of the game with tongue in cheeky goofiness.
However, the lackadaisical attitude surrounding the plot seems to have infected other, more crucial aspects of the game.
The game is broken up into missions strewn about the different regions of Gamindustri that all involve doing roughly the same thing: smacking around a bunch of enemies, or collecting some items between smacking around a bunch of enemies. Players may choose two girls to switch between in a mission, or fly solo with a single character. Each character gains experience depending on how much she contributes to wiping out the droves of enemies in a level, and each girl has a set of stats that increase with each level up.
Defeating enemies may sometimes yield enemy-specific medals that are collected to unlock special rewards, like new stat-boosting equipment and better weapons. Annoyingly, the process requires you to select every single batch of coins one by one to see if you’ve reached the next milestone, making it unnecessarily time-consuming and tedious.
Characters have basic combos that are initiated with a sequence of light attacks and topped off with a finisher that changes depending on when you press it in the sequence. Enemies mindlessly surround you in a perfect circle, eagerly waiting to eat the swing of your weapon. Room-clearing special attacks are at your disposal to drop on a whim. All of the pieces are in place for a decent Dynasty Warriors-esque experience.
But then you hit the enemies, and the game’s most glaring flaw is made immediately apparent: the sound effects are essentially broken.
When the swings of your blade aren’t met with jarring silence, they are punctuated with the most underwhelmingly stale sound effects imaginable. Most attacks elicit all of the impact and fanfare of rapping your pencil on a wooden desk, if that, and the rest is even more piddling – even your biggest, most extravagant attacks somehow manage to feel weak and hollow. Much of the audio in combat is dominated by the irritating wails emitted by defeated enemies that don’t quite sound like yelps of defeat, so battles become a nonstop barrage of the same awkward gibberish from beginning to end, with very little audio feedback between them. The soundtrack isn’t terribly memorable, either.
This issue might have been assuaged by a solid combat system, but the gameplay is starved of any interesting features to make it engaging. A few special attacks, an ultimate attack, and a quick dash is all that’s at the player’s disposal. With those tools, it’s just a matter of mindlessly swinging away at the ever-spawning mooks until the game turns off the AI and declares you a success. The practically nonexistent audio feedback, coupled with the limited mechanics, gives the player all of the satisfaction of swinging a weapon through empty air while dying hogs squeal incessantly nearby.
Fortunately, the game looks fairly nice, running at 60 fps on PC. Characters animate as smoothly as they do in Senran Kagura, and the environments are colorful, even if the levels themselves are extremely small. Character portraits in the VN-styled cutscenes are well drawn, and the lip syncing is spot-on for the Japanese dub. When characters take enough damage in battle, their clothing will rip to shreds, triggering a little in-game scene where they recoil in jiggling disbelief, much like they do in Senran.
The particle effects can look nice in combat, and some characters attack with gusto. Sadly, they do little to spice up the dreary boredom of slogging through level after level of muted fighting. Which is a shame, because some obvious care was taken to make the game look nice.
It couldn’t be more obvious that Hypderdimension Neptunia U: Action Unleashed was made on a crippling budget. The polish and shine of the Senran Kagura games, which Neptunia U apes at every opportunity, is in short supply here. The game simply feels like it was rushed out the door well before it was ready for human consumption. There was potential for a good game here, but atrocious feedback from player input ruins what enjoyment might be had from smacking around legions of dumb enemies. The character interactions can be cute and amusing at times, but they’re only a small diversion from the stale meat of the game.
In short, Hyperdimension Neptunia U: Action Unleashed is like Senran Kagura, but bad. If you need your Nep fix, just watch the cutscenes on YouTube.

**WARNING** - This is NOT for those of you that want to mindlessly click and play and have instant gratification for little or no work. Go play Great Big War Game for that. This game simply put is the best Turn Based Strategy title to come down the pike since Civ 5. It is hard, yes. Even on easy it is difficult to manage and balance all the things you need to manage and balance in these type games (Economy, happiness, army upkeep etc). There IS a way to accomplish it but it takes smarts and determination. The rewards are well worth he work. The Pros and Cons are as follows :
PROS :
1.) Easy to learn interface. If you cant master this interface in the first 10 minutes then you need to exit the game and delete it because you will be lost like a fart in a whirlwind. Go play solitare as it is more your speed.
2.) Tutorial brings you up to speed. Easy to learn, hard to master
3.) Very challenging. This is not a simple fast gratification game. Hard core TBS gamers only.
4.) The Risk vs Reward system is well balanced unlike other games.
5.) A Deep, rich game that has untold hours of replayability in it.
Cons :
1.) Poorly designed building tech tree. It has some good elements to it BUT the design of it makes it very difficult to know what to build to get the unit, spells, items you want. Could have been much better.
2.) The AI tends to take too long in making its moves on the overall map and in combat .... but at least in combat you can move your combat speed to max and that fixes the problem.
3.) The game sometimes will hang in combat and get stuck in the hourglass mode ... but you can hit ESC and then click "Quick Combat" and it will simulate the results for you ending the battle. They should patch that problem soon I hope.
Well that about sums it up. If you are a hardcore TBS gamer ... this is for you .... if you are a casual TBS gamer ... move along .... back to RISK for you :)

This is the worst stealth game I have ever played.
Upon starting up the game, you are told that your name is "John 'mad' Doe." You are a freelance stealth operative who works around for the different countries during WW2.  It is then up to you to choose a country to work for and do what you do best, that is sabatoge of enemy bases. After choosing your country, you will be brought to a menu where you are given a briefing on your mission.  Here, you can customize John's loadout, equipment and even choose apropriate camoflauge for the mission.  You are then thrown into a giant open world map, with multiple routes to complete your objective. you are also sometimes given a set of more than capable AI teamates.  This is all very nice and well implemented, it's just to bad that they didn't focus more on the "game" part of this "game"
The amount of controls for this game are absolutely ludicrous.  You will probably end up having to rebind and memorize over 100 different keystrokes just to make the game playable.  After that, you will of course try and move to your objective. However, the developers of this game didn't understand the concept of a "stealth" game.  Any time you try and move john around, you might as well be playing the sound of a b-52 bomber over a boombox at full volume.  It is not remotely possible to sneak around in this game.  On top of this, if you try to turn John around to fast or make to sudden a move, he will fall over to the ground faster than a boombox playing the sounds of a b-52 at full volume being hurled out the back of a b-52.
You might be thinking now "Well if I can't get close to the enemy, I'll just take them out from far away."  That's just the problem.  Every weapon in the game has no silencer. You might as well be firing rockets, dropping bombs or shooting a .50 cal machine gun at them.  Finally, there is also no way to see how visible you are to enemies.  Since the maps or so open, you can literally be seen by an enemy miles away.
Overall this is a poor excuse for a stealth game.  Stay away from it, and instead look at better stealth games like the original thief.

The music is pretty good, even great at times. This is probably the main reason quite some people like this game. This definitely gave the game a boost in my rating of it.
The animation isn't outstanding or anything, I mean, it's pixel-art, but even for pixel-art, this doesn't look good. The protagonist is in the middle of a tile, even during the cutscenes, so when he picks something up or gives something to someone, it looks weird, which is emplified by the fact that it's done right when he picks up his backpack. The transitions from place to place are done in a strange way, sometimes effectively, sometimes it just looks dumb. Its backgrounds are great though, mostly.
It's in the "game" part that this game fails; the "game" to this game is no more than walking from point A to point B and ocationally pressing directions to move the cutscenes along, which was pretty weird and it felt unnatural to do so. The parts where you walked around from point A to point B also just kind of plop you in like "Hey, remember that this is a game? Good. Now roll the next cutscene." It felt especially weird with the arrow keys showing up on screen after every cutscene, even though I had been using my controller for the past half an hour. If this were to be a YouTube short film, I'd say this is good, but it's a game, for which you have to pay 4 dollars (or pounds or euros or whatever), which is a bit expensive for what it is. The game drags on for way too long at times, it gets really boring.
It certainly doesn't help that the times that you do walk around, your movement is very limited and stiff. First of all, you have to use either a controller or the arrow keys, not WASD, which isn't a big problem, but it sucks you can't just change that in the settings. Second of all, you're being taken down a path, and there are invisable walls sprinkled across the place for no good reason I can think of. Third of all, and most importantly, you move from tile to tile. I thought we fixed this like 10 years ago!? Why is this still a thing? You can't go diagonally and you can't input-buffer your directions. This was frustrating to sit through for a person like me.
I don't know why the creators of this game decided not to add any dialog, but I find this to be an unnecessary detail. Like, it's implied that they talk, so why not just add some words and not by unnecessarily cryptic? The images in the speech bubbles were clear as day anyway, so just typing up a sentence wouldn't have made this a less complex work or whatever.
One particular thing that A:♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥me off and B: made my opinion of this game sink even deeper, was
Final thoughts:
Just go watch a playthrough of this on YouTube if you really want to know the story, and there is no more to this than just the story. Markiplier or jacksepticeye probably played this. It's free like that anyway. That's closer to the price this is actually worth.

This game demands that it be taken incredibly seriously from start to finish, and after playing To The Moon, I was willing to give it the benefit of the doubt. But at 60 minutes, this game was 59 too long. There is little to no interaction, the basic storytelling is very confusing (was a character hit? Was the sound effect indicating distress? A physical action that took place?). For a story with no dialog and little interaction, oversignts and problems like that leave you completely at a loss for what to think or take away from it.
The lack of dialogue is a neat idea, but without dialogue, there needs to be some form of interaction. Occasionally the game will grudgingly allow you to transport the character to the next scene or to open a door, but then it's back to absolute tedium. It is buggy as well. I lost progress twice when I accidentally wandered outside of the boundaries of the game's allowed geometry and couldn't get back. The movement was frustrating as well. It is both slow and difficult to control.
I feel bad being so incredibly negative about this game, but what happened?? This is not worth the time to play if it were free. Somewhere buried in this game is a deep and heartfelt message, but it's under too many layers of confusion and tedium for me to dig out.
I really hope that future games are more like To the Moon and less like this one. Hopefully just a minor experiment.

At first coming from reflex, I hated this game with a passion. But after having over 2k hours on reflex over the years, it was time to look for something else. 1st impression, no feel for the bike, couldn't turn, coudln't whip, could barely make any of the jumps. And why is the camera panning sideways in 3rd person? This of all things really screwed me over, this panning of the camera sideways in every turn, made it very easy to run off the track in every turn. I felt limited it what I could do.
Quit and played reflex some more, but the hours were wearing me down. Started playing Encore again when I heard KTM's were released as DLC. This time I gave it an honest try with an open mind, not allowing the sea of negativity to influence my opinion before I gave the game an real try. I would play to get to a point where I could get some clean laps in and start pushing, because this is where racing games come alive, when you are on the gas!
The biggest difference for me between liking and hating this game, (other than the KTM's), was forgetting about 3rd person and playing in 1st person. After I started getting some basic lines down it really felt like Encore was designed to be played in 1st person, not 3rd. The game just felt so much more fluid in this view, much closer to what I've come to expect from an MX vs ATV game. Looked way better and played better as you feel the bike more as you actually have a feel for the front of the bike. 3rd person by comparison feels very, VERY stiff and static.
I came to realize that my initial opinion of the game was compounded by friends saying "don't play this game it sucks." It was also influenced by the fact that the supercorss was different from Reflex, which is what I was used to. When I first started reflex I hated it, why? because it didn't play like unleashed. And reflex turned out to be one of my most played games of all time. Also bear in mind that reviews from early access are not seperated. It was a totally different game back then, and a lot of gripes have been addressed.
The tracks themselves offer a nice variety of content, though I do wish nordic would release the 2016 AMA supercross tracks which are all out there....somewhere. Not as much a fan of some of the outdoor tracks but they do offer a completly different challenge with those flat turns that require a completly different approach to how you attack the track. I do wish SX tracks would get rutted the same amount as outdoors though, Sounds are pretty well done, feels great when you open up the throttle, go though the whoops and rev the bike in the air.
At it's core this still is an MX vs ATV game. Lots of huge lines to be found, still feels great when you land the rythms clean and you put down a fast lap - Physics are pretty much on par with what you would expect with an Mx vs ATV game, not ultra realistic but not over the top arcadey. Feels like there is much more traction than reflex and the clutch will actually give you a decent boost. Unlike reflex, you actually have to use the clutch and brakes in encore, as you can very easily blow the turns. I do wish, however, that manual shifting was a little more refined so that there would be a real benifit to manually working your way though the gears instead of staying in 5th and using the clutch. That said automatic transmission works just as well and is what you would expect from an mx vs atv game without manual shifting. In the end I feel both are on par with eachother.
Preloading can seem over the top in 3rd person as it seem like the bike gets popped up and launched forward, but I find it much more mellow playing in 1st person. In my videos above, I do preload quite a few jumps but you don't see that huge pop up and forward that you see in 3rd person.
At this point, after hating encore for so long, I'm playing it a lot more. (but I still hate it's implemention of 3rd person which I think puts a lot of people off). Its not a perfect game, it still has it quirks and still could benifit from some elbow greese, but what game is perfect?
So if you're thinking of trying this game, ignore the sea of negativity. Stop by my page and check out some of my videos and see for yourself how much fun this game can be. See you on the track racers!

I think this game has gotten more hate than it deserves.
It is too often compared to Reflex, which was a fantastic game.  In terms of realism, I would agree that Reflex is the best game to this day.  However, this game targets a slightly different audience.  The objective here wasn't to have an ultra-realistic game that offers no forgiveness for messing up in a rhythm section.  The goal was to have a supercross game that gave players the sensation of realistic racing, while still allowing newer players to make small mistakes without throwing their entire race away.  There are more supercross tracks than Reflex, and the poor excuse for an upgrading system has been replaced.  The "physics" that everyone complains about are actually pretty good too.
Bottom line:  If you're looking for a new supercross game that takes a certain amount of skill and knowledge about sx, but doesn't have simulator-level difficulty, I think you'll enjoy this game.
Also, for anyone who says it's impossible to do a whip - it's possible; you just have to learn how.

So, I've had a chance to play this game for a couple hours now... or 300, I guess. I do like it a lot, so I feel like I owe the game and the developers my feedback, which might help some people decide that they should get this! (or not, I suppose).
Firstly, it's a turn based strategy game in a fantasy setting. Anyone who's a fan of that genre knows that it can be really difficult to tell a good one from a bad one by looking at screenshots on Steam. As a result, I own the complete collection of bad ones.
I classify this game as good. For me personally, it's probably one of my favorite games, and would be in the shortlist of titles that I might choose from if I were forced to play only one game forever. Other titles in this "shortlist" might be Dominions 3, and Heroes of Might and Magic III. Now that 75% of you have stopped reading this, I can speak specifically to the people who should be reading this.
Eador has a lot in common with those other two games I mentioned. Hiring heroes, outfitting them with gear and troops to roam the map conquering territory, building improvements in your castle, casting "adventure spells" and "combat spells" that you obtained from your buildings or looted scrolls. So many similarities, it captures all of the great things from the other games of this genre, so the decision whether to get this game hinges on what it does differently.
First of all, the scale of the game is enormous. The campaign is the primary game mode. You choose a "shard", which is a piece of a broken world, they are all just floating around in space, and each one has a unique set of properties that will alter the rules of the game on that shard. One shard might have magically infused crystals, making wizardry especially effective, or a desert shard makes it difficult for troops to move across a battlefield, etc. The shards also have a "size" (map size), and a reward for conquering the shard. The rewards are mostly centered around unlocking castle improvements, which will then be available to you in subsequent shards. With the exception of previous shard rewards, nothing carries over between shards, as your "character" is just the immortal calling the shots from above, and he can only pass on what he has learned. The shards all have their own inhabitants and a unique ecosystem. In addition, there will be other immortals, like yourself, on the shard trying to capture it. You capture the shard by conquering the castles of these other immortals. The winning immortal has the shard merge into his master shard, (a collection of all his previously captured shards). You can choose to attack these master shards, where it will be a 1v1 battle between you and the immortal who owns it. If an immortal loses a game on his master shard, he is eliminated from the campaign altogether, and all of his rewards go to the person who defeated him. This is true for you as well, some immortals will attack your master shard, and losing means game over. Also keep in mind that while you are attacking shards, the other immortals are going after them as well. Some shards might get snapped up while you are battling on a different one, so prioritize them if they contain technology that is part of your fundamental strategy.
All the while this is going on, there will be plenty of bantering, wheeling and dealing, smack talking, and good old fashioned back stabbing happening between the immortals. All of them want something from you, want you to hate the people they hate, or try to convert you to whatever their psychopathic vision might be for how the universe should operate. You can take them up on these things, and it can have a dramatic effect on the "storyline" of the game. You can kill them off if you choose, and they will do it to each other from time to time when the universe gets crowded. There are many of them, and more of them will keep springing up along the way, each with their own personality, back story, misguided morals, and gameplay strategies. The choices you make in game will affect their attitude toward you.
It's important to understand the whole shard and immortal concept of the game because this is a big turn off for some people. Conquering a single shard is like playing an entire game from start to finish in any other strategy title, something that can take 1 to 12 hours, depending on the map size. Then you move on to the next shard where all your heroes are level 1 again, and all your phat loot is gone, and your castle has no upgrades again. While 95% of your time will be spent battling on shards, the overall story arc and meaningful strategic decisions will happen outside of them. This is what makes the game feel like it has nearly infinite possibilities and replay value for me, but I've heard others comment that moving from shard to shard feels punishing as you have to keep "starting over". You definitely need to decide which camp you fall in.
The pace of the game is much slower and more nuanced than similar titles. You will be faced with MANY decisions in the game, and their impact is rarely immediate. These will come in the form of random events and encounters, where you will be making moral or monetary choices, which buildings you build will open other building possibilities while closing a bunch of others, and the troops you hire will have their own alignments and synergies. In a game like Heroes of Might and Magic, the outcome of the game might be decided on turn 9, by the guy who built his capital first, or captured the ultimate artifact, and the rest is just cleanup. In Eador, you build momentum. You pay 50 gold for +2 gold a turn, because in 30 turns, you're going to be glad you did. Your strategy is the culmination of all your decisions and how effectively you can align them with a particular end goal. Not to say that nothing significant happens, because it does, but for the most part you're playing from a macroeconomic perspective. This also frustrates some players because it can be hard to tell whether you are doing well, and there are so many choices to make without any clear indicator of what your priorities should be. It also doesn't help that the AI can be pretty brutal at times, so right when you are feeling way out of your element, someone is going to come along and crush you very unceremoniously, leaving you feeling pretty sour. I assure you that after a few shards, you will know what you are doing, and why you got crushed, and all that confusion and frustration will turn into excitement and possibilities.
Heroes and troops are the core of shard conquering, and the best ones require a robust economy to support. Heroes engage in combat just like troops. They also can become very formidable relatively quickly, making lower level troops more like obstacles in a battle between heroes. There are 4 ranks of troops, and it takes a lot of time and resources to obtain higher ranks. Consequently, the combat effectiveness between the ranks is very significant. A dragon, hydra, or phoenix would be a rank 4 unit. These are very powerful, and could easily clean up an entire army low rank troops like swordsmen or clerics. This huge disparity of power is another frequent complaint. Just know that while each troop will have his moment of glory, and play a pivotal role in your advancement, most of them are unlikely to be useful beyond that point in the shard.
The game has a ton of content. After 300 hours, I don't even have half of the achievements, and I'm constantly finding things I've never seen before. In combination with the stunning amount of replay value, this makes for a game that manages to stay fresh.
My only complaints are AI turn times in large maps with many opponents during the late game can be long. Patches have made it better, but it's still irritating sometimes.
It's had a history of bugs. The last patch introduced a pointer error that made it unplayable for me, but a reinstall seems to have alleviated it completely.
A very nice piece of work that does a great job sucking up hours.
Super deep and complex gameplay for the standard turn based strategy genre.
