Hearts of Iron IV is a somewhat flawed but nonetheless engrossing experience. The basic premise revolves around controlling a single nation up to and through WWII. You can be a political behemoth, such as the Soviet Union, Germany, or the United states, or you can be some pipsqueak country like Cuba or Bhutan. You muster your industrial resources and poltical power to create a capable military and shape your alliances. Each country has a "focus tree," a series of political decisions which grant you bonuses as you progress. The major powers all receive unique focus trees that let them recreate certain historical moments (or explore a little alternative history), and the smaller countries receive generic focus trees which grant additional military factories or ways to change your political alignment faster.
The most frequently noted problem with the game is that the AI can be a bit screwy. Germany sometimes implodes by 1941 after using its manpower bashing its head against French defensive lines. Your allies might fritter away their armies by sending them into harsh environments to slowly starve to death. Sometimes, your commanders seem to be doing their very best to get their troops surrounded and annihilated. Obviously, this is a bit obnoxious. Personally, I rarely find it outright frustrtating, though. Historically, WWII had a lot of indefensible choices by military and political leaders. That does nothing to forgive the fact that the AI has problems, but there is a weirdly satisfying authenticity when a country collapses due to poor choices. Every playthrough is a little different, and your mileage may vary when you see the AI shoot itself in the foot, but it can be sort of fun if you want to take it as a counterfactual. You'll either find this mildly annoying, or you'll hate it with a fiery, burning passion. I fall into the first camp.
Regardless of its problems (a few of which see fixes with each new patch), the game is actually fairly fun. A huge number of people play mostly as Germany. A human player who knows what they're doing can use a major nation to kick the rest of the world in the pants, and that can be quite satisfying. However, it's also quite enjoyable to blaze your own path. Want to be a fascist, atom bomb slinging Mexico determined to restore the old borders with the United States? You can do that. Want to be communist Thailand and help the USSR bring the peoples' revolution to Imperial Japan by force? Yeah, sure. You can do that. Want to annex the entire African continent as Liberia? Good luck fighting all the colonial powers, but you can do that.
As of late 2017, the game's DLCs mostly add unique focus trees for some of the medium-sized countries of the world. They're not essential, but they add some flavor if you like forging your own path as a smaller country.

I originally played Blade Kitten Episode 1 on the Playstation and I bought it again here on Steam, along with Episode 2. As a rule I do not play platform games, yet in this case I made and exception as, I have to admit, I'm a fan of giant sword wielding catgirls...
The game is simplistic and easy to get into. They make the gameplay more exciting by giving you the ability to scale walls and ceilings, opening up the possibility for more hidden treasures and motivating you to explore every nook and cranny of every level.
Combat is a bit limited, as 99% of all your fights will be to keep your head down and charge into your enemies wildly mashing the one button. Then you also have long attack, drop attack and slide attack.
The story may seem a bit convoluted as if the writers tried to make up the for lack of depth with complexity.

The player being pushed off the correct plane, dropping you through the world. No dead-zone on the control stick, so you are forced to move in a direction if you want to do a slide (which is mainly a combat move). Annoyances include: Fast stamina usage and slow regen. Run-jumping becomes a long-lump and you lose the ability to double-jump, meaning if you're running and want to do a jump up to a higher level, you will instead shoot off the side. No benefits to collecting collectables besides completionism.
Now, the gameplay itself is fine. Bland, but it works, for the most part. But this is no Strider, and the plot will send you to sleep, only to be woken up by the occasional cringe when the protagonist speaks.

Axiom Verge is a decent Metroidvania if you have that itch that needs to be scratched.  The game is a bit slow to get going, so I may as well address negatives first.
-	Movement initially stiff/not for sequence breaking
It takes a while before you so much as get high jump boots and prior to that, there’s nothing like dashing or means of navigating small spaces, so it feels as if you’re stuck running around a giant maze.  The movement isn’t rigid in the way that Castlevania III is, but there’s not much you can do to adjust your y-axis level for quite some time.  The multitude of walls and barriers subsequently ensure that you’re never in a spot the developer doesn’t want you to be in before you’re supposed to get there.
-	Game feels like it was made in phases
The initial few settings you’re involved in… well, despite the fact that you’re dealing with a formerly inhabited planet gone to semi-ruin, it’s hard to tell what purpose any of the environments served.  Some appear to have functions.  Others do not.  Additionally, the initial music tracks are a bit more chiptuney, culminating in a track in lower Kur with digitized singing that is not only bad, but doesn’t make sense in context of the caves you’re running around at present.
-	Passcode system because passcode system
The game wanted to consciously make the “JUSTIN BAILEY” nod, and well, okay, but the passcodes are not well-integrated other than to get you the capacity to read a few notes in translation/flesh out the lore or later jimmy open a few hidden passages, which you’d have to backtrack to and then seek out to find.  The rewards are worth it, but the reality is that after the game has been out and people have found the locations, it boils down to “find location, punch in code, grab item, forget you have the code system again.”
-	Story exists in fits and starts
This is either a plus or a minus.  Do you really care about a story?  Well, Axiom Verge is really trying to have a story here, with a bunch of potential interdimensional and/or time travel and ethical questions and morally ambiguous characters.  The trouble is that the story is usually used as a denouement in either reading the notes or immediately following a boss battle.  Despite the fact that you have the Ruskali stationed at various intervals throughout the planet and they’re your NPC helpers, you can’t really interact with them and you may go through periods of just poking your head in to see what they’re up to and getting no reaction at all.  Kind of a bummer.  As for the story itself, it’s trying to be deep and convoluted and while it’s nothing too extraordinary, it seems to be well-executed enough, if you’re thinking that specific slip-ups are intentional or could be made to be intentional.
It's a lot to complain about at the outset and I wasn’t initially a fan, but it does get better and more playable.
+ Pretty darned good soundtrack!
“Cellular Skies,” which plays in the overworld portion of Kur, might be one of my favorite tracks I’ve heard in a game in a while and from there, all the new regions have good, atmospheric tacks that are complementary of the overall atmosphere.  In particular, the Edin track, “Phosphene,” is very subdued and fits a backdrop where you can see open plains dotted by bits and pieces of ruined alien architecture.
+ WEEPONS!
Axiom really goes all out with the weapon selection for a shooty game.  If you’re comparing it to Metroid, you may be disappointed by the inability to combine weapons, but most of them have their own utilities and strategies and there are a bunch of them that one could conceivably use regularly during the game, discounting the fact that one is waaaaay better than the others and some, like the Firewall and Reversible Slicer, are unlikely to have any great functionality.
+ Glitch Gun!
It’s a sort of doofy method of changing enemy behaviors and opening up blocked off passages, but the Glitch Gun is pretty fun to use and handles well enough, along with having some interesting results.  I think that it makes the game a bit easy in stretches when you can get enemies to puke up health restoration.  I also don’t really get how you’re causing flora and fauna to trip out by shooting bio-mechanical whatsits at them, but whatever.
+ Drone Travel!
Midway through the game, Trace gets the ability to spit up a wee bitty squid that he can then use to navigate small spaces and fight enemies.  It's a plus over the "how does this work" morph ball of Metroid fame that, in Prime, led to countless space pirates getting mangled in confused attempts to replicate it. Your squid can shoot lasers and fight dudes and as you fill out your upgrades, it's finally possible to teleport to its location and go through silly processes to gain infinite height.  By then, you don't really need infinite height, but I explored one of my last map blocks that way.
+ Secret Worlds!
Remember when you played Metroid for the NES and bombed through some wall only to find yourself in an environment that you couldn’t tell whether you were supposed to continue on to get a prize or if it was even possible to do so.  Axiom Verge generates those on purpose and makes your screen look like a CRT to notify you it’s doing it.  Hot.
I’d say this is probably the second-most enjoyable Metroidvania I’ve played that was made by a single person, after Cave Story, which plays a bit better despite having not much reason to revisit a lot of the territories as you get in Axiom Verge.

I'll be blunt: The grappling absolutely killed this game for me.
I don't like Metroid, but I like Metroidvania-style games. I don't like the environments in Metroid games, and I dislike Metroid's reliance on the whole hey-try-shooting-through-random-blocks-to-find-your-way-into-or-out-of-a-room brand of traversal that's all too common in the series. So, color me surprised when I found myself legitimately enjoying Axiom Verge, despite it relying to some extent on these elements. Things were looking up, and I was engaged.
And then I found the grapple power-up.
Look, there are games that do grappling well. Hell, even Super Metroid did grappling well. I didn't like Super Metroid, but it handled most means of traversal quite well, and this is true of the grappling, as well. That said, I prefer grappling that's more along the lines of what you'd find in Castlevania: Bloodlines or The GG Shinobi II: The Silent Fury.
I absolutely *hate* Bionic Commando-style grappling, and this game uses it in full force. And it feels terrible.
For starters, the grappling in Axiom Verge models itself very closely after the grappling in Bionic Commando, right down to the janky feel and animation (in that it's not smooth at all). It just feels off.
Furthermore, holding left or right when you're swinging will cause you to automatically release yourself from the grapple whenever you swing all the way in that direction...some of the time. Other times, you'll have to press Jump in order to release yourself in that direction, because one stupid block that didn't even affect your swinging trajectory happens to be relatively close to your grapple point. The fact that you can't count on your character to automatically release himself from the grapple when you're simply holding the correct direction really messes up your flow at times.
The worst part about the grappling is that it becomes frustrating almost immediately after you get the ability to grapple. You need to use it to grapple across a ceiling, which requires multiple uses of the grapple in quick succession. Failing results in a really long fall, which results in you having to grapple your way back up a series of platforms that do nothing to prepare you for the aforementioned grappling segment, because they're too damn short to practice the timing on. You can't practice, and the time spent grappling your way back up for another try creates too long of a break between your attempts at getting across the ceiling for the process to be very intuitive. It's really bad.
Once I progressed enough to reach the next save point, I saved the game and uninstalled it. I have zero interest in continuing to play the game, because I know that I'll reach a point at which the grappling just isn't doable for me, given my discomfort with the grappling mechanics in general. I can deal with grappling in some other games, but there's just too much of a disconnect for me when the mechanics mimic those of Bionic Commando so closely.
If you like Metroid games and Bionic Commando, then you'll probably enjoy the game. If you can't get past elements of either of those two games, though, then steer clear.

Beautiful environmental design and music, set an incredible atmosphere in every unique area of the game. Level designs felt fresh and intuitive, rarely caused a sense of being directionless, and had many 'visual leads' that hinted at uses for later upgrades.
Puzzles were clever and made intuitive use of the game's unique mechanics, though some lategame puzzles were almost too obscure to be solved through anything but serendipity. (Often involving the use of the Address Disruptor on enemies, which sometimes have less-than-obvious effects while glitched.)
Tools and upgrades offered a decidedly cerebral approach to Metroid-like platforming while avoiding the common power spike that renders later challenges pointless. However, I got the impression that the endgame was lacking at least one more upgrade to mobility to aid in backtracking, such as a Speed Booster. (There were many long, straight hallways I was expecting to be used with one.)
Weapon variety was impressive, but the majority of the choices lacked a niche or purpose, or were completely outmoded by even some of the earlygame options. It would have been interesting to see more weapon-specific puzzles as were demonstrated in the first area of the game, or at least retooling the selections to have slightly fewer weapons with more useful applications.
Bosses often felt either underwhelming or frustrating, as most of them had a simplistic pattern with an unusual hitbox and loads of health. There was one boss (Gir-Tab) where the hitbox was placed behind the enemy entirely, while the front was completely invulnerable to shots. The only weapons I had that could reach that far were the Nova, which felt woefully underpowered, and the Voranj, which could only randomly hit that area. The sheer amount of shots it took to take down the boss was frustrating, and I'd died at least 14 times before then thanks to the discrepancy in firepower at that point in the game.
The writing definitely kept me hooked, and I was pleasantly surprised to find that it made up for what initially seemed to be an unfitting protagonist in an alien world. The foreboding hints at Athetos' history and the enigmatic nature of the Rusalki did leave me wanting more character development, or perhaps even an alternate ending considering there were some optional fights / interactions at key points in the game.
Overall, Axiom Verge is a wonderful take on the fairly small non-linear platforming genre that had me constantly going back to play more with few little nags. The game bleeds passion and attention to detail, especially in the lavish SNES-style spritework that paves every part of the game as a harrowing, but beautiful alien world. I'm finding myself wishing for a continuation already.

I'm glad I took a chance and bought this (on sale), despite all of the negative reviews.  Basically, it feels like mx vs atv supercross on the 360/ps3, except they cleaned up the handling a bit (feels like I have some traction now) and threw in the motocross tracks from alive.  I love reflex, but the 90mph tracks and doing a forward or back flip off of a tuff block at 10-20mph really got old.  This game has some quirks for sure, but I'm enjoying it.  For example, as with the console version, there are rare phantom inputs that will steer me off course, or throw my rider way forward off a jump.  Also, I can really feel the loss of forward speed (like crazy wind resistance) in the air.  On the other hand, though, I like the tighter tracks (especially the outdoor tracks from alive), the fact that I actually need the brakes, and the handling in the turns.  The clutch is crazy op as others say, but I like that I can goof a turn and make up for it with that.
As for the graphics, maybe some people are reviewing the game without launching the graphics settings program first (a seperate thing for some reason, just like reflex)?  I played at 4k and other than the inconsistent framerate and some lod popping, it looked just as good as reflex to me (even better in some places where texture resolution is higher and meshes have more detail).  I think rainbow/nordic REALLY need to force the settings program to launch before the first play, because the default settings look terrible, and leave a bad first impression.
As a fan of the series since the first motocross madness, I would have preferred that rainbow just tighten up the tracks and ease up on the crash-if-someone-nudges-me physics in reflex to make a follow-up game (instead of completely changing the engine for alive/supercross), but I'm definitely not in agreement with the chorus of bad reviews this game is getting.  Get it on sale if you have some doubts, but don't even launch the game without changing the graphics settings first (unless you want to get a laugh or something).

Grave Prosperity and I have an... interesting history, to say the least. Back at the last site I worked for (VGU.TV), I was given the opportunity to review the original form of this game given my history with streaming horror games, and presumably because I was the new guy and no one else wanted it. So I accepted, and... let's just say it wasn't great. Clumsy combat, awkward controls, unforgiving enemies, brutal bosses, and basically anything else you could think of to infuriate a player was present.
But this is the "Redux" up here on Steam, so let's not dwell too much on the past. I was genuinely surprised a new version had emerged at all, so I decided to give it a shot out of morbid curiosity. And, in fairness, things improved... slightly. I'm sorry I'm using so many ellipses in this. Anyway, a lot of fat had been trimmed from the game's initial version. Shorter intro, with some of the more ridiculous bits (like suriviving a sledgehammer to the head) cut out. Things felt a bit more navigable, and finding your way around wasn't quite as much a chore. At the same time, combat felt even more frustrating and impossible, and those ridiculous death animations still felt excessive and repetitive, especially given how often the game likes to kill you off.
I've never been a fan of the visuals, either; the enemies, whatever they are, mostly feel like generic "mutants" or "zombies" with no real appeal, and our heroine looks like a commission job from a Poser or Blender fetish artist on DeviantArt. Not feeling it. Despite all this, I made it to the end of the Redux version, which stops a great deal sooner than the first iteration. I'm guessing things are going to be more episodic this time around, between that and the "Part 1" designation. At least it didn't end on an impossible boss battle this time.
Despite my multiple fronts of frustration with Grave Prosperity, I give the developer some credit for stubbornness in sticking to its baby. Clearly, they believe in this property, and want to find a way to make it work. Whether it can, I can't say, but hopefully they at least take some lessons away from this and apply this to a different game or find a new format to tell the tale they want to.
As the game stands right now, I can't recommend it. I'm curious what the "major update" in the game's description will bring, so I may give it one more chance once that's done and released. If so, I'll update and amend this review accordingly. But in its current state? Nope.

Initially, Hatoful Boyfriend struck me as a purely comedic otome game. Like many who chose to play it, I decided to go through it for kicks. Eventually, I learned that it is not what it seems at all. The more I progressed through the game the more immersed I became in it. I forgot all about the fact that it was meant to be a dating simulator where you court birds. I learned that it possesses all the trappings of classic visual novels. It is rife with plot twists and angst. The story is surprisingly deep, something I found to be a relief. As you go through the routes you obtain more and more pieces of the proverbial puzzle. They fit together pretty nicely at the end. I was glad to know that it is more than just some silly thing.
Although it has many elements and troupes that are common in such games it presented them in a unique way, I think. However, my taste for it was admittedly acquired. After having went through a route in its entirety I became bored of many of the jokes and scenarios which had been scattered throughout it. For a time it was a bit of a chore to go through. Thankfully, the skip button helps you rush through the things you have already read, cutting out unnecessary game-time. You definitely need to be patient when going through Hatoful Boyfriend. I personally feel that in order to get the most enjoyment out of it you should go through one route at a time. That way you will have plenty of time to reflect on what happened as well as keep your interest in the plot fresh.
PROS:
> Overall, Hatoful Boyfriend is short and sweet. A basic route can be finished in an hour even if you are a slow reader. This makes it a great thing to play before going to bed or when you just need to kill some time for a while.
> The art is soft, and the scenery colorful, making the backdrops pleasant. It is simple, but is still able to add to the mood.
> While many of the characters and their stories are tried-and-true they are still ones you can get attached to (for the most part, anyway).
> There is more than one unlockable route.
> The story becomes more advanced as you progress through the game.
CONS:
> The protagonist is simple and impressionable.
> During the main routes you do not get a lot of route-exclusive content. A lot of the scenarios are the ones you go through during the main story, so you end up having to read through much of what you already have.
> The running gags get old fast.
> You are unable to save at decision screens and must do so just before you are about to make a choice.
> There are very few CGs.
> Sometimes your saves will bring you to a backdrop and you cannot do anything at all so you have to exit and re-open the game (save your game in multiple slots just in case!).
All in all, I think that Hatoful Boyfriend is enjoyable. I feel that it rewards you well for your diligence. The final, true story that is Hatoful Boyfriend is great. I absolutely love the BBL ending, and think that it was worth all the time I spent working to get it. I believe that it is a fairly solid purchase.

Ugly, alien aesthetic with an overall well-hidden but slightly covoluted narrative, and extremely familiar gameplay to anyone with any Metroidvania experience (especially the former half of the term). Varied and unique forms of movement allow for interesting platforming, and every weapon you find has a given niche that it works best in. Not quite as perfect as the codifiers of the genre (ie Super Metroid), but a well-done addition nonetheless.

the most metroid game since metroid
(also the best since zero mission)

Beautiful environmental design and music, set an incredible atmosphere in every unique area of the game. Level designs felt fresh and intuitive, rarely caused a sense of being directionless, and had many 'visual leads' that hinted at uses for later upgrades.
Puzzles were clever and made intuitive use of the game's unique mechanics, though some lategame puzzles were almost too obscure to be solved through anything but serendipity. (Often involving the use of the Address Disruptor on enemies, which sometimes have less-than-obvious effects while glitched.)
Tools and upgrades offered a decidedly cerebral approach to Metroid-like platforming while avoiding the common power spike that renders later challenges pointless. However, I got the impression that the endgame was lacking at least one more upgrade to mobility to aid in backtracking, such as a Speed Booster. (There were many long, straight hallways I was expecting to be used with one.)
Weapon variety was impressive, but the majority of the choices lacked a niche or purpose, or were completely outmoded by even some of the earlygame options. It would have been interesting to see more weapon-specific puzzles as were demonstrated in the first area of the game, or at least retooling the selections to have slightly fewer weapons with more useful applications.
Bosses often felt either underwhelming or frustrating, as most of them had a simplistic pattern with an unusual hitbox and loads of health. There was one boss (Gir-Tab) where the hitbox was placed behind the enemy entirely, while the front was completely invulnerable to shots. The only weapons I had that could reach that far were the Nova, which felt woefully underpowered, and the Voranj, which could only randomly hit that area. The sheer amount of shots it took to take down the boss was frustrating, and I'd died at least 14 times before then thanks to the discrepancy in firepower at that point in the game.
The writing definitely kept me hooked, and I was pleasantly surprised to find that it made up for what initially seemed to be an unfitting protagonist in an alien world. The foreboding hints at Athetos' history and the enigmatic nature of the Rusalki did leave me wanting more character development, or perhaps even an alternate ending considering there were some optional fights / interactions at key points in the game.
Overall, Axiom Verge is a wonderful take on the fairly small non-linear platforming genre that had me constantly going back to play more with few little nags. The game bleeds passion and attention to detail, especially in the lavish SNES-style spritework that paves every part of the game as a harrowing, but beautiful alien world. I'm finding myself wishing for a continuation already.

Yes it's a good game, but I wouldn't call it perfect.
The artwork is really good and gameplay is smooth and enjoyable. There's also a lot that's fresh and original aboutit, despite being a retro platformer firmly rooted in a lot of older gaming traditions. The music (while I couldn't really get into most apart from one track) is distinctive and well written, and there are a lot of powerups and mechanics that give an interesting dimension to the gameplay that are rarely seen in other games.
However, this is a two-edged sword. There is a bewildering number of weapons to find, each with it's own well thought out mechanic, but unfortunately most of them are entirely useless.
Another thing that is worth pointing out is the story. It seems a lot of people praise this game for that aspect, but I really don't think it's a strong point of the game. Yes, it has its share of reveals and little twists, but so do M Night Shyamalan movies and they are still mostly horrible.
I just didn't find myself investing in it at all, and for all its bluster about alternate dimensions and technology and the nature of reality (which already wasn't new when the Matrix did it 17 years ago), it really doesn't have anything interesting to say. Now, I don't think the quality of a game necessarily rests on the story (there have been plenty of good games without good stories), but don't automatically buy in to the idea that this game has a particularly good one.
My last minor gripe is that I think the game is just a shade too long for the first play-through. Granted, I took my time and tried to find as many secrets and powerups as I could, but at 16 hours I found myself wishing it would just be over for about the last quarter of it.
But still, overall I recommend this game. It's expertly crafted and rich, especially for a single dev, and it's one of the best realizations of a Metroidvania I've seen.

So for someone who comes from the background of playing racing titles mainly made by Codemasters, & Milestone I didn't expect much for this game.
Was I right? Simply put, no.
This game from what it seems is a Remastered Edition of MX vs. ATV Supercross converted to run on Higher End Systems, or just to bring the game to life with a few nifty updates. That, said, this is my first visit with these titles and I'm pleasantly surprised by the game.
It definitely fits into a niche crowd with people who just adore arcade style racers, people who wanna blow off time, and for others who are simply looking for an offroad game.
It provides, with things like the ever so beloved AI who can never seem to decide what part of the track they wanna take, let alone if they want to be in a straight line they'd rather scope out their own trail for the course.
It also maintains itself with an interesting take on outdoors style tracks, something the original version of the game didn't contain.
It truly lets you filter your adventuring.
Mixed racing, & other sorts to provide you with different style challenges, and learning to share a track with a quad-biker who just wants to try and cut your line off every time you catch him with his pants down.
I personally jumped into this game wanting a different experience, and telling myself I'd never actually lay hands on this game.
I EAT MY WORDS BIG TIME.
I was in search of a game that gave me mixed racing, and just an over all fun time, nothing to be taken seriously.
I can slightly copare this game to its younger brother MX vs. ATV Reflex as I bought it and played them side by side just to have more games to jump along and play.
I will say the two handle nothing at all like each other, and if you want to grab it just be expecting a more light feeling bike, and looser ATV's that seem to get stuck in one direction when riding through the carved patterns of someone elses bike. Besides that, it doesn't get itself too lost and feels slightly like the MXGP Bikes, both ATV, & MX.
Tricks, tracks, jumps, whips, all included. You won't be let down.
I really do recommend this game, but I'll add that it is choppy even for higher running rigs, mine being a computer that sits in the middle of every OP machine.

There's no doubt this game is rough around the edges, but under the surface lies strange, wonderful things. I'm trying to keep spoilers to a minimum for this, but there's gonna be some.
This game is about dating fictional birds. Fictional. Birds. The setting may be ridiculous and silly, and the game
ridiculous and silly, but it has a surprising amount of depth. Being a new student at St. Pidgeonation's high school, you have the option of dating a total of 9 birds. The first few routes (Ryouta, Sakuya, Nageki, etc.) are fairly easy to complete and find, but there are a few well hidden ones that grant a deeper (or more silly) look at the world that Mediatronic and co. built.
Speaking of the world, it has very little consistency. While the majority of it is explained away in
and
the story just doesn't hold for a lot of what we see. That is kind of expected - it isn't easy or even necessary to build a wholly consistent world for what is a mostly comedic game. But, strangely, there is a surprising amount of lore that is explained throughout the game, especially in the de-facto true ending.
That lore involves a rollercoaster of emotions. What is essentially a comedic game devolves into a tragedy by the end, if you're willing to stick through it. Mind you, good luck keeping that will. Some parts do drag on for too long (which is very annoying in a visual novel) and the bright and happy UI impairs the immersion when the situation is dire. If you like your story with twists, though, this game will not dissapoint. Just be prepared to sit through a few hours of glorious bird dating first. On the other hand, if you only want to date those birds, don't pick to complete the promise when you get the chance. It's a major change in tone and there's really no bird dating involved in that route.
Gameplay-wise, it's a visual novel with RPG elements. While the RPG elements are only useful in a couple of routes, they are important to getting some of the good endings for some characters as well as finishing them altogether. I suggest using a guide because things can get messy very quickly and you WILL miss some routes without one. The visual novel aspect, on the other hand... it's a ren'py game, and it is hard to say much beyond that. There are some minor bugs here and there, but they aren't game breaking.
It's a solid visual novel / dating sim with a surprising amount of depth and plot on the inside. As a bird dating sim, it's a 7/10. With all the twists and world involved, I'm willing to give it an 8 for the effort, even if it isn't executed perfectly.

What really gets me about this game isn't the whole thing about dating birds, but that this game is incredibly dark once you get underneath the cute otome surface. It's those hints of darkness in the setting's recent past that keep me playing even through the less appealing parts (some cheesiness, predictable angst, and Okosan... ugh, I do not like San.)
One thing I appreciate is that Hatoful Boyfriend doesn't try to convince you that characters that are unlikable and/or creepy ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s are appealing love interests. You pursue them for the sake of game completion, knowing full well that your character's getting into something unappealing and possibly even dangerous. In some cases you might be surprised at what you find out. So you keep doing it anyway.
I've played otome where you're wooing some misogynistic jerk or antisocial personality, and you're supposed to believe you'd actually willingly fall for that for the off chance he might turn out having some redeemable quality or sympathetic sob story. I can't stand that.
I like Hatoful Boyfriend--but keep in mind, the only other otome I've played that I liked was Idea Factory's Hakuoki, a game based on Japan's Meiji era where the members of the Shinsengumi basically become vampires to avoid their historical deaths. And yes, you romance them. It's glorious!
Played all 14 routes to unlock the final ending. 10/10 completely worth it even if it took me a few hours. Probably one of the best short visual novels I ever played. Totally recommended!

It's also interesting and well thought out how you can actually see hints of the true story if you go back to replay the game and pay careful attention to the dialogue during the normal routes.

Normally I have a "dollar per hour" rule of thumb but for this game I'll give it a pass. Why? Well, the developer.
It's plain to see, looking at the updates and just the attention to detail within the game itself, that this developer is doing their best to provide as best a gameplay experiance as possible.
The voice acting is solid.
The combat, though clunky, clearly had thought put into it with dodge moves, attack chains, counter attacks, etc.
And then there's the little things. Like the custom death animations for evey enemy based on where you are and how they killed you. Though guesome, it's things like that that go a long way to giving heart to the game.
Only real complaints I have is that the combat feels clunky, and buggy. (making playing this game on any difficulty higher than easy an exercize in masochism) The perspective can get annoying. And even though they're only asking 2 bucks for it, an hour an a half for a game is still pretty short...
However over all I don't regret playing it. And I'm eager to see more. What can I say, this developer has peaked my curiosity with their 2D silent hill.
So taking all that into account I'd have to give this game my recommendation. Although certainly not for everyone this game has had enough heart and effort put into it to earn this developer some recognition. And I look forward to seeing more from them in the future.

I think girls dressed up as cats are hot... There. I said it.
(Bonus points for the additional gothic dress for our cat girl heroine. Me-ow!)
Blade Kitten is a 2.5D, action-platforming game starring Kit Ballard, a cat girl (in an optional gothic dress) who controls a levitating AI sword and is followed around by some weird flying pet... thing, as she does battle against various factions out to get her while she tries to reclaim a data stick stolen from her and get payback for her destroyed ship. Or something. The whole story is a bit of a mess. There's very little real explanation for who anyone is or how they're all connected or ultimately what's going on. The story and apparent goal seems to shift dramatically from one level to the next with little real sense of focus for anything, just a vague over-arcing narrative that's sporadically dropped then brought up again at whim.
I presumed there was more to this than meets the eye and, indeed, found the game to be based on a web comic of the same name. It looks like it's been going for quite a while, but despite an intensive Google search for what must have been at least a good minute and a half, if not two whole minutes, I still couldn't really find out much about the material it's based on. The lack of explanation (aside from a brief in-game glossary) would suggest it's aimed at established fans, but if it's as obscure as it appears to be then that's a huge misstep and is essentially shooting itself in the foot from the start. The story elements aren't offensively bad or anything, and I guess you'll get the basic gist, but I just wish it would've kept its attention on one thing rather than feeling like it was cramming in every feature of its universe to appease fans who the developers probably thought would be annoyed if their favourite parts weren't included. The mostly useless pet, Skiffy, being a pretty glaringly obvious example of something from the lore being shoehorned into some kind of role in the game.
But despite the way it was presented, I did still really like the universe that we're shown (and the gorgeous art style in particular) and would be happy to learn more about it. I want to know more about this flying, AI sword, dammit! The lead is very well written and acted, and I never felt like the game was talking down to the player and treating us like idiots. In fact, the game, and Kit herself, come across as somewhat self-aware without ever breaking the fourth wall, and as a result feels far more inclusive and engaging. But as for the supporting cast? Mmm, not quite so much. They're more standard, video game fare.
The actual gameplay is far more successful, though. You'll run, leap and hack your way through 13 stages, searching for secrets, unlocking costumes and buying new swords and upgrades. But the main appeal of the game comes from Kit's agility and dexterity, as she sticks to just about every surface to climb along walls and ceilings, opening up huge potential for exploration. That's something that might actually throw some players, in fact. Most platformers are about running a gauntlet as you overcome obstacles of one kind or another to reach the finish. But in this one you'll spend far more time roaming the occasionally labyrinthine stages, sometimes wondering whether the path you've taken is where you're supposed to be going, or if you're unwittingly making your way towards the dead end with the collectibles. But once you know your way around and how to best deal with enemies (jump over them, innit), most of the stages can be speed run in around about five minutes.
When you are engaging in combat, you'll probably have a little less fun than when you're running around. There aren't a great deal of enemy types, and the majority of them will be dealt with in largely the same manner; either rush up to them with a flurry of light, but fast slashes, or send your floating sword off to deal heavy, ranged strikes. You can also jump on some enemies and toss them around, or do a jumping ground stomp attack for crowd control, but from moment to moment, you'll mostly just be cutting up the waves of fodder then running along. It's pretty trivial stuff for most of the game, thanks largely to your regenerating health as well. But, to be honest, I'd rather them be easy than have them kill the pace and become tedious roadblocks every time they're encountered. Also, the controls aren't quite tight enough for anything too challenging, either. Most of the time they're fine (I played it entirely with a game pad), but every so often it felt unresponsive and I'd suffer because of it. Was never too major, but enough to be a noticeable annoyance.
So, it's not perfect. The story is muddled, the combat and enemies are kinda uninspired and some more moves or combos would've been nice, the levels can sometimes confound, and the controls could be improved. But even so, I did still really enjoy this one and felt the fun and easy-going positives far outweighed the negatives. Especially the price. It's kind of a steal how much game you're getting for so little. So if you like platforming, exploring and cat girls in gothic dresses, then this has your name writing all over it. Well... at least if your name is Blade Kitten. Though I'm guessing it probably isn't, is it?

I have a love hate relationship with this game, and now that it RANDOMLY became F2P i've decided that I state my opinions on this game. If you don't know, Brink was a highly anticipated game back in 2011 that was developed by splash damage. The people behind Wolfenstein Enemy Territory, Enemy Territory: Quake Wars, and the most popular and quite successful Dirty Bomb. There are two factions you can play as right when you start it up and have two seperate campaigns but honestly they're not that different from each other. The maps are the same for both campaigns so if you finish one, you've already played all of the maps. The differences are how the faction looks, what weapons they use, and different objectives compared to the opposite faction. The parkour while a little clunky is an idea that has a lot of potential and is fun to mess around with. Now easily the WORST part of this game is the AI when you are playing the campaign by yourself. IT'S STRAIGHT UP AWFUL. You will get extremely frustruated with the godawful AI on your team since they rarely never do the main objectives or help you at all. To make it even worse, the enemy AI always knows what they're doing and cooperate with each other, so playing the campaign singleplayer is like a 1V8 for all the missions. A perfect example is Security day 6. I honestly think that mission is straight up IMPOSSIBLE by yourself. I only remember beating it ONCE a long time ago. It's just random if you will win or lose, the second half of that mission makes you play the weakest class in the game like I said earlier with the awful AI on your team and you'll have to fight off against 8 other bots. If you are trying to beat the campaign, NEVER PLAY IT BY YOURSELF. I recommend having a few friends to finish it especially now that it's free. Now I know it looks like I hate this game, but I don't. Playing this game with other people and friends is actually a great time and you won't have to worry about all your friends buying it now so you can all play. The customization with how your classes and guns look and the overall weaponry plus with the game being F2P and having a much larger player count at least for a while. I recommend playing it right now because of the peak in players and how much fun you can have with friends.

When I first saw this game I knew it was going to be a blast. Who doesn't want to pillage islands and destroy enemy pirate ships?
Starting the game I took the time to design a pirate and give him a name. Then I selected a back story for him. I was on the right track! After about 15 minutes of playing I realized that my character I took the time to customize had died, and was replaced with a new captain! I thought this was odd, but decided to keep playing. Maybe it wouldn't affect the story. I mean, I can get over the trivial loss of my new favorite character and learn to love his replacement that I hired from a tavern.
After about 4 hours of pillaging and ship fights I decided it was time to get to business and get more involved in the story. I needed to find my objectives. It was then that I realized that there is no story. No quests. Not objectives, aside from achievements. It really sucked, but I decided that I bought the game and have already wasted about 4 hours playing. Why not finish?
I began recruiting crew members. Trained them. Leveled them. I made my way to the first legendary boss. Sure, things got rough, but I managed to pull through. The ship battles got even better when I figured out how to work cannons. I could take down an enemy ship before they even had a chance to board! I was untouchable! When I got to the first legendary pirate boss I was excited. Then I realized that this legendary pirate didn't have a single cannon on his ship. None. I was able to destroy him and his ship before the boarding phase of combat. It was a total letdown. Not only that, he and his crew had fewer hit points than other pirates I'd already faced. Not much of a legendary pirate if you ask me.
It didn't take long before I stopped visiting islands and just headed straight for the other legendary pirates. It was a wholly underwhelming experience.
The laundry list of bugs and design flaws were also more than a minor pain.
• Poop gets stuck inside the ship. It manages to get stuck BETWEEN the blocks of hull, making it impossible for your crew to clean. You also can't remove blocks around poop, so it has to stay there until you take the time to clear out your entire ship build and start from scratch. But then it just happens again 15 minutes later.
• If you are sailing to an area and cross paths with an enemy pirate you can choose to fight or flee. If you flee successfully you don't continue your trip, but instead have to open the map again and select your destination. This makes travelling long distances very annoying.
• If a crew member gets stuck while trying to perform a task (like picking up poop or loading a cannon) no other crew member will attempt the same task. Now you're down a crew member until you notice and tell him to move somewhere.
• Trying to make a pirate flee is near impossible. If you tell him to run away and he is hit, he will target whatever hit him and attack. This results in you trying to get him to run by constantly clicking, but he just ends up dying.
• The controls are inconsistent. In some screens you have to use the keyboard to pan the view. In others only the mouse can be used. You also can't use the mouse wheel to scroll through lists of items, and clicking an item will take you back to the top of the list.
• Crew frequently have trouble targeting enemies. You can send your entire crew down to attack some enemies, but once they kill the enemy half of them will stand around doing nothing until you give them a new target.
• Pirates must be part of your "Ship Crew" group to get them to clean or repair the ship, even if they're idle with nothing else to do.
• Vertical panning of the camera has been disabled. You can build your ship very tall, but you won't be able to scroll up to see it.
• Some sounds come from the wrong stereo channel. For example, a crew member can be training on the ship on the left side of the screen, but the sound effects will come from the right speaker. If you scroll far enough to the right it will eventually move to the left speaker.
• Massive frame drops when you build a large ship. There were times I went from 200 FPS down to about 3 while trying to build my ship.
• Pets don't seem to have any real benefit, and because the captain is the only one that can carry them they are too cumbersome to be used in a fight.
• The crew needs to poop CONSTANTLY. They always end up piled up around the toilets and food. The ship will be a ghost town except in the bathroom, where you will find 30 guys in about 5 blocks of space. They will even stop fighting to run to the bathroom if they're on the ship.

If you've played games like Metroid or Castlevania: Symphony of the night, you'll be instantly familiar with this game, because it follows the same exact formula. As you explore the world you find health and damage powerups to make your life easier and also unlock new guns and abilities. which grant you access to the next area. There are a ton of weapons, some more practical than others, some better against certain types of enemies. Interestingly most of the bosses I've encountered so far (with the exception of one) can be beaten by your basic gun.
You'll also make use of all of your abilities to find secrets, which range from a basic notes detailing the world to hidden powerups and weapons. They usually aren't too hard to spot, but there are some, which are quite tricky. But because the secrets are tied to certain game mechanic also means you'll have to do a lot of backtracking in order to find everything. There is no fast travel of any description, which is a little annoying. But then again, this is completely optional.
The bosses are giant hunks of biomass and steel, which all have clear pattern you can take advantage off. The only "problem" with that is that they generally get faster as they take damage, which turns every encounter into an intense battle. While the boss encounters can be hard, they're never unfair, in fact they're quite the opposite. Not to mention the music is so good, that I didn't care I died, it simply meant I coul listen to it a little bit longer.
While Axiom Verge borrows from other games (Contra, Metroid, Castlevania, Bionic Commando, etc.), it also has it's own original ideas. The ability to "glitch" the enemies, effectively crippling them, or turning them into floating platforms/ health generators is unique, fun and incredibly useful.
, I have to say, this is the most inovative game mechanic I've seen in years.
This game is also quite heavily story driven for a metroidvania game, if you're into sci-fi, you'll enjoy it. And if you're here only for the gameplay, you'll enjoy it as well.
There is also built-in speedrun mode, which is just that. It bypasses all the custcenes and slaps a timer on the screen.
So far I haven't encountered any bugs, so good job there. One ability could use some little tweaking though. Later in the game you'll acquire the abiliy to dash through thin walls using the D-pad or the left stick. I use the left stick for movement and I've noticed that sometimes Trace dashes on his own while I'm moving the stick. Normally it's only supposed to happen if you rock the stick twice in the direction you want to go, but I swear it happened when I simply touched it. I hope it makes at least a little bit of sense, explaining controls is always the hardest part.
In conclusion, this game is incredible especially if you consider the fact that it's a single person project. That's all I have to say.

Devs went Early Access with their game much too early, because they desperately needed the money. There was, and still is, very little content and the gameplay becomes repetitive pretty soon. It's only really interesting for hardcore gamers that make a sport of improving their skills to the limit. And the game is heavily skill-based and definitely not recommended to casual gamers.
The team has consisted exclusively of amateurs from the start, who started out making the crpg-mod for mount & blade. If you think progress on the game is slow, you should know that it has been developed for at least 4 years even before EA - that's how slow it is. In my opinion, it's likely that the game will be abandoned before even half the promises have been realised. There are trailers on their youtube channel from years ago, which will give you a completely wrong impression of how finished the game is. Basically, nothing you see there is actually in the game.
The "epic", an overhyped (mostly by the devs themselves) board game type of meta game, that is supposed to add context and persistency to the melee fighting, is being delayed time after time. It was initially announced to be released one week after EA release. Many "soons" and months later, there is just silence now. Many initial buyers purchased the game believing that it would be an open world RPG. It's not. Maybe in 5 years from now, if you want to believe. Devs didn't do much to resolve this misunderstanding and many people kept playing with the expectation that "the epic" (which was supposed to release in a matter of days) would be that promised open world. And I'm assuming you are familiar with Steam's refund policy...
The first major patch also took months to release, and whatever balance in respect to combat mechanics there was before is mostly broken now. It also introduced voting for kicks, bans and muting, which are often abused by players.
The combat can be fun, but it is basically just a copy of mount & blade's combat system with twice or more the number of attack/block directions. This leads to missing the right direction more often than not, unless you practice 10 hours a day, and you will often swing at your enemy when you wanted to stab etc.
The "roleplaying" elements are an important part of the game as it is advertised, but the devs somehow refuse to decide on how much progression they want. They don't want to scare away new players, but they are probably also aware that without "grinding" even the ~50 players that regularly play the game will soon be gone as well, if progression just stops after a relatively short time, as it is now. They said they would try hard not to "wipe progress" after patches and wiped everything clean after the first major patch...
The game was supposed to feature battles of 100 vs 100 players. In reality there are rarely enough players for a 10 vs 10 battle most of the time.
I guess there is a chance that this game will be decent in a few years, but I wouldn't bet on it. The way I see it, players are basically a necessary evil to the devs at this point. They needed money. They got it. Now they need lots of time to make their game. And it's almost like they don't want any further publicity until they have, which is understandable somehow - negative reviews speak for themselves.
If you are undecided, come back for the final release in 2017 ^^

This review will first start with the pros and cons, before we then get into details. I strongly advice you to read this despite the low price of the game.
+ Good animations despite low budget
+ Good voice acting for the protagonist
+ Very good dark industrial/ambient and orchestral score
+ Several areas has their own death-scene
+ Good cutscene cinematography!
+ You'll feel sorry for protagonist's death...... because she wears glasses
+ Challenging combat gameplay
+ Game controls similaire to a Japanese PC port
- Game controls similaire to a Japanese PC port
- Extremely low quality backgrounds
- No key remapping?
- Think i noticed a Husk model from Mass Effect......ehm, copyright???
REVIEW:
Clearly rendered in DAZ 3D, this challenging platformer action-horror game takes place in a Silent Hill like town called Prosperity, and just like the protagonist says "ironyyyyy". Upon exploring a hotel in the town, the world turns into a hellish version where monsters pop out. The starting seconds are very stylish. First i expected it to be a quirky slick Japanese game with bad quality for the sake of humour, wich i would definately have supported.......if it was the intention. The protagonist is very well voice casted, wich just like the soundtrack, wich sounds like Diego Stocco's score for Chernobyl Diaries, came surprising as the visual quality was low.
Unfortunately the game had so many flaws wich prevented me from living into the game and fully enjoy it. First of all,
our heroine can only be seen from two angles even when you can move upward and downwards, this is seen as sloppy work and it looks weird when she is sidestepping in and out of the image. The backgrounds for this game is the biggest flaw i think. The backgrounds are clearly 3D at core, but they have been inserted as 2D image files and given a corny unclear look. This collides with the clear and solid look of the 3D models. The proportions of the background objects such as doors also collides, with some doors for instance being three times bigger than the models. Who lived in this town, descendants of Goliath? This is absolutely not needed, the game would have worked fine with 3D backgrounds!
I also happened to become disoriented because of this. However the inventory display is stylish and well composed.
When entering combat, things helped ease up the pain a bit. It was fast, furious (still platformer though) and challening. It also grants you Experience Points you'll going to use to upgrade your character. And yes you will be able to sprint later in the game. I also noticed something absolutely amazing imo, wich completely came surprising since i was so disappointed with the overall. Several areas had its own death scene! These cutscenes have not very good, but solid cinematography, who the hell are these guys?!
It was sad to see this cute woman with glasses die though :<
However, i also often experienced enemies not following me over to the next screen
(image changes when reaching end of one platform), wich was......weird. Oh well, good for my health i guess!
This would have been a beautiful game if the backgrounds and controls were much more better and comfortable and
if the combat design would have been a little bit more stabile. Many of the pros i have given does not really affect the gameplay and the gameplay is what separates a game from a movie.
It's extremely hard for me to not recommend this. I wouldnt feel comfy with recommending it, but it has a
solid potential. This game, deserves a remake or a fully 3D remake with over-the-shoulder camera.
I would love a open-world horror game with the Dark Souls difficulty!

I don't quite remember how I got Blade Kitten. Was it in one of the bundles I bought? Or did I buy it specifically because of the name (yes, I am that easy)? I have no idea. But no matter how I got the game, I'm glad I did.
While the story is quite simple (and not all that interesting, to be honest), the game has a lot of charm. The quirky protagonist can be funny at times, the levels are visually interesting and just plain pretty and the movement, ooh the movement.
I really like when a protagonist can move easily through levels and doesn't get stumped by the smallest walls or drops. ("Oh no, a hedge, I can't possibly LIFT MY LEG OVER IT, can I?") Blade Kitten is right up my alley. Kitty moves swiftly and with ease, climbing sheer clifs and overhangs like it's just a stretching excercise. The movement feels really fluid and pleasant. It's a joy to play.
I have noticed that some reviewers found it difficult to do precise platform-to-platform jumps and complained that the movement is perhaps "too fluid". I think that missing some jumps in a platformer game is to be expected ;) I guess it comes down to personal preferences, but it needs to be said that even when you do miss a jump for whatever reason, it's never fatal. You can easily climb back up and try again. This happened to me a few times but it never felt like a chore.
On the contrary, I felt such joy playing this game. It's just well-designed and well-made game. It throws new things and toys your way very often, so it always stays fresh. Even Kitty herself can be "customised" by buying new costumes. The pacing reminds me of the good old Prehistoric 2. When you got bored with running around and smacking dinosaurs, the game gave you a kite to fly for a whole level or so, which completely changed the dynamic. Blade Kitten's design works similarly and as a consequence never feels dull.
One small beef I have with the game is that in later levels it's very easy to get stun-locked between multiple enemies. Kitty, attacked from both sides, sometimes can't escape the onslaught, as there's no one-second-immortality-after-being-hit as in other platformers.
One larger beef I have with the game is that it essentially ends nowhere and prompts you to buy Episode 2. I had no idea that what I have is a story-wise incomplete game. It was a bit of an unpleasant surprise to find out just when the story got a bit more interesting. I don't know the reasoning behind the episodic format. Usually, tactics like these make me feel ripped off as a customer. Still, the game on the whole was a joy to play (and both episodes are quite cheap, anyways), so this time, there are no hard feelings.
This is the only platformer game I have played end-to-end in just about fifteen years. Because it's just good.

Well is this game real hidden gem or what! I put off buying it for a long time despite very low price because of a few negative reviews on game mechanics. Turns out those reviews dont know what they are talking about.
Yes this game has a few kinks that you should know about combat. There for instance is a kickback during which time you are stunned. This kickback+stun can be stacked on you by multiple enemies resulting in unexpected beatdowns and deaths. We are not talking about La-Mulana type of kickback here that defines the whole combat system but it's significant enough that it should be taken into account. Melee enemies dont let you go once they connect with their blows resulting in half your health going away. You regenerate fast but sometimes its not enough.
And what about your weapons and moves? Standard sword slash works well on 1-2 enemies but a group of enemies all at once? your DPS is not fast enough and you dont hit them all so the enemy will retaliate so adjust your tactics accordinly. You CAN take them out most of the time. but not always.
Enemies deliver their blows once they have progressed on their move and some of them are non-interruptible even if they die. The long range sword throw does not connect every time as it works bad in close range. In addition it consumes stamina which is important when you jump around trying to do your moves so it's better to be used when skirmishing or as an opener.
Use your head - your character can easily in normal situations just spam on the normal attack and win. But sometimes even the basic grunt can kick you down from a ledge if they have the height advantage or form a tag-team with another one to beat you up if you fool around too much.
Use that shield of yours.  Jump on top of enemies and throw them. Their bodies trigger doors, switches and even crumbling walls.
And what about platforming and levels? Well it sure is overdone. Just the start screens of levels, you can basically just spend 5-15minutes clearing the opening screen. See a ledge? there is a secret there - there always is. Every. single. time. at least money if not a chest or a teleporter to some other area.
Arrows tells you to move forward? nope. go back, there is still a ton of secrets or there is a alternative way forward with loot on the way.  I dont recall any other game overdoing secrets the way this game does. A typical level has the arrows pointing where to go but you must do the traditional 'uh-oh, game wants me to go here - i need to go back' -routine as much as possible and instead look for walls and ledges where to jump. or just hang from walls and make your way to seemingly impossible places - where there is a huge section of the level and here you will spend the next 5minutes. In another game called Limbo you got an achievement for 'going left'. this game takes 'go everywhere, there are so many secrets it will take time'  to a whole new level. On average levels last for a very long time so there is plenty to do.
To sum up the good this game has weapons, upgrades, costumes, nice artwork. good responsive platforming controls and easily learnable combat with small details that you can learn if you like but it's not mandatory. To get ahead in the game you dont need to learn all the details but it sure helps a lot.
I am very entertained this far. Unique game for me. Good looks and interesting stuff to do.
9/10.

PROS: Astoundingly well done for the price point. Fully voice acted, fairly good platformer controls. Give you flexibility to play it old school on a controller or do several keyboard+mouse  styles. Plot is... kinda disjointed, but evocative enough, especially with the voice acting.
CONS: It's a little wonky getting used to having your weapon float and learning how to time your attacks so your blade is actually available to launch another attack. Wall climbing is somewhat touchy and more than once I got stuck in a slide or to a wall.  Never permanent, but it happened enough that it makes some of the rapid movement and combat sections somewhat annoying.  Short. Two hours in I had completed more than half of the game.
MIXED FEELINGS: Some replayablility to find all the hidden collectibles, but it's no Metroid-vania. You don't revisit areas with new options, you just revisit them to find what you missed.  Despite the tooltips scattered around through the first few levels, They still leave some things out. Go into the options menu and read the manual first, as it also gives you some important context.
Overall, I definitely recomend it. It's low cost and it's a fun platformer for the price.  I picked it up on sale for under a dollar, but I'd definitely recommend it, even at the full $3 price tag.

A Bird Story was a short, but emotional and very charming little story that I enjoyed very much, and that touched my heart.
You play as a young boy who loves animals and loves the outdoors. When he's at home or at school, his life is often mediocre and boring, but you can see him enjoy himself outside when he can go to the forest. One day, he comes across a small bird in the forest, and its wing is broken. He takes the bird and rescues it, bringing it back to his apartment. Although the bird needs healing, the boy is afraid of anyone taking the bird away from him, and he tries to nurse it back to health himself.
The story is short, but beautiful and heartwarming, and I would recommend this game to anyone who enjoys a nice story, and bird-lovers like myself. I have to say I regret purchashing this game a little. I read the other reviews and said, "Maybe they're crazy and it runs just fine." And then I bought it and said "Nope, I am crazy for thinking it will be different." I have an NVIDIA GTX 960 with the game installed on a SSD and the frame rate drops are so horrible on the Nationals tracks that I can't stand to play it. The drops aren't too bad on Supercross style tracks, but it is annoying. Having said that, maybe if I upgrade my old AMD A6 processor and added more RAM, it might run better as I've noticed memory and CPU to be very,very high while running this game. Also, dropping some of the settings seems to have improved it a bit. Other newer games run just fine, so maybe this one is just not optimized for PC.
I will say that the handling does seem to be improved from the XBOX 360 version. My rider no longer does 360s on the ground a lot and doesn't seem to cross jump like a goon all the time. Is it the same as MX Simulator? No. But honestly, I haven't fallen over in real life as much as my MX Sim guy, so take it as you will.  Is it the same as MXGP? Not really. The turning still doesn't feel as nice. But, you can throw way better whips....in that you can actually control a whip. If you all ready own it on 360 or PS3, it's probably a waste of your time, but I am lazy and don't feel like walking to the other side of the house to turn on my 360, so I have it on here. It's just the same game though, there's not really anything new for you.
If you like motocross, well supercross, then it's a decent game, assuming you have an extremely powerful machine, maybe. I don't know, that frame rate thing could be present on all of them. Or I guess you could just wait for the May release of the Xbox One version and stream it to your PC. But I cannot honestly recommend it until it can be played without frame drops on a modest PC instead of a "Dude, I future-proofed the crap of my system" PC. Looks like after the recent update this game seems to be much better with my computer, usually getting a constant 60fps in SX and 30-45 in MX. I really do thank Rainbow for finally fixing the performane issues, so now I shall write a fair review in return. I'm gonna try and keep it short as possible, but looks like there's lots of things to cover here. I'm not trying to bash on Rainbow or Nordic in any way, just reviewing the game in my honest and opinion.
First off, the game itself is kinda fun, but doesn't really live up to what i was expecting. I was honestly hoping for a reflex2.0, but it turned out as a washed out Alive2.0.
To start here, the physics are honestly what i think are weighing down the rest of the game so much. I would have been fine if the same physics for reflex were used for supercross encore, because it really is the better of the motocross games out there. The new physics engine isn't terrible, but it feels like there was a step backwards from the right direction. The turning is like skating on brown ice simulator amped up a notch, and the whips are more like slightly maneuvering the bike sideways rather than flipping it which ever way you want like a sick pancake. scrubbing is alright but sometimes you'll end up turning sideways and transition into a super lame whip then proceed to land sideways because bringing back a whip is actually hard to do for some reason.
Braking seems to be a problem too. i had a few times when i hit the brakes and spun into a 720 noscope as if i were playing mw2 quickscope battles on rust. i know i had the oversized brakes updgrade on but jeez dude i dont think they have that kind of power.
Again, unlike reflex this game has your rider as a living tank that holds on to the bike with an absolute death grip and will only wreck if you are completely flatlining or upside down when landing a jump. Same with getting smacked into by other riders, instead of both wrecking, it just goes into bumper cars mode. and for the most part the AI is still dumb as it has been for generations now. most the time you can win a race going half speed as long as the opponents keep crashing into one another.
This game also really abuses the use of the clutch and seatbouncing, it's over powered what you can do if you just pop the clutch(which would stall the bike) and then seatbounce off a triple, you'll end up quading into the next section from the super mega ultrasanic speed boost. also it'd be real sweet if there was a manual gear shifting option, because no full sized racing dirtbike i've ever seen is automatic.
AND WHERE DID THE TRACK DEFORMATION GO?
that was one of  the coolest features for reflex, because you could carve out your out deep ruts and really rail it around berms with em, but in sx encore it seems like you cant even put an indention into the ground, sadly. Also... the rider reflex thing that you can use to save yourself from a crash is absent from this game, it's just an automatic animation. why would you do that?
so yeah it's apparent now that i really liked reflex, and lots of other mx vs atv fans can agree it's the best one out there.
Now that the biggest problem  is out of the way, i can get onto the little details and stuff i noticed were missing.
Ok, so the career mode isnt really much of a career, it's just racing after racing and getting some cool rewards, which is how it's been in pretty much all of the previous mx vs atv games. I'd like to see a career mode done differently, with sponsorships and all that fun stuff. You know another thing that's just completely missing from the supercross experience? where's all the qualifying, heats, semis, and lcq races? the race just starts off in the main event, which is really anticlimatic for me. Where's the 20 man gate drop too? i've been waiting around for that for years. This isnt much of a big deal, but it'd really add to the authenticity that makes this game "supercross".
Sountrack is good for the most part with some cool fitting music, but there were some songs i felt kinda killed the mood for me. BUT i did hear some of the old reflex songs and i was really excited to hear those again because they are amazing.
The customization is still nice with the variety of cool gears there are, but there's always gotta be more. Would be nice if there were even more added for free, or really really.... really cheap
Most of the tracks out there are actually great and feel like a SX track. so that's one good thing going for the game if i may say. The addition of the MX tracks from alive is definitely great, and im sure glad it happened, so why not also add tracks from other games too? reflex, untamed, and unleashed all had some good stuff and i'd like to see em again. why not throw in some of the older gears too?
also please dont make expensive dlc.  like seriosuly nobody likes that. if a company were to sell me dlc, it better be worth every penny
so im finally gonna wrap up this super long review. i didnt spend too much time organizing but i think i got my point across.best wishes to rainbow and nordic because i want to believe they can bring the series back to life. thanks to the developers again, but come on man you can surely do better, YOU JUST GOTTA BELIEVE!
TLDR: game is fun, but it aint no reflex. i wanna recommend this game but i just cant do it.

Since I'm a bit of a plane junkie, this game appealed to me greatly, so my review may be a bit biased.
If you're the type who wants something similar to Ace Combat, look elsewhere. You won't be zooming about in the air doing on a dime turns in some super OP plane, just blasting people out of the sky left and right. This game requires a great deal of patience and skill to really play well, especially online against other people. The modeling of planes and all their related systems is really good, as it should be for a WW2 flight simulator. You can fly most major aircraft from all major sides in the war, ranging from the eponymous IL-2 ground attack plane, to a Japanese Zero or a P-51.
That all being said, a joystick (preferrably HOTAS) is damn near a requirement to get the most out of this game. Without it you'll be stretching your fingers and your brain to remember all the controls on a keyboard. You can set the realism to lower levels so you won't have to worry about having to open radiator cowls, ammo counts, fuel status and the like, but IMO that takes away from the fun of the game.
If you're a flight simulator junkie like me, and am willing to drop a few bucks on a good joystick setup, this game is definitely worth the price.

Hell Yeah! is SEGA doing what it does best which is delivering another tight platformer. The game is silly but not in a bad way at all. The protaganist is an unlikely "hero" set out to exact revenge on his enemies who have publicly embarrassed him due to his love for "Duckies". The levels are crisp and detailed. The controls are tight and easy and simple to learn. The objective is to detroy all the monsters in a single level to open up the last door to the boss before moving on to the next area. The game is not serious at all and it is obvious from the short introduction during a new game and it finds several ways to make you crack a smile along the way. The only downside is the length of the game which is purely based on your level of skill with platforming. Players who are familiar with the game will find themselves having a good laugh and breezing through under 10 hours or so and others may find it a bit harder to purchase every unlockable and find every secret.
It may not be the blockbuster title you're looking for but this is definitely a game you should grab if you see it on sale! The platforming is perfect and it shows SEGA has mastered this genre over the last couple of decades.

Ignore my play time, I put 4 hours max into the game but even after closing it there was a background process for the game that made Steam think I was playing it. This happened multiple times, and is an extremely bizarre thing that I had to go into Task Manager to end.
A buggy, glitchy mess that somehow is still somewhat enjoyable through the suffering. The gameplay is very much a hack n slash. Victory is gained through the constant mashing of the two attack buttons and jumping around a lot. Enemies ragdoll around and the art design makes great use of the 2.5D style here, letting enemies come in from different plains of view and adding a great set of backdrops and visuals to an otherwise bland experience. The platforming is a bit wonky and prone to some bizarre physics, but was never too offensive and more than capable of moving you through the variety of areas, but don't even bother doing some of the bonus stuff; there were plenty of times that my pursuit for the more difficult unloaded the normal levels and led to me falling through the world multiple times; inexcusible for a game about all those hidden secrets.
Combat is also somehow a mess, even though it is quite truly just two different buttons to mash. Your sword floats and chops up enemies, either close to you or far away. Hitting guys far away usually takes them out within a hit or two, but if you get up close they deflect your attacks in some sort of arcane counter system, stun lock you, and kick you repeatedly. You learn quickly to not do close attacks. Like most aspects of this game, combat can also be fairly glitchy, often with enemies falling in the floor but still being able to attack making them virtually invincible. Thankfully, fodder is fodder, but in the decent amount of time I put into it, all I encountered was fodder.
The game does change it up a bit with the scenarios, although some can go on for far too long. Where the real redemption and where the over all worth is would be in the excellent animation that occurs in the cutscene. It's clearly all in engine, but whomever was in charge of doing all the lipsynching and animation overall has a lot of talent and skill. That is not to say those who put this together aren't; even at its worst the game clearly has a lot of love put into it, just not a lot of polish. Even though the story never really goes past "chase this one person to find this other person between one-liners," I still enjoyed what was there. The amount of utter brokenness I encountered within my few hours of playing are fairly unexcusable, but at the same time I'm glad this game has been successful. The second episode has been out for some time now and I hear it's a better over all experience, so it's good to hear that they're doing well and that they are so open with their audience.
All the same, Blade Kitten fails to hold on to the initial fun the first few minutes offers and offers little variation throughout its short campaign. While successful overall in its ambition, the amount of gamebreaking bugs and bland gameplay ruins my overall feeling for it. This game definitely has an audience, but it's not one I can recommend in good concscience, and makes me wish once again there was a "maybe" button. Worth getting in a bundle or sale to find out how you feel about it yourself, as I am clearly in the minority.
