Well if you'd like an actual or valid explanation as to why this game is not recommended rather than some edgy or trying to be cool statement, please read on. This is a game I was hoping to play for quite a while BUT the moment I got to play it made me realize how much of a disappointment the game as a whole really is. I now truly understand why the game community really is divided on this title in its rating and recommendation. This game has excellent concepts to build off of but fails miserably in its execution of all of these goods ideas. I'll just go the list of discrepancies to point out some of the game's most obvious and major flaws.
#1) A.I team members and enemies are both dumb as rocks
No real intelligent or tactical movement from either side just the same old "Let's all run in at the same time shooting" strategy. Even when either side is grouped up they really don't pay attention to each other's position or movement. I incapacitated 3 enemy squad members only to watch 2 of their medics prioritize engaging me with the rest of their team rather than prioritizing wounded team mates. Same thing happened with my A.I team mates also. Another big problem is A.I on either team does not retreat from combat when they are low on health or mortally wounded, rather they just kamikaze themselves straight through the middle of enemy ranks for no reason.
#2) Parkour/Free running in this game a joke
I remember long ago when Brink was first released (2011) they bragged about how the parkour system would be this great game changer for FPS games as a whole. Frankly speaking it could have been if it was done right. BUT the map design in this game is pretty claustrophobic and too cramped to make use of any meaningful pakour movement. The most you can do is leap over tables, desks and staircase rails. That about sums up all the free running you can do. And to make matters worse is that the parkour in this game SO PAINFULLY SLOW!
#3) Enemy A.I are massive bullet sponges
Even after you incapacitate an enemy, there is a chance he can be revived in this last stand condition only if an enemy medic is nearby. So to make sure he doesn't get that chance to revive you gotta put some extra bulets into him to make sure he stays dead. The problem with this arises when incapacitated enemies are able to tank an extra 6 or maybe 9 bullets to the face and body seriously depleting your ammo by more than it should. This is further made worse because like mentioned before the A.I is as dumb as rocks and rarely acknowledge each others presence including your own. So you might have soldier class team mate nearby but he won't toss out ammo to you 90% of the time sadly.
#4) Game is locked at 30FPS on single player/campaign mode but is unlocked at 60FPS in multiplayer
Now this one wouldn't be a big deal IF the game was optimized properly. This problem should have been remedied immediately the moment it came to PC. Anyone can clearly see that this game is a lazy or hastily put together port of the console version. No matter how good your system may be, you're going to have random and unnecessary FPS drops. Single player was painful because no matter what resolution you set it to and no matter what advanced features you turn off, the frame rate will bounce up and down between 15-30 frames. Even when people report getting 200+ frames they say the movement of gameplay looks and feels like it's in the low 20s
#5) Map design and gameplay are rather bland and boring
The Ark which is supposed to be this massive ship which kinda acts like an island for civilization is rather confined, tight, not very colorful or expansive. Each hallway, tunnel, lounge, facility or living sector all look and feel like they were all just copied and pasted over and over again with different furniture in it. Battles and skirmishes are ultimately unfufilling and don't feel rewarding. Gameplay just feels like a battle of attrition rather than anything fun. After you've shot down 15 or 16 enemies you start thinking "This is it? This is all I'm gonna do for the rest of the match?" Yes I'm well aware there are objectives and side objectives i.e Blow up this thing, Hack this thing blah, blah etc.. But your idiot A.I team members stink at covering you or watching your back, so expect objectives to only get done if you are doing them yourself.
Not to say this game did everything wrong but it's fair to say the bad outweighs the good on a massive scale. The graphics hold up quite well despite the age of the game. The animations on the other hand are nothing to write home about. Character customization is pretty in depth and fairly large. Voice acting is pretty good but wasted on throw away, meaningless dialogue. Plot is decent in concept but poor in execution and explanation. (Simply boils down either being a cop and keep the peace or become a rebel and escape the Ark)
If you still insist on playing this game despite what I have said thus far, do yourself a favor and play the more stable console version of this lazy port...

While the graphical style is something like 8-bit+, similar to Shovel Knight, the gameplay builds far beyond what was available in that era.
I especially like the variety of weapons available. It's much more than Super Metroid's different beams, as they vary in range firing pattern, and rate of fire.
Compared again, to Super Metroid, the combat is less forgiving. You've got less health and fewer opportunities to replenish between save points; however, at least the save points are pretty frequent, and basically only serve as respawn locations--your progress is saved even if you die, which is nice.
The art style is gorgeous, with a very H.R. Geiger feel, especially the game's trademark Rusalki--the giant heads nested in coils of tubing. I was a little disappointed with the design of the protagonist and some of the cutscenes; they stray a little too far from the rest of the game's look and feel. They're not BAD, but they could be more consistent.
The story is a little hard to follow, but it's supposed to be a bit of a mind trip. I only wish there were a full log so I could go back and review previous dialog in light of each new revelation. Also, part of the exposition is told in a broken-English style that is maybe a little over-wrought. I wasn't sure if the writer was going for 80s bad-Japanese-translation or trying to portray the character herself as a non-native English speaker. It's fine, but I'm not sure it adds more than it detracts. Over all, the story supports the weird sci-fi setting well with an interesting premise. I haven't finished the game, so time will tell if it delivers a satisfying conclusion.
The game mostly does interface very nicely. I like the ring menu for switching weapons; it takes clever advantage of the otherwise empty right analog stick that most 2D games ignore. The subscreen menu is fairly standard flip-left-and-right-to-change-pages. I'm not really sure why the menu screen pages scroll the opposite direction from what the buttons on the interface indicate (RB is in the top right and says "MAP" while you're looking at items, but when you press it, the items screen scrolls off to the right, and the map screen scrolls in from the LEFT.) It's like you're manipulating the screen itself rather than your viewport. A minor annoyance, but it messes with spatial learning of the interface which mostly just led to me pushing one direction or the other till I got the screen I wanted, even if it was the long-way-around. The other minor interface issue, and certainly more substantive is that some upgrade items in the item menu can't be highlighted for more information. So you have to remember the difference between the health fragments and power fragments if you want to know whether you're 3/5 to a new health upgrade or a new weapon power upgrade. Everything else is selectable with more info available. And I'm not sure if this is an interface thing, but I would have liked a fast travel/warp system like the Castlevania did in Symphony of the Night. There's a central "hub" area later on, but it can still take a while to get places.
The music is really cool, atmospheric chiptunes in the grand Metroid style. One of the tracks has these great synthy vocals that perfectly convey the otherworldly tone of the game.
And, to wrap this up, as far as I know, the game plays very "fair." It doesn't hide secrets in arbitrary places. It doesn't (to my knowledge) feature any secret timers or hidden conditionals. It's just pure, relaxing, explore-y Metroidvania. I really like it.

I've fully flopped from despising this game to enjoying it immensely. The launch was undeniably a disaster, and there was a lot to be frustrated with - I came back roughly a year later, and while I wouldn't say it's a totally different game; it's a ton better. Clans and raiding have afforded a great deal of depth in the absence of Epic (going to have to be patient), it really feels nice to be a part of a cohesive group.
Anecdotally, I used to fence - and I certainly wouldn't say that this game captures swordplay perfectly (especially considering we're talking about totally different styles of combat), but the tension and excitement is all there. I wasn't particularly good at fencing, but the key thing was always training: practice makes perfect and all that jazz. Same holds true with Of Kings and Men, you will watch yourself progress as a soldier, and if you're working with your clan to train it really starts to feel like a consecrated effort to improve your ability to fight.
Melee-combat is second to none. I've come to love this game, even though I originally detested its existence and wanted it purged from my library. I'm optimistic, and I would definitely recommend this to others - especially if clan-based games are your thing.

After reading all of the extremely bias reviews I thought I would give my two cents on this game since I have actually played for more than 5 hours. Yes it's true that the game servers have got a bit quieter recently due to lack of new content but that does't mean there is no new content. The devs have been really busy and have created a tonne of new features that are due to be implemented into the game late Dec 2016 in a big update instead of releasing lots of little ones. A lot of people don't understand that this game is "early access" and still has a some flaws that need ironed out. But by contributing to it now you also get a chance to help mould the game into it's final version and you also get a 1 up on all the new players that will join after the full game release. So, now that you know the reasons people are saying you shouldn't buy this game are false, let me tell you why you should buy this game.
Firstly the combat system is one of the best I have encountered, (and it's not even finished). The fluidity and control over your weapon gives such a satifying fighting experience as if you are actally on the battlefield yourself. You can choose between a sword, axe, spear or bow, 2 handed or 1 handed and they all respond different requiring different techniques and skills.
Secondly is the customisability. The amount of weapons and armour in the game at the moment is incredible, (and again it is far from being complete). Each weapon or armour item has it's own stats that will help you in specific battle situations, and it is up to you to decide which to choose. You can also upgrade your skills in HP, damage, attack and movement speed, each unique to your fighting style.
The last point is maybe the most important, comradery. This is a team game and in the heat of battle you must rely on those beside you to watch your back. It is a great feeling running in to battle with your team by your side knowing that you have each other covered, no matter what happens. It is never every man (or woman) for himself, you fight and die together as a team. And right now while there are slightly less people online, that is multiplied by a thousand.
I haven't even mentioned The Epic or the countless other features that the devs have in store for us as that would take you hours to read through, but you get the idea.
Overall this is a medieval warfare game like never before, and it isn't even finished yet!!!

In "A Bird Story" you experience the story of a boy and his new and only friend, a bird. After rescuing it from a badger he takes care of it and bonds with the bird while also keeping it safe from others and realizing that the bird must return to its own kind one day.
Think of it as a walking simulator in Super Nintendo graphic style.
If the game reminds you of "To the Moon" very much, don't worry: It is the same company "Freebird Games".
What you see and hear is pretty much the same concept: detailed, pretty retro graphics to a beautiful piano soundtrack.
Also the story is pretty much about life itself and important parts of it, like friendship and love.
Though, I must admit that "A Bird Story" disappointed me a bit because I had very little to do and even what I could do was laughably idiotproof (go a few steps in this direction, go to that room...). Most of the time it's like watching silent cutscenes from a SNES RPG game. True, the scenes are often very beautiful and dreamlike (like when you exit your house or classroom and you find yourself in the middle of the forest or when you ride that paper plane) but after a while I felt rather bored than impressed. And after 1 or 2 hours you should finished it completely.
The bond between the boy and the bird was nice, though but not too strong or something that would be stuck in my memory anytime soon.
So: I don't know if I should recommend this game even though it's not technically bad, it just offers not much.
It's pretty and relaxing, short and cute but no must-have. If you haven't tried out "To the Moon" yet, better check that out first.

When I first purchased Blade Kitten, it was because Funhaus (formerly Inside Gaming) played it during an episode of Steam Roulette, and it seemed terrible to me so I thought I could use it to crank out a few funny videos for my YouTube channel. Fast forward about a year, and my YouTube channel died along with my hopes and dreams, but I still had 50+ games sitting in my library that I had always planned on making videos in, but never got around to actually doing it. Since then I had been trying to level up, but I only wanted to level up in games that I either actually liked or at the very least could at least tolerate, and there was Blade Kitten among the list of unstarted badges. So I thought, "What the hell," and gave it a whirl. And now? I actually really like this game.
The story and animation style remind me of
in that even though there are some aspects that seem to have been thought of by an 8th grader whom even though was good at writing still listened to his friends who are the kind who like to LARP. And I mean cheap LARPing. But to be honest, it was because of Blade Kitten's likeness to
that I actually stuck around, since I really love
. Even though a lot of the story is nowhere near as good as the writing in
, it's still capable of having your attention.
As for the gameplay, I'm genuinely at a loss for words. While it is a side-scroller, it's still fun as hell, especially if you're the kind who when playing an open-world game tends to completely forget about the main story and instead prefers to get distracted by side quests and whatnot. Mind you, though, this game is definitely not open-world... I think... I honestly can't tell. Without a map, you're pretty much just wandering through the levels, with the only objective indacators being arrows that will only pop up at crossroads, so to speak, since the levels are still fairly linear in design. Still though, I found myself struggling at times trying to make sure I wasn't completing the objectives so that I could instead♥♥♥♥♥♥around with side stuff. Other than that, though, the gameplay is seriously fun as hell and very interesting.
All in all, I'd have to say this game is pretty deece in deece. 7.8/10

For an RPGmaker game, sure, it's good. There's a full, if cliche, story
and aesthetically, it's pleasing. But I can't recommend buying it unless it's only sale for maybe a tenth of its cost.
Unfortunately, the game is missing basic functionality that exists in even free games on RPGmaker communities, and if you're used to that, you're going to quickly find yourself frustrated. For example:
- There's the ability to craft in this game, but you have no idea of the specifics of what you're getting -- not the name of the item or what the stats are, both of which are kind of important. The crafting system goes by weapon or armor, then the class, and the level of the item depends on what crafting materials you're using up.
- The enemies have no health bars when you're fighting, which forces you to guess at which enemy to prioritise the first time you see them and then remember in subsequent encounters which ones are at which health and who dodged/missed, etc.
- As far as I can tell, enemies are limited, which means that you're stuck on what level you can be at for fights, and as you progress, you are painfully below the threshhold for having a fighting chance on bosses (unless you get lucky in one of your retries and the boss misses multiple times/you get criticals).
There's also very little interactivity with the environment. I may be nitpicking, but for a $14.99 game, I expect to be able to see snippets of lore when I try to interact with bookshelves, or extra houses that can be entered just for NPC conversation. The monster fights are all generic RPGmaker imps as well -- and actually, everything but the character portraits (and maybe the character sprites?) are generic RPGmaker portraits.
Ultimately, I can't justify paying for this game. I bought it on sale, but even then, I really feel like I would have been better off buying coffee.

I didn't really enjoy the protagonist, Claret, though. Claret felt a bit like a flat trope to me, whereas another character, Sullivan, narrowly managed to avoid that fate towards the end. The ending also seemed to come a bit out of nowhere (almost as if to create extra ~drama), but overall, it was refreshing and fun to play so I wouldn't think too much about it.
And that final scene though...

There'a a unique combat system with the idea of a character's "threat level," which forces the player to come up with a different sort of strategy to keep everyone alive.  There are no random encounters, so you have the opportunity to try to avoid any enemies you can see running around, unless it's a story battle.  All around great game, especially for RPG Maker.  I don't know if I would pay the full $15 for it, simply because it does only take a few hours to beat, but if you can get it on sale then there's absolutely no reason not to.

I'm reviewing this game again after ragequitting due to what was, to be honest, my own incompetence. However, I've recently discovered that there's still hours of gameplay left for me and a lot of it is rage inducingly difficult.
The Good: Characters. I like these characters! Even in battles, they were very in-character, with one of them constantly blocking attacks for the others. That was a nice touch. The dialogue is fun to read and the relationships between the characters are quite well done. Nothing really feels forced and they honestly come off like real people a lot of the time. Honestly, if this game were focused on the story and characters more than the battles, I'd probably love it. There's a fantastic game in here and if this team ever makes a sequel, I hope they'll actually go to the effort of making it more focused on the writing and story. There's a good setup, beautiful artwork, and genuinely lovable characters.
The Bad: These battles are fun... for the first hour or so. Then they get incessant, with few points to restore your HP and MP. And what's worse is that a lot of enemies are so difficult, you have to grind a LOT to get past them. Sometimes, they'll even wipe out half your team in their first move. I understand enemies need to get more difficult as it goes on but this is extremely frustrating. The battles near the end are almost unbeatable and the game forces you to go on several side quests just to be able to beat them, which is not good game design since I really just wanted to know what happened. The crafting system is pretty bad too, with no indication as to what materials you have, what the objects you craft can do, or what they'll require you to collect. It's a shot in the dark and quite pointless.
For that reason, it's pretty much a 5.5-6/10 for me. There's so much wasted potential, with a great story, great characters, and decent worlds. It's completely ruined by the battling though, which stretches the game out to insane lengths. If you like battle-heavy RPG Maker games, by all means play this one. But if you're interested in stories and characters, think about it before you buy it. Because while this game definitely delivers on both those elements, you have to go through a lot to get there. And the battle system is very unforgiving.
I'm saying I don't recommend this game but to be honest, I'm split. It's by no means a bad game but it's far too flawed and frustrating for me to feel comfortable recommending it.

This is another game I first discovered as a browser game on Notdoppler.  It's an incredibly fun game.  You create a party of up to 4 heroes and enter a dungeon.  Once you beat the "final" boss (at level 10) you can then enter an endless dungeon mode, which is exactly what it sounds like: a neverending dungeon generator.  "But MetalTreads, if it's a browser game, why wouldn't I just go play it for free there?" you ask.  Weeeeell, for one this version is saved to steam, not browser history so you can never lose progress unless you delete it. As well, you can access it from any computer that has steam. For two, you can use custom portraits for your heroes.  For three, full screen + good quality graphics = what more do I need to say?  For four, it's only $4.99 so even if you don't like it you're not down that much.  I love it and highly recommend it to anyone who likes WoW-ish type stuff.

"Super Metroid if you took mushrooms and LSD while listening to Pink Floyd played in reverse."
Axiom Verge is a 2D metroidvania that harkens back to the original era games, namely Super Metroid. Boasting a good 5+ hours of gameplay, it turns many of the conventional tropes on their head, creating a psychadelic and interesting game that can leave you wanting more.
The story begins with a lab explosion and you get very little else besides a voice. As the player navigates the alien world, you discover and slowly piece together a very strange and cryptic story that may or may not make sense at its conclusion. Along the way, your power grows as per a normal metroidvania but instad of getting staples of the genre, you get "different" types of movement. This is both a strength and weakness of the game, as navigate the map on a macro level feels very awkward and forced. Some of the movement items feel very awkward or even atrocious to use while others feel like a dream. This is a running theme of the game where experimentation creates both interesting items, weapons, or bosses while also creating trainwrecks.
Level design is mediocre at best, the surroundings and environment more lending to a surreal world. It is fairly easy to get lost without spending time making sure you are going the right way, and inconsistency plagues the game's design. Sometimes, the game forces you to use an item or movement ability on something that, before then, simply didn't work but does in that room. In one specific time, it even works on only part of the room despite there being other sections that are identical!
Difficulty tends to run in a feast or famine situation: Early on you have a fairly smooth curve but entering a new area often ends with you getting destroyed. Death can be used as a shortcut and is also part and parcel of a speedrun. Bosses are likewise hit or miss, serving more as puzzles than challenges, though some bosses can be a bit esoteric in terms of their gameplay or strategy.
All in all, Axiom Verge may not be a perfect game, but it's a unique and interesting one. If you look past its flaws, you can get a great sci fi experience and a story that will leave you thinking deeply. If you're afraid of complex designs (or just feel like you may get disoriented from the truly alien feel of the game), feel free to skip it, but watch a let's play.

ALOT of people will probably disagree, but I think this game is better than Reflex. There, I said it.
There are two major things about this game that annoy me.
The first is obvious; the framerate issues. From the poor console port of Reflex from 7 years ago, until now, these games have had poor framerate issues (and graphical issues on Reflex for some cards including mine). Whenever you're by yourself on a supercross track, the framerate is almost always above 60fps on newer hardware. Anywhere else (nationals, free ride, rhythm racing), it drops considerably. The developers have said that this is due to the trees, and the lag everywhere else is due to the dirt physics and terrain deformation. I kinda halfway believe that this is the case, but whatever.
The second is the clutch kick. It is WAY too strong. Yes, it gets you out of terrible situations whenever you don't hit a rhythm perfectly, but in no way should it be that strong, especially on hard packed dirt. Once they tone that down a bit, I'd say this game is pretty spot on with its physics.
Also, the track scaling is pretty big compared to real life like it has been for previous games (except Alive, which was rebranded to this. The smaller tracks in Alive had perfect scaling IMO), but I remember seeing an interview where a developer explained that this is because they want the game to have the pick-up-and-play aspect and that the game isn't too hard. Eh, I can live with that.
If the problems can be fixed in a timely manner, this game gets a solid 8.5/10 from me. If not, it's staying at a 6/10. I can still recommend this game based on its potential and current playability.

First played Evolved during its open beta weekend prior to launch. I was very interested because I played Left 4 Dead, and had my own ideas that ended up in that game. I was very excited about the game and found it had lots of polish. Superficially it was great to look at, if you had the computer to handle it. and It had fun and exciting game play not found anywhere else. But then i learned its price.. 60$. and that changed everything. Not only did i not have 60$, but, the game seemed to lack any real depth to earn that price. After all, it was a very simple arena game. Four hunters vs a single beast.. and there was only that one beast at the time. And far less hunters as well.. and maps.
Anyway, when i checked back in on its ratings and price over time. I noticed i wasnt the only one who wasnt digging the price tag. Although i could hear the devs thinking how AAA their game was. But, once it went free to play i was eager to play again. Even willing to put some money in. The problem? No community. even at peak times you can gurantee you're going to be sitting in lobby for many minutes. and will likely have someone leave once others are found.. putting you right back into the queue again. and, not only that.. a large fraction of the small community is cocky and toxic. Often times you will be on a team of people who have no idea what they are doing, or, people who apparently think are god's gift to this game and want to do their own thing entirely. and if you happen to be on their team during a loss.. they will refuse to play with you after that. and since the community is so small.. that basically means no one gets to play for a while. until more people happen to login and try and find a game.
another thing i have experienced is monsters that are too easy to kill.. either DC or quit, or, you have the overly cocky ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ who knows how to break the game and has found what over powered percs to use on what beast. and are essentially impossible to kill and they know it.. and rub it in your face. they don't run.. they attack immediately. just stand there and gloat and act like nothing matters and control the entire match and end it as they please.. often dragging it all out.  and its not something that skillful. you merely need to know a few things about the game and spend the points to unlock those percs. And daily login rewards that build make that super easy. thats one thing i like about the game.. the daily login rewards build over 30 days. and i just finished mine. and, if you want to collect all the characters, beasts and percs, especially without real money.. it will take an absurd amount of time. and with how small the community is, how toxic and bad at times.. its a fool's errand...
you see, i wanted to recommend this game to people so that the community could build.. and eliminate the many negative things about the experience. it deserves more people playing it. its a shame to see it in the state that it is. But, the devs have seemed to have abandoned this game. its a ghost ship.. skeleton crew.... and its a shame. if only they had not overcharged from the beginning.... they waited until their game had enough content to warrant a higher price tag, and they went free to play.  and it seems by then it was too late.
but... who knows. will Evolve reach Stage 3 and come back? the game has fun gameplay, great aesthetics. the world building or story telling through the simple dialogue between characters is also entertaining. but there is no community, and many of those within the community are buttheads.  and, i've played too many free to play games and done the whole grined routine.. the way it is set up could work only if there was a much larger community. wait times to get into a game are simply too long and troublesome seeing as people will leave the lobby if they don't get the exact class they want.

DO NOT BUY THIS GAME IF U ARE NOT A FAN OF THE HYPERDIMENSION NEPTUNIA SERIES!!
This is a game made for Hyperdimension Neptunia fans and as a non-fan I didn't really like this game. I missed my chance to refund it cus I totally forgot that i bought it. ;_; And yeah I finished the whole game lol, if I can't refund it, might as well try to enjoy it.
COMBAT
The combat in this game is probably one of it's weakest points which pains me a lot because I bought the game thinking it would at leat have a decent combat system. It felt very stale and repetitive. The game doesn't really encourage you to change up ur attack pattern and even if they did, there just isn't enough attack variety. A lot of time I just find myself spamming the same attack again and again. The combat is boring and it gets worse the moment you get into HDD form since the game just gets a hell lot easier, waaaaay too easy to even gain any sense of accomplishement from it. There is one thing I'll give this game's combat though, and that is it's flashy attacks. The playable character's attacks are flashy, although not he flashiest I've seen. Still it's probably the only redeeming quality for it's combat system.
ENEMIES
There are "some" variety in enemies. Well not really as the attacks of most of the enemies are basically the same and they are terrible. For most of the enemies, there is little to no indication in their animation that they are about to attack. This gives the player close to no time to dodge at all. Sometimes I don't even realise that I've been hit until I look at my health bar. The only indication you get most of the time is just a squeeky sound made by the enemies when they are about to attack. Could it be that they are trying to innovate with their combat system? Nah, I doubt so. And even if it was meant to be that way, they failed MISERABLY.
CHARACTERS
Ok, the characters are pretty good. They all have a wide range of personalities and it's fun to see them interact with each other. This is the first Hyperdimension Neptunia game I've played and man do I like the characters. But come on, it's a game, not an anime, not a book. Games are not meant to be a storytelling medium. Sure they can tell a story but the story should not be the main focus. The story of a game exist to give the player a motivation to play on, it's a tool to support the gameplay and the gameplay just simply isn't good.
UI
The interface isn't bad, it was pretty well designed and i didn't really find any problems navigating through it. The only one complain I have is that they didn't tell me that there was a medal collection. I only figured it out 3/4 through the games. The stat boost from the medals really helps in clearing the levels faster which is just about it. The game was already really easy to begin with, the medals just make it a lot easier. Although, without the medals you're going to find yourself stuck in one area trying to kill the enemies with what little damage you can deal.
OVERALL
I don't hate this game  but I didn't really like it either. As mentioned at the start, this game is made for fans of the Hyperdimension Neptunia series, even if it is a hack and slash. Don't buy the game if you're not a fan, you'll regret it. Trust me, it's not worth it.

Il2 is a realistic flight sim game featuring aircraft from pre world war 2 era to the late 40s. The aircraft are modeled very realistically featuring an advanced damage model where individual parts of your aircraft can take damage and affect the performance of the plane.
Most of the aircraft in the game are very realistically modeled using performance data from actual aircraft. (except the Nazi secret aircraft added in the 1946 edition).
You can play story campaigns, dynamic campaigns and single missions.The game includes a very advanced campaign editor that lets you create your own campaign and missions.
To truly have fun in this game you need to play multiplayer or get into the modding scene. However matchmaking is not possible from within the game and you need to get Hyperlobby (which is free). Once you have that installed you can easily join multiplayer matches.
A huge (and still active) modding community keeps adding new content and really adds to the games replay-ability. From extra missions to entire story campaigns, hundreds of downloadable aircraft and  semi official patches that steam will not install and you have to get it manually.
Il2 is a must play game for any flight sim fan or any aircraft enthusiast. With a friendly  community that promises to remain active for years,

A great platformer.  In each level you need to recapture the escaped prisoners and then reach the exit (your mecha).
The SWITCH mechanic is core - certain walls can switch on and off, to open up paths, or defeat enemies if the walls crush them.  The switches create a variety of snack-sized challenges - either hitting a tight timing window, or working out the puzzle of how to get from point A to point B.
It took me ~10 hours to complete all the levels (including the "hyper" levels, remixed and more challenging versions of the main levels).  Getting a par time on each level (or competing in the leaderboards) would be a bigger undertaking.
What I'll remember most is the catchy soundtrack that exceeds expectations.  The game feels a little like the Shantae series by the same developers - but without metroidvania-style upgrades and backtracking.  It also reminded me of Dustforce, but with more puzzles and gentler difficulty.

From the creative minds responsible for the Shantae series comes this wonderfully confusing action-puzzle game.
The artwork, world, and character designs are iconically Way Forward; everything is adorable and dances along with the background music in their idle pose. Mighty Switch Force takes place in an almost cyber-punk setting reminescient of Robocop crossed with Rockman.
Somehow, the backdrop of city lights and towering buildings does little to detract from the overall charm of the cartoon-like character designs, which I personally love.
Mighty Switch Force's gameplay is outwardly kind of like a scrolling action-platform game. Deep in its core, however, there's much more puzzle solving than action. The unique gimmick is based around the main character's ability to toggle specific background objects into the foreground or to do the reverse, hence the name, "Switch Force."
The game manages to sqeeze just about all it can out of this core gameplay concept, introducing a variety of different blocks that behave in unique ways. It isn't a particularly long game, even counting the optional stages, but it's very satisfying while it lasts.
The first of my only two complaints I have is in regards to the game's hit detection; it's pixel-perfect in all the wrong ways. Patricia is actually a few pixels larger than her art on a few sides, especially in her jumping animation. The result is the game has a very bad habit of deciding that the edge of one of the aglets on Patricia's shoelaces was slightly overlapping part of the shading on a nearby block that is entering the foreground, sending her smashing headlong into the screen and sending the player back to the previous checkpoint.
This is funny, charitably speaking, maybe twice. After that I started to get the impression that the game was out to get me.
The other annoyance, for me at least, was the game's health system. Being hit by some obstacles and enemies causes Patricia to lose a heart and flicker for a few seconds, while taking damage from other hazards causes her to fall off the screen and return to the previous checkpoint. The inconsistency gave the game an unpolished feel.
Nothing in those two drawbacks would ever stop me from recommending this, though. Mighty Switch Force is vibrant and fun, never losing its characteristic sense of humor, while still providing a good, meaty challenge,

I have a lot I want to say about this game, but I'll try to keep it short.
First off, the protagonist, Kit Ballard, is one of my favorite characters in recent memory: capable, sarcastic, and yet still genuinely kind as well as able to change her tune or admit she was wrong when someone provides a new piece of information. Not to mention that she just seems to be having so much fun with everything that she and all the other characters play off of each other nicely and make it enjoyable to both fight and watch cutscenes.
The combat is simplistic, mash the attack button and jump around like a kangaroo. Congrats, you've beaten most of the enemies in the game. There's an interesting mechanic where you can do the aerial wall grab move against certain vulnerable targets for an instant kill with an extra cash reward, but sometimes a move will leave an enemy vulnerable and sometimes the same move won't, so it can be really frustrating when someone blocks all your attacks and won't light up for the finish move. Also, the wall grab prefers to grab walls and ceilings rather than enemies, so if you jump up and try to insta-kill an enemy in a room with a low ceiling, you'll be gluing yourself upside down for a second in the middle of the fight. Also, the move is kind of hard to pull off with a keyboard since you need to use the q button in conjunction with wasd.
The programming is...well it's finicky. Usually the game works fine, but there are plenty of weird parts. For example, often on the instakill move, Kit or the enemy will be in the wrong location and will slowly drift into position while Kit says her taunt. There are some other weird situations like this, but there's one of these actually has the potential to break your game: for context, this is a 2D game with 3D graphics where you're supposed to run along the x-axis and jump on the y, but there are times where Kit accidentaly moves some distance in the z-direction. This can make her collide with background characters and objects which can actually make it impossible to proceed. If this happens, you had beetter hope you left an enemy alive in the current area so that they can kill you and send you back to the checkpoint. I know I'm not the only person who's had this problem as I've seen forum posts about the glitch as well.
The story has a REALLY bad problem of assuming the player has information that they have no way of learning. Nearly the entire game, I'm wandering around in random directions and eventually reach the place I was appreantly supposed to go to. I would travel right to get to the outskirts of town, Kit would get something that she needs to take to the top building in the town and instead of just backtracking a bit I would for some reason end up in a factory underground that I have to climb out of to get into the city. The entire story just keeps dropping you in random places and say "Okay, go to the Holy Island now" with no indication of which direction it's in or how far you are from it.
Honestly, I recommend the game as it's a fun diversion with some really nice characters. However, the game suffers from some issues with it's programming and its narrative conveyance, so just be aware of that going in.
PS: As a side note, on the first computer on which I played this game, a certain cutscene always crashed the game and made it impossible to proceed. Later, I got a new computer and tried the game again; I started a new game to remind myself about the controls, but then learned that there is only a single save slot in this game, so I had to play the whole thing again (learning that I previously had made it nearly to the end of the game). As such, I can confirm that the game doesn't have much replay value and the second playthrough was a chore. The "Skiffy" scenes where your pet uh, flying...rodent...thing goes off into the foreground or background to perform some task is completely unskippable and the little guy takes his sweet time doing them which made it really hard for me to stay immersed in the high-octane gameplay.

I really want to like the game. I dig the quasi-JRPG style and a lot of the game design is actually rock solid. It has good platforming elements, good exploration, secrets to find, weapon upgrades, costume unlocks. The combat seems a little sketchy at first, but it makes more sense once you realize that the game expects you to take a more leap-and-dodge, hit-and-run approach to combat (especially don't forget about that slide kick!) instead of  running in with blade swinging like a berserker.
Unfortunately, I don't feel like I can recommend the game because the controls are just way too sketchy. Controlling the character does not feel as responsive as it should, which really detracts from the fun of playing an ultra-agile type character. There are also a lot of buggy behaviors with walls and floor when you move the character eratically. For example, Kit is supposed to automatically cling to walls and climb them as easily as walking, which she normally does. But sometimes you'll attach to a wall and kit will automatically start climbing down and will keep climbing down even though you're not pressing the controls, and will keep climbing down even when you press up to get her to go the other way. I also experienced a situation several times where, if you throw up her shield/hold move where she stabs her blade into the ground, but you do it around an edge coming out of a fall, she will sometimes fall halfway through the floor, so only her head is sticking up out of the ground. Also, within the first ten minutes of playing, I somehow managed to get kit stuck in the shield/hold position where she would default back to shield/hold every time I stopped walking, and I had to leap around like a crazy monkey for a minute to get her to stop doing it. These are but a few of the "buggy but passable" behaviors you may experience.
The aesthetic is great, the attitude is great, the game design principles are rock solid. Really the only thing that truly hurts this game is that the character controls do not feel very tight. They are aaalllmost there. It's so close that some people will consider the other positives enough to overlook the loose and shaky controls, and if that's you then buy it up. But I think for a game that is supposed to be an action platformer with hit-and-run combat and ninja-agile character, the controls should be super tight, and they very simply are not.

Survival of the mismatched
I’m going set aside the debacle that followed the launch of Evolve and concentrate on the game since it went free-to-play, which is when I started playing it (it was on my wishlist and I probably would’ve bought it eventually). Coop gaming lives or dies with the team. They can be great fun to play provided you have a decent team, but if your team does not cooperate, or is poorly-matched, well, it soon goes down the pan. In this respect ES2 suffers more than most. If you’re lucky enough to get a cooperative, well-matched team of hunters, against a well-matched monster, it can be really enjoyable. If you don’t have such a team it can be extremely frustrating, especially if poorly-matched hunters are pitted against a high-level monster. Due to the low number of players (it averages around 400 at the time of writing) there is no matchmaking to speak of and teams are often badly balanced as a result. There are also too few players who enjoy playing as monster which can lead to long waiting times. And yet despite all of these gripes I keep going back to the game because I love coop, and when it does go well it really is a satisfying game. I think Turtle Rock missed an opportunity with Evolve: there is the basis for a really good game here but, for whatever reasons, they dropped the ball. And I can understand why many people lost patience or grew bored with the game. But if you enjoy coop, and have a little patience, EVOLVE STAGE 2 is worth a try – it is free after all. 3.5/5

The game runs through the original three Indy films and while it follows the stories well, there are some segments that have been added or tweaked to better fit the title. For example, after rescuing Marion from her bar towards the start of Raiders of the Lost Ark, you'll run through a section where you work along a snowy cliff side, take on some Germans and eventually head out of the area. Similarly, the temple at the end of the Last Crusade has much more than three tests to pass, with plenty of mostly non-deadly puzzles to complete before you get to the Grail. This all works well in terms of how the game plays as well as its pacing, and most all of the segments are fun, though there's certainly a bigger separation between game and films than what we saw with the LEGO Star Wars titles.
Though there's obviously a lack of Force powers this time around, Traveller's Tales has once again done a good job of providing distinct character groups. Indiana Jones' whip always comes in handy, and he's the only one that can open a number of the game's sections thanks to its numerous uses. Thugees, the bad guys from the Temple of Doom, are able to "talk" to statues of Kali and open up secret areas, while people with manuscripts, like Henry Jones Sr. or Elsa, are able to decipher hieroglyphs and open other secrets. Some characters come with shovels or wrenches, which allow them to dig up objects or fix broken items.
￼
Fights with armed enemies can be a nuisance when all you have is your fists.
The cool thing here is that aside from Indy's whip (or a tiny character's small stature), you're able to find all of these items in-game to help you solve puzzles. So even if you only have Junior and Willie at your disposal, you'll be able to dig up treasure if you can find a shovel nearby, or you can work with hieroglyphs if you can find a book. There are plenty of areas that won't have these things lying around, requiring that you come back in Free Play to unlock more goodies, but the puzzle variety is able to be mixed much better throughout the game thanks to the ability to pick up and use items.
Adding a bit more character to the main cast are phobias that a couple of them have. Indy, for instance, is afraid of snakes, while Willie is scared of spiders. Both will cower in fear when near them, so you'll need to use another character to either clear the way or go ahead and solve a puzzle without them. It's a small touch, but one that works well to bring about some of the characters' traits from the films to the game. Since the characters don't really talk though, Short Round lacks his funny quips and just winds up being short. Oh well.
A somewhat big difference between the Star Wars and Indiana Jones LEGO games is the focus of combat. While most characters either had a lightsaber or blaster in the Star Wars titles, the combat in LEGO Indy is largely hand-to-hand. You can pick up guns that enemies drop, but they're only good for a few shots before they expire. While this is mostly fine, it can be a little frustrating when there are a group of armed enemies on-screen and you have no choice but to repeatedly jump while running at them in order to try and dodge their shots. You will inevitably get hit and probably even die a few times in the scuffle. While you have infinite lives of course, it's still frustrating to know that you don't really have a good chance of coming out unscathed in these encounters and simply have to bear down and charge until everyone is dead.﻿

To the Moon hit me with an avalanche of emotions that left me speechless and in tears by the time the game was over. To this day, the profound and haunting storyline of To the Moon has stayed with me, and, it will probably always stay with me. I doubt that I will forget that game anytime soon.
I consider A Bird Story to be To the Moon's less intense little cousin. Fear not, this game will still take you on a ride on the feels train. This is a bittersweet and carefree story that will no doubt resonate with the inner child within us all. Did it move me to tears? Well, I'll admit, my eyes did get watery quite a few times. I wasn't exactly bawling my eyes out like I did with To the Moon, though. However, there's nothing wrong with that at all. To the Moon was definitely designed to be way more heavy. This game was obviously designed to be much more tame and mellow.
Gameplay is rather short, but, it still packs an emotional punch that'll leave a melancholy and bittersweet imprint. I was also overjoyed when I found out that Freebird Games was making a new game, called Finding Paradise, which will delve into the dying mind of the man who was the little boy in A Bird Story. So, it appears that A Bird Story is the prequel to Finding Paradise. That being said, I definitely suggest that anyone who loves To the Moon or is planning to play Finding Paradise checks this out. However, even as a stand alone game, this is a very sweet and bittersweet little game that'll no doubt tug on your heartstrings regardless of whether or not you have played To the Moon or are planning to play the sequel, Finding Paradise.
Freebird Games (the makers of the games I've been mentioning in this review) know how to make games that bring out raw and unadulterated emotions in people. Their games will make you cry, they will make you think about life, loss, death, and everything in between. I won't spoil the ending, so, I'll say as much as I can say without ruining the plot too much. In short, this is a story about a little boy who was lonely. Then, he made a new friend. A bird. And, for a while, they were inseparable and they were the best of friends.

Dishonored ist eins meiner absoluten Lieblingsspiele!
Es gibt nicht nur eine wundervolle Story, welche mitlerweile wundervolle Fortsetzung hat, sondern auch ein unglaublich gutes Storytelling, wunderschöne Maps  und eine prallgefüllte Welt voller Details die mit einer bombastischen Atmosphäre gefüllt ist!
Meiner Ansicht nach, wäre das Spiel um einiges besser wenn es eine Art Openworld innerhalb der Stadt wäre.
Es ist eine sich ständig verändernde Welt.
Am Anfang sieht man Dunwall noch ohne irgendwelche großen Probleme, die Seuche und zerstrittene Gesellschaft ist klar erkennbar, aber es gibt noch (vermeindlich) sichere Orte und die Armee wenn man sie so nennen kann ist ebenfalls gut geführt.
Im laufe des Spiels ändert sich allerdings alles!
Die Seuche bricht weiter aus, die Stadt geht langsam kaputt und verfällt.
Es gibt immer weniger Anzeichen von Leben und man trifft sehr selten auf andere Personen, die nicht gerade der Feind sind, also Armee/Polizei.
Es gibt für alle Level verschiedene Lösungsmöglichkeiten, während man den Zerfall der Stadt immer weiter ansehen kann.
Dabei muss man sich immer entscheiden ob man jetzt den guten, oder den schlechten Weg wählt was sich auf das Ende des spiels auswirkt.
Dishonored ist im Gesamtpaket ein wunderbares Spiel und hat eine Kaufempehlung für absolut jeden!
Dieses Spiel ist ein MUSS!

Dishonored has top-tier gameplay. You are a supernatural assassin on a brutal quest for vengeance, and that means you have access to powers beyond those of mortals. Bending the flow of time, traveling long distances near-instantaneously, and summoning swarms of rats are just some of the things you can do in Dishonored. You get these powers by exploring the environment and interacting with the world, and over the course of the game you can improve that which appeals to you.
The best part is, you aren't forced to use supernatural abilities. Dishonored has a lot of choice involved in everything from ability selection to the way you tackle the various levels of the game. While the story is mostly linear, with a few variants toward the end, each level presents an amazing array of choices from something like infiltration to combat and assassination.
The story is pretty good too. I find that the most interesting aspects of Dishonored's story are not relayed directly to the player. There is an air of mystery surrounding the Outsider, for example, who initially grants the main character supernatural abilities. The plague devouring Dunwall is also implied to have supernatural origins. All fascinating questions.
I would highly recommend the DLC, the Knife of Dunwall. It's arguably better than the base game with about 75% the scope. The challenge DLC is also fun if you want to mess around with powers, though it isn't strictly need-to-play.
Highly recommended.

It wasn't terrible and occupied me for quite a few hours, but eventually left me unsatisfied which is why I cannot recommend it.
Quite battle driven, lacking story sequences. There were times where in between battle grind I completely forgot why I was here in the first place. However, the battle system was quite well made and fun for the most part (except for the final game breaker).
The crafting system is abysmal. You click through choices over and over with no information given to you (e.g. your inventory, or at least what resources oyu have available). If you misclick or lack resources, you have to do it over. The "Okay, but it's an RPG Maker game" excuse doesn't work, this is still being sold as a 15 USD game.
And finally, towards the end of the game it feels like the developer(s) just got lazy in their battle design. First, you meet an optional battle (one of the achievements), which is completely ridiculous in comparison to all other battles you had fought. Barely takes any damage and will eventually one-hit your entire crew with an AoE attack. "Okay", I think, moving on. Good thing it's just optional, I guess they thought it would be a fun easter egg?
Well, I was wrong. While the final boss wasn't as bad as that easter egg character in terms of taking damage, it was completely impossible to defeat with my character builds. Eventually it would rain down AoE attacks that in one hit left only my 6000 HP guy alive. There was no point trying to revive others since they'd just be caught immediately by the next AoE attack, which went on forever. It feels as if they just set every stat of said final boss to the maximum value and went "lol ship it". You could say I'm just bad at RPGs, but even if I was, this battle was still nowhere near like any of the other tough battles I've had in this game. In relation to how the game played previously, it's just completely out of order. Keep in mind, this is WITH grinding through every single battle offered to me beforehand.

This was the start of my downward spiral into otome games, a fandom I am so deeply entangled with now, there is simply no return for me.
Hatoful Boyfriend wasn't supposed to be serious.  It wasn't supposed to make me FEEL.  But it did.  At first, you're so taken with the "Haha I'm dating birds" aspect, but then the game tricks you into seeing the characters, each nuanced in their own multilayered backstories, for more than what they are.  You start wanting to know more about them, wanting them to be happy, hurting when they hurt.  It's ridiculous.
And don't even get me started on the BBL stuff.  My face had melted by that point.
I would encourage basically everyone to play this game, especially since it goes on sale often enough, and the whole experience is worth the small amount of money for it.  The world needs more games like this one!

Mighty Switch Force is a fun time. It's pretty standard as platformers go, with a limited range of abilities and unique obstacles, but the level design is so heavily varied and the actions you perform feel exhilarating enough that it never got stale. The stages always find different intricate ways of using the elements they introduce, yet remain pretty straightforward in terms of finding your way around. It's an easy game to learn and control, pretty kind about health and checkpoints, and will certainly challenge you at times.
I will say, though, that it's a pretty short and linear game. There's a modest selection of levels, so if you really sit down and play through, you might have this done in just a few hours. The latter half consists of hard modes of previous levels, but they reconfigure enough to give them their own identity while remaining familiar to the originals, so there's still a fair amount of added variety and challenge there.
The par times will definitely keep you a lot more busy. They'll test your reflexes, accuracy, and familiarity with each level layout and feel great to complete. That said, however, certain minor issues with jump and crush damage thresholds that are negligible when playing the levels normally can become really inflated and punishing in this scenario. Don't get me wrong, par times are still really fun if you want something intense. They're fulfillingly difficult, and the goals you need to reach are cunningly defined.
Overall, I would very much recommend picking this up! There's easily enough to do here to be worth $10. Just go into it knowing that you probably won't spend thousands of hours on it. Still, everything that's here is a lot of fun, feels really good to perform, and is worth your attention while it lasts.

I would describe this game with the following sentence: an amazing idea that falls short because of bugs. This game in concept and excecution is amazing, but is littered by bugs, glitches and a couple of design flaws here and there that inhibit it from reaching it's true potential. For one, the framerate dips, especially when you have a bigger boat and more crew members, later in your play through. Another issue that comes with more crew members is poop (literally). Your crew members poop a lot, and poop manuals to teach pirates how to clean them are scarce. This means that your boat will always be a poopfest, and you'll have to keep on stealing other pirate's boats to keep a clean boat. Furthermore, scurvy. Scurvy is a status that a pirate gains when it doesn't eat enough lemons, fish, etc.. This wouldn't be a problem if these foods were easy to find. However, you have to travel all accross the world just to find a measly lemon, and that doesn't even fix it all, because you'll need way more. This makes your crews stats decrease, which affects the gameplay.
Although the game has many, many flaws, it's still very fun and I still recommend it due to the sheer enjoyment I got out of the gameplay, and creating fictional storylines with the events that occurred to me in my travels. Get this game, or wait till they fix the bugs. I would get it now because most of the flaws come in the late game, and you'll already have around 6 hours of enjoyment out of it.

HELL YEAH to HELL YEAH!!!   KILL KILL KILL!!!!!  A great indie game developed by Arkedo and published by SEGA.   Wait....does this make this indie or third party? ..... Both?  Well, alright then.~
Play as Ash, a mixture between Jumpy the Rabbit King from the cartoon Hero 108 and Laharl from Disgaea, who acts as the new ruler of Hell after his father mysteriously passes away (no, you won't find out why and the plot doesn't go that deep).  Ash rules hell with an iron paw...until one day, someone snapped photos of him f*cking a rubber ducky in a bathtub and posted them on the Internet.  Ash sees this and is infuriated to find 100 views on the article.  To quell his vengeance, he must kill 100 denizens of Hell.   Did they see the pictures?  Are they innocent?  Who cares?!  100 souls will quell his anger.  One for each view of that article.
With your primary weapon as a giant buzz-saw blade equiped with guns, rockets, grenades, lasers, etc., you can't really go wrong with killing.   Every finishing move is a mandatory minigame that often leads to a brutal demise of your victims.  Ash really is one ruthless rabbit who doesn't give a f*ck.
PROS:
Tons of ways to slaughter
Great humor
Memes here and there (spot them all)
Easy to pick up and play
Achievements  (easy 100%)
CONS:
Not worth full price ($15)
Obligatory jackpot achievement
Too short
No achievements for doing more than 10 side-missions
Some obligatory minigames can either be too easy or too repetitive (if you liked WarioWare type games, then you may enjoy it)
Ending song loops 5-6 times after you beat the game...gets annoying
Only one save file
Very limited replayability (you beat the game, you can roam around, play slots or complete challenges...or DLC challenges, but that's about it. Aside from that, the only thing you can do is reset your file to get additional gameplay.)
I grew up with Nintendo.  I'm starting to like SEGA more nowadays.  This game isn't worth full-price, but it is worth playing if you find it on sale.  Thank you, SEGA, you done good.  ^_^
So, do I recommend this game?  Hmm....what was the name of this game again?   Oh yeah.....HELL YEAH!

You play as a Cat Girl and you go around...helping I guess? The story is pretty disjointed, it seems like you just go on random favors for people as you go along. I'm not usually big into story in games so I didn't get much out of it anyhow, but even watching the cutscenes didn't give me much idea of what was going on.
The gameplay is a lot of 2D platforming. There is a ton of Hex (the currency) to collect in levels, so much so that you can probably find hundreds of different secret paths that can lead you to more. This is a nice touch as you can use the hex to upgrade your character and get more costumes. It encourages exploration, and can lead to spending a lot of time in levels just messing around and finding hex. The platforming itself is generally solid, and climbing allows you to get to a lot of areas without much trouble.
The combat is one area of the game I didn't much care for. It seems that more often then not the best way to fight is to just abuse overpowered energy skills rather then fight normally. Because of this, fighting becomes quite boring, and it's mostly optional anyhow, which lead me to skip most enemies in the game (of which there are a lot). The amount of enemy spawns which seem endless in some areas seems to encourage that run away playstyle. The combat itself just doesn't have much depth, you can shield, spam attack, or spam energy skills. The boss fights are also pretty
uninteresting.
I really like the art style of the game, which seems cel-shaded. The character are animated well and I feel like I'm playing an older style console game seeing them interact.
The game lasted me about 3 hours but it would take much more time to collect everything in the levels, so if you're a completionist you can definitely get your moneys worth. I guess the game is somewhat episodic because it ends without any type of real finish to the story, and there is a Part 2 DLC. This might be something to keep in mind if you want the complete story.
I did enjoy the game, but it could do with some improvements. I'm not sure if I'll go for the DLC at this point, but I might consider it in the future.

Mighty Switch Force! Hyper Drive Edition is a fun little platformer that branches out mostly in the Nintendo area of consoles, but has come to Steam for a neat release as well. I personally quite like this game and its related franchise, as well as the developer company themselves, so fair warning, I may be slightly biased. Please don't let that deter you from purchasing this game, however!
Let's start with the gameplay. It plays well, and doesn't take much to run. The player controls one Patricia Wagon as she sets off to capture, capture, and capture again the Hooligan Sisters, making use of large blocks that switch in and out of the game's playing field, making up a majority of the puzzles and action in the game itself. The concept is relatively simple enough, and is put to use pretty well. Along with that is fairly standard platforming mechanics, with Patricia carrying a gun to shoot enemies with as well, altogether making a pretty good gameplay experience in my opinion.
As for graphics, this is a two-dimensional platformer that uses sprites, but it looks good. The version of this game on Steam and some Nintendo consoles titled Hyper Drive Edition feature redone sprites of most everything in the game, in a nice and smooth artstyle. There is an option to turn Patricia Wagon, and only her, back into the pixelated version seen in the first versions of the game.
In terms of sound and music, I very much like the soundtrack of Mighty Switch Force! Composed by Jake Kaufman, or virt, it's a lovely electronic mix soundtrack, and is available to download for free or pay what you wish on Jake's bandcamp. Admittedly I believe the sequel's music is ever so slightly better, but that can be found in the little spinoff game also present on Steam. As for the sounds themselves, overall the game has good sound design. Patty's voice doesn't get annoying, and the rest complement the actions that occur.
Overall, I find the game great, if a little short perhaps, but still worth the price! If you do purchase and do like this game, I recommend obtaining another entry into its franchise, Mighty Switch Force! Academy, also available currently exclusively on Steam. If you like this type of game, I'd also suggest looking into the Shantae franchise! If I missed anything, please leave a comment below. Thanks for reading, and if you do purchase this game, have fun!

This is the best puzzle-platformer I've played in years!
In this game, WayForward, best known for the outstanding Shantae series, showcases their mastery of level design with a whopping 42 stages of hectic block-switching action.  By my standards, puzzle-platformers fail if they're too plodding, or if their signature mechanics are too one-dimensional.
, though, hits all the right notes with smoothly flowing stages that are meant to be played fast, and with the continual "switching up" of its simple-seeming handful of tricks into endlessly inventive combinations.  The dressing is great too:  the cartoon sprites are gorgeously animated and the candy-sweet electronica rocks.  I'm going to buy the soundtrack as soon as I finish writing this!
One more thing: I actually completed all achievements in this game!  I don't hundred-percent games very often, because so many of them require you to suffer the agonies of hell in order to do it, and I think that takes all the fun out of playing.  This game, however, let's you grab all the achievements in the ordinary course of skillful, (sanely) passionate play.  You might drop a few beads of sweat or let flee a few F-bombs in finishing the "hyper bonus" stages under par, but you'll never lose the sense of obsessive platforming fun that
engenders from the start!

I really loved MSF when it came out for 3ds, so I purchased it for a bit of a throwback. I wasn't expecting all the extra content, and was really impressed with the hyper and bonus stages!
Mighty Switch Force is a very original game idea. What I'd call "easy to learn and hard to master" is a big philosophy in the level design. Each level builds on concepts that are easy to understand at first, so there's plenty of time to "practice" before the tough levels come out. The puzzles themselves aren't actually that hard, and the platforming isn't THAT hard either. It's putting everything all together to get a "perfect run" that's the challenge, and I like a challenge.
Mighty Switch Force also has one of THE best soundtracks for a game ever made. Jake Kaufman is a legend. The music design really fits the levels too, with most of the BPM matching the animations of Patricia, which is a really cool feel.

I was expecting a story and dialogue. First and foremost, Mighty Switch Force is a puzzle/platforming game with a focus on fast gameplay and I respect that. It's good gameplay, and I have no complaints about it. But it kind of took me by surprise that there are pretty much no cutscenes and story, and zero character development. It's just stage after stage.
Be warned, this game isn't exactly Shantae-of-the-future.

If you've never played a Hyperdimension Neptunia game, brace yourself. The whole series is a glorious satire of the competition between Microsoft, Sony, Sega, and Nintendo. If you're an otaku and know what Hetalia Axis Powers is, then consider this series the Hetalia of Video Games.
You have the big consoles represented along with their portable counterparts (Microsoft doesn't have a portable counterpart though) and ALL of the characters are portrayed as anime styled girls, some of which obvious jiggle physics (looking at Vert/Green Heart, the XBox representative as the one with the most generous...physics). However, what sets this game apart from the rest, is that it's not a turn based game. Instead it's a hack and slash game similar to Senran Kagura (and even features the costume break mechanic of the latter, only not to such an extreme).
Plot wise, the game takes place during a lull in the fighting of the "Console War" (yeah...dead serious...this is just the beginning), which regularlly rocks the world of Gameindustri (I warned you). Basically it's not some big fate of the universe story. Rather these two journalists named Dengekiko and Famitsu (Blaitant satires of the Dengeki and Famitsu gaming magazines) are trying to write articles on the four consoles and arrange a series of quests to test the main cast and get a good idea of their performance.
The game itself is quite fun and enjoyable. The cutscenes are agonizingly long though but aside from that, the overall game is still fun. The humor is quite well played.
I do recommend you have an XBox controller for this game. It will make gameplay 10x easier than with a mouse and keyboard.

LONG REVIEW AHEAD BEWARE (TL;DR at the end)
This game is a lot of fun.  Really simple but I think that's what I find charming about it to be honest.  I originally saw it on FrozenFoxy's youtube channel and found that it was an interesting concept.  I go through bouts of playing it every now and then because deep down it's a time waster with a fair amount to do.
By no means am I an expert with this game.  I play on the easiest mode because I hate losing progress (Protip, don't dock your ship and walk away for like 20 minutes you'll still have mutiny aboard your ship LOL.)  I picked it up again recently (and played most of my gameplay recently too) and did notice that there HAVE BEEN updates.  Not a lot but there are noticeable differences from the last time I played.  TBH Don't remember when that was for a timeframe but they were updates for the better.  Honestly, the game doesn't need a lot of changes.  You go in knowing that this is a time waster with some strategy elements.
You create your campaign.  The maps are generated based on the things you select.  Create a character (cute customization etc) and Huzzah!  You're a pirate in a pixel world.
You start at a basic town.  Leave your ship as is for a while or mess around with it.  DO NOTE THAT IF YOU DO DELETE YOUR WHOLE SHIP YOU NEED TO ENSURE IT HAS AT LEAST ONE WALL PIECE WHEN YOU REBUILD.  If it hasn't got any wall pieces you can't sail.  It seems silly but part of the game IS customizing your ship so I guess it's to be expected.
Each Town has to be explored before you know what's there.  There are a variety of shops which don't show up at all towns.  Hire crew at Taverns, Food for the ship at Food, Weapons for fighting at Weapons, Items sells skills (GET CLEANING AND SWIMMING AS SOON AS POSSIBLE) and stuff like healing items, Ship sells stuff for your ship.  There are little mini quests too on bulletin boards.
Sail around, gain experience, fight stronger enemies.  Defeat the Legendary Pirates listed at the beginning.
I still haven't gotten pets or anything like that but I don't know how important that is tbh.
After you defeat enemies on a ship you can either PLUNDER (Blow up, take parts, money, etc) or You can take it as your own.  I haven't taken any either.  You get money from blowing ships up and I like the explosions.
Watch your food and moral.  You can get scurvy, wet and miserable, bleeding, etc.  Different things that affect your morale and health.
Overall I have to say give it a shot if you need something to do while you're bored.  I promise you'll realize you've just spent two hours controlling tiny pixel art pirates sailing and fighting other tiny pixel art pirates rather than sleeping.  It's charming.
Cute, Charming, Time Wasting Strategy Game.  Overall rating like idk 7.7/10.  Would lose track of time again.

HELL YEAH to HELL YEAH!!!   KILL KILL KILL!!!!!  A great indie game developed by Arkedo and published by SEGA.   Wait....does this make this indie or third party? ..... Both?  Well, alright then.~
Play as Ash, a mixture between Jumpy the Rabbit King from the cartoon Hero 108 and Laharl from Disgaea, who acts as the new ruler of Hell after his father mysteriously passes away (no, you won't find out why and the plot doesn't go that deep).  Ash rules hell with an iron paw...until one day, someone snapped photos of him f*cking a rubber ducky in a bathtub and posted them on the Internet.  Ash sees this and is infuriated to find 100 views on the article.  To quell his vengeance, he must kill 100 denizens of Hell.   Did they see the pictures?  Are they innocent?  Who cares?!  100 souls will quell his anger.  One for each view of that article.
With your primary weapon as a giant buzz-saw blade equiped with guns, rockets, grenades, lasers, etc., you can't really go wrong with killing.   Every finishing move is a mandatory minigame that often leads to a brutal demise of your victims.  Ash really is one ruthless rabbit who doesn't give a f*ck.
PROS:
Tons of ways to slaughter
Great humor
Memes here and there (spot them all)
Easy to pick up and play
Achievements  (easy 100%)
CONS:
Not worth full price ($15)
Obligatory jackpot achievement
Too short
No achievements for doing more than 10 side-missions
Some obligatory minigames can either be too easy or too repetitive (if you liked WarioWare type games, then you may enjoy it)

Only one save file
Very limited replayability (you beat the game, you can roam around, play slots or complete challenges...or DLC challenges, but that's about it. Aside from that, the only thing you can do is reset your file to get additional gameplay.)

Do you like Metroid? Do you like good Storytelling? Eerie Atmosphere? Yes, yes and yes? Then you
like Axiom Verge because it offers at least the Metroid'y parts you like and love. The game handles just like Samus on SNES, the upgrade and exploration system is quite similar while adding little interesting knacks to the powerups and their usage.
Axiom Verge is trying hard to be a homage to Metroid while struggling to define its own identity. The graphics have that distinct NES flair, even turning flickering and glitches into a smartly implemented mechanic. However the design overall more often than not looks bland and samey, alterated only by monotonous color schemes that quickly turn boring to the Samus-spoiled eye.
The soundtrack has its moments, driving the dark sci-fi shivers up your spine in rare moments. However there are also the flaws: sound assets and music parts are often unfitting, sometimes plain annoying to the ear. Music often appeared as very unfitting to the sceneries shown, taking me out of the immersion. The story offers great potential, but falls flat on its face during the later parts of the game. Boss fights look interesting at first glance, but quickly devolve into a "find the ideal position and fire away" fest.
In short: For every bit of light there are quite a lot of shadows lurking in the corner.
Overall Axiom Verge has some great ideas, but the "wow" moments are rarely spread. There's a huge load of backtracking involved and secrets are often discovered by hard trial and error instead of smart hints. The gameplay is overall fluid, without major flaws and the character controls are as tight as can be. Axiom Verge gives you 10-15h of "good" content to chew on, depending on your expertise within the genre.  If you're in desperate need for a "Metroid'y" game, give it a shot. However it's not a must-have in my book.

Don't jump straight into the campaign - this is a fairly realistic flight sim. Best way to start this game is to fly single missions in an easy to fly plane (I recommend the La-5FN) until you're comfortable with:
1. Taking off and landing
2. Performing aerobatics

It'll take a while to get comfortable, and you'll be pulling G's with sim (and real life!) pilots with 1000s of hours of flight time under their belts, but as stated in other reviews, it's a very enjoyable game once you finally straighen up and fly right.
