A fun puzzle/platformer with nice aesthetics and music.  MSF has 16 regular and 5 bonus stages, plus unlockable remixed versions of levels after you clear all the regular and bonus stages.  Game handles well and the controls are simple.  You can jump, shoot, switch and that's it.  You're always at max speed so there's no need to hold a button to run, which is always a plus.  Art is nice and clean and the soundtrack by Jake Kaufman is up-tempo and catchy.
Gameplay-wise, there's no fat.  No cut-scenes, no dialogue, no tutorials.  It feels very acadey in this sense, as most levels are designed to be beaten in a couple of minutes and are fairly compact.  There are a few variations to block-switching, but nothing too hard to grasp outside of initially figuring out how red/blue lock blocks work.  I hate red/blue lock blocks.
Each level's goal is to solve puzzles to find the five hooligan sisters scattered about.  You're not likely to find yourself annoyed at finding a missing sister since the game has a handy "pointer" system that directs you in the location of the nearest sister.  It's a simple thing but it helps keep the pace up.
The only two negatives I can see for this game are length and the last level.  Clearing the 16 normal and 5 bonus stages probably won't take more than 3-4 hours for most people.  The replayability comes from trying to "low-score"/speedrun the levels in the fastest amount of time.  If you're into that, you just added a lot of extra gameplay.  You also unlock a sort of easy mode gun by beating the game that lets you play through a number of levels in a different manner.
I'm much more about quality of gameplay over quantity, so I'd definitely rather play a 3-5 hour game that's really fun like MSF than a 12-25 hour game that's kind of okay.  If you have a "I need x amount of gameplay for every dollar spent" mentality, you'll probably find yourself cringing at the idea of paying 10 bucks for a short game like MSF, but if you don't think like that, you'll probably be happy with a full price purchase if you like puzzle/platformers.
Onto to the second negative, the last level of both the regular stages and bonus stages are pretty bad and do the terrible video game thing of taking the primary gameplay mechanic of a game and flipping it out its head.  Throughout the game, you have complete control of block switching and playing mostly compact, short stages.  For whatever reason, WayForward thought it was good idea to make the finales really long and with an automated switch mechanic.  There's also much more a focus on fast-twitch platforming and I could see people who are more interested in the puzzle part of puzzle/platformer giving up in frustration.  It also doesn't help that MSF has an archaic life system that really rears its head during the finales.  It's very annoying to get near the end of the level only to suffer a cheap death, and there are truly cheap deaths near the end of the finales, and have to start over from the beginning.  Then again, WayForward had a dumb life system in DuckTales, too.
In short,
+ a fun, nice-looking puzzle/platformer with a good soundtrack and replayability if you're into speedrunning levels.
- the last levels of both the regular and bonus modes are difficult in way the rest of the game isn't, and a short overall play time if you just one-and-done each level.

Garbage Day has an interesting concept where you'll be replaying the same day over and over again. The idea is to screw around in the world and make your own fun. The question is "are there enough to do for the player to have fun".
In the current version as of this review (Last update 25 Jan 2015), there isn't enough tools for the player to enjoy. You can pick up 1 of 5 weapons, cause some havoc, and call it a day. There is a slow motion button that you can use. It has no connection to the gameplay but is at least sort of interesting to mess around with. There's 1 car and a few dumb AI controlled NPCs. There's a wilderness area that you can discover, but there's nothing there except the edge of the map. If you walk off said edge, you fall forever. You can easily explore everything the game has to offer in a matter of minutes, and for $15, that's not reasonable.
The game is also clearly incomplete. It does get some leeway for being in Early Access, but having multiple full buildings with nothing inside, and the lack of content overall can not be excused simply because of the Early Access tag. Early Access or not, the game is incredibly incomplete, lacking in content, and even as a sandbox game, needs to have more of a focus to what it's trying to do.
Overall I did not enjoy Garbage Day. Not enough things to keep the player interested, clearly incomplete, and most will find this game boring after only minutes of play. Wait for it to be more developed before sinking any cash into this one.
Pros:
- Decent visual design
- Slow Motion is fun to play around with
Cons:
- Not enough content

Like many people, I played To the Moon before I played this game. I tried to come in without much expectations, and I even knew that it was mostly just a sit-back-and-watch "game." I mean, the title even calls it a story.
However, that ended up not quite true. A Bird Story does have you play, controlling the kid every so often, performing actions that are mostly super slow and tedious. The game basically just pops up with images of items and you have to walk somewhere in a room (or in an adjacent one), grab the item, and return to the original location. That was one piece that really bothered me and added arbitrary time to the story for not much reason at all, making the true length of A Bird Story even shorter.
Essentially, the story is rather predictable and cliche overall, despite the art direction being unique. The child, whose name we never learn because the game has no text or dialogue at all, is a rather lonely kid. He seems to have no friends, though his parent(s) do show love to him from what little we can see. And as the name implies, the game does literally involve a bird, which he befriends.
The game takes just around an hour, maybe a little more, to go through a handful of days of his life with the bird, as far as I can tell. The display is rather surreal, which is definitely a pro. For instance, as you walk around in short bits of the game, the environment will drastically change from the kid's memory, where you'll walk out a door into the forest, and then another door suddenly appears to take you into school. Trees will even move around while you're walking in a few places, forcing you down a certain path.
While I liked that art, as the kid's imagination and memory are all merging together for some uniqueness, those qualities of the game do not save it as a whole. As said above, almost no interaction from us was really worth it, considering the developers threw in many tedious or repetitive tasks, whereas To the Moon did not feel that way.
Really, the game is just trying to get people invested into the kid and his childhood. It is a teaser for the bigger sequel to To the Moon, called Finding Paradise as of right now. That is another reason that bothers me and somewhat explains why I didn't feel like the game brought anywhere near as much of an experience.
Despite the game getting some emotion from me, I think the best description of my experience is to say "I was simultaneously happy, sad, and bored."

When approaching writing this I went back and looked at my review for To The Moon; which was the other game by these Devs. That should have been warning enough for me to have not wasted my time on this. I am amazed at the good reviews. This "game" took all of my problems with the execution of their last game - then made it somehow worse.

The art style is not my thing, though I've overlooked it in the past. The clincher though is that there is no dialogue. You're just watching a poorly animated silence film where you occasionally Press E to Pay respects.
The reviews recommending implore me to spend an hour of my time playing through - I disagree. I would not recommend this to anyone.

tl;dr Not for everyone. Some may consider this pricey for a mere hour of story. I myself bought it during a sale. If on the fence for any reason, the best deal breaker: Developer supports refunds and no questions asked. Check forums for details.
Kan Gao's (the developer) use of the word "experimental" certainly describes the game well. The "gameplay" and interaction is minimal, even more so than his previous work, To the Moon. With so much of the game on auto pilot, it's hard to decide whether the entire thing should have just been that, and thus a video rather than game, or have more interaction to actually make the interaction meaningful. While the gameplay sometimes felt like it interrupted the narrative more than adding to it, there were more than a few sequences that were fun to control the character.
Its story, both in plot and execution, is worth discussing as well. It was simple enough and exactly as it says on the tin; 'a boy who found an injured bird, told through a blur between reality and imagination'. Surreal in many instances, yet relatable and interesting most of the time. Its initial few minutes were more confusing rather than intriguing, but I was invested once the titular bird appears. To be able to express a range of emotion with sprites is a commendable feat, as well as humour without any text whatsoever.
As ever, its music is a lovely accompaniment to the game and one that I will look forward to listening to in my spare time. The art and rather creative use of assets is something I hope to see more both from Kan Gao and other developers.
In summary, would I recommend the game? The thumbs up above is an obvious yes. It does come with a qualifier however; the game is definitely not for everyone. After finishing it, I was left with mixed feelings. No regret or buyer's remorse, but rather confusion as to what I just experienced. Even with that however, I'd recommend the game to people to encourage more experimentation like A Bird Story, even if they don't always work out. That Kan Gao also understand how divisive and different the game can be, offering full refunds no questions asked, is simply icing on the cake.

Pros:
+ Controls are responsive, and vehicle upgrades actually affect how your vehicle responds
+ Has free ride mode (which is most of what I do in these games)
+ AI is very balanced in difficulty, and can be very good
+ You don't have to unlock tracks in free-play
+ Can practice on any Supercross track in free-play mode
+ The different sizes of vehicles have a clearly different feel (much more difference than reflex)
Cons:
- Only one (very small) free roam map, and there is currently no modding comunity for adding more
- No cheats to unlock all bikes, so you will be grinding for a LONG time to unlock the 650's or the 50-pit bike
- No rebinding controls other than 3 premade controller layouts (although keyboard layout is quite nice)
- If you have multiple displays, the game will crash if you click outside of the game window, although alt-tabbing works fine
- Still has quite a few crashes
- haven't seen many updates since I've started playing the game
- Only looks marginally better than other MX vs ATV games, and in some cases actually looks worse.
- Menu's look much worse than Reflex (looks like they were from the PS2)
- No trucks or UTV's!
Other Notes:
The new clutch system is very odd, and can get you going much faster than you could in other games, and get you into rhythems that would have otherwise been impossible to get into, but if you don't know about it, then racing will be very hard for you as the AI almost always use it.
If there was one thing I would love the Dev's to add, it would be map support from other games in free-ride mode, or just more free-ride maps.
Verdict:
If you liked the Supercross modes from other MX vs ATV games, you'll like this game, because that is 90% of the game. If you were more like me and only ever played the free-ride from the other games (30+ hours of it on reflex on steam and 50+ hours on disc version of reflex) then you might want to pick up Reflex, as I had much more fun with it. The only redeeming quality of the game for me was the different bikes (didn't touch the ATV's). There is actually a variety of sizes of MX bikes that change how you play the game.

It's not my intention to insult anyone,  i'm just being honest and critical.   This game's physics feel like they've been dumbed down for children the ages of 3-5.  Any connection to real-world physics is lost here, unfortunately.   This is a problem in previous titles but here it's gone into turbo mode.   I dare say that this game isn't as fun as the original ExciteBike stand-up arcade game.  At least there you had control and things made sense.  Then there's the speed of this game.  It's mind-numbingly slow movements combined with the way the physics make no sense leaves me feeling a bit sick after just a few minutes of playing.
The graphics options...there are none.   I mean NONE.  Not even a screen size resolution option.  Not even a Full Screen option.  It starts (and stays) in 'windowed mode' at what looks like 1280x720.  The only way to get Full Screen is to Maximize the game window in the Task Manager.    The quality of the graphics is absolutely unacceptable in this day and age.   It's probably one of the worst looking and worst playing motocross game i've ever played.
Worth $24.00?  Absolutely not!  Real wotrh (using other Steam games and prices as a guide) - $4.
Unless they're considering a full replacement of everything in this game,  don't buy it.
There is one thing positive, though... The power the clutch has at low speeds is just right.  If Reflex had that i'd be happy with that game.

Blade Kitten is alright, I guess.
You play as Kit Ballard, a pink haired cat girl who is unfortunately not my girlfriend. Kit is a breaker, which is a bounty hunter, I don't know why they didn't just call her a bounty hunter, maybe due to her close resemblance to Dog the bounty hunter, they wanted to avoid a lawsuit. Kit is also apparently a comic book character, I have not read the comics, but they are probably a treat
Look at you sitting at the table, Marmaduke. Who are you to do that? You're just a dog.
In Blade Kitten, Kit arrives on the planet Hollow Wish in search of a bounty, go figure. But unfortunately, her bounty chip (card?) is stolen by a rival who is, sadly, also not my girlfriend, and Kit has to get it back. What happens after is a journey across Hollow Wish to both get your stuff back, stop the Sols (I think they're called the Sols), and track down your bounty.
The game uses a typical side scrolling jump and fight collectathon style. Kit, being a cat girl, is very nimble and can move around the terrain easily, and probably do that think where cats lick their legs and it sticks out all weird and stuff. This is the part where I talk about the environment.
The game, althought colorful, has rather generic set pieces for you to prowl along through. See what I did there? Cause she's a cat.

Kit's manages to get her personality across, but other than that, a bunch of her lines seem ham fisted or half heartily delivered. Much like the gameplay, it is stiff like the whiskey I fix myself every morning to help me forget. Why did I let them die?
And further mo- Wait, that's it? It's over? That was like... Two hours. Oh, there's an episode two coming soon, when did this game come out?
2010? Get out of here.
I guess you can say this game is short of purrfect. It's nothing to write home about, but it's also nothing to hate. If you can get this game for...Three dollars or so, you'll probably be good to go.

Let me start by saying I was wary of this game because I was afraid it was just going to be a "Oh look an anime girl with cat ears and a tail bouncing around doing vaguely action-y things and saying stuff like "nyan" every time she gets hit!!! How cute!!!". I was so happy to be wrong!
I love this game, the acrobatic platforming is so addictive. I love that Kit (the protag) is taken seriously as a character and is still cute and tough while not being turned into a fan-service joke.
Some of the problems I had with this game however is that this game has a LOT of controls to keep track of and almost no tutorial. I was playing on keybroad and almost all of the default controls were useless when I first started. I had to manually set all of them, which isn't that big of a deal. (I do strongly recommend playing with a controller though.)
Secondly the pacing of the story felt a bit rushed, in the beginning it was hard to keep track of what exactly was happening due to the fact that you're on to the next thing so quickly, the pervious thing was barely explained at all. But such is the life of a galatic bounty hunter I guess.
I only experienced one glitch in this game, and it was when you're blowing up the floor to get to a lower level of a temple (level 6 I believe). There was a pillar I couldn't move past, and I thought I had to do something to get it to move, but when I couldn't figure out what that something was (after about 20 minutes of screwing around) I decided to take a break and exitd the game. When I re-entered the game I found I could simply walk past that pillar that I was blocked by before. Turns out it was suppose to be part of the background, but like I said simply restarting the game fixed the problem and it was right after a save point anyway so no loss.
Overall:
Pro's: fun and addictive platforming, cute cartoony style while still taking the story line seriously and being respectful of all the characters.
Con's: pacing felt a bit rushed, default controls are wonky if you're using a keybroad.

Excellent game with a really great soundtrack (As expected from Jake Kaufman) and nice and colorful HD graphics. It's mostly a platforming game although it quickly goes into puzzle territory thanks to its mechanics.
The story is more of an excuse-plot so you're not going to find a deep storyline here, not like it's really needed though as the gameplay is quite engaging. Basically you're a cop named Patricia Wagon and your objective through 95% of the game is to capture 5 different sexy prisoners scattered across the stage. To do that you have a pellet gun (That is mostly used to break some blocks or detonate bombs) and the ability to switch "dimensions" which causes transparent blocks to become tangible and viceversa. The switching is what helps you move through most of the stages and solve puzzles.
Controls are quite simple, one button to jump, one to shoot, one to switch dimensions and one extra button you can hold to move the camera and scout the nearby area before moving on. Physics are great and the game is pretty fair when it comes to level design so whenever you lose is mostly your fault although be prepared for the latter stages as you'll need quick reflexes to get through many of the puzzles. Note that unlike most platformers holding or pressing the jump button has no difference, you'll still jump the same height.
The game has a total of 16 initial stages and upon finishing them you'll then have to go through 5 more bonus stages. If you finish those then another whole batch of 16 stages + 5 bonus stages will become available. Thers are FAR harder versions of the previous batch with remixed music, colors.
The game looks quite short at first but if you're willing to go towards 100% completion then you can sink 10 hours into it with ease as each stage has a PAR time to beat and beating them all requires you to master the mechanics of the game. In fact, playing the game just to beat it and not caring about the PAR times greatly reduces the overall experience.
Worth mentioning again: The soundtrack is AMAZING.

Mighty Switch Force! Hyper Drive Edition is a puzzle platformer.  You take on the role of Patricia Wagon, a cool robot cop that’s charged with bringing in the Hooligan Sisters.  The goal in each stage to capture all 5 sisters in the level and then proceed to the exit.  The gameplay comes first so if you were expecting much in the story department you might be disappointed.  The main gameplay gimmick involves switching blocks into and out of existence.  This creates some interesting puzzles that can give your brain a work out on your first play through.  There are 42 levels, each with wonderful level design and all can be cleared in under 5 minutes, some in under 30 seconds.  This is one of those games where half the fun is speed running levels and going for the fastest times.  In fact this version, unlike the Wii U version, also offers a leaderboard so you can compete with your friends and players from all over the world, which adds a whole new layer of fun.  It’s also worth noting the top notch soundtrack which alone is worth the price of admission.  The art is also fantastic with beautiful backdrops and wonderfully animated characters full of charm.

I might be a bit premature on the review for Mighty Switch Force! Hyper Drive Edition.  I've only played just over an hour so far, and if the level count is any indication I'm about half way through the incidents (incidents being levels).  I don't know if there is more, but the level count seems a little bit light.
If I were to summarize the rest of this review I would say this game is very well done, and I think it is a good game, but because of the nature of the game play I don't much care for it.  If I had known what it would be like to play before hand, I wouldn't have bought it.
At its core, this is a puzzle platformer, which I think is the genre it's tagged as.  It's a very well done game, but I do wish there was a way to distinguish between timing puzzle platformers and other styles.  This one is a timing platformer, with many bits reminiscent of the barrel cannon sequences in the old Donkey Kong Country games.  However, while I enjoyed those back in the day, I'm not a big fan of these ones.
The basic controls are that you run, jump and shoot much like you would in something like a megaman game.  However, shooting the bad guys isn't the focus.  The focus comes from a button that switches the state of things on the screen, which you can do whenever you want.  When a thing is switched off it is effectively not there.  If it is switched on it is a platform you can stand on and will block anything from walking past.  If you switch them on while something (including yourself) is standing in front of it, that creature will be killed with an amusing animation of them smashing into the screen of your monitor.
The first puzzles you'll come across feature you needing to switch the platforms so that they are physical when you land on them.  This will often need to be done while you're in the air, having jumped from the last platform you switched on.
Another thing you'll find are launcher blocks.  If anything is standing in front of them when they get turned on that creature (or yourself if it's you) will be launched in the direction of the arrow.  These are the sequences that reminded me of the DK Country barrel cannons and they have come to feature quite prominently.  You need to time your switch changes so that when you're flying through the air you get caught in another launch block that will launch you in the right direction.  Often times your target block is not visible from where you're launching from and you'll either need lightning reflexes, or to try again and again until you get it right.
There is a system of checkpoints and lives.  You have three "lives" when you start, and you can never have more then three.  Each time you get hit you lose a life.  If you land on spikes or activate a block while you're standing in front of it you lose a life and respawn at the last checkpoint.  There are pickups you can find to restore one life heart at a time.  Checkpoints come in the form of little dogs that you walk past, and you can activate then as many times as you wish, but you'll only ever have one checkpoint active at a time.  If you exhaust your "lives" you are booted back to the main menu to begin the level again.
All in all, it is a solid and well made game.  I just don't care for the gameplay, and that is more about me then it is about this game.  If anything I've described sounds like fun to you, you should buy this.

tl;dr Not for everyone. Some may consider this pricey for a mere hour of story. I myself bought it during a sale. If on the fence for any reason, the best deal breaker: Developer supports refunds and no questions asked. Check forums for details.
Kan Gao's (the developer) use of the word "experimental" certainly describes the game well. The "gameplay" and interaction is minimal, even more so than his previous work, To the Moon. With so much of the game on auto pilot, it's hard to decide whether the entire thing should have just been that, and thus a video rather than game, or have more interaction to actually make the interaction meaningful. While the gameplay sometimes felt like it interrupted the narrative more than adding to it, there were more than a few sequences that were fun to control the character.
Its story, both in plot and execution, is worth discussing as well. It was simple enough and exactly as it says on the tin; 'a boy who found an injured bird, told through a blur between reality and imagination'. Surreal in many instances, yet relatable and interesting most of the time. Its initial few minutes were more confusing rather than intriguing, but I was invested once the titular bird appears. To be able to express a range of emotion with sprites is a commendable feat, as well as humour without any text whatsoever.
As ever, its music is a lovely accompaniment to the game and one that I will look forward to listening to in my spare time. The art and rather creative use of assets is something I hope to see more both from Kan Gao and other developers.
In summary, would I recommend the game? The thumbs up above is an obvious yes. It does come with a qualifier however; the game is definitely not for everyone. After finishing it, I was left with mixed feelings. No regret or buyer's remorse, but rather confusion as to what I just experienced. Even with that however, I'd recommend the game to people to encourage more experimentation like A Bird Story, even if they don't always work out. That Kan Gao also understand how divisive and different the game can be, offering full refunds no questions asked, is simply icing on the cake.

Detail and opportunity lie in every corner of Dishonored. Even though the story is rather standard, the gameplay and level design are woven together so perfectly that it's easily forgiveable. Every location has an authentic atmosphere that amps the immersion to 11. The game can be rather short if you play guns blazing, but Dishonored doesn't have a reputation for being a combat focused game, does it? Stealth is the way to go here, choking out npcs, hiding them in dumpsters, and stealing every last coin hiding behind them. It's far more rewarding to play the levels slowly, gathering coins, upgrades, and side objectives. There is a lot of replayability that comes from choosing a different "power path." For your first playthrough, you may want to play nonlethal (as possible) with stealth powers and gadgets. For the second you may use lethal powers and gadgets. The third, try no powers and only gadgets.
If I can reccomend Dishonored with a $60 price tag, I can easily reccomend it for $10. Check it out

Why does Kimmy have no negative reviews? This is a good question, and one I asked myself on starting it. The text is slow with no way to skip and the gameplay is a bit ragged, involving reproducing the rules of various children's games to others in order to play them. None of the awesome alternate rule sets are valid.
At just about the time that I was about to quit and leave a negative review, however, I was sucked into the storyline. The children that you play with tell you their cares, and the overall setting is very nostalgic, making for a very comfortable way to tell a story that's still not so light in tone. There were portions that I still had issues with, but the storylines more than made up for them.
EDIT: Actually, there are negative reviews? I have no idea why the page says there are only 12.

Kimmy is a young girl who recently escaped her porch harness to wander the streets of 1964.  Dana finds her and takes daytime ownership of the girl.
This low pressure visual novel gives a rare look at white Americana back in the 1960s.  There are some missteps in some of the writing that makes characters seem awkward even for children.
When considered as a whole, this game does a sincere job building its world to tell a story, but it's unclear who this story would be for.

Man... Kimmy caught me off guard. I was appreciating its simple, sentimental approach to storytelling for the first half. Most of the characters are children, they have weird uninformed biases, they don't understand nuanced concepts and opinions, but they're kids. They act like real kids, and even the annoying/dumb ones have a reason for acting the way they do. It was only in Kimmy's second half that this became apparent and what starts off as simple and nostalgic turns macabre and dark.
It reminds me a lot of Stand by Me. I remember watching that movie like 15 times one summer, I was probably 12 or 13 years old and I found myself so enamored and entranced by how beautifully it captured the uneasiness and anxiety of growing up. Children can be mean for seemingly no reason, but they can also do the right thing for no greater reason than "it seems right". Kimmy drove that point home really well, they beg the question "Are people born cruel, or do they learn it?". I found myself thinking that before it was explicitly stated. Kimmy's writing is implicit in a way that I really loved. I found myself swept away by these characters I didn't have much attachment to at first, as I saw more and more of myself and people I knew grewing up in their dialogue. They're not caricatures or full-blown stereotypes, these are kids growing into adulthood, forming their own views and ideals.
When Kimmy started to reveal more of its adult world, I really started to love it. I felt this increasing sense of sadness wash over me, because I knew that it was only going to become more difficult to stomach. It creates a real sense of anxiety in such a short amount of time, and it just clicked so suddenly. If you had a difficult childhood concerning your friends and/or family, then you will probably get swept away too. Kimmy is legitimately great towards its second half, and I can definitely recommend it to anyone who liked Stand by Me or coming of age stories with a real-world perspective.

This is a platforming, beat 'em up game that doesn't quite get either aspect right.
None of the platforming is really that tricky, and there are no (or so few I've forgotten about them) bottomless pits and such, so the platforming isn't dangerous. And the super narrow perches you sometimes need to land on avoid being frustrating by automatically landing on them when you jump in their vicinity, which is almost worse, because it removes all of the challenge (except the challenge of getting caught in a wierd bug where you're suspended midair). Starting off the game with double jump and the ability to wall/ceiling climb on pretty much everything provides an opportunity to explore the rather large levels, but this is slightly hampered by lack of direction, which means you don't know if you're about to find an optional collectible, or just the next part of the stage. On top of this, there are times when progressing beyond certain points cuts you off from backtracking without warning.
As for the combat, the character controls a floating sword that follows her around, which is a small departure from conventional combat. Your basic attacks are a flurry of short range attacks, which you can direct in pretty much any direction around you, or a slightly slower flurry of long range attacks that are limited to more or less straight left and right. The blade strikes can pass through platforms, which makes for a safe way to dispatch enemies on platforms above you. The long range attack can also stab enemies and draw them closer, although it doesn't necessarily prevent them from attacking you in that half-second between releasing them and starting the follow up attack. There is also a ground-pound type of attack which is powerful, if a little slow, and sliding does damage as well (often taking out enemies more quickly than the sword). The problem is there is a very limited selection of enemies, so the combat, which isn't super interesting to begin with, quickly becomes very boring (at least, when it's not frustrating you with suprisingly long stun-lock attacks from enemies).
There is a story. I have no idea what it is. There are cutscenes between each level presumably letting you know what's going on, but the events and the protagonist's motivation are so loosely connected throughout that I have no idea what the current goal is, much less the end one. Repeatedly I feel like I've been thrown into an existing universe/franchise that makes zero effort to explain any context. One level begins in a ruined city with the protagonist seeing an alien and exclaiming "Not Darques! Not here!" That's all the explanation you get. It's apparently a horror themed level, because at various points you get brief nightmarish cutscenes, and the level ends with you getting after falling into a pit of the creatueres, you get KO'ed, but somehow wake up in a merchant camp outdoors to start the next level. A different level has you deliver a message to the commander of the mooks that have been your nearly exclusive enemies to that point, because, they're being attacked by someone else? And some of them will still attack you anyway.
Have I mentioned yet that the money you collect throughout the game is used in a second pause menu that the game doesn't tell you about until four levels in?
This whole game feels like a whole bunch of half thought out ideas mashed together.

After the sheer joy I had (for the most part) with their previous game "Deadly Sin 2", I figured I'd finally sit down and give this game a go, as it had been sitting in my Steam library for a long, long time after I'd bought it for a couple of bucks during a huge sale.
Let me say, boy, had I paid full price for this game, I'd be♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off. This game is SHORT. My playtime at completion is 5.4hrs, an hour of which was almost defintely spent AFK with the game running. Could I have done all the side quests? Of course, but the real issue here is the point of no return is just sprung on you out of nowhere. Imagine this, you're playing the game, greatly enjoying the story, then suddenly out of the blue you get notified that "you can't turn back from here" and you're thinking "surely just for this quest, right?". Well no, literally before you know it, the game is just over, and it feels rushed. For the content this game has to offer, I feel that the $14.99 price tag is vastly overpriced, but if you manage to get it 50% off or more, then its a decent bargain.
So, why am I giving the game a positive rating? For that exact reason, I got it on sale. Most things the game does, it does well. A fair amount of new things were added or fixed from Deadly Sin 2:
- You can augment gear while wearing it this time around, instead of having to unequip it first, which was a huge pain.
- Carries over the same quest system/log, that I found to be a nice touch in DS2.
- Crafting your own gear.
- Visible enemies on the map. No more random encounters every 6 seconds.
- "Mining" resources for crafting/augmenting gear.
- Option to disable the mouse.
- Actually has Steam achievements.
- Job branches (Pro Tip: Sniper is grossly overpowered).
Aside from being short, there aren't a whole lot of things to complain about, but here are a few:
- When crafting, you can't see how many items you actually have to craft with. A bit irritating!
- Items/Spell names are almost exactly the same from DS2. This just feels super lazy to me.
- Characters no longer visible during battle like they were in DS2. Now you just have character "cards".
Overall, I feel the story here is much better than "Deadly Sin 2", and there was SOOOOO much missed potential with this game in terms of plot development and lore exploration.
TLDR: Buy it on a super sale and you'll enjoy it for an afternoon/evening.
Sidenote: If you even remotely want a challenge, I'd suggest playing on hard and not upgrading your classes from the ones you start with, though even then the game is probably still too easy.

Let me point out something else instead: AXIOM VERGE is trippy. The right kind of trippy too. They totally chanelled Tsutomu Nihei's BLAME and BIOMEGA mangas in terms of story and aesthetics. People are calling this Metroidvania-style, but I don't think so. This feels way more like a pure Metroid game than anything. Gameplay wise, your character's strength is defined by the items they find; no amount of killing will make you healthier or faster. However, there's a massive amount of weapons that makes fights enjoyable, and exploration tools that open up the world around you, with pickups that increase your health, damage, weapon range and even projectile size, so exploration is well-rewarded. The main issue with this is that a good 20% of the items can only be found with one end-game item, and finding the right areas to plunder can become a massive hassle if you aim for 100%
The story was intriguing enough to keep me going to the credits. One scene near the midsection played out rather well, with the gameplay changing to match the character's state of mind... somewhat. I'd describe the ending, but I'd rather avoid spoilers so let's say that, on a personal note, I wasn't a fan. However, I liked the game's use of graphical glitches as a gameplay and story element, and was very pleased that the player-character, Trace, doesn't
remark on how the glitches reminds him of things he saw in a video game he once played. It's all played straight, with mentions of "artifacts" and "The Breach" being things that affect the world in unnatural ways.
The game-map is pretty big, or at least it
big. There's lots of things to be found, as was mentioned in the first paragraph, and returning to old areas with new tools not only makes exploration fun, but makes killing once-annoying enemies with new weapons all the more fulfilling to one-shot. One of my main gripes with the game (along with what makes me not want to dub it "Metroidvania") is that you have no method of warping to places late in the game; your main method of fast travel is to make for the hub-corridor and catch a ride with a local monstrosity. Which is pretty neat in how streamlined it is, but with the way lore is presented, I'm surprised there wasn't a way to get taken to specific save-points around the world. There's also an annoying habit of having secret areas hidden behind blocks that are identical to other blocks, so you'll spend a lot of time hugging walls near the end.
Sound is good. Music loops similar to how old PS1 games used MP3 tracks in that they finished the song, then played it again after a moment's silence. I wouldn't call it stuck-in-my-head-for-days memorable, seeing as it's mainly ambience. But the final boss fight is easily the exception, and I'm sure it'll find its way onto playlists here and there. One track ended up grating thanks to either dying and returning to a save point over and over again, or just revisiting said area and slowly losing patience for what started out as a really cool track. As a plus, if you go into low HP values, the game will do the usual "bdeep-bdeep" thing, but it's in time with the music, and will slowly dip in volume so that you're not being assaulted by "
" like some annoying £5 alarm clock.
There's also an optional Speedrun mode that adds a timer and cuts out story and "randomised" elements so you can try to beat the game as quickly as possible. It's something I might use, and I'm sure others would be pleased to see it.
I'll add in as a disclaimer that I got the game as a birthday gift so the value of the game is a bit nebulous. But I would easily recommend the game to people with £15 knocking around, if they're a fan of older 2D Metroid games. For anyone else, I'd say check out gameplay videos first.

First off, before anything.... I KNOW IT"S ON PC BUT FOR THE LOVE OF GOD USE A CONTROLLER. Just trust me, the way the game's built it feels so much better that way.
Okay now that that's been established... the actual gameplay.
The Reflex system IS in this game, but if the last game you played was Reflex, well, it handles a little differently, so be prepared. The rider control influences the bike a lot more in turns, you can easily accidentally 180-360 degree turn your bike if you aren't careful. Other than that, the responsiveness is a lot better and feels a lot more like your rider has weight. It does make the physics system a little wonky if you ignore the rider control though, as the bike feels a lot more like a slippery brick, Rainbow has done a wonderful job of weighting these systems together and the rider and bike feel separate and together at the same time (unlike Reflex where they often felt more separate than anything else).
Vehicle customization returns and changing off stock parts does change the performance of the bike/atv, although the fine tuning from Reflex is not there, (I'm very sad about this).
The AI still crashes into you, but it won't throw you off your ride. It actually drives like it isn't trying to commit a murder suicide constantly, although the AI doesn't compensate for slipperiness on the ATVs so be prepared to see more than one com flying at you from another track section. Other than that, it's no more easy or difficult, you just won't be forcibly wiped out by the AI every 10 secs if you get stuck in the group.
Your Bike is also more sturdy now, or at least it feels more sturdy (I've been told it's slipperry though if you don't pull back on the rider to increase traction), and wiping out isn't quite as easy unless you throw the bike and rider hard in one direction or ram your front wheel into the ground when landing. The actual Reflex (QTE to stay on the bike from Reflex game) is gone making some landings that seem like they should throw you off strange when they would have thrown the QTE to recover in your face before, you now have to recover (or break your riders neck) with your own decisions, the bike will not auto-recover via magical Analog stick flick anymore.
And finally we also see the return of the 50cc class. That's random but it's so fun.
Overall Score:
Pros-
- The Reflex system, after a minor adjustment period, feels a lot better
- The core gameplay is still there, however it leans heavily on the reflex system rather than steering.
- Bike customization affects performance to a degree
- Your placement is still determined more by the lines you picked and your ability to control the bike than your ability to out run the AI with blind speed. In fact, blind speed will  lose the race a lot of the time, even on rookie.
- There are 34 tracks. 17 Supercross, 12 National, and 5 Rhythm
- You can wear a chicken mask as a helmet
Cons
- The Gameplay is a bit more nuanced and weighted towards the rider than before. As such it feels very clunky if you ignore the rider controls.
- Bike can feel slippery and underperforming to new players. This is fixed with parts which are unlocked during play easily.
- Fine tuning is gone
Overall 7.5/10 It's good.

If you're a flight simulationr buff looking for an excellent WWII flight sim, look no further. This is the best one you'll find. Though it looks a tad clunky at first glance, it's the most accurate WWII flight sim you'll find. It's also got a tremendous amount of content, made virtually limitless by the mission designer available therein.

The best $10 you can possibly spend on Steam. This game is incredible. You won't find many other games that can match the challenge that IL-2 presents. The tactical depth is infinite and the difficulty is high but the satisfaction of improving your skills is immense. This is a hardcore flight simulator, so don't expect a shallow learning curve. Speed, accuracy and finesse with the controls are a must. Situational awareness is equally critical, as are reflexes, decisionmaking and tactical analysis, teamwork and communication, etc. The demands are high, but the reward is great. Of course you also have to fly your plane; proper engine management is very important, as is a basic understanding of aerodynamics and flight physics.. However, while the game DOES expect alot from you, it does also strike a near-perfect balance by introducing the challenge of a flight simulator while avoiding overly-complicated modern avionics and difficult-to-learn computer systems. cont'd..

"Kimmy is a visual novel game about a young babysitter in 1968". You play as Dana, who runs across Kimmy thinking she is her child. She then agrees to look after her, throughout the summer holidays. Your main goal is playing games with other kids to make Kimmy friends, but the main focus of the story is much darker.
I definitely would use the term "visual novel" over "game", because there is barely any gameplay involved. The whole focus of the game is the story - geting to know the relationships between the characters, and the secrets behind Kimmy's family.
With the budget of 25 cents a day for babysitting Kimmy, you can buy game pieces. This is where the "gameplay" comes in - you have to explain to the other kids various street games. It all comes from previous knowledge of popular games, and a couple of games I had never heard of took a couple of attempts. I didn't have much fun at these segments personally, because they were quite boring and I think it could of been better if their were actually minigames that you play instead.
The ending was genuinely sad and moving, because you feel so attached to all the characters by the end. The speech from the kids is so perfect, and the game is so realistic that it creates an immersive experience.
It's also unlike any other game I have experienced. I have never played a 'visual novel'so didn't know what to expect. Although at first I was dissapointed, when I found out the street games were really just you having to test your knowledge of the rules, it somehow gripped me with it's unusual plot.
I have just finished my first playthrough, with exactly 2 hours of playtime in one sitting, but I didn't have time to talk to all the kids so I think I missed about half the dialogue. This isn't much content for 7 pounds - so I would argue that it's overpriced - but the game felt like it was the right length. If you're interested I would recommend picking it up on sale.

The latest game from designer Nina Freeman (Cibele, Tacoma), Kimmy is a visual novel with a quirky style courtesy of artist Laura Knetzger (who had also worked with Nina on Freshman Year). The game is very simple to play, with the player primarily making a few choices through dialogue and who to interact with. You play as Dana, who becomes a babysitter to younger girl Kimmy. During the days that you babysit, you have a limited amount of time to play with other kids, buy toys and games, and learn more about the residents of your town. As with many of Nina Freeman’s games, what appears on the surface to be a normal 1960’s summer is in fact a dark, mature tale of the struggles that many families face. The game moves along at a good pace, taking you from interaction to interaction without much fuss and hardly a single wasted word throughout the entire game. It is very interesting to see the world through the eyes of a young girl at that time – I can’t think of any other game where the player takes the role of a middle-school-aged-girl.
Overall, it is a very interesting and impactful game that doesn’t take too long to tell its story. If you are a big fan of story in games, or just find this premise interesting, I’d definitely recommend picking Kimmy up! There is a demo on Steam, and the game is available on PC and Mac.

As the game went on, I found myself increasingly disinterested in it. In fact, a few of the hours I've logged in this game have been spent on the pause menu as I got so bored I started doing other things instead.
The music is pretty good, and level design isn't half bad. At times it feels like a (good) Crash Bandicoot game, even to the point I'd call it fun! However, that's about all this game does well.
The game has a currency/upgrade system, which is fine until you realize there's only one weapon worth getting. Most of your money goes into stamina upgrades, as the alternate costumes are bland and uninteresting. Health upgrades should normally be as effective as stamina boosts, but the only times your health hits zero are instant-death situations.
Most of the combat in this game revolves around hitting the attack button until something happens. If you don't have the (very inexpensive, you can get it during the first level) final sword, almost every attack will bounce off and you have to use 'special' attacks which consist of swinging your sword out a bit further and sliding. There's also a ground-pound attack that takes far too much stamina to use.
Platforming in this game relies mostly on physics. That's not a good thing. You often find yourself stuck on a wall, pushed through the level, or outright unable to run and jump. The game has an aspect of velocity to it that doesn't make much sense in an action platformer. The entire game feels like a poorly programmed ice level with a stamina bar.
Nitpicking time? Nitpicking time. There's a section at the end of the game where you're forced to climb long sections of walls while flying bugs attack you. Being attacked while climbing makes you fall. There are enemies with shields that can deal minor damage while stunlocking you, and if there are two surrounding you then you'd better hope you didn't buy any health upgrades. It's best just to run past them as you need to use a special grab attack to take away their shield. Special attacks take stamina, also known as the make-the-game-go-by-faster meter.
The final boss is well designed. Brings together a culmination of the game's essentials: climbing, running, jumping, and attacking. However it's heavily dampened by the horribly annoying four or so lines of dialogue being constantly spewed and the fact that all of the things I just mentioned are broken. I ended up exiting the game and watching the ending on youtube for a sense of finality. The plot's not even that great, considering you have to read the (not so good by any means) comic series that the game neglects to tell you about.
Overall it's a good port in terms of additional content and playability, but you can't just paint a brick wall red and call it art.

The story presentation is done through animated cutscenes instead of stills or simply the in-game character models. The voice acting is also excellent, which makes for watching them a much more enjoyable experience.
The game can feel a bit short, but the amount of unlockables and exploration greatly make this game worthy of revisits and its replayability makes it much more inviting.

+ Art style is nice to look at. Cel shading will age well and always give a nice clean look.
- Some of the murky sections with the pale greens and brown looked out of place.
+ A wide variety of combat and movement mechanics. Can lead to interesting platforming and fights.
- Controls feel sluggish, especialy when enemies hit you. Most of their attacks will stun you, which will lead to very slow and frustrating fights, especially when you get swarmed by enemies all stunning you with their multiple attacks.
+ Excellent audio. The sound effects work and the soundtrack is awesome. I've listened to the OST a couple of times for fun.
- Voice acting can be a little annoying at times, especially with the main shopkeeper. His accent will really get to you and his dialogue can get really repetitive. More variety in his dialogue and an accent easier on the ears would've been much nicer.
+ The game features 13 levels, 4 different blades, 13 costumes and 10 passive upgrades. This all adds up to more content than usually expected for such a cheap game. Additionally, more content is on the way when Episode 2 release.
- The following is what I find the most annoying about the game. While the levels are open, which is nice, the are littered with the ingame currency, treasure chests and a multitude of collectibles. The game for me went from a fun action-filled light-hearted adventure, to a game about walking to every single corner of each level, making sure that I hadn't missed some sort of collectable. I don't enjoy spending all of my time searching for the 142 Treasure Chests, 20 Skiffs, 20 Datapaks and the seemingly infinite amount of hex across every level. Sure, a couple of treasure chests for each level would've been great. It would've been fun exploring each location for that 1 or those 2 treasure chests, however, having 142 makes every single one seem sort of meaningless. That's not even taking into account the other 40 collectables that you have to find. I feel that this game could've easily been much better if there were far less collectables. I eventually just gave up crawling around every location to collect every Hex, and instead tried just running through every level. I found that much more enjoyable.
If you enjoy the Blade Kitten Webcomics or you are a fan of sidescrollers, you will probably enjoy this. For everyone else, just expect a few hours of fun. There are a few minor problems, as listed above, that could be easily fixed. Change the colours of some areas. Change the effects of most of the enemy attacks so most of them don't stun the player. Change the voice actor for the shopkeeper and give him more lines of dialogue. I doubt that fixing these should take up too much time, and in my opinion it will bump up the game from a 6 or 7/10 to a 7 or 8/10.
The biggest problem, in my opinion, is that there are collectables scattered everywhere, and too much of my time playing the game was spent look for every single one of theses. I gave up in the end, but making the levels smaller and reducing the amount of collectables could allow the players to focus their time on the combat, platforming and story. Still allow some exploration, and keep a few collectables, but having 182 things to find over 13 levels is too overwhelming, and just makes the game kind of boring. Fixing this, along with the minor problems, would make this game a solid 8/10, or even possibly a 9/10. For now, the game is 7/10 from me.

This is a bit of a hard one to reccomend, just because it is such a niche thing. The game is in the style of the Senran Kagura games, but with the charm and setting of Hyperdimension, but it doesn't play as well as them. The gameplay very quickly (pretty much right after the tutorial) becomes "hit quick attack until you have a 4000 combo and win" on every level. The game also does away with all the rpg aspects of the previous games sans item equiping-though without item crafting- and basic leveling. Story is also very thread bare, being the shortest of the Hyperdimension games on PC and just sort of putting an enemy there and saying "oh no, shes invincible, better keep doing the same type of missions over and over again until we have this power to kill her." Also, in the fashion of this series, you have seen most of the enemies and all of these levels before.
But I still recomend it, because if you have played any of the previous games in the series, you know what you are in for if you watch a gameplay trailer. It has the characters you love from this series. It has the self referential and self aware comedy of the series. It has the same enemies and levels from the series. It is just like all the other games in this series, just with a different way of playing it. I enjoyed my time with the game, and absolutely recomend getting if you are okay with spending $30 on 7-10 hours of gameplay. If not, I highly recommend getting it on sale, as I did.

Hyperdimension Neptunia U Action Unleashed is an action game set in the Neptunia universe. If you like the regular RPG games, then you will likely enjoy this one as well. It isn’t as good, for a couple of reasons. Firstly, it has more action, but a lot less plot and I like the stories in the other games better. There’s not even multiple endings to explore. Secondly, the fighting can get a little too repetitive, especially when grinding the final few achievements.
It is still worth checking out, but I can’t be as enthusiastic as I was with the other games.

Hyperdimension Neptunia is a series of games which does what it intends to do extremely well: Advertise skimpily clad anime girls!
The game is largely about a group of girls and their younger sisters who set out to become....Well pretty much cute cuddly teddy bear murderers for hire? Honestly, as with many Japanese storylines, I can't make heads or tails of it. It seems to be sort of all over the place.
The only thing truly consistent about it, though, is that girls strip and kill a whoooole lotta cute things, for reasons I cannot even begin to comprehend. Trust me, I googled it, and I still don't understand.
So instead of trying to put a logic lable on this game, I'll just put an 18+ on it instead.
Graphics wise, the game is mediocre at best. There's little to no shaders in the game, and the enemies are all large or small cookie cutter editions of themselves. Really not at all impressive.
The art style, however, is a whole lot different. It's wonderfully drawn, and clearly the artist(s) knew what they were doing when making these scenes and characters.
Voice acting for English is, as per usual, awkward and kinda crappy. I don't suggest playing this in English. Then again I didn't even check if there IS a Japanese version....Well if there is, use it. There's no way it's worse than the English dub.
There...really is little to nothing else for me to say about this...I mean what did you expect? This is literally one, maybe one and a half, steps above Sakura Clicker. It's a bunch of girls, with powers inspired by some 60 year old tech-♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ person's ideas of what technology and computers are about, whose clothes are the CHEAPEST knockoff crap I've ever seen, considering just how easily it breaks! If you can actually fill an entire review with useful, concrete information to give about a game whose entire selling point is that it caters to the weeaboos need for skimpy waifu material, then you seriously need to re-evaluate your life.

Maybe I'd feel better if the enemies didn't look like they want to hug you. I can only recommend this game to real Neptunia fans. I have 180 hours in the game and I love it.  At first I sucked at melee and now I'm halfway decent although I still get owned by most good players.  The game as is can host 75 vs 75 combat in a capture the flag type gameplay.  Its very addicting and very fun.  You have attributes to level up.  You can get to lvl 10 and for each level you gain one attribute.  This can be placed in damage, hit points, speed, attack speed.  Also there are many different weapons and armours that you can unlock.  For example there is helmet, chest, feet, gloves, shield, 1 hand weapons, 2 hand weapons, bows.  This game is in development so its by no means a finished product.  The epic is supposed to be released soon which will offer a ton more game play and a lot more players that currently play crpg and other medieval games will flock back here.  The combat is very fluid.  Its easy to pick up but hard to master.  You use left mouse to attack and depending on where you have your mouse (the direction) depends where you will swing.  To block is similar.  You have poke attack, right and left attack,  right and left high and low and overhead smash.  You can also shield bash, kick, parry, and yell.  The next big patch should be in the next week or two so now is a good time to pick this game up.  If your a fan of mount and blade, crpg, and other similar combat oriented games, strategy games, medieval games, rpg, open world, chess, risk, pick it up.  Most players are melee but there is ranged combat as well ie archery at the moment.
The epic will feature 200 vs 200 real players fighting over land, castles, resouces.  There will be 4 factions and 2 set times to fight during the day and whoever controls 51 percent of the map will be declared winner.  And they will be reset every 3-4 months.  There will be horses, crossbows, and tons and tons of new improvements added to the game.  Pick it up guys its a great bargain at 25 dollars.

I love this game! It's like all of the fast-paced Metroid elements but without the grand story and it's more episodic. It's a game built for speedrunning. If you enjoy constantly trying to be faster and faster at a game and trying to find better paths for better time and such, this game is for you. Also if you like a fun side-scrolling shooter platformer that's easy to get into with beautiful art that doesn't take itself too seriously, you'll love this.
Also, don't even get me started on the soundtrack. It's all wonderful electro-housey stuff that is candy for the ears. Jake Kaufman's official Mighty Switch Force soundtrack can be bought at a price you name (literally as low as $.01 if you want) on his Band Camp profile. I have the soundtrack actually on my phone and play some of the tracks now and then on the way to and from work. If you're a fan of electronic music, I definitely recommend picking the soundtrack up because all of the tracks in the game's stages are actually full-length songs that are beautifully produced.

WayForward's best work is when they're working with their own IPs, and the Mighty games certainly show it.
Mighty Switch Force is a solid (if short) time attack platformer that is well worth the price of admission.

From the same people who brought Shantae and DuckTales Remastered among other great platforming titles we have Mighty Switch Force! Hyper Drive Edition. If you are familiar with any of previous titles that should tell that you are in for a good platforming experience.
Mighty Switch Force! Hyper Drive Edition is a puzzle platformer with some action elements. While killing enemies is a big part on the game, it focuses a lot more on finding the five Hooligan Sisters on each level and to do that you'll need to smart up and use a combination of thinking and reflexes to finish most levels, which are called Incidents here.
The controls in this game are fantastic. They are precise, responsive and whenever you get hit or make a mistake you'll hardly feel like it was the game's fault. From jumping to shooting everything is as quick as you can react.
As the name of the game implies there's a lot of switching here. You do it to activate or deactivate platforms ranging from the common usage to avoid hazard or overcome obstacles to the not so common use of killing enemies by literally throwing them on your screen, but watch out; you can do it to your own self if you are not careful with it.
As you progress through the game the level becomes harder and more intricate with some of them being really challenging, especially if you are aiming for the Par Time. The difficulty curve is steady but it never feels like it spiked in any level, whenever you are presented with a new obstacle, the game makes sure to give you a chance to test it to understand how it works.
Just like Mighty Switch Force! Hose It Down!, Mighty Switch Force! Hyper Drive Edition gives you a nice and gratifying experience when playing the game as you'll feel great when you overcome that puzzle that was getting you stuck. And if that is not enough for you there are Par Time challenges which requires you to finish the level as fast as you can. Most of the Par Times are not very generous and a single mistake will force you to start all over again in a lot of cases.
There are several other challenges for achievements in specific levels that can be also very difficult to do. Something perfect for those who may think this game is too easy.
If beating the Par time isn't enough challenge for you, how about doing it in even harder versions of the levels you just did?
Hyper Drive Edition features bonus levels and once you finish them you'll unlock the Hyper version of all levels (i.e: Hard difficulty). Unlike many lazy developers, WayForward changed considerably most of the levels and you'll notice right away as soon as you pick any level to play.
The game will non-verbally, non-written say the gloves are off by making the very first level, the one you probably laughed at, a good deal more challenging forcing you to use platofrming techniques and finesse in execution that was only demanded from you in the last levels of the game.
Mighty Switch Force! Hyper Drive Edition has cartoony graphics of the highest caliber. The animations are fluid and extremely pleasant to the eyes and you can also have the option to turn the protagonist into her older pixel-modeled version which is just as well animated. This shows the carefulness of WayForward's craft and for those who don't know: animation, especially from pixel-art, can be VERY difficult and time consuming to do.
The music is something worth noting. Jake Kaufman (same composer from Shovel Knight and Shantae series) did an extraordinary job with it, sometimes you may just pause for a moment and forget about that clock ticking just to hear it. Now, how many games does that to you?
This game is amazing. I've longed to play it since 2013 and had very high expectations from it. Unlike other titles it wasn't a letdown and so far it's been a great experience with its charming graphics and great soundtrack and the good dosage of challenge from level to level.
Mighty Switch Force! Hyper Drive Edition is considered one of the finest games of its genre (even though it's quite underrated) and for the right reasons. It's a game that can be difficult but enough to make you go for it even more, not shoo you away.
If you enjoy platformer with puzzle elements or are looking for the first game of its genre, Mighty Switch Force! Hyper Drive Edition is definitely worth trying, especially since it's rather cheap.

Wayforward is one of those companies that impress me with pretty much everything they put out lately, and this is no exception. The solid gameplay and fantastic level design and progression is the star here, as the reuse of elements and mix of them up makes every level feel new and interesting. The HD upgrade is definitely appreciated for this 3DS port, and the game runs fantastically on pretty much all levels, and I love the animation quality and the characters designs. Honestly, when it comes down to it, there's not a lot I can really say that really doesn't work for the game as a whole: everything works together to make a solid experience. It's not a GOTY candidate by any means, but it's definitely a game that puts enjoyment as one of its core experiences, and I can't argue against a game for less then 10 dollars that delivered on almost every level. Definitely worth a pickup for the puzzle-platform lover, and even for those who may not like the genre regardless.

I'm not going to lie, Mighty Switch Force and its sequel were the reason I purchased a Nintendo 3DS and it's a decision I am glad I went with.
You play as Patricia Wagon who is on the pursuit to repromand the Hooligan Sisters in a 2D puzzle platformer.
MSF gameplay involves switiching blocks from transparency to be used as platforms, defeat enemies and traverse the stages to re-arrest the Hooligans. It's a simple mechanic that is all done with the press of a button but as you progress the stages and blocks become more varied and difficult. When switching blocks the others that are already physical will disapear, some blocks are needed to be used as cannons and some can be altered by stepping on them. The puzzles won't leave you stumped but do excpect some challange. The game is more about it's arcade like time attack then it's puzzle solving and nothing illustrates this point more than the superb soundtrack created by Jake Kauffamn (Virt) who creates a highly intense, hyperactive 16 bit score a kin to the Megaman series. (seriously go get his album it's even free on his website but give him something you won't regret it).
The PC version throws away the pixel art from clean animatied sprites and a much higher resolution that makes the stages pop with colour and vibrance in a techno city. If you miss the sprites you have the option to turn them on.
I'm a big fan of Wayforwards work and if you enjoy your classic platofrming mixed with varied puzzles, ♥♥♥♥♥♥ic music and colourful worlds you owe yourself to give Mighty switch Force the attention it so rightfully deserves.

I only played this game for a little while, and it has some problems, but the reason I stopped playing is that I was getting motion sickness from the camera zooming in and out, which is my problem rather than a problem with the game.
I was on the border about how to rate this. The controls are 'iffy', and I really hate that I can't map movement to the d-pad instead of the gorram analog stick, especially since the game requires quick turns during combat and analog sticks can 'whiplash' and make you end up facing the wrong direction (this happened to me A LOT during play). Most of the control issues are really because the character just has too much going on and the controls aren't really locked down to any single mechanic, so even walking around feels floaty, and jumping is pretty ridiculous in some cases. You can stick to walls and cielings and climb around on them, you can also do Metroid-style wall jumps in cases where you can't stick to the wall. There's also these weird glowy things that try to make you land on them while jumping if you're anywhere near them. The tip sign says they're only supposed to draw you in if you hold the L-trigger, but it seems that they're always on instead. In any case, the controls are functional but need work before they can feel natural and repsonsive.
Combat is sort of bad. I mean I was only in the first stage, but the problems were immediately evident, and I expect them to get worse as the game progresses. The main problem is that your stun animation is extremely slow, and you're not invulnerable during it, so it's incredibly easy to get stunlocked just by standing too close to an enemy, let alone between two. To add to the frustration, the enemies seem to be invulnerable during their close-range attacks, so you can get into some really crappy situations that aren't fun or challenging, but simply frustrating.
The character dialog isn't childish, but simply corny. I had though that we had advanced as a society since the early 90's, but clearly I was wrong: We've simply added memes into the vocabulary of "things that kids say".
Despite all that, this is a workable platformer, and some of the moves are cool when you pull them off. I got the game on sale, and I don't really feel bad about it, despite not being able to play because of my motion sickness, which - again - is not the game's fault; I'm just overly sensitive to certain camera movements.
In the end I decided to vote up because when I was originally considering the purchase I saw a number of very concerning issues being raised in the negative reviews. They almost all turned out to be bunk, or at least far less of a problem than was being indicated. For instance, a couple reviewers said that there's no way to block. There are - in fact - two ways to block. You can simply hold the attack button for half a second, or you can use the L-Trigger to activate your shield and grab onto the ground. There doesn't appear to be any limitation on this either. You can sit there for days and the shield soaks up all the damage, so I'm not sure what that was all about. Additionally, some reviews rightfully cited control issues, but wrongfully exaggerated them to apocalyptic proportions. The controls feel floaty and sometimes wall-gymnastics don't go how you planned them, but they are entirely workable, and I've certainly seen a lot worse on more expensive games. Finally, the stunlock issue was presented by some as game-breaking. It's annoying and frustrating, but it's also very easy to deal with if you just activate the shield for a moment and then jump out of the crossfire between attacks.
Anyway, that's my 2 bits.

I got this game in one of the Humble Bundles from a few months back. Decided to finally play it. But after finishing this game, I can't recommend it to anyone.
Skyborn is not a bad game. It's no good game either. It's just average. And the fact, that it's an average RPG Maker game just doesn't cut it, because there are so many free games you could play instead. If I have to pay money for a RPG Maker game, I at least expect something unique that warrants it. Yes, the games soundtrack was made by harmonic and it's good (not my favorite, but much better than RTP music). Yes, the game has nice edits and new Char- and Tileset graphics. But then you get to the story, which starts out interesting but then... just looses steam. The characters get less and less screentime as the game continues and more characters join, especially Chaska and Corwin.
Gameplay also has some nice ideas, like the forging and the augmenting system, but aside from the whole augmenting, gameplay just... lacks. Dungeons have no puzzles (you can't call the "press the button/lever once" puzzles), there are only 3 or 4 sidequests in the whole game and battles all play out like this:
You try to kill enemies before they kill you. If that is not possible, you buff/debuff and then kill them. Since I played on the highest difficulty, enemies could 2-3 shot most non tanks with their attacks. And since this whole threat system is implemented, each fight basically plays out exactly the same, unless a random crit happens. And this just gets boring after a while. There was 1 battle in the whole game which I liked, and that was the final battle in the Venom Depths. The final boss and optional boss in the final dungeon both were ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t difficulty with their abilities to oneshot the whole party if you even did a tiny mistake. And sometimes you couldn't even prevent it. It's nothing impossible, but those 2 fights, especially on hard, are just stupidly designed.
There are other aspects which annoy me because I myself work with the engine. Stuff like simply wrong perspective, some "ugly" looking tiles I know could easily be done better without even editing them or these loooong wooden plank ways you find in most of the dungeons, especially the waterfall and Venom Depths lava area. Most people won't even notice this, but if you do it annoys you.
Now, again, Skyborn is no bad game. But it's no good game either. And since it costs 15€, I have at least higher expectations that "average". Else, I could just play one of the hundred free RPG Maker games. What I find especially sad is the fact that I loved Legacies of Dondoran, a really old RPG Maker 2003 game made by the same people. That was REALLY GOOD. And I think even today it's a better game than this one.

There's even an arena/colisseum to test your mettle (which I'd advise taking on as soon as you get your final party member). The story isn't anything new, but it is interesting and fun nonetheless. The banter between the characters is humorous and entertaining, especially Claret and Sullivan. Skyborn is ultimately an unfortunately somewhat short RPG but fun nonetheless. You will be glad you played it but will be left wanting more. So in the mean time, play Echoes of Aetheria afterwards.

I've been following this game since the prototype launched forever ago, and I've been extremely excited to finally play the game. When I heard the game was gonna finally be released on Steam in January, I was ecstatic. I kept money aside until release and bought it immediately when it launched. In hindsight, that was probably a silly move, but I'm not wholly dissatisfied.
The game is great to play. Fun gameplay, unique visual style (for the genre, at least,) pretty cool destruction physics (even if the places in which they actually work are few and far between.) I was having an absolute blast with the game until about half an hour in when I asked myself "Is this really all there is right now?"
I understand that the game is early access, and I probably should've anticipated that, but the lack of content here is kind of inexcusable. The game has a huge amount of potential to expand on itself, and if you're willing to wait for content to be released, it's probably worth getting eventually, but probably not now.
Another huge problem (which I assume will be resolved as development goes on, but my point still stands) is the performance. Now look, my PC isn't fantastic. I have a GTX 560ti GPU and an AMD A6-3670 quad core CPU. I struggle to run the game at max settings at 60fps. That might sound like some PC first world problems to some people, but considering the actual visual quality of the game, it's baffling that I can't hit 60 at all times. I would've thought at least some of this would be down to the destruction physics, but the game seemingly doesn't take even a slight hit in performance when I destroy anything, so I'm unsure what's really causing this other than a lack of optimisation.
Another absolutely massive problem with the performance is the abundance of crashes. In my <2 hours of playtime at the time of writing this I've suffered over 10 crashes, usually tied to resetting the level but sometimes just random and inexplicable crashes occur. I hope and assume this will be resolved in the near future because this is a huge issue.
If you want a game with a justifiable amount of content for the price tag, don't get this right now. $15 is far too much for what is essentially 30 minutes of gameplay at most, and on top of the lack of decent optimisation and abundance of crashes it really brings down the quality of what could be, and probably will be a fantastic game when it's finished.
I would love to recommend this game, I really would, but potential isn't enough for a lot of people to drop $15 on a game. Svajūnas, if you're reading this, I'm really looking forward to what you have in store for this game, but for the love of god bring down the price even just a tad until you've added more content.
